matrix_cell_text_full: The UNDP executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the UNDP's vision, mission, directions of change, signature solutions, and enablers. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2021-09/UNDP-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025_1.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Paris Agreement, and is structured around “3x6x3” - 3 directions of change, 6 signature solutions, and 3 enablers - to help countries expand human capabilities and development choices, build a more equitable world, and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The three directions of change are structural transformation, leaving no one behind, and resilience. The six signature solutions are poverty and inequality, governance, resilience, environment, energy, and gender equality. The three enablers are strategic innovation, digitalization, and development financing. Secondly, an annual integrated budget and workplan, devised by the UNDP and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each signature solution. The budget and workplan for 2024 is tailored to the countries' needs and stakeholders' priorities (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2023-12/dp2024-CRP1_3.pdf). The UNDP also maintains the SDG Accelerator Lab Network, a key aspect of the innovation and digitalisation of the UNDP (https://www.undp.org/acceleratorlabs). UNDP proposes a total budget of $5.4 billion for 2022-2025, comprising $1.4 billion for institutional effectiveness and $4 billion for development activities based on projected income and in alignment with the strategic plan outcomes and outputs. In order to achieve its mandate, UNDP relies entirely on voluntary contributions from UN Member States, multilateral organizations, private sector and other sources, in the form of unrestricted regular resources (core), and contributions earmarked for a specific theme, programme or project (https://www.undp.org/funding). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the UNDAF, the UNDP Strategic Plan, and the SDGs, addressing poverty and inequality, governance, resilience, environment, energy, and gender equality (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2022-07/UNDP%20Strategic%20Plan%202022-2025.pdf).

To fulfil these objectives, the Organization shall perform various functions, such as encouraging and assisting the developing countries in their industrialization efforts, initiating and coordinating the activities of the United Nations system in the field of industrial development, creating and developing new concepts and approaches for industrial development, providing a forum and an instrument for international cooperation and dialogue on industrial matters, serving as a clearing-house for industrial information, promoting and encouraging the development, transfer and use of industrial technology, organizing and supporting industrial training programmes, assisting in the exploitation, conservation and transformation of natural resources, developing special measures for the least-developed and other disadvantaged developing countries, and assisting in obtaining external financing for industrial projects (Article 2). matrix_cell_text_full: ITU derives its mandate from the Constitution (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf) and the Convention of the International Telecommunication Union, which is an international treaty signed and ratified by almost all countries of the world (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Convention-E.pdf). The treaty is the founding document of the ITU, a specialized agency of the United Nations (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). Specifically, Article 1 of the Constitution defines the purposes and functions of the ITU, which include maintaining and extending international cooperation among all its Member States for the improvement and rational use of telecommunications of all kinds, promoting the development and efficient operation of technical facilities, and harmonizing the actions of Member States and Sector Members (https://www.itu.int/en/history/Pages/ConstitutionAndConvention.aspx). Additionally, ITU's jurisdiction is influenced by the resolutions and decisions of the Plenipotentiary Conference (https://search.itu.int/history/HistoryDigitalCollectionDocLibrary/5.23.61.en.100.pdf), which is the supreme organ of the ITU and has the power to amend the Constitution and the Convention (Article 8 of the Constitution). ITU also adopts and supervises the Administrative Regulations, such as the Radio Regulations and the International Telecommunication Regulations, which are binding on all ITU Member States and provide the legal framework for ITU's jurisdiction over the use of the radio-frequency spectrum, satellite orbits, and international telecommunication services (Article 4 of the Constitution). Also, The ITU Constitution and Convention are complemented by the Administrative Regulations, which comprise the ITU International Telecommunication Regulations and ITU Radio Regulations, and are binding on all ITU member states as well (https://www.itu.int/en/history/Pages/RegulationsCollection.aspx#:~:text=ITU's%20Administrative%20Regulations%20contain%20provisions,operation%20of%20international%20telecommunication%20services).

These resolutions and decision reflect the support and recognition of the UN General Assembly for the UN Global Compact as a strategic partner and a leading initiative for corporate sustainability and social responsibility.

The IAEA also finds its mandate from the implementation of other international legal instruments related to nuclear safety, security, and cooperation, such as Article 5, 18 and 23 of the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/infcirc274r1.pdf), and Article 8 and 18 of the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/2005/04/20050413%2004-02%20PM/Ch_XVIII_15p.pdf). These instruments and initiatives provide further legal frameworks and mechanisms for the IAEA's jurisdiction over specific nuclear issues and challenges.

The WBG derives its mandate from the Articles of Agreement, Conventions, or equivalent governance documents of its five constituent institutions: the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), the International Development Association (IDA), the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), and the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). These documents outline the conditions of membership, the general principles of organization, management, and operations, and the status, immunities, and privileges of each organization ((https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). The IBRD Articles of Agreement (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/722361541184234501/IBRDArticlesOfAgreement-English.pdf), which came into effect on December 27, 1945, define the purposes and functions of the IBRD, the capital stock and voting power of the members, the loans and guarantees of the IBRD, the operations and transactions of the IBRD, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IBRD. Similarly, the IDA Articles of Agreement (https://ida.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/ida-articlesofagreement.pdf), which came into effect on September 24, 1960, define the purposes and functions of the IDA, the resources and management of the IDA, the terms and conditions of financing by the IDA, the operations and transactions of the IDA, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IDA. The IFC Articles of Agreement (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/6a4a091b83577eb35e881dbf9016c5c3-0330032020/original/IFCArticlesOfAgreement.pdf), which came into effect on July 20, 1956, define the purposes and functions of the IFC, the capital stock and voting power of the members, the loans, guarantees, and other operations of the IFC, the operations and transactions of the IFC, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IFC. The MIGA Convention (https://www.miga.org/sites/default/files/archive/Documents/miga_convention_november_2010.pdf), which came into force on April 12, 1988, defines the purposes and functions of the MIGA, the membership and capital of the MIGA, the guarantees and other operations of the MIGA, the relations with other international organizations, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the MIGA. Lastly, the ICSID Convention (https://icsid.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/ICSID%20Convention%20English.pdf), which entered into force on October 14, 1966, defines the purposes and functions of the ICSID, the jurisdiction of the ICSID, the recognition and enforcement of awards, the administrative and financial provisions of the ICSID, the amendment and interpretation of the ICSID Convention, and the final provisions of the ICSID Convention.
The WBG’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Boards of Governors, the Boards of Executive Directors, and the Council of Governors (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/leadership). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for the WBG’s activities and programs, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. The WBG’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/259801562965232326/2030Agenda-2019-final-web.pdf), the Paris Agreement on Climate Change ((https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/english_paris_agreement.pdf), and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/frameworks/addisababaactionagenda), which provide further legal frameworks for the WBG’s jurisdiction over specific development issues and domains.

The IBRD Articles of Agreement (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/722361541184234501/IBRDArticlesOfAgreement-English.pdf) state that the WBG through IBRD aims to assist in the reconstruction and development of territories of members by facilitating the investment of capital for productive purposes, promoting private foreign investment by means of guarantees or participations in loans and other investments, and supplementing private investment by providing finance for productive purposes out of its own capital, funds raised by it and its other resources (Article I, Section 1). As specified in the IDA Articles of Agreement (https://ida.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/ida-articlesofagreement.pdf), the WBG through IDA aims to promote economic development, increase productivity and thus raise standards of living in the less-developed areas of the world by providing finance to projects and programs that contribute to the economic or social development of the members whose per capita income is low, and to those members in the opinion of the Association are not able to borrow from the IBRD on suitable terms (Article I, Section 1). The WBG through the IFC Articles of Agreement (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/6a4a091b83577eb35e881dbf9016c5c3-0330032020/original/IFCArticlesOfAgreement.pdf) aims to further economic development by encouraging the growth of productive private enterprise in member countries, particularly in the less-developed areas, by assisting in financing the establishment, improvement and expansion of private productive enterprises, and by stimulating and helping to create conditions conducive to the flow of private capital, domestic and foreign, into productive investment in member countries (Article I, Section 1). According to the MIGA Convention (https://www.miga.org/sites/default/files/archive/Documents/miga_convention_november_2010.pdf), the WBG through MIGA aims to encourage the flow of investments for productive purposes among member countries, and in particular to developing member countries, by providing guarantees against non-commercial risks in respect of investments in member countries, by establishing and operating a trust fund to provide technical assistance to member countries in connection with the promotion of foreign investment, and by exercising such other incidental powers as shall be necessary or desirable in the furtherance of its objective (Article 2, Section 1). Lastly, the WBG through the ICSID Convention (https://icsid.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/ICSID%20Convention%20English.pdf) aims to provide facilities for conciliation and arbitration of investment disputes between contracting states and nationals of other contracting states, and to bring together parties who have agreed to use such facilities, in order to facilitate the settlement of such disputes and to contribute to the development of international law on investments (Article 1, Section 2).

The IMF mainly derives its mandate from its Articles of Agreement, which is a treaty that establishes the legal framework and objectives of the Fund. The Articles of Agreement were adopted at the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944, and entered into force in December 1945 (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/pam/pam45/pdf/chap1.pdf). The most recent amendment, which became effective in January 2016, was aimed at enhancing the representation and voice of emerging and developing countries in the Fund’s governance (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf).
The Articles of Agreement define the obligations and rights of the Fund and its members, as well as the procedures and principles for the Fund’s operations and transactions. In addition to the Articles of Agreement, the Fund’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions of the Board of Governors, the decisions of the Executive Board, the agreements with other international organizations, and the jurisprudence of the Administrative Tribunal (https://www.imf.org/external/imfat/report.htm).

The IMF’s capacity development strategy is reviewed every five years to ensure its relevance and effectiveness (https://www.imf.org/-/media/Files/Publications/PP/2022/English/PPEA2022056.ashx). The latest review, conducted in 2023, reaffirmed the two main objectives of increasing the impact and efficiency of capacity development, and proposed several recommendations to achieve them. The review also highlighted the importance of integrating capacity development with surveillance and lending, tailoring and modernizing delivery, enhancing internal and external coordination and communication, and improving management processes and systems. The IMF’s capacity development strategy is guided by the principles and priorities set out in document IMF/18/4/Rev.1 (https://www.imf.org/~/media/Files/Publications/PP/2018/pp021518cd-strategy-review.ashx). The IMF’s surveillance strategy is also reviewed periodically to adapt to the changing global environment and the needs of the membership. The most recent review, completed in 2019, focused on enhancing the quality, traction, and evenhandedness of surveillance, and identified four priority areas for action: strengthening the analysis of macro-financial linkages, governance and corruption, external sector assessments, and policy trade-offs and spillovers. The IMF’s surveillance strategy is based on the principles and modalities specified in document IMF/19/68/Rev.1 (https://www.imf.org/~/media/Files/Publications/PP/2019/PP041719-2018-Review-of-Program-Design-and-Conditionality.ashx). The IMF’s lending strategy is designed to help members restore macroeconomic stability, foster growth and reduce poverty, and safeguard the stability of the international monetary system. The IMF’s lending strategy is informed by regular reviews of its lending policies and facilities, as well as the lessons learned from its program experience. The latest review, conducted in 2019, assessed the adequacy and effectiveness of the Fund’s lending toolkit, and proposed some modifications and enhancements to better meet the diverse needs of the membership. The IMF’s lending strategy is governed by the rules and procedures established in document IMF/19/69/Rev.1 (https://www.imf.org/~/media/Files/Publications/PP/2019/PP041719-2018-Review-of-Program-Design-and-Conditionality.ashx).

It also has a system of committees, more than 100 working groups, symposia, and an Annual Science Conference (https://ices-library.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/33403040). Finally, ICES is committed to building a foundation of science around one key challenge: integrated ecosystem understanding of marine ecosystems. IPBES derives its mandate from the 2010 Busan Outcome document (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/3115), which was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly resolution 65/162 on 20 December 2010 and Decision 26/4 
of 24 February 2011. The first session of Plenary convened in Nairobi in 2011 to determine modalities 
and institutional arrangements for IPBES (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/3377) and a second session of Plenary in Panama in 2012 established IPBES as an independent intergovernmental body to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/history-establishment). Specifically, paragraph 4 of the Busan Outcome defines the objectives and functions of IPBES, and paragraph 5 outlines the operating principles and modalities of IPBES. Additionally, the IPBES rules of procedure, rule 2 on the functions of the IPBES secretariat (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2675), states the duties of the secretariat in servicing and supporting the sessions of the Plenary and other subsidiary bodies, and in performing other tasks entrusted to it by the Plenary. IPBES's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its Plenary, such as the IPBES work programme (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme), the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework), and the IPBES assessment process (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/18538#:~:text=An%20IPBES%20assessment%20is%20a,ensure%20legitimacy%2C%20relevance%20and%20credibility.). These resolutions and provisional documents provide guidance and direction for IPBES's activities and deliverables, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/24663). IPBES's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the Convention on Migratory Species (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for IPBES's jurisdiction over specific biodiversity and ecosystem services issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: The IPBES Secretariat executes its defined objectives and functions via several strategies: firstly, a rolling work programme up to 2030 backed by Decision IPBES-7/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/27458) and based on requests, inputs and suggestions from relevant bodies under multilateral environmental agreements as well as governments and other stakeholders. The rolling work program aims to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, long-term human well-being and sustainable development. This work programme corresponds to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, including the Sustainable Development Goals (http://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/sustainable-development-goals/), the biodiversity-related conventions and other biodiversity and ecosystem service processes (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). It initially focuses on three topics: the interlinkages between biodiversity and other relevant issues reflected in the 2030 Agenda, the determinants of transformative change, and the tools and solutions for conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). Secondly, a biennial budget and work programme, approved by the Plenary, detail the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each deliverable of the work programme (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). The current budget and work programme for 2022-2023 is based on the priorities identified by the Plenary and the available resources, as outlined in decision IPBES-8/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/102793). It also supports the development and use of policy support tools and methodologies, such as the IPBES online catalogue of policy support tools and methodologies (https://www.ipbes.net/catalogue-policy-support-tools-and-methodologies), the IPBES guide on the production and integration of assessments from and across all scales (https://www.ipbes.net/guide-production-assessments), and the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework). Finally, various assessments, task forces, expert groups, and platforms provide an evidence base for informing policy and decision-making, addressing the state of knowledge on the interactions between human societies and the natural world, the drivers and impacts of biodiversity change, and the options and pathways for achieving conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/104403). Some of the key assessments include the global assessment report on biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/global-assessment), the assessment report on invasive alien species (https://www.ipbes.net/ias), the assessment report on the sustainable use of wild species (https://www.ipbes.net/sustainable-use-assessment), and the assessment report on the diverse conceptualization of multiple values of nature and its benefits (https://files.ipbes.net/ipbes-web-prod-public-files/downloads/IPBES-4-INF-13_EN.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The IPCC derives its mandate from the Decisions and Resolutions of its parent organisations, WMO and UNEP, which established the IPCC in 1988 as an intergovernmental body to assess the scientific information on climate change and its impacts, and to formulate response strategies for the management of the climate change issue. Specifically, the WMO Executive Council Resolution 4 (EC-XL) (https://archive.ipcc.ch/docs/WMO_resolution4_on_IPCC_1988.pdf) defined the initial terms of reference and objectives of the IPCC. The IPCC's mandate was subsequently updated and refined by various resolutions and decisions of the governing bodies of WMO and UNEP, as well as by the IPCC itself, to reflect the evolving needs and challenges of the climate change issue. Over the years, key resolutions and decisions have shaped the IPCC's mandate including the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) (https://unfccc.int/files/essential_background/background_publications_htmlpdf/application/pdf/conveng.pdf); the IPCC Principles Governing IPCC Work (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/09/ipcc-principles.pdf), which were adopted by the IPCC at its 14th Session in 1988 and approved by the WMO Executive Council and the UNEP Governing Council, and which define the IPCC's organisation, procedures, functions, and products; and the IPCC Procedures (https://www.ipcc.ch/documentation/procedures/), which were adopted by the IPCC at various sessions and approved by the WMO Executive Council and the UNEP Governing Council, and which provide detailed rules and guidelines for the IPCC's work, such as the preparation, review, approval, and publication of its reports, the election of its bureau and chair, and the participation of experts and observers. The IPCC's jurisdiction is also influenced by the requests and guidance received from the UNFCCC and other relevant bodies, which provide the policy context and demand for the IPCC's assessments and products (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2021/07/AR6_FS_What_is_IPCC.pdf). The IPCC's mandate is also supported by the scientific community and the public, which provide the knowledge base and the legitimacy for the IPCC's work (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/).

As defined in Paragraph 2 of Resolution 4 (EC-XL) of the WMO Executive Council (https://archive.ipcc.ch/docs/WMO_resolution4_on_IPCC_1988.pdf), the IPCC's objectives include the following main tasks:
(1) Assessing the scientific information that is related to the various components of the climate change issue, such as emissions of major greenhouse gases and modification of the Earth's radiation balance resulting therefrom, and the environmental and socio-economic consequences of climate change; (2) Formulating realistic response strategies for the management of the climate change issue; (3) Providing scientific and socio-economic information and advice, initially for the development and negotiations of a UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and after its entry into force, to continue to work closely with the UNFCCC and provide scientific, technical and socio-economic information and advice; and (4) Reporting on its activities to the governing bodies of WMO and UNEP and communicating the results of the assessments broadly. These tasks enable the IPCC to fulfil its role as an intergovernmental panel on climate change that provides authoritative and comprehensive assessments of the current state of knowledge on climate change and its potential impacts.

matrix_cell_text_full: The IPCC executes its objectives via several strategies. The IPCC operates through three Working Groups (WGs) and a Task Force on National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (TFI), each supported by a Technical Support Unit (TSU) (https://www.ipcc.ch/working-groups/). The WGs assess the scientific literature on the physical science basis of climate change (WG I), the impacts, adaptation and vulnerability (WG II), and the mitigation of climate change (WG III). The TFI develops and refines methodologies for the estimation and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions and removals. The IPCC also produces reports (https://www.ipcc.ch/reports/) in forms of Special Reports, Methodology Reports, Technical Papers and Synthesis Reports like AR6 reports (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_SYR_SPM.pdf) on cross-cutting topics. The IPCC develops its work programme based on the requests and guidance from its member governments and observer organizations and the work programme is reviewed and approved by the IPCC Plenary, which is the main decision-making body of the IPCC (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/structure/). The IPCC budget is funded by voluntary contributions from its member governments and other organizations. The budget covers the operational costs of the IPCC Secretariat, the Technical Support Units, and the travel and meeting expenses of the IPCC Bureau members, authors, reviewers, and other experts involved in the IPCC work. The budget is prepared by the IPCC Secretariat in consultation with the IPCC Bureau and the Technical Support Units, and is submitted to the IPCC Plenary for approval for each assessment cycle, which typically lasts six to seven years. The budget is subject to an annual audit by an external auditor. The budget cycle is also aligned with the calendar year (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/decision_p35_budget.pdf). In addition, the IPCC Scholarship Programme provides funding for young scientists from developing countries to pursue studies on climate change (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/scholarship/).

matrix_cell_text_full: The WTO derives its mandate from the Marrakesh Agreement Establishing the World Trade Organization (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf), which entered into force on 1 January 1995 and established the WTO as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/agrmntseries2_gatt_e.pdf). Specifically, Articles II and III of the Marrakesh Agreement define the scope and functions of the WTO, and Article IV outlines the structure and decision-making of the WTO. Additionally, the WTO's Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU), which is annexed to the Marrakesh Agreement, sets out the rules and procedures for the settlement of disputes between WTO members (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dispu_e/dsu_e.htm). The DSU establishes the jurisdiction of the WTO panels and the Appellate Body, which are the adjudicating bodies of the WTO dispute settlement system. The DSU also provides for the implementation and enforcement of the rulings and recommendations of the panels and the Appellate Body. The WTO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the other agreements and arrangements that are annexed to the Marrakesh Agreement, which are collectively known as the "covered agreements" of the WTO (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/utw_chap2_e.pdf). These agreements and arrangements cover various aspects of trade in goods, services, intellectual property, and trade policy reviews, and they contain specific rights and obligations for WTO members (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/legal_e.htm). The covered agreements also provide for the application of the DSU to disputes arising under them, unless otherwise specified (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dispu_e/dsu_e.htm). The covered agreements are an integral part of the WTO legal framework and constitute the primary source of law for the WTO dispute settlement system. The WTO's mandate is also supported by the participation of the WTO in various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Agreement on Trade Facilitation, the Trade and Environment Committee, and the Trade and Development Committee, which provide further legal frameworks for the WTO's jurisdiction over specific trade-related issues and domains (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/agrm1_e.htm). These agreements and frameworks also aim to enhance the cooperation and coordination between the WTO and other international organisations and stakeholders.

matrix_cell_text_full: The WTO has a comprehensive strategy in place to achieve its objectives and mandates in ensuring that trade flows as smoothly, predictably, and freely as possible. It operates a non-discriminatory trading system that spells out the rights and obligations of its members (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/inbrief_e/inbr_e.htm). The WTO agreements, which are the result of negotiations, cover a wide range of activities including agriculture, textiles and clothing, banking, telecommunications, government purchases, industrial standards and product safety, food sanitation regulations, intellectual property, and more (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/fact2_e.htm). The WTO’s strategic plans are largely the outcome of negotiations between the members. The current round of trade negotiations, known as the Doha Development Agenda, was launched in 2001 (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dda_e/dda_e.htm) to succeed the Uruguay Round negotiations (1986–94) (https://www.wto.org/gatt_docs/english/sulpdf/92160001.pdf). The WTO has expanded its scope to include cooperation with the UN system, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), and other international partners on a wide range of issues (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/mdg_e/global_partnership_e.htm). The WTO’s annual budget is contributed by its members based on their proportion of international trade (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/secre_e/budget_e.htm). The current budget proposal for the WTO Secretariat for the biennium 2024-2025 (https://docs.wto.org/dol2fe/Pages/SS/directdoc.aspx?filename=q:/WT/BFA/W643.pdf&Open=True) requests a modest increase of 7.4% in 2024 and 0.9% in 2025, amounting to CHF 211.76 million and CHF 213.7 million respectively. The WTO’s regulatory mechanisms are based on a number of simple, fundamental principles that run throughout all of its documents. These principles include trade without discrimination, national treatment (treating foreigners and locals equally), and the commitment to lowering trade barriers (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/utw_chap1_e.pdf).

Articles IV-VIII of the Constitution establish procedures for Council, Administration, Headquarters, Finance, and Legal Status respectively. IOM's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Council, the Executive Committee, and the Standing Committee on Programmes and Finance (https://governingbodies.iom.int/standing-committee-programmes-and-finance). matrix_cell_text_full:
UN-Habitat derives its mandate from several UN General Assembly resolutions, which established UN-Habitat as the focal point for all urbanization and human settlement matters within the UN system. Specifically, resolution 3327 (XXIX) of 1975 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/3327(XXIX)) created the United Nations Habitat and Human Settlements Foundation (UNHHSF), the first official UN body dedicated to urbanization. Resolution 32/162 of 1977 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/32/162) transformed the Committee on Housing, Building, and Planning into the Commission on Human Settlements, an intergovernmental body serviced by the Centre for Human Settlements (also known as “Habitat”). Resolution 56/206 of 2002 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/56/206) merged the UNHHSF, the Commission on Human Settlements, and Habitat into UN-Habitat, a fully-fledged UN programme managed by its own secretariat and headed by its own Executive Director. UN-Habitat's mandate is also shaped by the outcomes of the three UN conferences on human settlements: Habitat I in Vancouver (1976), Habitat II in Istanbul (1996), and Habitat III in Quito (2016). These conferences resulted in the adoption of the Vancouver Declaration on Human Settlements (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/1396335538wpdm_Vancouver_Declaration_EN.pdf), the Istanbul Declaration on Human Settlements (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/Istanbul_Declaration_EN.pdf) and the Habitat Agenda (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/Habitat_Agenda_EN.pdf), and the New Urban Agenda (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/The%20New%20Urban%20Agenda%20_%20Revised%20Low%20Res.pdf), respectively. These documents define the global standards and principles for achieving sustainable urban development and adequate shelter for all. UN-Habitat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the alignment of its work with other internationally agreed upon development goals, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (2015) (https://unhabitat.org/sustainable-development-goals), and the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (2015) (https://unhabitat.org/climate-change). These goals provide further legal frameworks and targets for UN-Habitat's jurisdiction over specific urban issues and domains. UN-Habitat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Framework Convention on Climate Change (https://unfccc.int/files/essential_background/background_publications_htmlpdf/application/pdf/conveng.pdf), the Vienna Convention on the Protection of the Ozone Layer (https://ozone.unep.org/sites/default/files/2019-12/The%20Ozone%20Treaties%20EN%20-%20WEB_final.pdf), and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/UNDRR%20Presentation_Sendai%20Framework-GGA6%20%281%29.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The World Food Programme (WFP) derives its mandate from the General Assembly Resolution 2095 (XX) of 20 December 1965 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/2095(XX)), which extended the WFP on a continuing basis for as long as multilateral food aid is feasible and desirable, Resolution 1714 (XVI) of 19 December 1961 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/1714(XVI)), which established WFP as an experimental programme, and Resolution 3404 (XXX) of 28 November 1975 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/3404(XXX)), which named Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes oversight of WFP. In addition, pursuant to Resolution 50/8 of 1 November 1995 (https://documents.un.org/doc/resolution/gen/n95/257/30/img/n9525730.pdf?token=lBOUzh2cYTpOtGNhBZ&fe=true), the Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes (CFA) was reconstituted as the WFP Executive Board with effect from 1 Jan. 1996. The General Assembly Resolutions 1714 (XVI) and 2095 (XX) define the objectives and scope of WFP, and Resolution 50/8 outlines the structure and membership of the United Nations/FAO Intergovernmental Committee of the WFP, which is the governing body of the programme. Specifically, Article II of the General Regulations and Rules of the WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150) defines the purposes and functions of WFP; Article III outlines the cooperation of WFP with the United Nations and FAO and with other relevant agencies and organizations, and the modalities of such cooperation; Article IV specifies the location of the headquarters of WFP in Rome, Italy; Article V lists the organs of WFP, which are the Executive Board and the Secretariat, and their composition and functions; Article VI details the powers and functions of the Board; Article VII establishes the WFP Secretariat, headed by an Executive Director, and its organization and functions; Article VIII grants WFP legal capacity, drawing on the legal personality of the United Nations and FAO; Article IX sets the eligibility criteria for assistance from WFP, which include being a member of the United Nations or any specialized agency or the IAEA, or being a recipient of emergency food aid requested by the Secretary-General; and Article XIII governs the contributions to WFP, which shall be on a voluntary basis and may be in the form of commodities, cash, or acceptable services. WFP's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Intergovernmental Committee, the FAO Council, and the Economic and Social Council, which provide guidance and direction for WFP's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/about-board). WFP's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Rome Declaration on World Food Security (https://www.fao.org/3/w3548e/w3548e00.htm#adopt05), the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.wfp.org/sdgs), and the Agenda for Humanity (https://agendaforhumanity.org/stakeholder/291.html), which provide further legal frameworks for WFP's jurisdiction over specific food security and humanitarian issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: The World Food Programme (WFP) executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan establishes the organization’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000132205), outlines the many ways for WFP, working in synergy with others, to most efficiently and effectively save and change lives. It is grounded within renewed global commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its associated Sustainable Development Goals 9https://www.wfp.org/publications/wfp-strategic-plan-2022-25). Secondly, a biennial Management Plan, presented to the Executive Board, details the projected operational needs, the provisional global implementation plan, the programme support and business operations budget, and the use of reserves and general fund. The current Management Plan for 2024-2026 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000151658) highlights the corporate budget required to implement WFP’s programme of work, based on the funding forecasts and prioritization criteria. It also outlines WFP’s key drivers of hunger, such as conflict, climate change, and economic shocks, and how WFP responds to them through various programmes, operations, and platforms (https://www.wfp.org/publications/wfp-management-plan-2024-2026). Thirdly, the Corporate Results Framework (CRF) 2022-2025 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000136871) guides the planning, implementation, monitoring, and reporting of WFP’s programmes towards the objectives identified in the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan. The CRF, supplemented by the policy on country strategic plans (CSPs) (https://www.wfp.org/publications/policy-country-strategic-plans), provides a performance and accountability framework that enables WFP to measure and demonstrate its response to humanitarian needs. In addition, the WFP has over 32 policies in effect under the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan. An update of the portfolio of policies is submitted annually and can be found as the “Compendium of Policies” on the Executive Board website (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000151657). Finally, various policies, frameworks, agreements, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the WFP Strategic Plan, addressing food security, nutrition, resilience, capacity strengthening, social protection, and innovation (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000132607).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNWTO derives its mandate from the Statutes of the World Tourism Organization (https://webunwto.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/imported_images/51970/unwtostatuteseng.pdf), which established UNWTO as a specialized agency of the United Nations. Specifically, Article 3 of the Statutes defines the aims and objectives of UNWTO, Articles 4-7 outlines the provisions for membership of the UNWTO, Article 8-24 define organizational structure and governance, and Articles 25-26 describe budgets and expenditures. Additionally, the General Rules of Procedure of UNWTO ((https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2019-11/130718basicdocumentsenweb.pdf) also govern the functioning and decision-making of UNWTO's governing bodies, namely the General Assembly, the Executive Council, and the regional commissions. The rules of procedure specify the composition, powers, duties, sessions, agenda, voting, languages, and other aspects of these bodies, as well as the role and responsibilities of the UNWTO secretariat. The rules of procedure are based on the Statutes of UNWTO, and can be amended by the General Assembly or the Executive Council, as appropriate. The rules of procedure also provide for the participation of other UNWTO members, such as associate members and affiliate members, as well as observers and guests, in the meetings and activities of UNWTO. UNWTO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the General Assembly, the Executive Council, and the regional commissions (https://www.unwto.org/unwto-general-assembly). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNWTO's policies and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. It also maintains the UNRISD Flagship Report, a key publication that synthesizes the Institute’s research and policy analysis on the social dimensions of contemporary development issues (https://www.un-ilibrary.org/content/books/9789290851332#:~:text=This%20UNRISD%20Flagship%20Report%20shows,are%20built%20in%20by%20design.). UNRISD receives no funding from the regular budget of the United Nations but depends entirely on voluntary contributions from national governments, multilateral donors, foundations and other sources and must fully mobilize all the financial resources necessary to cover the institutional and staff costs required to implement the UNRISD Strategy 2021–2025 ((https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4A1D94EBE95DA31A802586D8004198E8/UNRISD-Strategy-2021-2025.pdf). The underlying assumption in terms of delivering results, therefore, is that UNRISD will design and successfully implement a fundraising strategy that will diversify the Institute’s funding sources, and generate predictable, stable and increased revenues. Various institutional initiatives, collaborations, and regulatory mechanisms also provide an operational framework for implementing the Institute's objectives. For instance, the work programme of the UNRISD Bonn office aims to create new interagency collaborations and enhance synergies between research and learning activities (https://www.unbonn.org/UNRISD#:~:text=The%20work%20programme%20of%20the,and%20contributing%20to%20training%20and). The Institute also organises regular Seminar Series to provide a space for open, informed, and insightful conversation around contemporary issues of concern to social development research and policy (https://www.unrisd.org/en/activities/events).

These decisions and resolutions provide guidance and direction for the BRS Secretariat's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other international bodies and stakeholders. The BRS Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx), the Minamata Convention on Mercury (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/MEAs/MinamataConvention/tabid/4083/language/en-US/Default.aspx), and the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/UNEP/SAICM/tabid/4073/language/en-US/Default.aspx), which provide further legal frameworks for the BRS Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific issues and domains related to the sound management of chemicals and wastes.

matrix_cell_text_full: The CBD derives its mandate from the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), which is the international legal instrument for "the conservation of biological diversity, the sustainable use of its components and the fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the utilization of genetic resources" that has been ratified by 196 nations (https://www.un.org/en/observances/biological-diversity-day/convention). Specifically, Article 1 of the Convention states the objectives of CBD, which are to conserve biological diversity, to use its components sustainably, and to share the benefits of genetic resources fairly and equitably; Article 23 establishes a Conference of the Parties, which shall be the supreme body of the convention and shall keep under review the implementation of the convention. It also specifies the functions, procedures and frequency of the meetings of the Conference of the Parties, and the participation of observers; Article 24 establishes the CBD Secretariat, which shall arrange for and service the meetings of the Conference of the Parties and perform other functions assigned to it by the convention or by any protocol. It also requires the Conference of the Parties to designate the secretariat from among the existing competent international organizations that have signified their willingness to carry out the secretariat functions; and Article 25 establishes a subsidiary body on scientific, technical and technological advice, which shall provide the Conference of the Parties and its other subsidiary bodies with timely advice relating to the implementation of the convention. The CBD's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations adopted by its governing bodies, including the Conference of the Parties (https://www.cbd.int/cop), the Subsidiary Body on Scientific, Technical and Technological Advice (https://www.cbd.int/sbstta), and the Subsidiary Body on Implementation (https://www.cbd.int/sbi). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for the CBD's work programmes and thematic areas, as well as cooperation and coordination with other conventions and organisations. The CBD's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various protocols and frameworks, such as the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (https://bch.cbd.int/protocol/#:~:text=The%20Cartagena%20Protocol%20on%20Biosafety%20to%20the%20Convention%20on%20Biological,diversity%2C%20taking%20also%20into%20account), the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-sharing (https://www.cbd.int/abs#:~:text=The%20Nagoya%20Protocol%20on%20Access%20to%20Genetic%20Resources%20and%20the,a%20fair%20and%20equitable%20way.), and the Post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/409e/19ae/369752b245f05e88f760aeb3/wg2020-05-l-02-en.pdf), which provide further legal instruments and targets for the CBD's jurisdiction over specific biodiversity issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: The CBD Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a post-2020 global biodiversity framework, adopted by the Conference of the Parties at its fifteenth meeting, provide the vision, mission, goals and targets for biodiversity conservation and sustainable use for the next decade, aligning with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Paris Agreement (https://www.cbd.int/doc/strategic-plan/Post2020/Bubb.pdf). This framework, based on extensive consultations and inputs from various stakeholders, build on the achievements and lessons learned from the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011-2020 and the Aichi Biodiversity Targets (https://www.cbd.int/doc/strategic-plan/2011-2020/Aichi-Targets-EN.pdf), as well as the current state of knowledge and science on biodiversity and ecosystem services. Secondly, a four-year medium-term programme of work, approved by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the activities, expected outcomes, indicators and budget of the Secretariat for the period of interest, in support of the implementation of the Convention and its Protocols (https://www.cbd.int/information/adm-fin). This programme of work is structured around six core functions of the Secretariat, namely: servicing meetings of the governing bodies and subsidiary bodies; facilitating implementation; providing policy advice and support; fostering communication, outreach and partnerships; managing information and knowledge; and ensuring sound management and administration, as detailed in Article 24 of the Convention document (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf). The programme of work also includes a results-based management framework and a resource mobilization strategy. The major source of funding for the CBD Secretariat is the General Trust Fund for the Convention on Biological Diversity (BY Trust Fund), which is funded from the assessed contributions of Parties to the CBD, based on the United Nations scales of assessment (https://www.cbd.int/convention/parties/contributions.shtml). In addition, various mechanisms, initiatives and partnerships provide a platform for cooperation and coordination among Parties, other Governments, international organizations, civil society, indigenous peoples and local communities, and the private sector, on various thematic and cross-cutting issues related to biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/programmes). Some of these include: the Clearing-House Mechanism (https://www.cbd.int/chm), which facilitates the exchange of information and technical and scientific cooperation; the Global Taxonomy Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/gti/default.shtml), which enhances taxonomic knowledge and capacity; the LifeWeb Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/undb/media/factsheets/undb-factsheet-lifeweb-en.pdf), which supports the establishment and management of protected areas; the Bio-Bridge Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/biobridge/), which fosters technical and scientific collaboration among Parties; the Global Partnership for Plant Conservation, which supports the implementation of the Global Strategy for Plant Conservation (https://www.cbd.int/gspc/default.shtml); and the Biodiversity for Development Initiative ( Biodiversity for Development Initiative), which promotes the integration of biodiversity into development policies and plans.

matrix_cell_text_full: The CITES Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a ten-year Strategic Vision, adopted by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the Convention’s direction for the 2021-2030 timeframe in fulfilment of its mandate (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/reports/Implementation/E-SV-indicators.pdf). This vision, annexed to Resolution Conf. 18.3 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-18-03.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its Sustainable Development Goals, as well as the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/409e/19ae/369752b245f05e88f760aeb3/wg2020-05-l-02-en.pdf) being developed by Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It also recognizes the importance of global cooperation to address the threats posed by illegal trade in wildlife, as acknowledged by the United Nations General Assembly. The vision sets five broad goals and corresponding objectives and indicators to measure progress and performance. Secondly, a triennial budget and work programme, proposed by the Secretariat and approved by the Conference of the Parties, details the activities, outputs, and resources required to implement the Convention and the decisions of the Parties. The current budget and work programme for 2023-2025 is based on the priorities identified by the Parties and the Secretariat, as well as the expected income from the Trust Fund and external sources, as specified in Resolution Conf. 19.1 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-19-01.pdf). Thirdly various resolutions, decisions, agreements, and partnerships provide guidance and support for the implementation and enforcement of the Convention at the national, regional, and international levels, addressing legal and sustainable trade, compliance and enforcement, capacity-building, cooperation and collaboration, and awareness-raising, with key instruments listed here (https://cites.org/eng/res/index.php). The Convention is financed by core and external funds. The core funding, known as the CITES Trust Fund (CTL), finances the administrative costs of the Secretariat, the Conference of the Parties and its subsidiary bodies, the Standing Committee and other permanent committees. The CITES Trust Fund is replenished from contributions of the Parties to the Convention based on the United Nations scale of assessment, adjusted to take account of the fact that not all members of the United Nations are Parties to the Convention. The external funds, known as the CITES External Trust Fund (QTL) funds the voluntary programmes/projects activities costs. The CITES External Trust Fund consists of extrabudgetary contributions from Parties and other entities on a purely voluntary basis. Each offer of funding to the CITES External Trust Fund is negotiated and vetted by the Secretariat (https://cites.org/eng/disc/fund.php).

matrix_cell_text_full:
The CMS Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies:
Firstly, the CMS Secretariat has a Strategic Plan. This plan, proposed for 2024-2032, aligns with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, as stated in the draft resolution UNEP/CMS/COP14/CRP14.2 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop14_crp14.2_spms_e.docx). The plan is revised periodically, with the latest revision published in February, 2024. The Strategic Plan outlines the Secretariat’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. It aligns with the Convention’s mandate to conserve migratory species of wild animals. Secondly, the CMS operates on triennium budgets to fulfill its strategic plans, but may also operate interim budgets as deemed fit. The interim budget for 2024 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/036_Interim%20Budget%20for%202024_ExCOP1%20%281%29_2.pdf) provides for the same funding levels as the 2023 budget that was approved by COP13. The budget period covers the calendar year, from January 1 to December 31 and details activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. In February 2024, the CMS COP14 will adopt a budget for the triennium 2024-2026, which will supersede the interim budget for 2024 (https://www.cms.int/en/news/2023028-process-adoption-interim-cms-budget-2024-through-silence-procedure-and-convening). Thirdly, the CMS Secretariat promotes and supports the development of Agreements. These agreements are designed to address the conservation needs of specific groups of migratory species or specific migratory species that have an unfavorable conservation status (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/agreements). The CMS Secretariat engages closely with UNEP through various mechanisms to enhance cooperation and policy coherence between UNEP and the multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs). This includes periodic meetings with UNEP Executive Director and the Director of Law Division and the MEAs Focal Points Network coordinated by Law Division (https://www.cms.int/en/news/cms-and-unep-strengthen-mea-coordination). The Secretariat also collaborates with a number of organizations outside the framework of formal agreements (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships). The CMS Secretariat crafts different action and strategic plans for different programs with varying cycles based on the decisions and resolutions of the Conference of the Parties (COP), the Scientific Council (ScC) and the Standing Committee (StC), while also accepting inputs from other environmental treaties and organizations (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/action-plans). It also supports the implementation of CMS instruments, such as Memoranda of Understanding (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/mou), Action Plans (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/action-plans) and Concerted Actions (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/concerted-actions), which provide cooperative frameworks for the conservation and management of migratory species, as listed here (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments). Finally, various partnerships, mechanisms, platforms and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Convention and its instruments, addressing threats, habitats, knowledge, governance and synergies, with key examples listed here (https://www.cms.int/en/partnerships).

These resources feed its work program, and are supplemented by co-financing from beneficiary countries and other donors. Contributions are voluntary and multi-year in nature. Every three years, IFAD organizes a replenishment conference, corresponding to a work program. it also receives supplementary funds from various sources, such as climate financing and bilateral grants (https://www.ifad.org/en/finance). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Strategic Framework, addressing rural poverty, food security, nutrition, gender equality, resilience, innovation, partnerships and financing.

matrix_cell_text_full:
The Minamata Convention derives its mandate from the Minamata Convention on Mercury, which established the Convention as an international treaty to protect human health and the environment from mercury and mercury compounds (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf). Article 1 of the Convention defines the objective of the Convention, and Article 15 lays out the mechanism for Implementation and Compliance Committee to promote implementation 
of, and review compliance with, all provisions of the Convention. Similarly Article 23 establishes the Conference of Parties to the Convention while Article 24 outlines the functions of the Convention's Secretariat. Additionally, the Convention's articles and annexes, which were adopted by the Conference of Plenipotentiaries on 10 October 2013 (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf), specify the obligations and commitments of the Parties to the Convention, such as regulating the sources and trade of mercury, controlling the emissions and releases of mercury, managing the mercury waste and contaminated sites, providing information and public awareness, and facilitating technical and financial assistance and cooperation. The Convention's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and resolutions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Conference of the Parties, the Implementation and Compliance Committee, and the Secretariat (https://minamataconvention.org/en/meeting-documents?f%5B0%5D=document_type_2%3A307). These decisions and resolutions provide guidance and direction for the Convention's implementation and review, as well as cooperation and coordination with other relevant organisations and stakeholders. The Convention's mandate is also supported by the participation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and their Disposal (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2019.English.pdf), the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf), and the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for the Convention's jurisdiction over specific mercury-related issues and domains.

Firstly, the Secreatariat develops a programme of work and budget for each biennium, which is approved by the Conference of the Parties. The programme of work and budget, applicable for 2024-2025 (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/2024-01/Programme_work_budget_for_2024-2025.pdf), outlines the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources for implementing the Convention based on the needs and priorities of the Parties and other stakeholders, as reflected in COP-5 decision document (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/information_document/UNEP-MC-COP.5-INF36-POWB-Fact-sheets_English.pdf). Secondly, various mechanisms and tools provide technical and financial support to the Parties, especially developing countries and countries with economies in transition, to assist them in fulfilling their obligations under the Convention. These include the Implementation and Compliance Committee (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/implementation-and-compliance-committee), the Specific International Programme (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/specific-international-programme), the Global Environment Facility (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/gef), the Special Programme (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/special-programme), the Global Mercury Partnership (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/partners/global-mercury-partnership), and the Minamata Online platform (https://minamataconvention.org/es/node/3136). The main sources of funding for the Minamata Convention are the Global Environment Facility Trust Fund (GEF) and the Specific International Programme (SIP) to support capacity-building and technical assistance (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/financial-mechanism). The GEF has pledged $265 million for the four-year cycle starting in July 2022 (https://www.thegef.org/newsroom/news/minamata-convention-receives-increased-funding-pledge-global-environment-facility). Finally, various partnerships, initiatives, and platforms provide a framework for cooperation and information exchange among Parties, scientific communities, civil society, and other relevant stakeholders, on issues such as mercury supply and trade, mercury-added products, mercury waste, health and environmental impacts of mercury, and mercury-free technologies and alternatives (https://minamataconvention.org/en/resources/partnerships).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNOOSA derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly resolution 1472 (XIV) of 12 December 1959, which established the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) and its secretariat, later renamed as UNOOSA (https://www.unoosa.org/pdf/gares/ARES_14_1472E.pdf). Specifically, paragraph 1 of the resolution defines the objectives and functions of COPUOS. Additionally, UNOOSA's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and principles, such as the five treaties and five declarations on outer space, which provide the legal framework for UNOOSA's jurisdiction over the exploration and use of outer space for peaceful purposes (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties.html). The five treaties on outer space are: (1) The Outer Space Treaty (1967) on the Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introouterspacetreaty.html), (2) The Rescue Agreement (1968) on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introrescueagreement.html), (3) The Liability Convention (1972) on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introliability-convention.html), (4) The Registration Convention (1976) on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introregistration-convention.html), and (5) The Moon Agreement (1984) governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/intromoon-agreement.html). UNOOSA's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by COPUOS and the General Assembly, such as the Space2030 Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which provide guidance and direction for UNOOSA's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/resolutions.html).

As stated in its constitution, the FAO maintains relations with the United Nations as a specialized agency (Article XII), and with other international, regional, and national organizations and authorities related to food and agriculture (Article XIII). The FAO may also enter into agreements with Member Nations for the establishment of international institutions dealing with food and agriculture (Article XV) (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf). The FAO engages with a diverse array of institutions to advance its mission. It partners with Member States and various stakeholders, including civil society, the private sector, academia, and research centers, to combat food insecurity and malnutrition (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/en/). The FAO’s collaboration with academia and research institutions is crucial for mobilizing knowledge and innovations, as well as for providing evidence-based solutions to policy processes (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/academia/en/). 
Furthermore, the FAO works closely with international organizations to facilitate partnerships for food and nutrition security, agriculture, and rural development3. For instance, the FAO’s Strategy for Private Sector Engagement aims to strengthen strategic engagement with the private sector towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (https://doi.org/10.4060/cb3352en). In addition, the FAO is involved in South-South Cooperation, which is a key instrument for delivering on its mandate and achieving the SDGs (https://www.fao.org/3/i5163e/i5163e.pdf). This cooperation is facilitated through the FAO’s Partnerships and UN Collaboration Division, which develops strategic cooperation with non-state actors (https://www.fao.org/3/cc7997en/cc7997en.pdf).

It liaises with the International Seabed Authority (ISA), implementing a relationship agreement effective since 25 July 1996, as per UNCLOS Annex III Article 4 and the 1994 Agreement Article 177, detailed in resolution 48/263 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n94/332/98/pdf/n9433298.pdf?token=YhD8GNV5K9pWhEpVuW&fe=true). Similarly, DOALOS maintains a relationship with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), providing administrative support based on an agreement aligned with the Tribunal's Statute Article 5 (https://www.itlos.org/fileadmin/itlos/documents/basic_texts/statute_en.pdf) and the 1994 Agreement Article 178, detailed in resolution 51/204 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n97/769/51/pdf/n9776951.pdf?token=FFhG7JOPZn4wAkSphS&fe=true). It also services the Informal Consultative Process (ICP) on Oceans and the Law of the Sea, preparing related reports, with its mandate in resolution 54/33 (http://www.worldlii.org/int/other/UNGA/1999/71.pdf). Moreover, DOALOS facilitates the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, established in 2002, to enhance scientific understanding and decision-making, involving a Group of Experts and a Working Group, with terms detailed in resolution 57/141 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf). excerpt_<=50w: According to Part XI, Section 4 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the International Seabed Authority's objectives encompass several key functions: organizing and controlling activities in the Area, particularly with a view to administering the resources of the Area (Article 157, paragraph 1); establishing specific
matrix_cell_text_full: According to Part XI, Section 4 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the International Seabed Authority's objectives encompass several key functions: organizing and controlling activities in the Area, particularly with a view to administering the resources of the Area (Article 157, paragraph 1); establishing specific policies for the Authority in conformity with the Convention and the general policies established by the Assembly (Article 162, paragraph 1); adopting and applying provisionally the rules, regulations and procedures of the Authority relating to prospecting, exploration and exploitation in the Area, as well as the financial management and internal administration of the Authority (Article 162, paragraph 2 o); supervising and coordinating the implementation of the provisions of Part XI and inviting the attention of the Assembly to cases of non-compliance (Article 162, paragraph 2 a); exercising control over activities in the Area in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 4, and the rules, regulations and procedures of the Authority (Article 162, paragraph 2 l); and ensuring the equitable sharing of financial and other economic benefits derived from activities in the Area, taking into account the interests and needs of developing States and peoples who have not attained full independence or other self-governing status (Article 160, paragraph 2 f and g; Article 162, paragraph 2 g). These functions enable the Authority to fulfil its role as the organization through which States Parties shall carry out their rights and obligations under the Convention with respect to activities in the Area (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm).

matrix_cell_text_full: The International Seabed Authority (ISA) fulfills its objectives through diverse strategies: firstly, a five-year Strategic Plan (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Strategic_Plan_Booklet.pdf), adopted in 2018 by the ISA Assembly (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba24_a10-en.pdf), aligns with UNCLOS, the 1994 Agreement (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). Additionally, a High-Level Action Plan for 2019-2023, adopted in 2019 (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/25a-15-e.pdf), outlines necessary actions to achieve the Strategic Plan's objectives, including priorities, standards and guidelines (https://www.isa.org.jm/the-mining-code/standards-and-guidelines/). The ISA also employs a data management strategy initiated in August 2016 (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba-22ltc-15_1.pdf), focusing on enhancing data collection, storage, analysis, and dissemination, supported by the ISA DeepData database (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/DeepData-Brochure-final.pdf), as detailed in ISBA/23/A/3. Furthermore, ISA issues 15-year contracts for mineral resource exploration in the Area to various contractors, covering polymetallic nodules, polymetallic sulphides, and cobalt-rich ferromanganese crusts (https://dsm.gsd.spc.int/public/files/Deep%20Sea%20Minerals%20in%20the%20Pacific%20Islands%20Region%20Brochure%2015%281%29.pdf), governed by ISA's rules and requiring contractors to provide data and support training for personnel from developing States (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba_25_c_wp1-e_0.pdf). These strategies collectively ensure effective management and sustainable utilization of seabed resources.

matrix_cell_text_full: The ISA cooperates with various organizations to achieve its objectives and mandates. It maintains a relationship with the United Nations (UN), as an observer to the UN General Assembly, based on an agreement in accordance with UNCLOS Article 156, paragraph 2, and the 1994 Agreement Article 169 (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/UN-ISA-Agrmnt-1.pdf). Similarly, it maintains a relationship with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), as the principal judicial organ for the settlement of disputes relating to the activities in the Area, based on an agreement in accordance with UNCLOS Article 187 and the 1994 Agreement Article 178, detailed in resolution 51/205. Additionally, it consults and collaborates with the relevant specialized agencies of the UN, such as the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), and the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC), as well as other international and regional organizations, such as the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO), and the regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs), on matters of common interest, in accordance with UNCLOS Article 156, paragraph 3, and the 1994 Agreement Article 170 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/publication/CTC/Ch_XXI_6_english_p.pdf). It also participates in the Informal Consultative Process (ICP) on Oceans and the Law of the Sea, providing inputs and updates on its activities, with its role recognized in resolution 54/33 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N00/237/93/PDF/N0023793.pdf?OpenElement). Moreover, it contributes to the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, providing data and information on the environmental aspects of the activities in the Area, with its involvement encouraged in resolution 57/141 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNEP fulfills its objectives through diverse strategies: firstly, a four-year Medium-Term Strategy (MTS) for the period 2022–2025 set by and adopted by the UN Environmental Assembly (UNEA), adopted in 2021 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/35162/Doc3%20Reve1%20EnglishK2100501.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment, and the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development. The MTS defines UNEP’s vision, mission, strategic objectives, core functions, subprogrammes and indicators for measuring progress (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/policies-and-strategies). Secondly, a biennial Programme of Work and Budget 2022-2023, based on the MTS, devised by UNEP and ratified by UNEA, details the activities, outputs, resources, and partnerships corresponding to each subprogramme (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/38040/MTS_PoW2022.pdf?sequence=3&isAllowed=y). UNEP also supports the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans, which provide legal frameworks and operational mechanisms for addressing specific environmental issues and regions (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/why-does-un-environment-matter/secretariats-and-conventions). Furthermore, UNEP's work is guided by a number of over-arching strategies, policies and guidelines for ensuring access to information, preventing and responding to misconduct and fraud, enhancing sustainability, and engaging with civil society and the private sector, etc. (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/policies-and-strategies). Every two years, UNEA also adopts resolutions and decisions on various environmental topics, which guide UNEP’s implementation of its objectives and mandates (https://www.unep.org/news-and-stories/story/what-you-need-know-about-un-environment-assembly). These strategies collectively ensure effective coordination and promotion of environmental action within the United Nations system and beyond.
