matrix_cell_text_full: UNEP fulfills its objectives through diverse strategies: firstly, a four-year Medium-Term Strategy (MTS) for the period 2022–2025 set by and adopted by the UN Environmental Assembly (UNEA), adopted in 2021 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/35162/Doc3%20Reve1%20EnglishK2100501.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment, and the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development. The MTS defines UNEP’s vision, mission, strategic objectives, core functions, subprogrammes and indicators for measuring progress (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/policies-and-strategies). Secondly, a biennial Programme of Work and Budget 2022-2023, based on the MTS, devised by UNEP and ratified by UNEA, details the activities, outputs, resources, and partnerships corresponding to each subprogramme (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/38040/MTS_PoW2022.pdf?sequence=3&isAllowed=y). UNEP also supports the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans, which provide legal frameworks and operational mechanisms for addressing specific environmental issues and regions (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/why-does-un-environment-matter/secretariats-and-conventions). Furthermore, UNEP's work is guided by a number of over-arching strategies, policies and guidelines for ensuring access to information, preventing and responding to misconduct and fraud, enhancing sustainability, and engaging with civil society and the private sector, etc. (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/policies-and-strategies). Every two years, UNEA also adopts resolutions and decisions on various environmental topics, which guide UNEP’s implementation of its objectives and mandates (https://www.unep.org/news-and-stories/story/what-you-need-know-about-un-environment-assembly). These strategies collectively ensure effective coordination and promotion of environmental action within the United Nations system and beyond.

matrix_cell_text_full: UNDP derives its mandate from the United Nation's General Assembly resolution 2029 (XX), establishing it in 1965 as a merger of two previous programmes, the United Nations Expanded Programme of Technical Assistance (EPTA) (1949) and the United Nations Special Fund (1958) to provide technical assistance to developing countries and to be responsible for the coordination of development activities on the country level, as well as the monitoring and reporting of the progress made in achieving the development goals (UNDP-MX-SpecialFundandTechnicalAssistanceMX.pdf). Specifically, Paragraph 4 of the Resolution states that a single inter-governmental committee of thirty-seven members, to be known as the Governing Council of the UNDP, shall be established to perform the funtions previously exercised by the Governing Council of the Special Fund and the Technical Assistance Committee, including the consideration and approval of projects and programmes and the allocation of funds, and Paragraph 5 requests the Economic and Social Council to elect the members of the Governing Council from among States Members of the United Nations or members of the specialized agencies or of the International Atomic Energy Agency, providing for equitable and balanced representation. Similarly, Paragraph 6 of the Resolution establishes the Inter-Agency Consultative Board of the UNDP to meet under the chairmanship of the Administrator or Co-Administrator. UNDP’s mandate is also influenced by the quadrennial comprehensive policy review of operational activities for development of the United Nations system (QCPR), which provides guidance and direction for UNDP and other UN development agencies (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/dp2022-17_Annex%203.docx). Its mandate is likewise supported by its Financial Regulations Rules (https://popp.undp.org/document/undp-financial-regulations-and-rules) and by its Programme and Operations Policies and Procedures (https://popp.undp.org/). In addition, the UNDP's mandate is influenced by the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.undp.org/sustainable-development-goals/life-on-land?gad_source=1&gclid=CjwKCAiA_tuuBhAUEiwAvxkgTs0LJirFb70iqfh78qtj276maQH96QDdTQEyrmw-FYYh6IPHZd3pDxoCO5IQAvD_BwE).

matrix_cell_text_full: The UNDP executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the UNDP's vision, mission, directions of change, signature solutions, and enablers. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2021-09/UNDP-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025_1.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Paris Agreement, and is structured around “3x6x3” - 3 directions of change, 6 signature solutions, and 3 enablers - to help countries expand human capabilities and development choices, build a more equitable world, and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The three directions of change are structural transformation, leaving no one behind, and resilience. The six signature solutions are poverty and inequality, governance, resilience, environment, energy, and gender equality. The three enablers are strategic innovation, digitalization, and development financing. Secondly, an annual integrated budget and workplan, devised by the UNDP and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each signature solution. The budget and workplan for 2024 is tailored to the countries' needs and stakeholders' priorities (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2023-12/dp2024-CRP1_3.pdf). The UNDP also maintains the SDG Accelerator Lab Network, a key aspect of the innovation and digitalisation of the UNDP (https://www.undp.org/acceleratorlabs). UNDP proposes a total budget of $5.4 billion for 2022-2025, comprising $1.4 billion for institutional effectiveness and $4 billion for development activities based on projected income and in alignment with the strategic plan outcomes and outputs. In order to achieve its mandate, UNDP relies entirely on voluntary contributions from UN Member States, multilateral organizations, private sector and other sources, in the form of unrestricted regular resources (core), and contributions earmarked for a specific theme, programme or project (https://www.undp.org/funding). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the UNDAF, the UNDP Strategic Plan, and the SDGs, addressing poverty and inequality, governance, resilience, environment, energy, and gender equality (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2022-07/UNDP%20Strategic%20Plan%202022-2025.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNDP collaborates with various partners to advance sustainable development. It works with governments, providing policy advice, technical assistance, and financial support, based on the UN Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) and the Country Programme Documents (CPDs) that outline the country-specific priorities and results (https://www.undp.org/our-partners). It coordinates with the UN development system, ensuring coherent and effective support to countries, with its Administrator as the Vice-Chair of the UN Sustainable Development Group, which unites the 40 UN entities that contribute to the attainment of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development at the country level (https://popp.undp.org/policy-page/managing-partnerships). Furthermore, UNDP partners with international financial institutions, mobilizing non-core funding and implementing joint projects, such as the World Bank, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, with whom UNDP has formal agreements (https://www.undp.org/our-partners). It likewise collaborates with other UN entities, such as the UN Environment Programme, the UN Human Settlements Programme, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, and the UN Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women, on various thematic areas and initiatives, while also engaging with the private sector to foster innovation and entrepreneurship, and with foundations, civil society organizations, and goodwill ambassadors, leveraging their knowledge, networks, and resources, through various platforms and initiatives like the SDG Philanthropy Platform, the Business Call to Action, and the UNDP Innovation Facility (http://web.undp.org/evaluation/documents/directors-desk/papers/UNDPs_partnership_with_private_sector-12_2017.pdf). These partnerships are essential for UNDP to fulfill its strategic plan and contribute to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

matrix_cell_text_full: As per the  General Assembly resolution 1995 (XIX) of 30 December 1964 (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf),  Key objectives of UNCTAD include promoting international trade, especially to accelerate economic development, and enhancing trade between countries at varied development stages, including developing countries and those with different economic systems (section II, paragraph 3 a). It formulates principles and policies on international trade and economic development (section II, paragraph 3 b), proposes effective implementation strategies, considering economic system diversity and development stages (section II, paragraph 3 c). UNCTAD reviews and coordinates United Nations system activities in international trade and economic development, collaborating with the General Assembly and Economic and Social Council (section II, paragraph 3 d). It initiates actions for negotiating and adopting multilateral trade legal instruments (section II, paragraph 3 e), harmonizes trade and development policies of governments and regional groups (section II, paragraph 3 f), and addresses other relevant matters (section II, paragraph 3 g). Additionally, UNCTAD evaluates and recommends institutional arrangement improvements, including comprehensive organization establishment within the UN system (section III, paragraphs 30 and 31). These functions establish UNCTAD as the General Assembly's principal organ in trade and development (section I, paragraph 1).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNCTAD collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives and mandates. It engages with 195 Member States and various stakeholders through the UNCTAD conference, held every four years, serving as the highest-level decision-making body on trade and development issues (https://unctad.org/about/partnership). As the main organ of the General Assembly in the field of trade and development, UNCTAD's relationship with the UN is based on resolution 1995 (XIX), which established UNCTAD in 1964 (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf). Additionally, UNCTAD leads the UN Inter-Agency Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity, involving 15 UN agencies, providing a mechanism for the coordination of trade and development operations at the national and regional levels within the UN system, as endorsed by the UN Chief Executives Board for Coordination (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/tc2010d1rev9_en.pdf). It also cooperates with other international and regional organizations, such as WTO, OECD, World Bank, ILO, and CITES, UNDP, UNIDO, IMF, etc addressing common trade and development challenges (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/dom20092rev1_en.pdf). Moreover, UNCTAD supports the implementation of the UN development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, offering research and analysis, technical assistance, intergovernmental consensus-building, and policy advice for developing countries, as recognized in resolution 71/215 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N16/459/44/PDF/N1645944.pdf?OpenElement).

excerpt_<=50w: According to Chapter I of the Constitution of the UNIDO, the Organization's objectives are to promote and accelerate industrial development in the developing countries, with a view to assisting in the establishment of a new international economic order, and to promote industrial development and cooperation on global, regional and national,
matrix_cell_text_full: According to Chapter I of the Constitution of the UNIDO, the Organization's objectives are to promote and accelerate industrial development in the developing countries, with a view to assisting in the establishment of a new international economic order, and to promote industrial development and cooperation on global, regional and national, as well as on sectoral levels (Article 1). To fulfil these objectives, the Organization shall perform various functions, such as encouraging and assisting the developing countries in their industrialization efforts, initiating and coordinating the activities of the United Nations system in the field of industrial development, creating and developing new concepts and approaches for industrial development, providing a forum and an instrument for international cooperation and dialogue on industrial matters, serving as a clearing-house for industrial information, promoting and encouraging the development, transfer and use of industrial technology, organizing and supporting industrial training programmes, assisting in the exploitation, conservation and transformation of natural resources, developing special measures for the least-developed and other disadvantaged developing countries, and assisting in obtaining external financing for industrial projects (Article 2). These functions enable the Organization to play the central role in and be responsible for reviewing and promoting the coordination of all activities of the United Nations system in the field of industrial development, in conformity with the responsibilities of the Economic and Social Council under the Charter of the United Nations and with the applicable relationship agreements (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf).

UNIDO executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Medium-Term Programme Framework (MTPF), revised biennially by the Industrial Development Board, which defines the strategic guidance, directions, and priorities of the Organization (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/unido-publications/2023-02/2022-2025-MEDIUM-TERM-PROGRAMME-FRAMEWORK-en.pdf). This framework, applicable for 2022-2025, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals, detailed in document IDB.48/14 (https://downloads.unido.org/ot/21/32/21329747/PBC.37_14_E_United%20Nations%20Development%20System%20reform_V2101499.pdf?_ga=2.15564982.1264381354.1702429546-1974414734.1702429546). Secondly, a biennial programme and budgets, prepared by the Secretariat and approved by the General Conference, which specify the outputs, indicators, and resources for each focus area of expertise and core function of the Organization. The current programme and budgets for 2022-2023 reflect the needs and expectations of the Member States and the development partners, as outlined in document GC.20/5 (https://downloads.unido.org/ot/20/98/20989988/PBC.37_5_E_Programme%20and%20budgets%202022-2023_V2101337.pdf?_ga=2.83258390.1264381354.1702429546-1974414734.1702429546). It also maintains the Country Programme Frameworks (CPFs) and the Regional Programme Frameworks (RPFs) established under the MTPF, which provide the operational framework for implementing the Organization’s mandate at the country and regional levels (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/unido-publications/2023-02/2022-2025-MEDIUM-TERM-PROGRAMME-FRAMEWORK-en.pdf). In addition, UNIDO is operationalising  the Third Industrial Development Decade for Africa
(2016–2025) (IDDA III)  through the Roadmap Implementation of the Third Industrial Development Decade for Africa (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2018-09/IDDA3_Roadmap_0.pdf) derived from General Assembly resolution 70/293 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N16/234/02/PDF/N1623402.pdf?OpenElement), to drive Africa on a path towards inclusive and sustainable industrial development. Likewise, UNIDO maintains various partnerships, platforms, initiatives, and networks that provide the collaborative framework for enhancing the impact and effectiveness of the Organization’s interventions, addressing cross-cutting issues such as gender, youth, innovation, and digitalization (https://www.unido.org/about-us/partnerships).

UNIDO executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Medium-Term Programme Framework (MTPF), revised biennially by the Industrial Development Board, which defines the strategic guidance, directions, and priorities of the Organization (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/unido-publications/2023-02/2022-2025-MEDIUM-TERM-PROGRAMME-FRAMEWORK-en.pdf). This framework, applicable for 2022-2025, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals, detailed in document IDB.48/14 (https://downloads.unido.org/ot/21/32/21329747/PBC.37_14_E_United%20Nations%20Development%20System%20reform_V2101499.pdf?_ga=2.15564982.1264381354.1702429546-1974414734.1702429546). Secondly, a biennial programme and budgets, prepared by the Secretariat and approved by the General Conference, which specify the outputs, indicators, and resources for each focus area of expertise and core function of the Organization. The current programme and budgets for 2022-2023 reflect the needs and expectations of the Member States and the development partners, as outlined in document GC.20/5 (https://downloads.unido.org/ot/20/98/20989988/PBC.37_5_E_Programme%20and%20budgets%202022-2023_V2101337.pdf?_ga=2.83258390.1264381354.1702429546-1974414734.1702429546). It also maintains the Country Programme Frameworks (CPFs) and the Regional Programme Frameworks (RPFs) established under the MTPF, which provide the operational framework for implementing the Organization’s mandate at the country and regional levels (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/unido-publications/2023-02/2022-2025-MEDIUM-TERM-PROGRAMME-FRAMEWORK-en.pdf). In addition, UNIDO is operationalising  the Third Industrial Development Decade for Africa
(2016–2025) (IDDA III)  through the Roadmap Implementation of the Third Industrial Development Decade for Africa (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2018-09/IDDA3_Roadmap_0.pdf) derived from General Assembly resolution 70/293 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N16/234/02/PDF/N1623402.pdf?OpenElement), to drive Africa on a path towards inclusive and sustainable industrial development. Likewise, UNIDO maintains various partnerships, platforms, initiatives, and networks that provide the collaborative framework for enhancing the impact and effectiveness of the Organization’s interventions, addressing cross-cutting issues such as gender, youth, innovation, and digitalization (https://www.unido.org/about-us/partnerships).

matrix_cell_text_full: ILO derives its mandate from the Treaty of Versailles, cum The Covenant of the League of Nations, which established it as the first specialised agency of the League of Nations in 1919 (https://libraryresources.unog.ch/ld.php?content_id=32971179). Specifically, Article 23 of the Treaty provides the legal basis for ILO's jurisdiction over the improvement of labour conditions, the regulation of hours of work, the prevention of unemployment, and the protection of workers' rights (https://www.foundingdocs.gov.au/resources/transcripts/cth10_doc_1919.pdf). ILO also adopts and supervises international labour standards, such as Conventions and Recommendations, (including he Maritime Labour Convention - Maritime Labour Convention, 2006  - https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---normes/documents/normativeinstrument/wcms_090250.pdf) which provide further legal frameworks for ILO's jurisdiction over specific labour issues and regions.

matrix_cell_text_full: The ILO collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It works closely with its tripartite constituents - governments, employers and workers - through the International Labour Conference, the Governing Body, and the Regional Meetings, which are the supreme organs of the ILO and set its policies and programmes (https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/how-the-ilo-works/lang--en/index.htm). As the first specialized agency of the UN, the ILO's relationship with the UN is based on the Agreement between the United Nations and the International Labour Organization, which was approved by the General Assembly in 1946 and by the International Labour Conference in 1947 (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---dgreports/---jur/documents/genericdocument/wcms_433792.pdf). Additionally, the ILO cooperates with other UN agencies and regional and subregional organizations, such as the UN Economic and Social Council, the UN Development Group, UNEP, UNIDO, UNDP, UNITAR, the World Bank, the IMF, the OECD, the African Union, the European Union, and the Organization of American States, on various aspects of labour and social issues, as stipulated in Article 12 and Article 13 of the ILO Constitution (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf; https://www.ilo.org/pardev/partnerships/partnerships-and-relations/interagency-partnerships/lang--en/index.htm). The ILO is member of the UN Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity   through which it works with UNCTAD, ITC, UNIDO and UNOPS to enhance horticulture supply and sustainable tourism to develop business linkages in developing countries (https://tii.unido.org/sites/default/files/publications/TII_ImpactStory_SECO_Myanmar.pdf)  It also participates in the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, providing data on the social and economic dimensions of the marine sector, as recognized in resolution 57/141, paragraph  (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: ITU derives its mandate from the Constitution (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf) and the Convention of the International Telecommunication Union, which is an international treaty signed and ratified by almost all countries of the world (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Convention-E.pdf). The treaty is the founding document of the ITU, a specialized agency of the United Nations (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). Specifically, Article 1 of the Constitution defines the purposes and functions of the ITU, which include maintaining and extending international cooperation among all its Member States for the improvement and rational use of telecommunications of all kinds, promoting the development and efficient operation of technical facilities, and harmonizing the actions of Member States and Sector Members (https://www.itu.int/en/history/Pages/ConstitutionAndConvention.aspx). Additionally, ITU's jurisdiction is influenced by the resolutions and decisions of the Plenipotentiary Conference (https://search.itu.int/history/HistoryDigitalCollectionDocLibrary/5.23.61.en.100.pdf), which is the supreme organ of the ITU and has the power to amend the Constitution and the Convention (Article 8 of the Constitution). ITU also adopts and supervises the Administrative Regulations, such as the Radio Regulations and the International Telecommunication Regulations, which are binding on all ITU Member States and provide the legal framework for ITU's jurisdiction over the use of the radio-frequency spectrum, satellite orbits, and international telecommunication services (Article 4 of the Constitution). Also, The ITU Constitution and Convention are complemented by the Administrative Regulations, which comprise the ITU International Telecommunication Regulations and ITU Radio Regulations, and are binding on all ITU member states as well (https://www.itu.int/en/history/Pages/RegulationsCollection.aspx#:~:text=ITU's%20Administrative%20Regulations%20contain%20provisions,operation%20of%20international%20telecommunication%20services).

The current budget and operational plan for 2022-2023 are tailored to the Member States' and Sector Members' needs and priorities, as outlined in Resolution 154 (Rev. It also maintains the databases and registries for the allocation and assignment of radio frequencies, satellite orbits, and numbering resources, which are essential for the coordination and management of the global telecommunication network (https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-R/terrestrial/Pages/by-categories-faq.aspx?subcategorizedby=6). Finally, various standards, regulations, resolutions, recommendations, and initiatives provide a technical and regulatory framework for implementing the Constitution and Convention of the ITU, addressing connectivity, digital transformation, innovation, and partnership, with key instruments listed here (https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-s/opb/conf/S-CONF-ACTF-2022-PDF-E.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNICEF implements its objectives through several key strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan (2022-2025), revised by the Executive Board, outlining UNICEF’s vision, mission, and goals aligned with the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (https://www.unicef.org/sites/default/files/2022-02/UNICEF-strategic-plan-2022-2025-publication-EN.pdf), detailed in document E/ICEF/2021/11 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N21/108/01/PDF/N2110801.pdf?OpenElement). Secondly, a biennial Integrated Results and Resources Framework (2022-2025) specifies expected results, indicators, and resources for each Strategic Plan outcome, based on a theory of change and results-based management (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/7426/file/2021-25-Add1-Strategic_Plan_2022-2025-IRRF-EN-ODS.pdf), as outlined in document E/ICEF/2021/12 (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/5316/file/2021-12-Draft_Strategic_Plan_2022-2025-EN-2021.05.04.pdf). UNICEF also focuses on monitoring the implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.unicef.org/child-rights-convention/unicef-role). Additionally, UNICEF's Data for Children Strategic Framework sets principles for data work, including action, innovation, and trust, with strategic objectives like improving data quality and fostering data partnerships (https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Data-for-Children-Strategic-Framework-UNICEF.pdf). The UNICEF Disability Inclusion Policy and Strategy (DIPAS) 2022-2030 aligns with the CRPD, CRC, and UNDIS, setting priorities for disability-inclusive services and participation (https://www.unicef.org/media/134511/file/An%20inclusive%20world,%20starts%20with%20me,%20with%20you,%20with%20all%20of%20us.pdf). Finally, the UNICEF 2021-2030 Child Protection Strategy aligns with the CRC and SDGs, focusing on strengthening child protection systems, addressing harmful social norms, leveraging partnerships, and enhancing evidence for child protection (https://www.unicef.org/media/104416/file/Child-Protection-Strategy-2021.pdf). These comprehensive strategies enable UNICEF to deliver results for children globally, including in humanitarian and fragile contexts.

Additionally, UNICEF's Data for Children Strategic Framework sets principles for data work, including action, innovation, and trust, with strategic objectives like improving data quality and fostering data partnerships (https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Data-for-Children-Strategic-Framework-UNICEF.pdf). matrix_cell_text_full: WHO collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It works with 194 Member States and various stakeholders through the World Health Assembly (WHA), established in 1948 by the Constitution of the WHO, serving as the supreme decision-making body for health (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). As a specialized agency within the UN system, WHO's relationship with the UN is based on the Agreement between the United Nations and the World Health Organization, effective since 10 July 1948, which defines the respective responsibilities and cooperation of the two organizations (https://apps.who.int/gb/bd/pdf_files/BD_49th-en.pdf). Additionally, WHO supports various health-related conventions and treaties, providing legal and normative frameworks for specific health issues and situations, such as the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/42811/9241591013.pdf?sequence=1) and the International Health Regulations (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/246107/9789241580496-eng.pdf?sequence=1). It also collaborates with other UN agencies and partners, such as Gavi, The GFF, the Global Fund, UNAIDS, UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF, UNITAID, UN Women, World Bank Group and WFP and WHO, addressing common health challenges (https://www.who.int/news/item/24-09-2019-multilateral-agencies-launch-a-joint-plan-to-boost-global-health-goals#:~:text=The%2012%20signatory%20agencies%20to,Bank%20Group%2C%20WFP%20and%20WHO.&text=Quotes%20from%20the%2012%20Principals%20are%20available%20below.). Moreover, WHO participates in the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC), contributing to the coordination and delivery of humanitarian assistance, as endorsed by resolution 46/182 of the UN General Assembly (https://ngocoordination.org/system/files/documents/resources/ga-resolution-46-182.pdf).

It works with the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) to provide technical support and guidance to Member States and other stakeholders on disaster risk reduction, as stated in paragraph 48 (a) of the Sendai Framework (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..). It also coordinates with the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) to ensure coherence and synergies among the relevant instruments and frameworks, as stated in paragraph 48 (b) of the Sendai Framework (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..). Moreover, UNDRR supports the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction, the regional and subregional platforms for disaster risk reduction, and the thematic platforms, as well as the United Nations Scientific and Technical Advisory Group, to facilitate dialogue, cooperation, and knowledge-sharing on disaster risk reduction, as stated in paragraph 48 of the Sendai Framework (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_69_283.pdf).

Additionally, the UN Global Compact's jurisdiction is influenced by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (https://www.un.org/en/udhrbook/pdf/udhr_booklet_en_web.pdf), the International Labour Organization's Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---declaration/documents/publication/wcms_467653.pdf), the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_CONF.151_26_Vol.I_Declaration.pdf), and the United Nations Convention Against Corruption (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/UNCAC/Publications/Convention/08-50026_E.pdf), which provide the basis for its ten principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption (https://unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc/mission/principles). The UN Global Compact also supports the implementation of the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, which provide further guidance for its participants and stakeholders on advancing societal goals with an emphasis on collaboration and innovation (https://unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc/mission).

Furthermore, the UN Global Compact's jurisdiction is endorsed by the UN General Assembly, which has adopted several resolutions and a decision that recognize its role and activities, encourage its expansion and participation, and call for its strengthening and alignment with the UN's values and principles. These include resolutions 55/215 of 21 December 2000, 56/76 of 11 December 2001, 58/129 of 19 December 2003, 60/215 of 22 December 2005, 62/211 of 19 December 2007, 64/223 of 21 December 2009, 66/223 of 22 December 2011, 68/234 of 20 December 2013 and 70/224 of 22 December 2015, as well as decision 72/543 of 20 December 2017 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement). These resolutions and decision reflect the support and recognition of the UN General Assembly for the UN Global Compact as a strategic partner and a leading initiative for corporate sustainability and social responsibility.

matrix_cell_text_full: The IAEA derives its mandate from the Statute of the IAEA, which was approved by the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in 1956 and entered into force in 1957 (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). The Statute provides the legal basis for the IAEA's jurisdiction over the promotion and control of the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and technology, as well as the verification of compliance with non-proliferation and disarmament obligations (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). Additionally, the IAEA's jurisdiction is influenced by the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), particularly Article III, which entrusts the IAEA with the responsibility of applying safeguards to all non-nuclear-weapon states parties to the treaty, as well as other states that have concluded safeguards agreements with the IAEA (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/publications/documents/infcircs/1970/infcirc140.pdf). The IAEA also finds its mandate from the implementation of other international legal instruments related to nuclear safety, security, and cooperation, such as Article 5, 18 and 23 of the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/infcirc274r1.pdf), and Article 8 and 18 of the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/2005/04/20050413%2004-02%20PM/Ch_XVIII_15p.pdf). These instruments and initiatives provide further legal frameworks and mechanisms for the IAEA's jurisdiction over specific nuclear issues and challenges.

matrix_cell_text_full: The IAEA derives its mandate from the Statute of the IAEA, which was approved by the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in 1956 and entered into force in 1957 (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). The Statute provides the legal basis for the IAEA's jurisdiction over the promotion and control of the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and technology, as well as the verification of compliance with non-proliferation and disarmament obligations (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). Additionally, the IAEA's jurisdiction is influenced by the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), particularly Article III, which entrusts the IAEA with the responsibility of applying safeguards to all non-nuclear-weapon states parties to the treaty, as well as other states that have concluded safeguards agreements with the IAEA (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/publications/documents/infcircs/1970/infcirc140.pdf). The IAEA also finds its mandate from the implementation of other international legal instruments related to nuclear safety, security, and cooperation, such as Article 5, 18 and 23 of the Convention on the Physical Protection of Nuclear Material (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/infcirc274r1.pdf), and Article 8 and 18 of the International Convention for the Suppression of Acts of Nuclear Terrorism (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/2005/04/20050413%2004-02%20PM/Ch_XVIII_15p.pdf). These instruments and initiatives provide further legal frameworks and mechanisms for the IAEA's jurisdiction over specific nuclear issues and challenges.

matrix_cell_text_full: The IAEA executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a six-year Medium Term Strategy, prepared through a joint consultation process among Member States and the Secretariat, which establishes the Agency's strategic direction and roadmap for the preparation of its programme and budget, by identifying priorities among and within its programmes for the achievement of its statutory objectives in an evolving international environment (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/23/02/mts2024_2029.pdf). This strategy, applicable for 2024-2029, draws upon the previous Medium Term Strategy 2018-2023 and may be updated, if deemed necessary by the Board of Governors, adapting to new developments and evolving needs and priorities of Member States (https://www.iaea.org/about/overview/medium-term-strategy). Secondly, a biennial programme and budget, approved by the General Conference, which details the expected results, performance indicators, and resources corresponding to each major programme area. The current programme and budget for 2022-2023 are aligned with the Medium Term Strategy 2018-2023 and reflect the Agency's response to the COVID-19 pandemic, as well as its support to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/gc/gc67-5.pdf). It also maintains the safeguards system, which verifies the compliance of States with their non-proliferation and disarmament obligations, as well as the technical cooperation programme, which assists Member States in the peaceful application of nuclear science and technology (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/safeguards_web_june_2015_1.pdf). Finally, various legal instruments, initiatives, platforms, and networks provide an operational framework for implementing the Agency's mandate, addressing nuclear safety, security, and cooperation (https://www.iaea.org/topics/nuclear-knowledge-management).

matrix_cell_text_full: The IAEA collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It engages with 178 Member States and various stakeholders through the General Conference, which is the highest policy-making body of the Agency and meets annually to approve the programme and budget, as well as the Board of Governors, which consists of 35 Member States and meets five times a year to examine and make recommendations to the General Conference on the IAEA's accounts, programme and budget, and to consider applications for membership (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/18/08/the-iaea-policy-making-organs-providing-guidance-for-the-agencys-work.pdf). As an autonomous organization within the UN system, the IAEA's relationship with the UN is guided by an agreement signed in 1957, which stipulates that the Agency shall report annually to the General Assembly and, when appropriate, to the Security Council, and shall cooperate with the Economic and Social Council and other specialized agencies (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/207456/files/A_RES_1145%28XII%29-EN.pdf?ln=en). Additionally, the IAEA supports the implementation of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) and other international legal instruments and initiatives related to nuclear safety, security, and cooperation, providing verification and inspection services, technical assistance, and policy guidance for Member States, as detailed in the IAEA Statute, Article III (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf). It also cooperates with other UN agencies and organizations, such as WHO, FAO, UNEP, and OECD/NEA, as well as regional and intergovernmental organizations, such as the European Union, the African Union, and the Organization of American States, addressing common nuclear issues and challenges, as recognized in various resolutions and agreements (https://www.iaea.org/about/partnerships), (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/publications/magazines/bulletin/bull29-3/29301081418.pdf), (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/publications/magazines/bulletin/bull37-3/37305381015.pdf).

Secondly, a  Results-based Budget, devised by the secretariat and ratified by the World Meteorological Congress, detail resources for implementation of the Strategic Plan, including the functioning of constituent bodies and the Secretariat (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/56690?medianame=1236_en_#page=33&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q=).

These regulatory provisions make it possible to operate the 24/7/365 global systems for observations, data exchange and management, forecasting and provision of authoritative scientific assessments and standardized service products to a variety of users in each WMO Member State and Member Territory (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/55618/download?file=EC-69_Progress_report_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). 
The WMO also has a Competency Framework that helps Members design their services for effective delivery, assist in staffing decisions, guide the performance assessment of staff members, and offer recommended learning outcomes to use in planning training programmes (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/56877/download?file=1209_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1).  In addition to these, the WMO has Resolutions, Decisions and Recommendations adopted by the Congress, Executive Council, Regional Associations and Technical Commissions in force (https://tools.wmo.int/wmo-resolutions/). These resolutions and decisions guide the overall progress towards achieving departmental targets and organizational objectives and goals.

The WMO collaborates with key organizations to fulfill its objectives. It engages with 193 Member States and various stakeholders through the World Meteorological Congress, serving as the highest-level meteorological decision-making body (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/overview). As the primary meteorological authority within the UN system, WMO's relationship with the UN is grounded in Part XII, Article 25 of the Convention of the World Meteorological Organization (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1), pursuant to Article 57 of the Charter of the United Nations (https://www.un.org/en/about-us/un-charter/full-text). 
Additionally, WMO supports National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs) and advances the application of meteorology and hydrology in many societal and economic areas (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/overview). Pursuant to Part XIII, Article 26 of its convention, WMO collaborates with UN specialized agencies, multilateral development banks, climate funds and others, addressing shared meteorological concerns (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). 
Moreover, WMO contributes to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/partnerships).
Furthermore, WMO maintains a relationship with the public, private, and academic sectors operating in the global weather arena through its Public-Private Engagement (PPE) initiative (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/public-private-partnerships). This initiative encourages and enables Members to pursue mutually beneficial partnerships and engagement with all sectors and stakeholders in order to enhance weather, climate, and water services for businesses, individuals, and society as a whole (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/public-private-partnerships). 
Finally, WMO facilitates the Voluntary Cooperation Programme (VCP), which focuses on meeting urgent needs of Members through direct financing, small grants and transfer of expertise and technology (https://old.wmo.int/extranet/pages/prog/dra/vcp_en.php).

matrix_cell_text_full: The OECD derives its mandate from the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which established OECD as an intergovernmental organisation with 38 member countries, to stimulate economic progress and world tradem (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Specifically, Article 1 of the Convention defines the aims and objectives of OECD, and Article 2 outlines the functions and activities of OECD (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Additionally, OECD’s rules of procedure, rule 18 on the functions of the OECD secretariat, states that the secretariat shall assist the Council and its subsidiary bodies in carrying out their work and shall perform any other tasks entrusted to it by the Council (https://www.oecd.org/legal/Rules%20of%20Procedure%20OECD%20Oct%202013.pdf). OECD’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions, agreements, recommendations, etc adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Council, the Ministerial Council, and the committees (https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for OECD’s work and policy advice, as well as the cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. OECD’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international standards and frameworks, such as the Common Reporting Standard (https://www.oecd.org/tax/automatic-exchange/common-reporting-standard/), the Base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS) (https://www.oecd.org/tax/beps/about/), which provide further legal and technical frameworks for the OECD.

matrix_cell_text_full: OECD collaborates with various organizations to promote economic co-operation and development. It maintains relations with the European Communities, established by the Treaties of Paris and Rome of 18th April, 1951, and 25th March, 1957, as defined in Supplementary Protocol No. 1 to the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD Convention), article 13 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). It also enters into agreements with Members, non-member States and international organizations, as provided for in OECD Convention, article 5 (c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Additionally, OECD participates in the activities of other international organizations or institutions, such as the UN, the World Bank, the IMF, and the WTO, in a manner consistent with its obligations, as stated in OECD Convention, article 1 (c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). It also contributes to the economic development of both Member and non-member countries in the process of economic development, by appropriate means and, in particular, by the flow of capital to those countries, as agreed in OECD Convention, article 2 (e) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Moreover, OECD supports the further expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis, as one of the most important factors favouring the economic development of countries and the improvement of international economic relations, as affirmed in OECD Convention, article 1 (c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf).

The WBG derives its mandate from the Articles of Agreement, Conventions, or equivalent governance documents of its five constituent institutions: the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), the International Development Association (IDA), the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), and the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). matrix_cell_text_full: The objectives of the WBG are established in the Articles of Agreement and Conventions of its constituent institutions (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). The IBRD Articles of Agreement (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/722361541184234501/IBRDArticlesOfAgreement-English.pdf) state that the WBG through IBRD aims to assist in the reconstruction and development of territories of members by facilitating the investment of capital for productive purposes, promoting private foreign investment by means of guarantees or participations in loans and other investments, and supplementing private investment by providing finance for productive purposes out of its own capital, funds raised by it and its other resources (Article I, Section 1). As specified in the IDA Articles of Agreement (https://ida.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/ida-articlesofagreement.pdf), the WBG through IDA aims to promote economic development, increase productivity and thus raise standards of living in the less-developed areas of the world by providing finance to projects and programs that contribute to the economic or social development of the members whose per capita income is low, and to those members in the opinion of the Association are not able to borrow from the IBRD on suitable terms (Article I, Section 1). The WBG through the IFC Articles of Agreement (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/6a4a091b83577eb35e881dbf9016c5c3-0330032020/original/IFCArticlesOfAgreement.pdf) aims to further economic development by encouraging the growth of productive private enterprise in member countries, particularly in the less-developed areas, by assisting in financing the establishment, improvement and expansion of private productive enterprises, and by stimulating and helping to create conditions conducive to the flow of private capital, domestic and foreign, into productive investment in member countries (Article I, Section 1). According to the MIGA Convention (https://www.miga.org/sites/default/files/archive/Documents/miga_convention_november_2010.pdf), the WBG through MIGA aims to encourage the flow of investments for productive purposes among member countries, and in particular to developing member countries, by providing guarantees against non-commercial risks in respect of investments in member countries, by establishing and operating a trust fund to provide technical assistance to member countries in connection with the promotion of foreign investment, and by exercising such other incidental powers as shall be necessary or desirable in the furtherance of its objective (Article 2, Section 1). Lastly, the WBG through the ICSID Convention (https://icsid.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/ICSID%20Convention%20English.pdf) aims to provide facilities for conciliation and arbitration of investment disputes between contracting states and nationals of other contracting states, and to bring together parties who have agreed to use such facilities, in order to facilitate the settlement of such disputes and to contribute to the development of international law on investments (Article 1, Section 2).

matrix_cell_text_full: The World Bank Group executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a World Bank Group Strategy adopted in 2013, based on the principles of country ownership, evidence-based solutions, and global and regional integration (https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/16093/32824_ebook.pdf?sequence=4&isAllowed=y). Secondly, a World Bank Group Evolution Roadmap that outlines the key actions and reforms to implement the WBG Strategy and enhance the WBG's effectiveness and efficiency (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/evolution-roadmap). This roadmap, endorsed by the Board of Governors in 2020, focuses on four pillars: (i) strengthening country platforms and partnerships, (ii) enhancing the WBG's financial and operational capacity, (iii) improving the WBG's business model and internal processes, and (iv) fostering a culture of innovation and learning. Thirdly, a set of thematic and sector strategies that provide the strategic framework and guidance for the WBG's engagement in specific areas of development, such as gender, climate change, fragility and conflict, human capital, infrastructure, and private sector development. These strategies are aligned with the WBG Strategy and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and are informed by global knowledge and evidence (https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/sdgs-2030-agenda). In addition, the WBG prepares Country Partnership Frameworks (CPFs) and Regional Partnership Frameworks (RPFs) that define the WBG's support to individual countries and regions, based on their development priorities, challenges, and opportunities. These frameworks are developed in consultation with the governments, civil society, and other stakeholders, and are aligned with the WBG Strategy and the country's own development strategy (https://www.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/country-strategies). The WBG also maintains various initiatives, platforms, and funds that provide the operational and financial instruments for addressing specific development challenges and opportunities (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/what-we-do/brief/initiatives-platforms-and-funds) while engaging in partnerships, coalitions, and networks that provide the collaborative framework for enhancing the impact and effectiveness of the WBG's interventions, leveraging the comparative advantages and resources of different actors, and addressing cross-cutting issues such as governance, data, and innovation (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/partners).

The IMF mainly derives its mandate from its Articles of Agreement, which is a treaty that establishes the legal framework and objectives of the Fund. The Articles of Agreement were adopted at the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944, and entered into force in December 1945 (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/pam/pam45/pdf/chap1.pdf). The Articles of Agreement have been amended several times to reflect the changes in the global economic and financial system. The most recent amendment, which became effective in January 2016, was aimed at enhancing the representation and voice of emerging and developing countries in the Fund’s governance (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf).
The Articles of Agreement define the obligations and rights of the Fund and its members, as well as the procedures and principles for the Fund’s operations and transactions. In addition to the Articles of Agreement, the Fund’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions of the Board of Governors, the decisions of the Executive Board, the agreements with other international organizations, and the jurisprudence of the Administrative Tribunal (https://www.imf.org/external/imfat/report.htm).

matrix_cell_text_full: The IMF implements its objectives through several strategies. The IMF’s capacity development strategy is reviewed every five years to ensure its relevance and effectiveness (https://www.imf.org/-/media/Files/Publications/PP/2022/English/PPEA2022056.ashx). The latest review, conducted in 2023, reaffirmed the two main objectives of increasing the impact and efficiency of capacity development, and proposed several recommendations to achieve them. The review also highlighted the importance of integrating capacity development with surveillance and lending, tailoring and modernizing delivery, enhancing internal and external coordination and communication, and improving management processes and systems. The IMF’s capacity development strategy is guided by the principles and priorities set out in document IMF/18/4/Rev.1 (https://www.imf.org/~/media/Files/Publications/PP/2018/pp021518cd-strategy-review.ashx). The IMF’s surveillance strategy is also reviewed periodically to adapt to the changing global environment and the needs of the membership. The most recent review, completed in 2019, focused on enhancing the quality, traction, and evenhandedness of surveillance, and identified four priority areas for action: strengthening the analysis of macro-financial linkages, governance and corruption, external sector assessments, and policy trade-offs and spillovers. The IMF’s surveillance strategy is based on the principles and modalities specified in document IMF/19/68/Rev.1 (https://www.imf.org/~/media/Files/Publications/PP/2019/PP041719-2018-Review-of-Program-Design-and-Conditionality.ashx). The IMF’s lending strategy is designed to help members restore macroeconomic stability, foster growth and reduce poverty, and safeguard the stability of the international monetary system. The IMF’s lending strategy is informed by regular reviews of its lending policies and facilities, as well as the lessons learned from its program experience. The latest review, conducted in 2019, assessed the adequacy and effectiveness of the Fund’s lending toolkit, and proposed some modifications and enhancements to better meet the diverse needs of the membership. The IMF’s lending strategy is governed by the rules and procedures established in document IMF/19/69/Rev.1 (https://www.imf.org/~/media/Files/Publications/PP/2019/PP041719-2018-Review-of-Program-Design-and-Conditionality.ashx).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to Article II f the IHO Convention (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf), the International Hydrographic Organization's objectives cover several key areas: promoting the use of hydrography for the safety of navigation and all other marine purposes and raising global awareness of the importance of hydrography (Object a); improving global coverage, availability and quality of hydrographic data, information, products and services and facilitating access to such data, information, products and services (Object b); improving global hydrographic capability, capacity, training, science and techniques (Purpose, Object c); establishing and enhancing the development of international standards for hydrographic data, information, products, services and techniques and achieving the greatest possible uniformity in the use of these standards (Object d); giving authoritative and timely guidance on all hydrographic matters to States and international organizations (Object e); facilitating coordination of hydrographic activities among the Member States (Object f); and enhancing cooperation on hydrographic activities among States on a regional basis (Object g). These objectives enable the Organization to fulfil its vision of being the authoritative, worldwide hydrographic body that actively engages all coastal and interested states to advance maritime safety and efficiency and supports the protection and sustainable use of the marine environment.

The IHO collaborates with various organisations to achieve its objectives. It engages with its 99 Member States and other stakeholders through the Assembly (https://iho.int/en/iho-welcomes-99th-member-state). The IHO enjoys observer status in the United Nations and is particularly active in a number of its subordinate organisations, most notably the International Maritime
Organisation (IMO) and the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC) (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/Member%20States/Attachment_1-Brief_info_about_the_IHO.pdf). Additionally, the IHO supports the implementation of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 14 on Life Below Water, by providing hydrographic data and information for safe, secure and sustainable use of the oceans (https://legacy.iho.int/mtg_docs/circular_letters/english/2017/Cl39.pdf). It also cooperates with other UN specialized agencies and programmes, such as IMO, IOC, UNEP, UNDP, and WMO, and other organizations, such as ISA, ITLOS, IALA, and ICG/IOC, addressing shared hydrographic and oceanographic issues (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/Work_Programme_for_2022.pdf). Moreover, the IHO contributes to the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development (2021-2030) (https://iho.int/en/the-un-ocean-decade-and-the-iho-join-forces-to-change-the-gender-climate-in-hydrography), offering expertise and standards for ocean mapping and observation, as acknowledged in UN resolution 72/73, paragraph 14 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N17/421/90/PDF/N1742190.pdf?OpenElement).

It engages with its 99 Member States and other stakeholders through the Assembly (https://iho.int/en/iho-welcomes-99th-member-state). The IHO enjoys observer status in the United Nations and is particularly active in a number of its subordinate organisations, most notably the International Maritime
Organisation (IMO) and the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC) (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/Member%20States/Attachment_1-Brief_info_about_the_IHO.pdf). Additionally, the IHO supports the implementation of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 14 on Life Below Water, by providing hydrographic data and information for safe, secure and sustainable use of the oceans (https://legacy.iho.int/mtg_docs/circular_letters/english/2017/Cl39.pdf). It also cooperates with other UN specialized agencies and programmes, such as IMO, IOC, UNEP, UNDP, and WMO, and other organizations, such as ISA, ITLOS, IALA, and ICG/IOC, addressing shared hydrographic and oceanographic issues (https://iho.int/uploads/user/About%20IHO/Work_Programme_for_2022.pdf). Moreover, the IHO contributes to the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development (2021-2030) (https://iho.int/en/the-un-ocean-decade-and-the-iho-join-forces-to-change-the-gender-climate-in-hydrography), offering expertise and standards for ocean mapping and observation, as acknowledged in UN resolution 72/73, paragraph 14 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N17/421/90/PDF/N1742190.pdf?OpenElement).

matrix_cell_text_full: ICES derives its mandate from the 1964 Convention for The International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/who-we-are/Documents/ICES_Convention_1964.pdf). This Convention established ICES as a leading multidisciplinary scientific forum for the exchange of information and ideas on all aspects of marine sciences pertaining to the North Atlantic, including the adjacent Baltic Sea and North Sea. Specifically, Article 1 of the Convention defines the duty of ICES, which includes promoting and encouraging research and investigations for the study of the sea, particularly those related to the living resources thereof while Article 2 outlines that the Council shall be concerned with the Atlantic Ocean and its adjacent seas, and primarily concerned with the North Atlantic. Additionally, ICES's jurisdiction is influenced by the decisions adopted by its principal decision and policy-making body, the Council (https://www.ices.dk/community/groups/Pages/COUNCIL.aspx). The Council comprises a President and two delegates appointed by each of the 20 Member Countries. ICES's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international cooperation agreements (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/global-cooperation/Pages/Cooperation-agreements.aspx). These agreements provide further legal frameworks for ICES's jurisdiction over specific marine issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: ICES executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, ICES has a Strategic Plan (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/strategicplan/Pages/default.aspx) that defines its direction and priorities relating to science, data, and advice, and to develop the capacity needed to fulfill this commitment. This plan is supported by a Science Plan and an Advisory Plan (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/how-we-work/Pages/Our-strategy.aspx). The Science Plan highlights seven interrelated scientific priorities and how ICES network will address them. Secondly, ICES is a leading multidisciplinary scientific forum for the exchange of information and ideas on all aspects of marine sciences. It promotes, encourages, develops, and coordinates marine research through data sharing (https://www.ices.dk/data/dataset-collections/Pages/default.aspx). It also publishes and disseminates results of research and provides non-biased, non-political scientific advice to member nation governments and international regulatory commissions (https://www.ices.dk/Science/publications/Pages/Home.aspx). Thirdly, ICES has a collection of helpful guides and policies that help understand how to work with data, and how ICES receives and outputs data (https://www.ices.dk/data/guidelines-and-policy/Pages/default.aspx). It also has a system of committees, more than 100 working groups, symposia, and an Annual Science Conference (https://ices-library.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/33403040). Finally, ICES is committed to building a foundation of science around one key challenge: integrated ecosystem understanding of marine ecosystems. ICES advances this through the coordination of oceanic and coastal monitoring and research, and advises international commissions and governments on marine policy and management issues (https://www.ices.dk/sites/pub/CM%20Doccuments/2001/GEN/gen0201.pdf).

This plan is supported by a Science Plan and an Advisory Plan (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/how-we-work/Pages/Our-strategy.aspx). The Science Plan highlights seven interrelated scientific priorities and how ICES network will address them. Secondly, ICES is a leading multidisciplinary scientific forum for the exchange of information and ideas on all aspects of marine sciences. It promotes, encourages, develops, and coordinates marine research through data sharing (https://www.ices.dk/data/dataset-collections/Pages/default.aspx). It also publishes and disseminates results of research and provides non-biased, non-political scientific advice to member nation governments and international regulatory commissions (https://www.ices.dk/Science/publications/Pages/Home.aspx). Thirdly, ICES has a collection of helpful guides and policies that help understand how to work with data, and how ICES receives and outputs data (https://www.ices.dk/data/guidelines-and-policy/Pages/default.aspx). It also has a system of committees, more than 100 working groups, symposia, and an Annual Science Conference (https://ices-library.figshare.com/ndownloader/files/33403040). Finally, ICES is committed to building a foundation of science around one key challenge: integrated ecosystem understanding of marine ecosystems. ICES advances this through the coordination of oceanic and coastal monitoring and research, and advises international commissions and governments on marine policy and management issues (https://www.ices.dk/sites/pub/CM%20Doccuments/2001/GEN/gen0201.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full:
IPBES derives its mandate from the 2010 Busan Outcome document (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/3115), which was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly resolution 65/162 on 20 December 2010 and Decision 26/4 
of 24 February 2011. The first session of Plenary convened in Nairobi in 2011 to determine modalities 
and institutional arrangements for IPBES (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/3377) and a second session of Plenary in Panama in 2012 established IPBES as an independent intergovernmental body to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/history-establishment). Specifically, paragraph 4 of the Busan Outcome defines the objectives and functions of IPBES, and paragraph 5 outlines the operating principles and modalities of IPBES. Additionally, the IPBES rules of procedure, rule 2 on the functions of the IPBES secretariat (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2675), states the duties of the secretariat in servicing and supporting the sessions of the Plenary and other subsidiary bodies, and in performing other tasks entrusted to it by the Plenary. IPBES's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its Plenary, such as the IPBES work programme (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme), the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework), and the IPBES assessment process (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/18538#:~:text=An%20IPBES%20assessment%20is%20a,ensure%20legitimacy%2C%20relevance%20and%20credibility.). These resolutions and provisional documents provide guidance and direction for IPBES's activities and deliverables, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/24663). IPBES's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the Convention on Migratory Species (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for IPBES's jurisdiction over specific biodiversity and ecosystem services issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Resolution on the IPBES during second session of Plenary in 2012 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2674), the overarching objective of the IPBES platform is to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, long-term human well-being and sustainable development (Section I, Paragraph 1). matrix_cell_text_full: The IPBES Secretariat executes its defined objectives and functions via several strategies: firstly, a rolling work programme up to 2030 backed by Decision IPBES-7/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/27458) and based on requests, inputs and suggestions from relevant bodies under multilateral environmental agreements as well as governments and other stakeholders. The rolling work program aims to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, long-term human well-being and sustainable development. This work programme corresponds to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, including the Sustainable Development Goals (http://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/sustainable-development-goals/), the biodiversity-related conventions and other biodiversity and ecosystem service processes (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). It initially focuses on three topics: the interlinkages between biodiversity and other relevant issues reflected in the 2030 Agenda, the determinants of transformative change, and the tools and solutions for conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). Secondly, a biennial budget and work programme, approved by the Plenary, detail the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each deliverable of the work programme (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). The current budget and work programme for 2022-2023 is based on the priorities identified by the Plenary and the available resources, as outlined in decision IPBES-8/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/102793). It also supports the development and use of policy support tools and methodologies, such as the IPBES online catalogue of policy support tools and methodologies (https://www.ipbes.net/catalogue-policy-support-tools-and-methodologies), the IPBES guide on the production and integration of assessments from and across all scales (https://www.ipbes.net/guide-production-assessments), and the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework). Finally, various assessments, task forces, expert groups, and platforms provide an evidence base for informing policy and decision-making, addressing the state of knowledge on the interactions between human societies and the natural world, the drivers and impacts of biodiversity change, and the options and pathways for achieving conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/104403). Some of the key assessments include the global assessment report on biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/global-assessment), the assessment report on invasive alien species (https://www.ipbes.net/ias), the assessment report on the sustainable use of wild species (https://www.ipbes.net/sustainable-use-assessment), and the assessment report on the diverse conceptualization of multiple values of nature and its benefits (https://files.ipbes.net/ipbes-web-prod-public-files/downloads/IPBES-4-INF-13_EN.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The IPCC derives its mandate from the Decisions and Resolutions of its parent organisations, WMO and UNEP, which established the IPCC in 1988 as an intergovernmental body to assess the scientific information on climate change and its impacts, and to formulate response strategies for the management of the climate change issue. Specifically, the WMO Executive Council Resolution 4 (EC-XL) (https://archive.ipcc.ch/docs/WMO_resolution4_on_IPCC_1988.pdf) defined the initial terms of reference and objectives of the IPCC. The IPCC's mandate was subsequently updated and refined by various resolutions and decisions of the governing bodies of WMO and UNEP, as well as by the IPCC itself, to reflect the evolving needs and challenges of the climate change issue. Over the years, key resolutions and decisions have shaped the IPCC's mandate including the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) (https://unfccc.int/files/essential_background/background_publications_htmlpdf/application/pdf/conveng.pdf); the IPCC Principles Governing IPCC Work (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/09/ipcc-principles.pdf), which were adopted by the IPCC at its 14th Session in 1988 and approved by the WMO Executive Council and the UNEP Governing Council, and which define the IPCC's organisation, procedures, functions, and products; and the IPCC Procedures (https://www.ipcc.ch/documentation/procedures/), which were adopted by the IPCC at various sessions and approved by the WMO Executive Council and the UNEP Governing Council, and which provide detailed rules and guidelines for the IPCC's work, such as the preparation, review, approval, and publication of its reports, the election of its bureau and chair, and the participation of experts and observers. The IPCC's jurisdiction is also influenced by the requests and guidance received from the UNFCCC and other relevant bodies, which provide the policy context and demand for the IPCC's assessments and products (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2021/07/AR6_FS_What_is_IPCC.pdf). The IPCC's mandate is also supported by the scientific community and the public, which provide the knowledge base and the legitimacy for the IPCC's work (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/).

As defined in Paragraph 2 of Resolution 4 (EC-XL) of the WMO Executive Council (https://archive.ipcc.ch/docs/WMO_resolution4_on_IPCC_1988.pdf), the IPCC's objectives include the following main tasks:
(1) Assessing the scientific information that is related to the various components of the climate change issue, such as emissions of major greenhouse gases and modification of the Earth's radiation balance resulting therefrom, and the environmental and socio-economic consequences of climate change; (2) Formulating realistic response strategies for the management of the climate change issue; (3) Providing scientific and socio-economic information and advice, initially for the development and negotiations of a UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and after its entry into force, to continue to work closely with the UNFCCC and provide scientific, technical and socio-economic information and advice; and (4) Reporting on its activities to the governing bodies of WMO and UNEP and communicating the results of the assessments broadly. These tasks enable the IPCC to fulfil its role as an intergovernmental panel on climate change that provides authoritative and comprehensive assessments of the current state of knowledge on climate change and its potential impacts.

The IPCC operates through three Working Groups (WGs) and a Task Force on National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (TFI), each supported by a Technical Support Unit (TSU) (https://www.ipcc.ch/working-groups/). The WGs assess the scientific literature on the physical science basis of climate change (WG I), the impacts, adaptation and vulnerability (WG II), and the mitigation of climate change (WG III). The TFI develops and refines methodologies for the estimation and reporting of greenhouse gas emissions and removals. The IPCC also produces reports (https://www.ipcc.ch/reports/) in forms of Special Reports, Methodology Reports, Technical Papers and Synthesis Reports like AR6 reports (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/syr/downloads/report/IPCC_AR6_SYR_SPM.pdf) on cross-cutting topics. The IPCC develops its work programme based on the requests and guidance from its member governments and observer organizations and the work programme is reviewed and approved by the IPCC Plenary, which is the main decision-making body of the IPCC (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/structure/). The IPCC budget is funded by voluntary contributions from its member governments and other organizations. The budget covers the operational costs of the IPCC Secretariat, the Technical Support Units, and the travel and meeting expenses of the IPCC Bureau members, authors, reviewers, and other experts involved in the IPCC work. The budget is prepared by the IPCC Secretariat in consultation with the IPCC Bureau and the Technical Support Units, and is submitted to the IPCC Plenary for approval for each assessment cycle, which typically lasts six to seven years. The budget is subject to an annual audit by an external auditor. The budget cycle is also aligned with the calendar year (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/decision_p35_budget.pdf). In addition, the IPCC Scholarship Programme provides funding for young scientists from developing countries to pursue studies on climate change (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/scholarship/).
