matrix_cell_text_full: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) collaborates with key organizations to support climate change governance. It liaises with the United Nations (UN), implementing a relationship agreement effective since its establishment in 1988 (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2021/07/AR6_FS_What_is_IPCC.pdf), as per the UN's mandate to provide policymakers with regular assessments of the scientific basis of climate change, its impacts, future risks, and adaptation and mitigation options. Similarly, IPCC maintains a relationship with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), providing vital scientific information to limit climate change and establish a strong link between sustainable economic development, climate change, and vulnerability (https://www.undp.org/blog/five-key-takeaways-latest-ipcc-report). Additionally, IPCC supports the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) by assessing the scientific literature and providing vital scientific information to the climate change process (https://unfccc.int/topics/science/workstreams/cooperation-with-the-ipcc/background-cooperation-with-the-ipcc). It also services the Conference of the Parties (COP) and the Subsidiary Body for Scientific and Technological Advice (SBSTA) (https://unfccc.int/process/bodies/subsidiary-bodies/sbsta), by preparing related reports within its mandate. Moreover, IPCC facilitates the assessment process through its Task Force on Greenhouse Gas Inventories, carrying out important work on methodologies for estimating and reporting GHG emissions (https://www.ipcc.ch/working-group/tfi/).

matrix_cell_text_full: The WTO derives its mandate from the Marrakesh Agreement Establishing the World Trade Organization (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf), which entered into force on 1 January 1995 and established the WTO as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/agrmntseries2_gatt_e.pdf). It operates a non-discriminatory trading system that spells out the rights and obligations of its members (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/inbrief_e/inbr_e.htm). The WTO agreements, which are the result of negotiations, cover a wide range of activities including agriculture, textiles and clothing, banking, telecommunications, government purchases, industrial standards and product safety, food sanitation regulations, intellectual property, and more (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/fact2_e.htm). The WTO’s strategic plans are largely the outcome of negotiations between the members. The current round of trade negotiations, known as the Doha Development Agenda, was launched in 2001 (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dda_e/dda_e.htm) to succeed the Uruguay Round negotiations (1986–94) (https://www.wto.org/gatt_docs/english/sulpdf/92160001.pdf). The WTO has expanded its scope to include cooperation with the UN system, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), and other international partners on a wide range of issues (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/mdg_e/global_partnership_e.htm). The WTO’s annual budget is contributed by its members based on their proportion of international trade (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/secre_e/budget_e.htm). The current budget proposal for the WTO Secretariat for the biennium 2024-2025 (https://docs.wto.org/dol2fe/Pages/SS/directdoc.aspx?filename=q:/WT/BFA/W643.pdf&Open=True) requests a modest increase of 7.4% in 2024 and 0.9% in 2025, amounting to CHF 211.76 million and CHF 213.7 million respectively. The WTO’s regulatory mechanisms are based on a number of simple, fundamental principles that run throughout all of its documents. These principles include trade without discrimination, national treatment (treating foreigners and locals equally), and the commitment to lowering trade barriers (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/utw_chap1_e.pdf).

The WTO agreements, which are the result of negotiations, cover a wide range of activities including agriculture, textiles and clothing, banking, telecommunications, government purchases, industrial standards and product safety, food sanitation regulations, intellectual property, and more (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/fact2_e.htm). The WTO’s strategic plans are largely the outcome of negotiations between the members. The current round of trade negotiations, known as the Doha Development Agenda, was launched in 2001 (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dda_e/dda_e.htm) to succeed the Uruguay Round negotiations (1986–94) (https://www.wto.org/gatt_docs/english/sulpdf/92160001.pdf). The WTO has expanded its scope to include cooperation with the UN system, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), and other international partners on a wide range of issues (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/mdg_e/global_partnership_e.htm). The WTO’s annual budget is contributed by its members based on their proportion of international trade (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/secre_e/budget_e.htm). The current budget proposal for the WTO Secretariat for the biennium 2024-2025 (https://docs.wto.org/dol2fe/Pages/SS/directdoc.aspx?filename=q:/WT/BFA/W643.pdf&Open=True) requests a modest increase of 7.4% in 2024 and 0.9% in 2025, amounting to CHF 211.76 million and CHF 213.7 million respectively. The WTO’s regulatory mechanisms are based on a number of simple, fundamental principles that run throughout all of its documents. These principles include trade without discrimination, national treatment (treating foreigners and locals equally), and the commitment to lowering trade barriers (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/utw_chap1_e.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The WTO cooperates with various institutions to promote trade and development. It works with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, based on the coherence mandate in the Marrakesh Decision of 1994 (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/marrakesh_decl_e.htm), to ensure consistency and complementarity of global economic policies (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/coher_e.htm). Likewise, the WTO collaborates with the United Nations (UN) and its specialized agencies, such as the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), under the arrangements for effective cooperation signed in 1995, to address the linkages between trade and other policy areas, as specified in Article V of the WTO Agreement (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf). Furthermore, the WTO partners with the International Trade Centre (ITC), a joint agency of the WTO and the UN, to provide trade-related technical assistance and capacity building for developing countries, as stated in the Doha Ministerial Declaration of 2001 (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/ddec_e.pdf). It also engages with the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), an international organization of national parliaments, to enhance the parliamentary dimension of the WTO and foster dialogue and accountability on trade issues, as agreed in the Memorandum of Understanding of 2018 (https://www.wto.org/english/forums_e/parliamentarians_e/parliamentarians_conf_e.htm). Additionally, the WTO participates in various collaborative initiatives with like-minded groups of members and other stakeholders, such as the Joint Statement Initiative on E-commerce (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/ecom_e/joint_statement_e.htm), the Joint Statement on Investment Facilitation (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/minist_e/mc12_e/briefing_notes_e/bfinvfac_e.htm#:~:text=Originally%20launched%20by%20a%20group,of%20the%20economy%20(goods%20and), and the COVAX Facility on COVID-19 vaccines (https://www.wto.org/english/news_e/roadmap_igo_01jun21_e.htm), to advance discussions and actions on emerging and pressing trade challenges.

matrix_cell_text_full: IOM derives its mandate from the Constitution of the International Organization for Migration (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf), which established IOM as an intergovernmental organization in the field of migration. The present Constitution is an incoporation of the Constitution of 19 October 1953 of the Intergovernmental Committee for European Migration (former designation of the Organization), which entered into force on 30 November 1954, the amendments adopted on 20 May 1987 by the 55th Session of the Council (Resolution no. 724), which entered into force on 14 November 1989, the amendments adopted on 24 November 1998 by the 76th Session of the Council (Resolution No. 997), which entered into force on 21 November 2013 and the amendments adopted on 28 October 2020 by the Fourth Special Session of the Council (Resolution No.1385), which entered into force on 28 October 2020 (https://publications.iom.int/books/constitution-and-basic-texts). Specifically, Article 1 of the Constitution defines the purposes and functions of IOM, and Article 2 outlines the procedures of membership. Articles IV-VIII of the Constitution establish procedures for Council, Administration, Headquarters, Finance, and Legal Status respectively. IOM's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Council, the Executive Committee, and the Standing Committee on Programmes and Finance (https://governingbodies.iom.int/standing-committee-programmes-and-finance). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for IOM's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. IOM's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration 9https://refugeesmigrants.un.org/sites/default/files/180711_final_draft_0.pdf), the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol (https://www.unhcr.org/sites/default/files/legacy-pdf/4ec262df9.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for IOM's jurisdiction over specific migration issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: According to Chapter I (Article 1) of the Constitution of the International Organization for Migration (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf), the defined purposes and functions of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) are: (1) To arrange the transfer of migrants who need special assistance or who lack adequate facilities to move to countries offering opportunities for orderly migration, (2) To provide migration services such as recruitment, selection, processing, language training, orientation, medical examination, placement, integration, and return migration, at the request and in agreement with the States concerned, (3) To provide a forum for cooperation and coordination on international migration issues, including studies, research and consultation, among States and other relevant actors, such as international organizations and civil society, (4) To cooperate closely with other international organizations concerned with migration, refugees and human resources, in order to facilitate the harmonization of international activities in these fields, and (5) To recognize the linkages between migration and other areas such as economic, social and cultural development, human rights, humanitarian assistance, and environmental sustainability.

matrix_cell_text_full: UNOPS derives its mandate from the 2010 General Assembly resolution 65/176 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n10/523/10/pdf/n1052310.pdf?token=YpwFrn88GVoLxo0p9e&fe=true) and Executive Board Decisions (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/executive-board/executive-board-documents) which reaffirmed the role of UNOPS as a central resource for the United Nations system in procurement and contracts management as well as in civil works and physical infrastructure development, including the related capacity development activities. The resolution also recognized the operational capacity of UNOPS to implement projects in support of peacebuilding, humanitarian and development operations. Specifically, paragraph 1 of the resolution defines the vision and mission of UNOPS, and paragraph 2 outlines the core values and principles of UNOPS. Additionally, UNOPS’s financial regulations and rules (https://content.unops.org/documents/libraries/policies-2020/executive-office-directives-and-instructions/financial-regulations-and-rules/en/EOD.ED-Financial-Regulations-and-Rules.pdf), regulation 1.01 on the scope and applicability, states that UNOPS shall operate in accordance with the policies and procedures established by the Executive Director in consultation with the Executive Board. UNOPS’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and directives adopted by its Executive Board, such as the strategic plan 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en), the organizational structure (https://content.unops.org/documents/libraries/policies-2020/executive-office-directives-and-instructions/organizational-principles-and-governance-model/en/EOI.ED-Organisational-Structure.pdf), and the anti-bribery and anti-corruption policy (https://content.unops.org/publications/EB-for-docs-not-going-in-library/UNOPS-Anti-Bribery-and-Anti-Corruption-Policy-December-2023.pdf). UNOPS’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/english_paris_agreement.pdf), and the New Urban Agenda (https://habitat3.org/wp-content/uploads/NUA-English.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for UNOPS’s jurisdiction over specific development issues and domains.

This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en), aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf). Secondly, UNOPS operates in accordance with a strict legislative framework comprised of Directives and Instructions (https://www.unops.org/policies). matrix_cell_text_full: UN-Women derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly resolution 64/289 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/64/289), which established UN-Women as a multi-tiered intergovernmental governance structure. Specifically, Paragraphs 48-56 define the Purpose and General Principles of UN-Women, Paragraphs 57-67 outline the structure of Governance of the Entity, Paragraphs 68-74 define the provisions for Administration and Human Resources, Paragraphs 75-80 define Financing operations, and 81-89 describe Transitional arrangements and Review of Implementation. Additionally, UN-Women's strategic plan (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2021/UN-Women-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025-brochure-en.pdf), which is approved by the Executive Board, states the vision, goals, and outcomes of UN-Women, and guides its operational activities and resource allocation. UN-Women's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Commission on the Status of Women (https://www.unwomen.org/en/csw), the Economic and Social Council (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/intergovernmental-support/economic-and-social-council#:~:text=The%20UN%20Economic%20and%20Social,bodies%2C%20particularly%20its%20functional%20commissions.), and the General Assembly (https://www.un.org/womenwatch/ianwge/resolutions/ga_res_by_topic.htm). These resolutions and decisions provide policy guidance and recommendations for UN-Women's work on gender equality and women's empowerment, as well as cooperation and coordination with other UN entities and stakeholders. UN Women's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2016/CEDAW-for-Youth.pdf), the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/CSW/PFA_E_Final_WEB.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/2030-agenda-for-sustainable-development), which provide further legal frameworks for UN Women's jurisdiction over specific gender issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: UN-Women derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly resolution 64/289 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/64/289), which established UN-Women as a multi-tiered intergovernmental governance structure. Specifically, Paragraphs 48-56 define the Purpose and General Principles of UN-Women, Paragraphs 57-67 outline the structure of Governance of the Entity, Paragraphs 68-74 define the provisions for Administration and Human Resources, Paragraphs 75-80 define Financing operations, and 81-89 describe Transitional arrangements and Review of Implementation. Additionally, UN-Women's strategic plan (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2021/UN-Women-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025-brochure-en.pdf), which is approved by the Executive Board, states the vision, goals, and outcomes of UN-Women, and guides its operational activities and resource allocation. UN-Women's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Commission on the Status of Women (https://www.unwomen.org/en/csw), the Economic and Social Council (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/intergovernmental-support/economic-and-social-council#:~:text=The%20UN%20Economic%20and%20Social,bodies%2C%20particularly%20its%20functional%20commissions.), and the General Assembly (https://www.un.org/womenwatch/ianwge/resolutions/ga_res_by_topic.htm). These resolutions and decisions provide policy guidance and recommendations for UN-Women's work on gender equality and women's empowerment, as well as cooperation and coordination with other UN entities and stakeholders. UN Women's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2016/CEDAW-for-Youth.pdf), the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/CSW/PFA_E_Final_WEB.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/2030-agenda-for-sustainable-development), which provide further legal frameworks for UN Women's jurisdiction over specific gender issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Report of the Secretary-General A/64/588 on the Comprehensive Proposal for the Composite Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n10/202/88/pdf/n1020288.pdf?token=g8uLB3qijkKMoS6hAv&fe=true), the objectives of the UN-Women are to (1) Work for the elimination of discrimination against women and girls; the empowerment of women; and the achievement of equality between women and men as partners and beneficiaries of development, human rights, humanitarian action and peace and security (Paragraph 5), (2) Lead and coordinate United Nations system efforts to ensure that commitments on gender equality and gender mainstreaming translate into action throughout the world (Paragraph 5), (3) Provide strong and coherent leadership in support of Member States’ priorities and efforts, building effective partnerships with civil society and other relevant actors (Paragraph 5), (4) Perform eight functions, as outlined in the Deputy Secretary-General’s papers of August 2007 and July 2008, which include providing substantive support to intergovernmental bodies, supporting national efforts through innovative and catalytic programming, undertaking advocacy on critical issues, supporting Member States in implementing and monitoring intergovernmental agreements, undertaking research and analytical work, leading and coordinating United Nations system strategies and actions, strengthening the accountability of the United Nations system, and monitoring and reporting on system-wide compliance with gender balance (Paragraphs 5-6), and (5) Add value by providing capacity to meet the need for a strong voice for women and girls at the global, regional and local levels; better support for Member States as they enhance the normative and policy environment for accelerating progress towards full equality for women and girls; assistance for national partners as they respond to critical gaps and challenges; and an enhanced United Nations response to the country-defined needs and priorities of women and girls (Paragraph 21).

matrix_cell_text_full: UN-Women executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the organization’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets (https://www.unwomen.org/en/un-women-strategic-plan-2022-2025). This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2021/UN-Women-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025-brochure-en.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/CSW/PFA_E_Final_WEB.pdf). Secondly, an integrated results and resources framework (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2021-02/irrf_updated%20on%2028%20may.pdf), devised by UN-Women and approved by the Executive Board, details the specific results that UN Women aims to achieve and their respective set of indicators and resources. The current framework for 2022-2025 is based on the needs and priorities of women and girls worldwide, as outlined in the Annex I of the UN Women Strategic Plan 2022–2025. It also monitors and reports on the progress and challenges of achieving gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls, a key aspect of the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/in-focus/women-and-the-sdgs). Thirdly, a biennial Integrated Budget and work plan, devised by the entity and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current Budget for 2024-2025 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2023-05/Integrated%20Budget%202024-2025%20final.pdf) is tailored to the needs and priorities of the countries and regions where UN-Women operates, as outlined in the integrated results and resources framework. It also maintains the Women Count programme (https://data.unwomen.org/women-count), a global initiative to improve the production, accessibility and use of gender data for evidence-based advocacy and policy-making. Finally, various partnerships, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the UN-Women Strategic Plan, addressing governance and participation in public life, women’s economic empowerment, ending violence against women and girls, and women, peace and security, humanitarian action, and disaster risk reduction (https://www.unwomen.org/en/partnerships/businesses-and-foundations/why-un-women).

matrix_cell_text_full: UN-Women executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the organization’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets (https://www.unwomen.org/en/un-women-strategic-plan-2022-2025). This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2021/UN-Women-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025-brochure-en.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/CSW/PFA_E_Final_WEB.pdf). Secondly, an integrated results and resources framework (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2021-02/irrf_updated%20on%2028%20may.pdf), devised by UN-Women and approved by the Executive Board, details the specific results that UN Women aims to achieve and their respective set of indicators and resources. The current framework for 2022-2025 is based on the needs and priorities of women and girls worldwide, as outlined in the Annex I of the UN Women Strategic Plan 2022–2025. It also monitors and reports on the progress and challenges of achieving gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls, a key aspect of the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/in-focus/women-and-the-sdgs). Thirdly, a biennial Integrated Budget and work plan, devised by the entity and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current Budget for 2024-2025 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2023-05/Integrated%20Budget%202024-2025%20final.pdf) is tailored to the needs and priorities of the countries and regions where UN-Women operates, as outlined in the integrated results and resources framework. It also maintains the Women Count programme (https://data.unwomen.org/women-count), a global initiative to improve the production, accessibility and use of gender data for evidence-based advocacy and policy-making. Finally, various partnerships, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the UN-Women Strategic Plan, addressing governance and participation in public life, women’s economic empowerment, ending violence against women and girls, and women, peace and security, humanitarian action, and disaster risk reduction (https://www.unwomen.org/en/partnerships/businesses-and-foundations/why-un-women).

matrix_cell_text_full: UN-Women collaborates with key institutions to advance gender equality and women's empowerment. It supports UN Member States as they set global standards for achieving gender equality, and works with governments and civil society to design laws, policies, programmes and services needed to ensure that the standards are effectively implemented and truly benefit women and girls worldwide (https://www.unwomen.org/en/about-us/about-un-women). Similarly, UN-Women liaises with the UN Development Programme (UNDP), implementing a relationship agreement effective since 1 January 2011, as per General Assembly resolution 64/289 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Executive%20Board/GA-Res-64-289-en-Adopted%20by%20the%20General%20Assembly%20on%202%20July%202010%20pdf.pdf), which established UN Women as a composite entity of the UN system, comprising the Division for the Advancement of Women, the International Research and Training Institute for the Advancement of Women, the Office of the Special Adviser on Gender Issues and Advancement of Women, and the United Nations Development Fund for Women (Paragraph 53). Additionally, UN-Women facilitates linkages and influences between women’s lived experiences and efforts with regional intergovernmental policy and programme processes, and leverages spaces for women leaders to directly engage regional institutions, participate in mediation and other conflict resolution and peace initiatives (https://africa.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/peace-and-security_africa). It also services the Commission on the Status of Women (CSW) (https://www.unwomen.org/en/csw#:~:text=The%20Commission%20on%20the%20Status,II)%20of%2021%20June%201946.) with its mandate in Economic and Social Council resolution 11(II) of 21 June 1946(https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3845514/files/E_2ndsess-_Resolutions-EN.pdf?ln=en) by preparing related reports. Moreover, UN-Women maintains a relationship with the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) (https://www.ohchr.org/en/treaty-bodies/cedaw#:~:text=The%20Committee%20on%20the%20Elimination,rights%20from%20around%20the%20world.), providing substantive support and servicing its sessions, with its functions detailed in the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/ProfessionalInterest/cedaw.pdf) and its Optional Protocol.

matrix_cell_text_full: WIPO derives its mandate from the Convention Establishing the World Intellectual Property Organization (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833), which established WIPO as a specialized agency of the United Nations. Specifically, Article 3 of the Convention states the objectives of the Organization; Article 4 lists the functions of the Organization; Article 5 specifies the conditions for membership in the Organization, which are open to any State that is a member of any of the Unions, or a member of the United Nations or related agencies, or invited by the General Assembly; Article 6 defines the composition, functions, voting, and procedures of the General Assembly, which is the supreme organ of the Organization consisting of the States party to this Convention that are members of any of the Unions; Article 8 defines the composition, functions, voting, and procedures of the Coordination Committee, which is an organ of the Organization consisting of the States party to this Convention that are members of the Executive Committees of the Paris Union and the Berne Union, or both; Article 11 outlines the sources and management of the finances of the Organization; Article 12 grants the Organization the legal capacity necessary for the fulfillment of its objectives and the exercise of its functions; and Artice 13 authorizes the Organization to establish working relations and cooperate with other intergovernmental organizations, and to make suitable arrangements for consultation and cooperation with international and national non-governmental organizations, in matters within its competence. WIPO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the General Assembly, the Coordination Committee (https://www.wipo.int/meetings/en/topic.jsp?group_id=104), and the Assemblies of the Unions (https://www.wipo.int/about-wipo/en/assemblies/#:~:text=Assemblies%20of%20WIPO%20%E2%80%93%202024,July%209%20to%2017%2C%202024.). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for WIPO's activities and programs, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. WIPO's mandate is also supported by the administration of various international treaties and agreements, such as the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/287556), the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283693), and the Marrakesh Treaty to Facilitate Access to Published Works for Persons Who Are Blind, Visually Impaired or Otherwise Print Disabled (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/301019), which provide further legal frameworks for WIPO's jurisdiction over specific intellectual property issues and domains.

Specifically, Article 3 of the Convention states the objectives of the Organization; Article 4 lists the functions of the Organization; Article 5 specifies the conditions for membership in the Organization, which are open to any State that is a member of any of the Unions, or a member of the United Nations or related agencies, or invited by the General Assembly; Article 6 defines the composition, functions, voting, and procedures of the General Assembly, which is the supreme organ of the Organization consisting of the States party to this Convention that are members of any of the Unions; Article 8 defines the composition, functions, voting, and procedures of the Coordination Committee, which is an organ of the Organization consisting of the States party to this Convention that are members of the Executive Committees of the Paris Union and the Berne Union, or both; Article 11 outlines the sources and management of the finances of the Organization; Article 12 grants the Organization the legal capacity necessary for the fulfillment of its objectives and the exercise of its functions; and Artice 13 authorizes the Organization to establish working relations and cooperate with other intergovernmental organizations, and to make suitable arrangements for consultation and cooperation with international and national non-governmental organizations, in matters within its competence. WIPO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the General Assembly, the Coordination Committee (https://www.wipo.int/meetings/en/topic.jsp?group_id=104), and the Assemblies of the Unions (https://www.wipo.int/about-wipo/en/assemblies/#:~:text=Assemblies%20of%20WIPO%20%E2%80%93%202024,July%209%20to%2017%2C%202024.). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for WIPO's activities and programs, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. WIPO's mandate is also supported by the administration of various international treaties and agreements, such as the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/287556), the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283693), and the Marrakesh Treaty to Facilitate Access to Published Works for Persons Who Are Blind, Visually Impaired or Otherwise Print Disabled (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/301019), which provide further legal frameworks for WIPO's jurisdiction over specific intellectual property issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Convention Establishing the World Intellectual Property Organization (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833), WIPO's objectives encompass two main aspects: promoting the protection of intellectual property throughout the world (Article 3(i)) and ensuring administrative cooperation among the Unions (Article 3(ii)). To achieve these objectives, the Organization, through its appropriate organs, has several functions, such as: developing measures to facilitate the efficient protection of intellectual property and to harmonize national legislation in this field (Article 4(i)); performing the administrative tasks of the Paris Union, the Berne Union, and other international agreements related to intellectual property (Article 4(ii)); encouraging the conclusion of international agreements to promote the protection of intellectual property; offering legal-technical assistance to States requesting it (Article 4(iv)); assembling and disseminating information concerning the protection of intellectual property (Article 4(vi)); maintaining services facilitating the international protection of intellectual property (Article 4(vii)); and taking all other appropriate action in relation to the stated objectives (Article 4(viii)). These objectives and functions enable WIPO to contribute to better understanding and cooperation among States for their mutual benefit on the basis of respect for their sovereignty and equality, and to encourage creative activity in the industrial, scientific, literary or artistic fields (Preamble).

Firstly, a five-year Medium-Term Strategic Plan (MTSP), prepared by the Secretariat and noted by the Assemblies of WIPO, provides high-level strategic guidance for the corresponding Program and Budgets covered by the MTSP. This plan, applicable for 2022-2026 (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/wo_pbc_32/wo_pbc_32_3.pdf), outlines WIPO's vision, mission, strategic pillars, and foundation. Secondly, a biennial Program of Work and Budget, approved by the Assemblies of WIPO, details the expected results, performance indicators, and resources for each program and strategic goal. The current Program of Work and Budget for 2022-2023 (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo_pub_360_pb22_23.pdf) is based on the MTSP and reflects the priorities and needs of the Member States and stakeholders (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/wo_pbc_32/wo_pbc_32_3.pdf). It also supports the implementation of the WIPO Development Agenda, which consists of 45 recommendations to enhance the development dimension of WIPO's activities (https://www.wipo.int/export/sites/www/ip-development/en/agenda/docs/recommendations.pdf). Finally, various initiatives, platforms, and projects provide an operational framework for delivering WIPO's services and advancing its goals, such as WIPO Re:Search (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo_pub_gc_18.pdf), which facilitates research and development for neglected tropical diseases, malaria, and tuberculosis; WIPO IP and Gender Action Plan (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo-pub-rn2023-1-en-wipo-intellectual-property-ip-and-gender-action-plan-the-role-of-ip-in-support-of-women-and-girls.pdf), which aims to promote gender equality and women's empowerment in the IP ecosystem; and WIPO GREEN (https://www3.wipo.int/wipogreen/en/), which connects providers and seekers of green technologies and fosters innovation and diffusion of environmentally sound solutions.

UNFPA receives overall policy guidance from the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC). It reports to its governing body, the UNDP/UNFPA Executive Board, on administrative, financial and programme matters (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-un-system). The Programme of Action (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/programme_of_action_Web%20ENGLISH.pdf) defines the scope and objectives of UNFPA's work on population and development issues, with an emphasis on reproductive health and gender equality. UNFPA's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Resolution_A_RES_70_1_EN.pdf), the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/beijing-at-ten.pdf), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Statement_of_CEDAW.pdf), and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/ProfessionalInterest/crc.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for UNFPA's jurisdiction over specific population and development issues and domains.

It reports to its governing body, the UNDP/UNFPA Executive Board, on administrative, financial and programme matters (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-un-system). UNFPA's jurisdiction is also influenced by the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD), which was convened by the General Assembly in 1994 and adopted the Programme of Action 9https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/event-pdf/icpd_eng_2.pdf). The Programme of Action (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/programme_of_action_Web%20ENGLISH.pdf) defines the scope and objectives of UNFPA's work on population and development issues, with an emphasis on reproductive health and gender equality. The Programme of Action also provides a framework for cooperation and coordination with other UN entities, governments, civil society and other stakeholders. UNFPA's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Resolution_A_RES_70_1_EN.pdf), the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/beijing-at-ten.pdf), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Statement_of_CEDAW.pdf), and the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/ProfessionalInterest/crc.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for UNFPA's jurisdiction over specific population and development issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: The UN-Habitat executes its objectives via several strategies. Its programmes and initiatives are currently guided by a four-year Strategic Plan (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/documents/2019-09/strategic_plan_2020-2023.pdf), endorsed by the Committee of Permanent Representatives and approved by the UN-Habitat Assembly, which sets out the vision, mission, objective, domains of change, drivers of change, and organizational performance enablers of the organization. This plan, applicable for 2020-2023, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the New Urban Agenda, and other global frameworks (https://unhabitat.org/about-us/our-strategy). Some of the specific strategies in place for UN-Habitat to achieve its objectives and mandates according to the Strategic Plan include: (1) Refocusing its niche as the thought leader and go-to agency that sets the global discourse and agenda on sustainable urban development, (2) Aligning its work with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the New Urban Agenda, and other relevant global frameworks and commitments, (3) Delivering four domain-specific goals that address the key challenges and opportunities of urbanization: reduced spatial inequality and poverty, enhanced shared prosperity, strengthened climate action, and effective urban crises prevention and response, (4) Integrating cross-cutting themes such as social inclusion, resilience, and safety throughout its programmes and projects, (5) Strengthening its partnerships with various stakeholders, including national and local governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and media, and (6) Improving its organizational effectiveness by enhancing its governance, accountability, transparency, innovation, and resource mobilization.  According to the document, the estimated budget for the strategic plan for 2020-2023 is $1.2 billion, of which $500 million is expected to come from the regular budget and $700 million from extrabudgetary sources. The budget is based on the projected resource requirements for the implementation of the four domains of change, the drivers of change and the organizational performance enablers.

matrix_cell_text_full: The World Food Programme (WFP) derives its mandate from the General Assembly Resolution 2095 (XX) of 20 December 1965 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/2095(XX)), which extended the WFP on a continuing basis for as long as multilateral food aid is feasible and desirable, Resolution 1714 (XVI) of 19 December 1961 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/1714(XVI)), which established WFP as an experimental programme, and Resolution 3404 (XXX) of 28 November 1975 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/3404(XXX)), which named Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes oversight of WFP. In addition, pursuant to Resolution 50/8 of 1 November 1995 (https://documents.un.org/doc/resolution/gen/n95/257/30/img/n9525730.pdf?token=lBOUzh2cYTpOtGNhBZ&fe=true), the Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes (CFA) was reconstituted as the WFP Executive Board with effect from 1 Jan. 1996. The General Assembly Resolutions 1714 (XVI) and 2095 (XX) define the objectives and scope of WFP, and Resolution 50/8 outlines the structure and membership of the United Nations/FAO Intergovernmental Committee of the WFP, which is the governing body of the programme. Specifically, Article II of the General Regulations and Rules of the WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150) defines the purposes and functions of WFP; Article III outlines the cooperation of WFP with the United Nations and FAO and with other relevant agencies and organizations, and the modalities of such cooperation; Article IV specifies the location of the headquarters of WFP in Rome, Italy; Article V lists the organs of WFP, which are the Executive Board and the Secretariat, and their composition and functions; Article VI details the powers and functions of the Board; Article VII establishes the WFP Secretariat, headed by an Executive Director, and its organization and functions; Article VIII grants WFP legal capacity, drawing on the legal personality of the United Nations and FAO; Article IX sets the eligibility criteria for assistance from WFP, which include being a member of the United Nations or any specialized agency or the IAEA, or being a recipient of emergency food aid requested by the Secretary-General; and Article XIII governs the contributions to WFP, which shall be on a voluntary basis and may be in the form of commodities, cash, or acceptable services. WFP's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Intergovernmental Committee, the FAO Council, and the Economic and Social Council, which provide guidance and direction for WFP's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/about-board). WFP's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Rome Declaration on World Food Security (https://www.fao.org/3/w3548e/w3548e00.htm#adopt05), the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.wfp.org/sdgs), and the Agenda for Humanity (https://agendaforhumanity.org/stakeholder/291.html), which provide further legal frameworks for WFP's jurisdiction over specific food security and humanitarian issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: The World Food Programme (WFP) derives its mandate from the General Assembly Resolution 2095 (XX) of 20 December 1965 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/2095(XX)), which extended the WFP on a continuing basis for as long as multilateral food aid is feasible and desirable, Resolution 1714 (XVI) of 19 December 1961 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/1714(XVI)), which established WFP as an experimental programme, and Resolution 3404 (XXX) of 28 November 1975 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/3404(XXX)), which named Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes oversight of WFP. In addition, pursuant to Resolution 50/8 of 1 November 1995 (https://documents.un.org/doc/resolution/gen/n95/257/30/img/n9525730.pdf?token=lBOUzh2cYTpOtGNhBZ&fe=true), the Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes (CFA) was reconstituted as the WFP Executive Board with effect from 1 Jan. 1996. The General Assembly Resolutions 1714 (XVI) and 2095 (XX) define the objectives and scope of WFP, and Resolution 50/8 outlines the structure and membership of the United Nations/FAO Intergovernmental Committee of the WFP, which is the governing body of the programme. Specifically, Article II of the General Regulations and Rules of the WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150) defines the purposes and functions of WFP; Article III outlines the cooperation of WFP with the United Nations and FAO and with other relevant agencies and organizations, and the modalities of such cooperation; Article IV specifies the location of the headquarters of WFP in Rome, Italy; Article V lists the organs of WFP, which are the Executive Board and the Secretariat, and their composition and functions; Article VI details the powers and functions of the Board; Article VII establishes the WFP Secretariat, headed by an Executive Director, and its organization and functions; Article VIII grants WFP legal capacity, drawing on the legal personality of the United Nations and FAO; Article IX sets the eligibility criteria for assistance from WFP, which include being a member of the United Nations or any specialized agency or the IAEA, or being a recipient of emergency food aid requested by the Secretary-General; and Article XIII governs the contributions to WFP, which shall be on a voluntary basis and may be in the form of commodities, cash, or acceptable services. WFP's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Intergovernmental Committee, the FAO Council, and the Economic and Social Council, which provide guidance and direction for WFP's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/about-board). matrix_cell_text_full: The World Food Programme (WFP) executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan establishes the organization’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000132205), outlines the many ways for WFP, working in synergy with others, to most efficiently and effectively save and change lives. It is grounded within renewed global commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its associated Sustainable Development Goals 9https://www.wfp.org/publications/wfp-strategic-plan-2022-25). Secondly, a biennial Management Plan, presented to the Executive Board, details the projected operational needs, the provisional global implementation plan, the programme support and business operations budget, and the use of reserves and general fund. The current Management Plan for 2024-2026 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000151658) highlights the corporate budget required to implement WFP’s programme of work, based on the funding forecasts and prioritization criteria. It also outlines WFP’s key drivers of hunger, such as conflict, climate change, and economic shocks, and how WFP responds to them through various programmes, operations, and platforms (https://www.wfp.org/publications/wfp-management-plan-2024-2026). Thirdly, the Corporate Results Framework (CRF) 2022-2025 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000136871) guides the planning, implementation, monitoring, and reporting of WFP’s programmes towards the objectives identified in the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan. The CRF, supplemented by the policy on country strategic plans (CSPs) (https://www.wfp.org/publications/policy-country-strategic-plans), provides a performance and accountability framework that enables WFP to measure and demonstrate its response to humanitarian needs. In addition, the WFP has over 32 policies in effect under the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan. An update of the portfolio of policies is submitted annually and can be found as the “Compendium of Policies” on the Executive Board website (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000151657). Finally, various policies, frameworks, agreements, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the WFP Strategic Plan, addressing food security, nutrition, resilience, capacity strengthening, social protection, and innovation (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000132607).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNWTO derives its mandate from the Statutes of the World Tourism Organization (https://webunwto.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/imported_images/51970/unwtostatuteseng.pdf), which established UNWTO as a specialized agency of the United Nations. Specifically, Article 3 of the Statutes defines the aims and objectives of UNWTO, Articles 4-7 outlines the provisions for membership of the UNWTO, Article 8-24 define organizational structure and governance, and Articles 25-26 describe budgets and expenditures. Additionally, the General Rules of Procedure of UNWTO ((https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2019-11/130718basicdocumentsenweb.pdf) also govern the functioning and decision-making of UNWTO's governing bodies, namely the General Assembly, the Executive Council, and the regional commissions. The rules of procedure specify the composition, powers, duties, sessions, agenda, voting, languages, and other aspects of these bodies, as well as the role and responsibilities of the UNWTO secretariat. The rules of procedure are based on the Statutes of UNWTO, and can be amended by the General Assembly or the Executive Council, as appropriate. The rules of procedure also provide for the participation of other UNWTO members, such as associate members and affiliate members, as well as observers and guests, in the meetings and activities of UNWTO. UNWTO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the General Assembly, the Executive Council, and the regional commissions (https://www.unwto.org/unwto-general-assembly). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNWTO's policies and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. UNWTO's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Global Code of Ethics for Tourism (https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2019-10/gcetpassportglobalcodeen.pdf), the Convention on the Protection of Tourists (https://webunwto.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/imported_images/47266/6_report_on_the_convention_of_tourists_en_0.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwto.org/tourism-in-2030-agenda), which provide further legal frameworks for UNWTO's jurisdiction over specific tourism issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: The United Nations World Tourism Organization (UNWTO) executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, the UNWTO has a strategic plan that is directed towards governments of UNWTO Member States and aims to support and strengthen the capacity of National, regional, and local tourism Administrations (https://www.unwto.org/UNWTO-strategy). This strategic plan involves a sectorial analysis of tourism education and training, identifying weaknesses in the system as well as gaps between the educational offering and the real needs of the sector. The final product of this action is a strategic document containing plans and programmes in education and training at the national or regional level (https://www.unwto.org/UNWTO-strategy). Secondly, the UNWTO has a Programme of Work for 2024-2025, which is a wide-reaching plan built around clear priorities, including key pillars and landmarks (https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2023-10/A25_4_c_Draft_Programme_Work_2024_2025_rev1_En.pdf?VersionId=f87QHlfdEF31lDDrbrms82gFO2NCQZu5). This plan is aimed at restoring tourist confidence by developing and harmonizing minimum international standards, and providing sufficient guarantees for the protection of international tourists in the post COVID-19 world (https://www.unwto.org/international-code-for-the-protection-of-tourists). Thirdly, the UNWTO has established policy frameworks to effectively support the tourism sector at different levels: national, regional, and local (https://www.unwto.org/policy-destination-management). These policies focus on tourism policy and strategic planning, governance and vertical cooperation, and public-private partnerships. Finally, the UNWTO has instituted several collaborative initiatives. For example, it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the African Civil Aviation Commission (AFCAC) to promote sustainable tourism and the implementation of the Single African Air Transport Market (SAATM) (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-and-afcac-partner-around-air-connectivity-in-africa). It also has a partnership with Google to lead global tourism’s recovery through innovation, education, and market intelligence (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-and-google-launch-global-partnership-to-lead-tourism-recovery). The UNWTO's strategic plans and initiatives are typically aligned with global agendas such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, indicating a long-term perspective (https://www.unwto.org/reports/from-crisis-to-transformation/agenda-2030.html). The UNWTO also works with its members and partners on an ongoing basis to achieve its objectives (https://www.unwto.org/europe/partnerships).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNRISD derives its mandate from the Statutes of UNRISD (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n63/166/83/pdf/n6316683.pdf?token=yYyPtTVGKo5T95bmTP&fe=true), which established UNRISD as an autonomous research institute within the United Nations that undertakes multidisciplinary research and policy analysis on the social dimensions of contemporary development issues. Specifically, the Statutes defines the Purposes and general organization of the Institute (Articles 1-3); Administrative and financial arrangements (Articles 4-9); and Personnel arrangements (Articles 10-14). matrix_cell_text_full: The UNRISD pursues its objectives and mandates through several strategies: firstly, a five-year institutional strategy, developed through consultation with its stakeholders, defines the Institute’s vision, mission, research programmes, and expected results. The current strategy, applicable for 2021-2025 (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4A1D94EBE95DA31A802586D8004198E8/UNRISD-Strategy-2021-2025.pdf), focuses on overcoming inequalities and achieving a new eco-social contract. This plan aligns with the UN's Sustainable Development Goals and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The present strategy sets out five research programmes: Transformative Social Policy, Gender Justice and Development, Alternative Economies for Transformation, Environmental and Climate Justice, and Translating Research into Policy and Practice—Bonn Programme. UNRISD engages with its network and partners through a co-production process (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/about/outreach-unrisd-2023.pdf). The Institute is committed to comprehensive consultation with its stakeholders on where its research activities are directed, as well as how UNRISD conducts and communicates about its research (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/C393FC7BBDCA9A1B8025859D00490220/UNRISD-Institutional-Strategy-2021-2025-Consultation-Document-V1.2.pdf).  It also maintains the UNRISD Flagship Report, a key publication that synthesizes the Institute’s research and policy analysis on the social dimensions of contemporary development issues (https://www.un-ilibrary.org/content/books/9789290851332#:~:text=This%20UNRISD%20Flagship%20Report%20shows,are%20built%20in%20by%20design.). UNRISD receives no funding from the regular budget of the United Nations but depends entirely on voluntary contributions from national governments, multilateral donors, foundations and other sources and must fully mobilize all the financial resources necessary to cover the institutional and staff costs required to implement the UNRISD Strategy 2021–2025 ((https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4A1D94EBE95DA31A802586D8004198E8/UNRISD-Strategy-2021-2025.pdf). The underlying assumption in terms of delivering results, therefore, is that UNRISD will design and successfully implement a fundraising strategy that will diversify the Institute’s funding sources, and generate predictable, stable and increased revenues. Various institutional initiatives, collaborations, and regulatory mechanisms also provide an operational framework for implementing the Institute's objectives. For instance, the work programme of the UNRISD Bonn office aims to create new interagency collaborations and enhance synergies between research and learning activities (https://www.unbonn.org/UNRISD#:~:text=The%20work%20programme%20of%20the,and%20contributing%20to%20training%20and). The Institute also organises regular Seminar Series to provide a space for open, informed, and insightful conversation around contemporary issues of concern to social development research and policy (https://www.unrisd.org/en/activities/events).

matrix_cell_text_full: The BRS Secretariat derives its mandate from the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions, which established the BRS Secretariat as a joint secretariat serving the three conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Specifically, Article 16 of the Basel Convention (https://www.basel.int/Portals/4/Basel%20Convention/docs/text/BaselConventionText-e.pdf), Article 19 of the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf) and Article 20 of the Stockholm Convention (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf) define the functions and responsibilities of the BRS Secretariat, which include providing administrative, technical and legal support to the parties and their subsidiary bodies, as well as receiving and conveying information from and to the parties. Additionally, the memoranda of understanding between the conferences of the parties and the entities administering the secretariats of the conventions, namely the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-RC-COP.9-RC-9-14.En.pdf), clarify the institutional relationship between the parties and UNEP/FAO, including the delegation of authority, financial matters, reporting and programmatic cooperation. matrix_cell_text_full: The BRS Secretariat cooperates with key entities to support the sound management of chemicals and waste. It is administered by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), as per Article 16 of the Basel Convention (https://www.basel.int/Portals/4/Basel%20Convention/docs/text/BaselConventionText-e.pdf), Article 19 of the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf) and Article 20 of the Stockholm Convention (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf). It also implements memoranda of understanding with UNEP and FAO, clarifying the institutional relationship and responsibilities of the entities (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners2/CooperationWithPartners/tabid/2841/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Furthermore, the BRS Secretariat coordinates with other international bodies, such as the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM), the Minamata Convention on Mercury, the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, and the World Health Organization (WHO), to promote synergies and avoid duplication of efforts (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/MEAs/MinamataConvention/tabid/4083/language/en-US/Default.aspx). It also engages with various stakeholders, such as industry, civil society, academia and media, to raise awareness and mobilize resources for the implementation of the conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners2/CooperationWithPartners/tabid/2841/language/en-US/Default.aspx). It also coordinates with the International Seabed Authority (ISA), the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS), the Informal Consultative Process (ICP) on Oceans and the Law of the Sea, and the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/TechnicalAssistance/Partnerships/tabid/4900/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Furthermore, the BRS Secretariat engages with stakeholders, such as regional centres, non-governmental organizations, industry associations, and scientific institutions, to provide technical assistance, capacity building, and information exchange (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners2/CooperationWithPartners/tabid/2841/language/en-US/Default.aspx).

matrix_cell_text_full: The CBD derives its mandate from the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), which is the international legal instrument for "the conservation of biological diversity, the sustainable use of its components and the fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the utilization of genetic resources" that has been ratified by 196 nations (https://www.un.org/en/observances/biological-diversity-day/convention). Specifically, Article 1 of the Convention states the objectives of CBD, which are to conserve biological diversity, to use its components sustainably, and to share the benefits of genetic resources fairly and equitably; Article 23 establishes a Conference of the Parties, which shall be the supreme body of the convention and shall keep under review the implementation of the convention. It also specifies the functions, procedures and frequency of the meetings of the Conference of the Parties, and the participation of observers; Article 24 establishes the CBD Secretariat, which shall arrange for and service the meetings of the Conference of the Parties and perform other functions assigned to it by the convention or by any protocol. It also requires the Conference of the Parties to designate the secretariat from among the existing competent international organizations that have signified their willingness to carry out the secretariat functions; and Article 25 establishes a subsidiary body on scientific, technical and technological advice, which shall provide the Conference of the Parties and its other subsidiary bodies with timely advice relating to the implementation of the convention. The CBD's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations adopted by its governing bodies, including the Conference of the Parties (https://www.cbd.int/cop), the Subsidiary Body on Scientific, Technical and Technological Advice (https://www.cbd.int/sbstta), and the Subsidiary Body on Implementation (https://www.cbd.int/sbi). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for the CBD's work programmes and thematic areas, as well as cooperation and coordination with other conventions and organisations. The CBD's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various protocols and frameworks, such as the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (https://bch.cbd.int/protocol/#:~:text=The%20Cartagena%20Protocol%20on%20Biosafety%20to%20the%20Convention%20on%20Biological,diversity%2C%20taking%20also%20into%20account), the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-sharing (https://www.cbd.int/abs#:~:text=The%20Nagoya%20Protocol%20on%20Access%20to%20Genetic%20Resources%20and%20the,a%20fair%20and%20equitable%20way.), and the Post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/409e/19ae/369752b245f05e88f760aeb3/wg2020-05-l-02-en.pdf), which provide further legal instruments and targets for the CBD's jurisdiction over specific biodiversity issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: The CBD Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a post-2020 global biodiversity framework, adopted by the Conference of the Parties at its fifteenth meeting, provide the vision, mission, goals and targets for biodiversity conservation and sustainable use for the next decade, aligning with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Paris Agreement (https://www.cbd.int/doc/strategic-plan/Post2020/Bubb.pdf). This framework, based on extensive consultations and inputs from various stakeholders, build on the achievements and lessons learned from the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011-2020 and the Aichi Biodiversity Targets (https://www.cbd.int/doc/strategic-plan/2011-2020/Aichi-Targets-EN.pdf), as well as the current state of knowledge and science on biodiversity and ecosystem services. Secondly, a four-year medium-term programme of work, approved by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the activities, expected outcomes, indicators and budget of the Secretariat for the period of interest, in support of the implementation of the Convention and its Protocols (https://www.cbd.int/information/adm-fin). This programme of work is structured around six core functions of the Secretariat, namely: servicing meetings of the governing bodies and subsidiary bodies; facilitating implementation; providing policy advice and support; fostering communication, outreach and partnerships; managing information and knowledge; and ensuring sound management and administration, as detailed in Article 24 of the Convention document (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf). The programme of work also includes a results-based management framework and a resource mobilization strategy. The major source of funding for the CBD Secretariat is the General Trust Fund for the Convention on Biological Diversity (BY Trust Fund), which is funded from the assessed contributions of Parties to the CBD, based on the United Nations scales of assessment (https://www.cbd.int/convention/parties/contributions.shtml). In addition, various mechanisms, initiatives and partnerships provide a platform for cooperation and coordination among Parties, other Governments, international organizations, civil society, indigenous peoples and local communities, and the private sector, on various thematic and cross-cutting issues related to biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/programmes). Some of these include: the Clearing-House Mechanism (https://www.cbd.int/chm), which facilitates the exchange of information and technical and scientific cooperation; the Global Taxonomy Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/gti/default.shtml), which enhances taxonomic knowledge and capacity; the LifeWeb Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/undb/media/factsheets/undb-factsheet-lifeweb-en.pdf), which supports the establishment and management of protected areas; the Bio-Bridge Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/biobridge/), which fosters technical and scientific collaboration among Parties; the Global Partnership for Plant Conservation, which supports the implementation of the Global Strategy for Plant Conservation (https://www.cbd.int/gspc/default.shtml); and the Biodiversity for Development Initiative ( Biodiversity for Development Initiative), which promotes the integration of biodiversity into development policies and plans.

The Executive Secretary of the Secretariat is accountable to the Conference of the Parties for programme delivery and policy-related issues and to the Executive Director of UNEP for administrative and financial issues (https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/asg_cbd-2023-nv-english.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The CITES Secretariat derives its mandate from the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES-Convention-EN.pdf), which established CITES as an international agreement between governments to regulate wildlife trade. Specifically, Article XII of the Convention defines the functions of the Secretariat, which include arranging and servicing meetings of the Parties and the committees, communicating with the Parties and other relevant organizations, preparing reports and studies, and providing advice and assistance to the Parties. Additionally, the CITES guidelines for developing legislation (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/prog/Legislation/guidelines_legislation.pdf), which were adopted by the Conference of the Parties in Resolution Conf. 8.4 (Rev. CoP15) (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-Res-08-04-R15_0.pdf), state that the Secretariat has the authority to review and assess the national legislation of the Parties and to provide them with recommendations and assistance to ensure compliance with the Convention. The CITES Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by other resolutions and decisions adopted by the Conference of the Parties and the committees, such as the Standing Committee (https://cites.org/eng/disc/sc.php#:~:text=The%20Standing%20Committee%20provides%20policy,management%20of%20the%20Secretariat's%20budget.) and the Animals and Plants Committee (https://cites.org/eng/disc/ac_pc.php), which provide guidance and direction for the Secretariat's activities and projects, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/prog/Legislation/guidelines_legislation.pdf). The CITES Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetailsIII.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=XXI-6&chapter=21&Temp=mtdsg3&clang=_en), the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/cooperation/final-report-CITES%20CBD_Vilm_Workshop_Report.doc#:~:text=The%20Convention%20on%20International%20Trade,international%20concerns%20about%20biodiversity%20loss.), and the United Nations General Assembly Resolution on Sustainable Fisheries (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n23/397/27/pdf/n2339727.pdf?token=d5POlAgiWYC8Gzyjxu&fe=true), which provide further legal frameworks for the Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific wildlife issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: According to Article XII of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES-Convention-EN.pdf), the CITES Secretariat's objectives include the following tasks: (1) To arrange for and service meetings of the Parties (paragraph 2 a); (2) To perform the functions entrusted to it under the provisions of Articles XV and XVI of the Convention, which relate to amendments to Appendices I and II and Appendix III and amendments thereto (paragraph 2 b); (3) To undertake scientific and technical studies in accordance with programmes authorized by the Conference of the Parties as will contribute to the implementation of the Convention, including studies concerning standards for appropriate preparation and shipment of living specimens and the means of identifying specimens (paragraph 2 c); (4) To study the reports of Parties and to request from Parties such further information with respect thereto as it deems necessary to ensure implementation of the Convention (paragraph 2 d); (5) To invite the attention of the Parties to any matter pertaining to the aims of the Convention (paragraph 2 e); (6) To publish and distribute to the Parties current editions of Appendices I, II and III together with any information which will facilitate identification of specimens of species included in those Appendices (paragraph 2 f); (7) To prepare annual reports to the Parties on its work and on the implementation of the Convention and such other reports as meetings of the Parties may request (paragraph 2 g); (8) To make recommendations for the implementation of the aims and provisions of the Convention, including the exchange of information of a scientific or technical nature (paragraph 2 h);and (9) To perform any other function as may be entrusted to it by the Parties (paragraph 2 i).

matrix_cell_text_full: The CITES Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a ten-year Strategic Vision, adopted by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the Convention’s direction for the 2021-2030 timeframe in fulfilment of its mandate (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/reports/Implementation/E-SV-indicators.pdf). This vision, annexed to Resolution Conf. 18.3 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-18-03.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its Sustainable Development Goals, as well as the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/409e/19ae/369752b245f05e88f760aeb3/wg2020-05-l-02-en.pdf) being developed by Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It also recognizes the importance of global cooperation to address the threats posed by illegal trade in wildlife, as acknowledged by the United Nations General Assembly. The vision sets five broad goals and corresponding objectives and indicators to measure progress and performance. Secondly, a triennial budget and work programme, proposed by the Secretariat and approved by the Conference of the Parties, details the activities, outputs, and resources required to implement the Convention and the decisions of the Parties. The current budget and work programme for 2023-2025 is based on the priorities identified by the Parties and the Secretariat, as well as the expected income from the Trust Fund and external sources, as specified in Resolution Conf. 19.1 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-19-01.pdf). Thirdly various resolutions, decisions, agreements, and partnerships provide guidance and support for the implementation and enforcement of the Convention at the national, regional, and international levels, addressing legal and sustainable trade, compliance and enforcement, capacity-building, cooperation and collaboration, and awareness-raising, with key instruments listed here (https://cites.org/eng/res/index.php). The Convention is financed by core and external funds. The core funding, known as the CITES Trust Fund (CTL), finances the administrative costs of the Secretariat, the Conference of the Parties and its subsidiary bodies, the Standing Committee and other permanent committees. The CITES Trust Fund is replenished from contributions of the Parties to the Convention based on the United Nations scale of assessment, adjusted to take account of the fact that not all members of the United Nations are Parties to the Convention. The external funds, known as the CITES External Trust Fund (QTL) funds the voluntary programmes/projects activities costs. The CITES External Trust Fund consists of extrabudgetary contributions from Parties and other entities on a purely voluntary basis. Each offer of funding to the CITES External Trust Fund is negotiated and vetted by the Secretariat (https://cites.org/eng/disc/fund.php).
