matrix_cell_text_full: The CITES Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a ten-year Strategic Vision, adopted by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the Convention’s direction for the 2021-2030 timeframe in fulfilment of its mandate (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/reports/Implementation/E-SV-indicators.pdf). This vision, annexed to Resolution Conf. 18.3 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-18-03.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its Sustainable Development Goals, as well as the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/409e/19ae/369752b245f05e88f760aeb3/wg2020-05-l-02-en.pdf) being developed by Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It also recognizes the importance of global cooperation to address the threats posed by illegal trade in wildlife, as acknowledged by the United Nations General Assembly. The vision sets five broad goals and corresponding objectives and indicators to measure progress and performance. Secondly, a triennial budget and work programme, proposed by the Secretariat and approved by the Conference of the Parties, details the activities, outputs, and resources required to implement the Convention and the decisions of the Parties. The current budget and work programme for 2023-2025 is based on the priorities identified by the Parties and the Secretariat, as well as the expected income from the Trust Fund and external sources, as specified in Resolution Conf. 19.1 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-19-01.pdf). Thirdly various resolutions, decisions, agreements, and partnerships provide guidance and support for the implementation and enforcement of the Convention at the national, regional, and international levels, addressing legal and sustainable trade, compliance and enforcement, capacity-building, cooperation and collaboration, and awareness-raising, with key instruments listed here (https://cites.org/eng/res/index.php). The Convention is financed by core and external funds. The core funding, known as the CITES Trust Fund (CTL), finances the administrative costs of the Secretariat, the Conference of the Parties and its subsidiary bodies, the Standing Committee and other permanent committees. The CITES Trust Fund is replenished from contributions of the Parties to the Convention based on the United Nations scale of assessment, adjusted to take account of the fact that not all members of the United Nations are Parties to the Convention. The external funds, known as the CITES External Trust Fund (QTL) funds the voluntary programmes/projects activities costs. The CITES External Trust Fund consists of extrabudgetary contributions from Parties and other entities on a purely voluntary basis. Each offer of funding to the CITES External Trust Fund is negotiated and vetted by the Secretariat (https://cites.org/eng/disc/fund.php).

matrix_cell_text_full: The CMS Secretariat derives its mandate from the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), which established CMS as an environmental treaty that aims to protect and conserve terrestrial, aquatic and avian migratory animals and their habitats (https://www.cms.int/en/convention-bodies/secretariat). Specifically, Article IX of the Convention defines the functions of the CMS Secretariat, which include organizing and servicing meetings of the Conference of the Parties, the Scientific Council and the Standing Committee, promoting and supporting the development of Agreements, stimulating and supervising research and conservation projects, promoting the exchange of information between the Parties and liaising with international governmental and non-governmental organizations. The CMS Secretariat is provided and administered by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) (https://www.cms.int/en/convention-bodies/secretariat). The CMS Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by the Conference of the Parties, the Scientific Council and the Standing Committee, which provide guidance and direction for the CMS Secretariat's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders 9https://www.cms.int/en/documents/cop-resolutions). The CMS Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/int_exp_regs_part1_1_e.pdf), and the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for the CMS Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific migratory species and issues.

maintaining and making available to the Parties a list of AGREEMENTS and, if so required by the Conference of the Parties, providing any information on such AGREEMENTS (paragraph 4 h); maintaining and publishing a list of the recommendations made by the Conference of the Parties pursuant to subparagraphs (e), (f) and (g) of paragraph 5 of Article VII or of decisions made pursuant to sub-paragraph (h) of that paragraph (paragraph 4 i); providing for the general public information concerning this Convention and its objectives (paragraph 4 j); and performing any other function entrusted to it under this Convention or by the Conference of the Parties (paragraph 4 k). matrix_cell_text_full:
The CMS Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies:
Firstly, the CMS Secretariat has a Strategic Plan. This plan, proposed for 2024-2032, aligns with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, as stated in the draft resolution UNEP/CMS/COP14/CRP14.2 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop14_crp14.2_spms_e.docx). The plan is revised periodically, with the latest revision published in February, 2024. The Strategic Plan outlines the Secretariat’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. It aligns with the Convention’s mandate to conserve migratory species of wild animals. Secondly, the CMS operates on triennium budgets to fulfill its strategic plans, but may also operate interim budgets as deemed fit. matrix_cell_text_full: The CMS Secretariat works with various partners to implement the Convention and conserve migratory species. It cooperates with the secretariats of other biodiversity-related MEAs, such as CBD, CITES, Ramsar, and UNCCD, to harmonize policies and activities (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships), as per Paragraph 4(b) of Article IX of the Convention (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF) and resolution 11.10 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop12_res.11.10%28rev.cop12%29_e.pdf). It also collaborates with other inter-governmental bodies, such as UNESCO, IWC, and ITTO, to promote joint initiatives and projects on specific species or habitats, as per resolution 12.7 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop13_res.12.7_rev.cop13_e.pdf). It engages with non-governmental organizations, such as IUCN, BLI, OceanCare, and IFAW, to support scientific research, conservation action, and public awarenes (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships). It partners with the private sector, such as TUI AG, to raise funds and foster corporate social responsibility, following a code of conduct (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/basic_page_documents/code_of_conduct.pdf) adopted in resolution 10.21 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/10_21_synergies_e_0_0.pdf). It participates in the IPBES as an observer and contributes to its assessments and work programme (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/Doc_04_1_IPBES_E.pdf). It also supports the development and implementation of regional and thematic agreements and initiatives under the Convention, such as EAAFP, WHMSI, and SCF, as per Article IV and V of the Convention and Paragraph 6 of resolution 12.3 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop12_res.12.3_manila-declaration_e_1.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: IFAD derives its mandate from the Agreement Establishing the International Fund for Agricultural Development, which established IFAD as an international financial institution and a specialized agency of the United Nations (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421015/agree_e.pdf/b06d3b8f-6fb5-4db1-8054-b1ef21d746a5). Specifically, Article 2 of the Agreement defines the objectives and functions of IFAD; Article 3 outlines the membership and voting rights of IFAD; Article 6 describes the organization and management of IFAD; Article 7 specifies the use of resources and conditions of financing by IFAD; Article 8 establishes the relations of IFAD with the United Nations and other organizations, institutions and agencies; Article 9 regulates the withdrawal, suspension of membership, and termination of operations of IFAD; and Article 10 of the Agreement grants the legal status, privileges and immunities of IFAD. Additionally, the By-laws for the Conduct of the Business of IFAD (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421006/bylaw_e.pdf/d96589cb-8970-4862-af2e-c7fb4ed03c72?t=1651150969488) states that the by-laws shall govern the conduct of the business of IFAD, and that the by-laws may be amended by the Governing Council or the Executive Board (Preamble). IFAD's jurisdiction is also influenced by the policies and criteria for IFAD financing 9https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421030/ifad_financing_e.pdf/46846eb9-1053-4bcc-acf1-1e8756831fbb?t=1653556237925), which provide the general principles and operational guidelines for IFAD's lending and grant activities. These policies and criteria are periodically reviewed and updated by the Executive Board to reflect the changing needs and priorities of IFAD's target groups and member states. IFAD's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development, which provide further legal frameworks for IFAD's jurisdiction over specific rural development issues and domains (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38714170/40237917/IFAD+Strategic+Framework+2016-2025/d43eed79-c827-4ae8-b043-09e65977e22d).

matrix_cell_text_full: IFAD executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a ten-year Strategic Framework (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38714170/40237917/IFAD+Strategic+Framework+2016-2025/d43eed79-c827-4ae8-b043-09e65977e22d), revised every four years by the Governing Council, establishes the IFAD's vision, mission, strategic objectives, outcomes and pillars of results delivery that will guide its operations over the 2016-2025 period. This framework aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.ifad.org/en/strategic-framework) and responds to the commitments of the Thirteenth Replenishment of IFAD's Resources (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/repl/13/1/docs/IFAD13-1-R-7-PPT-on-Workplan-and-Sessions.pdf). Secondly, an annual Result-Based Programme of Work and Budget, devised by the IFAD and approved by the Executive Board, details the activities, outputs, indicators and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The Indicative Programme of Work and Budget for 2024 is based on the principles of efficiency, effectiveness and value for money, as outlined in document GC 47/L.8 (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/gc/47/docs/GC-47-L-8.pdf). It also supports the implementation of the Environment and Climate Change Strategy, which consolidates and updates IFAD's strategy and policy frameworks on environment and climate change for the 2019-2025 period (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/eb/125/docs/EB-2018-125-R-12.pdf). IFAD's budgeting process is based on a results-based approach that aligns the Fund's resources with its strategic objectives and operational priorities. IFAD reports periodically on its budget performance and achievements to its Executive Board. IFAD has four major funding sources: (1) contributions from its members, (2) investment income, (3) loan repayments by recipient countries, and (4) borrowing from its member states. These resources feed its work program, and are supplemented by co-financing from beneficiary countries and other donors. Contributions are voluntary and multi-year in nature. Every three years, IFAD organizes a replenishment conference, corresponding to a work program. it also receives supplementary funds from various sources, such as climate financing and bilateral grants (https://www.ifad.org/en/finance). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Strategic Framework, addressing rural poverty, food security, nutrition, gender equality, resilience, innovation, partnerships and financing.

This framework aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.ifad.org/en/strategic-framework) and responds to the commitments of the Thirteenth Replenishment of IFAD's Resources (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/repl/13/1/docs/IFAD13-1-R-7-PPT-on-Workplan-and-Sessions.pdf). Secondly, an annual Result-Based Programme of Work and Budget, devised by the IFAD and approved by the Executive Board, details the activities, outputs, indicators and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The Indicative Programme of Work and Budget for 2024 is based on the principles of efficiency, effectiveness and value for money, as outlined in document GC 47/L.8 (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/gc/47/docs/GC-47-L-8.pdf). It also supports the implementation of the Environment and Climate Change Strategy, which consolidates and updates IFAD's strategy and policy frameworks on environment and climate change for the 2019-2025 period (https://webapps.ifad.org/members/eb/125/docs/EB-2018-125-R-12.pdf). IFAD's budgeting process is based on a results-based approach that aligns the Fund's resources with its strategic objectives and operational priorities. IFAD reports periodically on its budget performance and achievements to its Executive Board. IFAD has four major funding sources: (1) contributions from its members, (2) investment income, (3) loan repayments by recipient countries, and (4) borrowing from its member states. These resources feed its work program, and are supplemented by co-financing from beneficiary countries and other donors. Contributions are voluntary and multi-year in nature. Every three years, IFAD organizes a replenishment conference, corresponding to a work program. it also receives supplementary funds from various sources, such as climate financing and bilateral grants (https://www.ifad.org/en/finance). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Strategic Framework, addressing rural poverty, food security, nutrition, gender equality, resilience, innovation, partnerships and financing.

In addition, IFAD facilitates the Global Environment Facility (GEF), established in 1991, to enhance environmental sustainability and resilience (https://www.ifad.org/en/gef). It also engages with the Green Climate Fund (GCF), established in 2010, to mobilise climate finance and support adaptation and mitigation actions (https://www.greenclimate.fund/ae/ifad).

matrix_cell_text_full: ITC derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly Resolution 2297 (XXII) (https://documents.un.org/doc/resolution/gen/nr0/236/32/pdf/nr023632.pdf?token=KPeCl92Q67Vpf1B3TZ&fe=true), which established The International Trade Centre as a joint subsidiary organ of the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the United Nations (UN) through the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) in accordance with the recommendations of the 1964 Global Agreement on Tariff and Trade (GATT) (https://docs.wto.org/gattdocs/q/GG/SPEC/64-151.pdf). The Resolution defined the objectives and functions of ITC and also outlined the governance and administrative arrangements. Additionally, ITC is subject to the relevant provisions of the UN Charter, the WTO Agreement, and the UNCTAD resolutions ((https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/wto_itc_e.htm).). ITC's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations of its governing bodies, such as the Joint Advisory Group (JAG), the Consultative Committee of ITC Trust Fund (CCITF), and the parent organizations (WTO and UNCTAD) (https://intracen.org/about-us/governance). These decisions and recommendations provide strategic direction and oversight the for ITC's activities and programmes, as well as resource mobilization and partnership development (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). Furthermore, ITC's mandate is supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and the Aid for Trade Initiative, which provide further legal frameworks for ITC's jurisdiction over specific trade and development issues and domains (https://intracen.org/file/operationalplan2023pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: ITC executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Joint Advisory Group, establishes ITC's vision, mission, strategic goals, core services, and impact areas. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its mandates (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). The plan also articulates ITC's vision of a world where trade builds inclusive, sustainable and prosperous economies, one where the recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic creates resilience and ensures a green transition. Secondly, an annual Operational Plan, devised by ITC and approved by the Consultative Committee of the ITC Trust Fund, details activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current Operational Plan for 2023 is tailored to the clients' needs and partners' priorities (https://intracen.org/file/operationalplan2023pdf). It also maintains the Trade Map, a key aspect of the provision of trade intelligence to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) (https://intracen.org/resources/tools/trade-map). The plan also specifies how ITC will assist MSMEs in creating jobs through entrepreneurship and value chain development, with a focus on women, youth, people with disabilities, and those in vulnerable situations. ITC operates on an annual budget for its work programmes, and the 2024 budget is aligned with the ITC Strategic Plan 2022-2025 and the Operational Plan 2023, which focus on the 5 'Ps' of the Global Agenda - prosperity, people, planet, peace, and partnership 9https://intracen.org/file/proposedprogrammebudgetfor2024pdf). ITC’s Regular Budget (RB) is funded in equal parts by the UN and the WTO. Its extra budgetary resources (XB) consist of pledges from donor governments, governmental organizations, other international organizations and civil society, including NGOs, the business sector and a variety of foundations. These commitments often extend over multiyear periods (https://intracen.org/about-us/funding). In addition, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing ITC's vision, mission, and principles, addressing trade competitiveness, inclusiveness, sustainability, and digitalization (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). Finally, ITC Annual Report offers a comprehensive review of the organization’s activities and detailed information on the results and effectiveness of its work. The latest report for 2022 (https://intracen.org/file/itcannualreport2022eng-interactive20junepdf) showcases how ITC delivered above and beyond the call of duty to set the Sustainable Development Goals back on track and help small enterprises continue finding new pathways to prosperity through trade, despite the challenges posed by the ‘four Cs’ – COVID, climate, conflict and cost-of-living. The report also presents results from the first year of ITC’s Strategic Plan 2022–2025, which pushes its value proposition further than before, laying out a bold roadmap for creating trade that is sustainable, inclusive and transformative.

matrix_cell_text_full: The UNCCD Secretariat derives its mandate from the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), which established the UNCCD as a legally binding framework to address desertification and the effects of drought (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf). Specifically, Article 23 of the Convention defines the functions and location of the Secretariat, Article 22 establishes modalities for the Conference of Parties, and Articles 20-21 outline the financial resources and funding mechanism of the Secretariat. Additionally, the UNCCD 2018-2030 Strategic Framework, adopted by the Conference of the Parties (COP) in 2017, specifies the vision, mission, strategic objectives, and expected impacts of the UNCCD for the period 2018-2030 (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/ICCD_COP%2813%29_L.18-1716078E_0.pdf). The Strategic Framework also defines the roles and responsibilities of the Secretariat, the COP, and its subsidiary bodies, as well as the affected country Parties and other stakeholders. The UNCCD Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations adopted by the COP and its subsidiary bodies, such as the Committee for the Review of the Implementation of the Convention (CRIC) and the Committee on Science and Technology (CST) (https://www.unccd.int/convention/governance/cric). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for the implementation of the Convention and the Strategic Framework, as well as cooperation and coordination with other relevant international bodies and conventions. Furthermore, UNCCD Secretariat's mandate is supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and the African Union Agenda 2063, which provide further legal frameworks for the UNCCD Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific land and soil-related issues and domains (https://www.unccd.int/land-and-life/sdgs/unccd-cbd-and-unfccc-joint-liaison-group).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to Article 23 of the UNCCD Convention (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf), the UNCCD Secretariat's objectives encompass several key functions: making arrangements for sessions of the Conference of the Parties (COP) and its subsidiary bodies established under the Convention, and providing them with services as required (Article 23, paragraph 1); compiling and transmitting reports submitted to it (Article 23, paragraph 2); facilitating assistance to affected developing country Parties, on request, particularly those in Africa, in the compilation and communication of information required under the Convention (Article 23, paragraph 3); and coordinating its activities with the secretariats of other relevant international bodies and conventions (Article 23, paragraph 4). Additionally, according to the UNCCD 2018-2030 Strategic Framework, the UNCCD Secretariat's objectives also include: acting as an advocate for land, ensuring land-related issues are put front and center on the development agenda; championing for healthy, productive and accessible land around the world; supporting countries in achieving land degradation neutrality, integrating strategies for poverty eradication, and promoting cooperation among affected country Parties; and providing access to the latest data and knowledge, ensuring that best practices are shared and opportunities for capacity-building are increased. These functions enable the Secretariat to fulfil its role as the main facilitator of the implementation of the Convention and the Strategic Framework (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/ICCD_COP%2813%29_L.18-1716078E_0.pdf).

It aims to restore the productivity of vast expanses of degraded land, improve the livelihoods of more than 1.3 billion people, and reduce the impacts of drought on vulnerable populations (https://www.unccd.int/convention/secretariat#:~:text=It%20aims%20to%20restore%20the,is%20located%20in%20Bonn%2C%20Germany.). Secondly, the Secretariat prepares a triennial programme and budget. The Programme and budget for the triennium 2022–2024 as detailed in Decision 10/COP.15 provides an overview of the human and financial resources requirements as well as the programme priorities (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/2022-10/10_cop15.pdf). Thirdly, the Secretariat supports countries that want to achieve national/regional land degradation neutrality, identify how land and soil are critical for climate change adaptation and mitigation, implement land management practices, design programmes and projects that transform communities, and provide science and research needed to take informed decisions (https://www.unccd.int/convention/secretariat). Finally, the Secretariat has been granted additional mandates to play a leading role with regards to operational objectives on advocacy, awareness raising and education, policy framework, and science, technology, and knowledge, as well as a support role in other operational objectives on capacity building and financing and technology transfer (https://knowledge.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/The%20secretariat.pdf). The Secretariat also collaborates with various partners at all levels, from global to local, to advance the implementation of the Convention (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/2022-02/Partnership%20evaluation%20report%20%20final%20corrected.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Charter of the United Nations University (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf), the University's objectives are as follows: (1) To contribute, through collaborative research and education, to efforts to resolve the pressing global problems of human survival, development, and welfare that are the concern of the United Nations, its Peoples, and Member States (Article I, paragraph 1); (2) To disseminate the knowledge gained in its activities to the United Nations and its agencies, to scholars and to the public, in order to increase dynamic interaction in the worldwide community of learning and research (Article I, paragraph 4), (3) To assist in the development of vigorous academic and scientific communities everywhere and particularly in the developing countries, devoted to their vital needs in the fields of learning and research within the framework of the aims assigned to those centres and programmes in the present Charter (Article I, paragraph 6); and (4) To grant and confer master’s degrees and doctorates, diplomas, certificates and other academic distinctions under conditions laid down for that purpose in the statutes by the Council of the University (Article I, paragraph 8). matrix_cell_text_full: The United Nations University (UNU) implements its objectives and mandates through a variety of strategies: (1) The UNU has a strategic plan that guides the development and implementation of the institute’s research, policy development, teaching, and capacity-building initiatives. The current strategic plan spans from 2020 to 2024 (https://i.unu.edu/media/unu.edu/attachment/100694/UNU-Strategic-Plan-2020-2024.pdf). This plan is closely aligned with the overall strategic direction of the UNU (https://unu.edu/ias/about-unu-ias/strategic-plan). It was produced through an inclusive process of internal stocktaking and dialogue, reflecting the outcomes of a comprehensive external evaluation of UNU-IAS conducted in 2020 (https://unu.edu/ias/about-unu-ias/strategic-plan), (2) The UNU Council is responsible for considering and approving the UNU budget and work programme. The Work Program and budget estimate for the biennium 2022-2023 is designed to support the United Nations University’s (UNU) vision of promoting sustainable human development and its mission to contribute, through research and capacity building, to efforts to resolve the pressing global problems that are the concern of the United Nations, its Peoples and Member States. The budget of USD 124.8 million, a 10.9% increase from the previous biennium, is funded through various sources including project fundraising, institutional fundraising, income from the endowment fund, cumulative surplus carried forward, and other income (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-01/Approved-UNU-Work-Programme-and-Budget-Estimates-for-the-2022-2023-Biennium.pdf), (3) The UNU has established the UNU SDG–Universities Platform through the UNU-IAS in 2020, which provides opportunities for Japanese universities to proactively collaborate with different stakeholders to promote research and educational activities advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (https://unu.edu/ias/unu-sdg-universities-platform), and (5) The UNU Council devises the principles and policies that govern the University’s operations. The Council holds two regular sessions per year (https://unu.edu/about/unu-council). Finally, the UNU has 13 institutes located in 12 countries around the world, each contributing to the mission of the UNU through their specific programmes of work. The global UNU system is coordinated by UNU Headquarters in Tokyo (https://unu.edu/unu-system).

matrix_cell_text_full: The Ramsar Secretariat derives its mandate from the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat, also known as the Ramsar Convention, which was signed in Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, entered into force in 1975, and ammended in 1994 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf). Specifically, Article 8 of the Convention assigned bureau duties to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources as a body to carry out the day-to-day coordination of the Convention's activities, as detailed in Paragraph 2 of article 8. Additionally, Rule 27 of the Convention's Rules of Procedure (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/ramsar_rules_of_procedure_e_0.pdf) defines the functions of the Secretariat, which include performing all other work that the Conference of the Parties requires and directs (Rule 27 g), and Rule 26 states the duties of the Secretary General. The Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by the COP, the Standing Committee, and the STRP, which provide guidance and direction for the Secretariat's work, as well as cooperation and coordination with other conventions, intergovernmental institutions, and national and international NGOs (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/2023-07/list_resolutions_recommendations_e_1.pdf). The Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Convention on Migratory Species, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, and the UN Convention to Combat Desertification, which provide further legal frameworks for the Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific wetland-related issues and domains (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships/partnerships-other-conventions).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Ramsar Convention (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf), Ramsar Secretariat’s objectives include the following key aspects: promoting the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, recognizing their ecological, economic, cultural, and recreational value (Preamble; Article 3, paragraph 1); encouraging countries to identify and designate Wetlands of International Importance, which represent the best examples of wetland ecosystems of global significance (Article 2, paragraph 2); promoting international cooperation on wetland conservation and management, recognizing that the conservation of wetlands and their resources is a global concern that requires coordinated efforts (Article 5); equiring regular monitoring and reporting on the status of wetlands and their resources, the measures taken for their conservation and sustainable use, and the effectiveness of these measures (Article 3, paragraph 2; Article 6, paragraph 2 e); and promoting public awareness and education on the importance of wetlands and their conservation, recognizing that public support and involvement are essential for the success of wetland conservation efforts (Article 4, paragraph 3).

This plan has three strategic goals: 1) address the drivers of wetland loss and degradation; 2) effectively conserve and manage the Ramsar Site Network; and 3) wisely use all wetlands. The Secretariat also has a Workplan that is structured around the seven core functions of the Secretariat and sets out principal activities and corresponding annual and triennial indicators for each, together with indicative lead responsibilities and principal funding source. The most recent Workplan is applicable for 2023-2025 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/2023-09/secretariat_workplan_2023_2025_e.pdf). Ramsar Secretariat's core funding is based on contributions from Contracting Parties to the Convention 9https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat also prepares an annual core budget which is approved by the Conference of the Contracting Parties. The core budget for 2022 was presented in Annex 1 of Resolution ExCOP3.2 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/excop3_2_financial_budgetary_matters_e.pdf). Finally, the Secretariat develops cooperation with other conventions, intergovernmental institutions, and national and international NGOs (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships). It also organizes Ramsar Advisory Missions at the request of Contracting Parties and contributes to the follow-up of RAM reports (https://www.ramsar.org/our-work/activities/ramsar-advisory-missions). These strategies and mechanisms provide an operational framework for implementing the Convention's mission of conservation and wise use of all wetlands through local and national actions and international cooperation.

It is based at the headquarters of the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) in Gland, Switzerland (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat develops cooperation with other conventions, intergovernmental institutions, and national and international NGOs (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships) . It also works to strengthen collaboration with the World Bank and UN agencies, particularly UNEP, UNDP, FAO, WHO, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), and the Intergovernmental Science Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES). This collaboration is detailed in the draft resolution on enhancing the Convention's visibility (Ramsar COP14 Doc.18.8 Rev.2) (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/cop14_18_8_rev2_dr_synergies_e.pdf). Furthermore, the Secretariat has interface procedures with the Joint Environment Unit (JEU) of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) (https://www.ramsar.org/document/interface-procedures-between-ramsar-secretariat-joint-environment-unit-jeu-un-office).

The Minamata Convention derives its mandate from the Minamata Convention on Mercury, which established the Convention as an international treaty to protect human health and the environment from mercury and mercury compounds (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf). Article 1 of the Convention defines the objective of the Convention, and Article 15 lays out the mechanism for Implementation and Compliance Committee to promote implementation 
of, and review compliance with, all provisions of the Convention. Similarly Article 23 establishes the Conference of Parties to the Convention while Article 24 outlines the functions of the Convention's Secretariat. Additionally, the Convention's articles and annexes, which were adopted by the Conference of Plenipotentiaries on 10 October 2013 (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf), specify the obligations and commitments of the Parties to the Convention, such as regulating the sources and trade of mercury, controlling the emissions and releases of mercury, managing the mercury waste and contaminated sites, providing information and public awareness, and facilitating technical and financial assistance and cooperation. The Convention's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and resolutions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Conference of the Parties, the Implementation and Compliance Committee, and the Secretariat (https://minamataconvention.org/en/meeting-documents?f%5B0%5D=document_type_2%3A307). These decisions and resolutions provide guidance and direction for the Convention's implementation and review, as well as cooperation and coordination with other relevant organisations and stakeholders. The Convention's mandate is also supported by the participation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and their Disposal (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2019.English.pdf), the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf), and the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for the Convention's jurisdiction over specific mercury-related issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: The Minamata Convention Secretariat executes its objectives through specific strategies. Firstly, the Secreatariat develops a programme of work and budget for each biennium, which is approved by the Conference of the Parties. The programme of work and budget, applicable for 2024-2025 (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/2024-01/Programme_work_budget_for_2024-2025.pdf), outlines the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources for implementing the Convention based on the needs and priorities of the Parties and other stakeholders, as reflected in COP-5 decision document (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/information_document/UNEP-MC-COP.5-INF36-POWB-Fact-sheets_English.pdf). Secondly, various mechanisms and tools provide technical and financial support to the Parties, especially developing countries and countries with economies in transition, to assist them in fulfilling their obligations under the Convention. These include the Implementation and Compliance Committee (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/implementation-and-compliance-committee), the Specific International Programme (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/specific-international-programme), the Global Environment Facility (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/gef), the Special Programme (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/special-programme), the Global Mercury Partnership (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/partners/global-mercury-partnership), and the Minamata Online platform (https://minamataconvention.org/es/node/3136). The main sources of funding for the Minamata Convention are the Global Environment Facility Trust Fund (GEF) and the Specific International Programme (SIP) to support capacity-building and technical assistance (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/financial-mechanism). The GEF has pledged $265 million for the four-year cycle starting in July 2022 (https://www.thegef.org/newsroom/news/minamata-convention-receives-increased-funding-pledge-global-environment-facility). Finally, various partnerships, initiatives, and platforms provide a framework for cooperation and information exchange among Parties, scientific communities, civil society, and other relevant stakeholders, on issues such as mercury supply and trade, mercury-added products, mercury waste, health and environmental impacts of mercury, and mercury-free technologies and alternatives (https://minamataconvention.org/en/resources/partnerships).

These relationships enable the Convention to fulfill its role as a global legally binding instrument on mercury to address the risks to human health and the environment from mercury pollution.

matrix_cell_text_full: UNOOSA derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly resolution 1472 (XIV) of 12 December 1959, which established the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) and its secretariat, later renamed as UNOOSA (https://www.unoosa.org/pdf/gares/ARES_14_1472E.pdf). Specifically, paragraph 1 of the resolution defines the objectives and functions of COPUOS. Additionally, UNOOSA's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and principles, such as the five treaties and five declarations on outer space, which provide the legal framework for UNOOSA's jurisdiction over the exploration and use of outer space for peaceful purposes (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties.html). The five treaties on outer space are: (1) The Outer Space Treaty (1967) on the Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introouterspacetreaty.html), (2) The Rescue Agreement (1968) on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introrescueagreement.html), (3) The Liability Convention (1972) on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introliability-convention.html), (4) The Registration Convention (1976) on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introregistration-convention.html), and (5) The Moon Agreement (1984) governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/intromoon-agreement.html). UNOOSA's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by COPUOS and the General Assembly, such as the Space2030 Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which provide guidance and direction for UNOOSA's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/resolutions.html).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to Part A, Section III of UNOOSA's working document "The 'Space2030' Agenda: Space as a Driver of Sustainable Development" (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf), the United Nations UNOOSA has been mandated to fulfil the following objectives: Enhance space-derived economic benefits and strengthen the role of the space sector as a major driver of sustainable development (Overarching objective 1); Harness the potential of space to solve everyday challenges and leverage space-related innovation to improve the quality of life (Overarching objective 2); Improve access to space for all and ensure that all countries can benefit socioeconomically from space science and technology applications and space-based data, information and products, thereby supporting the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (Overarching objective 3); and Build partnerships and strengthen international cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space and in the global governance of outer space activities (Overarching objective 4). These objectives are structured around the four pillars of space economy, space society, space accessibility and space diplomacy, and are complemented by four core objectives that outline the specific actions to be taken by Member States, UNOOSA and other stakeholders to implement the "Space2030" Agenda (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The UNOOSA executes its objectives through certain strategies: firstly, a vision and strategy for UNOOSA 2024-2030, presented by the Director of UNOOSA to the Member States in February 2024 (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf), establishes the Office's vision, mission, strategic objectives, and core functions. This strategy, aligned with the "Space2030" agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, reflects the high expectations and feedback from the Member States and other stakeholders (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/outreach/events/2018/spacetrust.html). Secondly, an annual programme plan and budget, prepared by UNOOSA and approved by the General Assembly. The proposed UNOOSA budget for 2024 (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2023/a78/a786_sect_6_0_html/A_78_06_Sect06E.pdf) supports its proposed 2024 programme plan (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2023/aac_1052023crp/aac_1052023crp_3_0_html/AC105_C2_2023_CRP03E.pdf), which aims to make the most of the economic opportunities that space offers and to use the space sector as a catalyst for sustainable development; to tap into the potential of space to solve everyday problems and to enhance the quality of life through space innovation; to enable access to space for all and to ensure that all countries can use space applications and data for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals; and to foster partnerships and cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space and in the global governance of outer space activities. The budget is mainly funded by the regular budget of the United Nations, but also relies on voluntary contributions from Member States and other entities for some of its activities.

Serving as the central drug control entity with exclusive responsibility for coordinating and providing effective leadership for all United Nations drug control activities and serving as the repository of technical expertise in international drug control for the Secretariat of the United Nations, including the regional commissions, and other United Nations organs, as well as Member States (Section 2.2 a); Acting on behalf of the Secretary-General in fulfilling his or her responsibilities under the terms of international treaties and resolutions of United Nations organs relating to international drug control (Section 2.2 b); Providing substantive services to the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council and committees and conferences dealing with drug control matters (Section 2.2 c); Carrying out activities in the field of international crime prevention and control; strengthening regional and international cooperation in preventing and combating transnational crime, in particular organized and economic crime, money-laundering, illicit trafficking in women and children, financial crimes and terrorism in all its forms; and promoting effective and fair administration of justice, with due respect for the rights of all those affected by crime or involved in the criminal justice system (Section 2.3 a); Promoting adherence to the international treaties on drug control, crime prevention and terrorism and their effective implementation by States (Section 6.2 f); and Providing assistance to Member States in the implementation of relevant General Assembly resolutions and declarations related to action against terrorism (Section 6.2 g).

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within the IOC involves collaboration with various levels of institutions and authorities. The IOC, under UNESCO, engages with Member States, United Nations bodies, and other international organizations to achieve its objectives. This coordination is structured under the IOC’s statutes and strategic plans, which outline the framework for cooperation with entities at different levels. The IOC operates through its Assembly, Executive Council, and Secretariat, which are responsible for implementing the decisions and strategies of the organization. The IOC also has subsidiary bodies, such as regional sub-commissions and working groups, that address specific regional and thematic areas. matrix_cell_text_full:
The FAO’s vertical coordination involves collaboration with various levels of governance and institutions, including the United Nations, specialized agencies, regional and intergovernmental organizations, national governments, and local authorities. The FAO operates through the Conference of all the members, the Council, and a secretariat headed by a Director-General  (Articles III, IV, V, and VII). It also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies that assist members in implementing standards, policies, and programmes, providing technical cooperation and assistance upon request (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf)
The FAO’s work is organized around five major programme areas, each overseen by a Deputy Director-General who works closely with the Director-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.fao.org/3/ne576en/ne576en.pdf). The Senior Management Team, consisting of the Director-General and Deputy Directors-General, provides strategic and operational guidance to ensure coherence and alignment between the different departments and divisions of the Organization and the governing bodies https://www.fao.org/about/org-chart/en/). Furthermore, the FAO’s structure includes Regional, Liaison, and Country Offices, Subregional Offices, and Partnership and Liaison Offices, which facilitate the FAO’s work on the ground, ensuring that its global mandates are translated into local action (https://www.fao.org/about/who-we-are/worldwide-offices/en/). The Governing Bodies, such as the Conference, Council, Regional Conferences, Committee on World Food Security, Council Committees, and Technical Committees (https://www.fao.org/unfao/govbodies/home/en/) and the Statutory Bodies (https://www.fao.org/unfao/govbodies/gsb-subject-matter/subject-matter/en/) , play a pivotal role in decision-making and oversight. The Oversight Advisory Committee further supports this structure by providing independent advice on issues related to governance, risk management, and internal control https://www.fao.org/about/oversight-advisory-committee/en/). In alignment with the UN Development System reform, the FAO leverages the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework and UN Common Country Analysis to integrate food security and agrifood systems transformation within the broader UN support to national governments (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/fao-un-system/en). This approach ensures that the FAO’s efforts are harmonized with the UN’s overarching goals and contribute effectively to sustainable development initiatives globally.

matrix_cell_text_full:
Horizontal coordination within the FAO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the food and agriculture domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that food security and nutrition are considered in all policies and that agricultural policies are aligned with other sectoral policies (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/en/). This coordination is guided by Article 1 of the Constitution of the FAO (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf). For example, FAO works with the environmental sector to address climate change impacts on food security (https://www.fao.org/3/i5188e/I5188E.pdf), or with the economic sector to enhance rural development and livelihoods (https://www.fao.org/agrifood-economics/areas-of-work/en/), and with the ocean sector  to enhance underwater food systems and ensure sustainable aquatic food production for the growing global population (https://news.un.org/en/story/2022/06/1121602). Horizontal coordination within FAO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Action Programme on Food Security and Nutrition in Small Island States (https://www.fao.org/3/i7297e/i7297e.pdf), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, such as the Committee on World Food Security (https://www.fao.org/sustainable-development-goals-helpdesk/champion/article-detail/committee-on-world-food-security/en), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, such as the Voluntary Guidelines on Food Systems and Nutrition (https://www.fao.org/cfs/vgfsn/en/),
(4) Advocacy campaigns like World Food Day (https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/world-food-day--global-ceremony-highlights-water-s-role-against-troubled-backdrop/en) or The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report (https://www.fao.org/publications/home/fao-flagship-publications/the-state-of-food-security-and-nutrition-in-the-world/en). The FAO provides leadership on global food security, shapes the agricultural research agenda, sets standards, offers evidence-based policy options, provides technical support, and monitors food and nutrition trends (https://www.fao.org/3/cb7099en/cb7099en.pdf). It facilitates the participation of diverse actors in the agricultural sector and enhances cooperation within the UN system on food and agriculture matters (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/en/)

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within IMO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with Other Organizations section of the IMCO Convention, specifically in Articles 45-48. The IMO operates through an Assembly of all the members, a Council of 40 members, and a Secretary-General (Articles 12-18 of the Convention) The IMO operates through its Assembly, Council, and a series of committees and sub-committees, Legal Committee, Technical Cooperation Committe, Facilitation Committee and the Secretariat that address various aspects of maritime safety, security, and environmental protection (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/Structure.aspx). It also works closely with Member States to implement and enforce international maritime conventions and standards (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf).  . The IMO also has committees, sub-committees, and other subsidiary bodies (Articles 19-24). The IMO assists members in the implementation of its conventions, codes, standards, and guidelines, and provides technical assistance and capacity building upon request (Articles 25-26).  This coordination is also structured under the IMO’s framework for cooperation with intergovernmental organizations, as established in resolution A.1168(32) adopted by the IMO Assembly (https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/KnowledgeCentre/IndexofIMOResolutions/AssemblyDocuments/A.1168(32).pdf).  The World Maritime University (WMU) and the IMO International Maritime Law Institute (IMLI) are key educational pillars of the IMO, fostering expertise and knowledge in maritime law and policy (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/WMUandIMLI.aspx). There are also some affliated bodies to the IMO including  the Global MTCC Network (GMN)  focusing on improving energy efficiency in the maritime sector and supports developing regions in moving towards maritime decarbonization (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/PartnershipsProjects/Pages/IMO-EuropeanUnionProject.aspx) . IMO has regional coordinators/advisors for technical cooperation activities, in Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, Kenya, Philippines and Trinidad and Tobago (https://www.imo.org/en/about/pages/structure.aspx#9). The IMO operates a network of regional centers, including NOWPAP MERRAC, REMPEITC-Caribe, MEMAC, ROPME, REMPEC, PEMSEA, and PERSGA, which play crucial roles in regional maritime safety, security, and environmental protection efforts

For example, the IMO works with the education sector to promote maritime training and capacity building through institutions like the World Maritime University (WMU) and the International Maritime Law Institute (IMLI) (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/WMUandIMLI.aspx), with the environmental sector to address issues like biofouling and greenhouse gas emissions through initiatives like the GloFouling Partnerships project (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/PartnershipsProjects/Pages/GloFouling-Project.aspx), or with the development sector to enhance maritime capabilities in regions like Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean through its Integrated Technical Cooperation Programme (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/ITCP.aspx). Horizontal coordination within the IMO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global SAR Plan (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Safety/Pages/GlobalSARPlan.aspx), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Global Integrated Shipping Information System (https://gisis.imo.org/Public/Default.aspx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for maritime sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) COde (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Security/Pages/SOLAS-XI-2%20ISPS%20Code.aspx) , (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for maritime issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Day of the Seafarer (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Events/Pages/Day-of-the-Seafarer-2024.aspx). The IMO provides leadership and direction on matters critical to maritime safety and security, shapes the maritime research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses maritime trends (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/Geo-Coverage.aspx). The IMO facilitates the participation of various actors in the maritime sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on maritime matters (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/Geo-Coverage.aspx)

source_title: General's Bulletin ST/SGB/2021/1, which organizes the Office of Legal Affairs and details the functions of DOALOS (
excerpt_<=50w: General's Bulletin ST/SGB/2021/1, which organizes the Office of Legal Affairs and details the functions of DOALOS ([URI]).
matrix_cell_text_full: DOALOS engages in vertical coordination with various levels of institutions, including the United Nations, specialized agencies, regional bodies, national governments, and local authorities, as outlined in section 9.2 of its governing document.  The structure of this coordination is outlined in the Secretary-General's Bulletin ST/SGB/2021/1, which organizes the Office of Legal Affairs and details the functions of DOALOS (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en). It operates under the guidance of the Under-Secretary-General for Legal Affairs and the Director of the Division, with specialized sections and units handling distinct functions (section 9.3). DOALOS aids in implementing the Convention and related Agreements, offering technical cooperation and capacity building (section 9.4). It maintains liaison with entities like the International Seabed Authority and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, and provides support to the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, the General Assembly, and the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, incuding Socioeconomic Aspects (section 9.5) (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en).  DOALOS operates through the Meeting of States Parties to the Convention, providing substantive servicing to this and other related bodies². It also assists members in implementing the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and related agreements, offering training, fellowships, and technical assistance (https://www.un.org/depts/los/doalos_activities/about_doalos.htm). DOALOS's work is structured to ensure the consistent application of the Convention across various levels of governance, supporting the development of maritime policies that align with international law (https://www.un.org/depts/los/doalos_activities/about_doalos.htm). The Division also engages with the International Seabed Authority and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, maintaining liaison and providing administrative support as necessary¹. Additionally, DOALOS supports the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf and facilitates the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the State of the Marine Environment (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en).

igo: Division for Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea (UN DOALOS)
source_title: Horizontal coordination within DOALOS involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the ocean domain, such as fisheries,
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination within DOALOS involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the ocean domain, such as fisheries, environment, security, trade, science, private sector, civil society, and other UN agencies to ensure that ocean affairs and the law of the sea are integrated into all policies ([URI]).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within DOALOS involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the ocean domain, such as fisheries, environment, security, trade, science, private sector, civil society, and other UN agencies to ensure that ocean affairs and the law of the sea are integrated into all policies (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). This is structured under the section 9.5 of the document, which outlines the inter-agency cooperation and coordination of the Division (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en).  This coordination is guided by the mandate of DOALOS to promote the uniform and consistent application of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and related agreements (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). The DOALOS participates in the inter-agency mechanism UN-Oceans, which seeks to enhance the coordination, coherence and effectiveness of competent organizations of the United Nations system and the International Seabed Authority on ocean issues (https://www.un.org/depts/los/coop_coor/un_oceans.htm). The DOALOS also liaises with other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, non-governmental organizations, and academic institutions on matters related to ocean affairs and the law of the sea (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/). DOALOS conducts consultations with regional intergovernmental organizations and others in Africa, Asia-Pacific, and Latin America/Caribben to gain insight in ongoing regional programmes and activities on ocean governance and to identify capacity-building needs and priorities in the region (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/consultations).  The DOALOS facilitates the exchange of information and best practices among governments and other interested parties on issues under its consideration. For example, DOALOS works with the scientific community to support marine scientific research and with environmental sectors to address marine biodiversity conservation (https://www.un.org/depts/los/general_assembly/general_assembly.htm). Horizontal coordination within DOALOS can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders (https://www.un.org/depts/los/biodiversity/prepcom.htm), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as UN-Oceans, the inter-agency coordination mechanism on ocean and coastal issues (https://www.un.org/depts/los/consultative_process/consultative_process.htm), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for engagement with other sectors and stakeholders (https://www.un.org/depts/los/), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for ocean issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/5214236EGM%20Report%20on%20Oceans.pdf). DOALOS provides leadership and direction on matters critical to oceans and the law of the sea, shapes the ocean governance research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses trends related to oceans and maritime affairs (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). DOALOS facilitates the participation of various actors in the ocean sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on ocean matters (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos).

matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the ISA involves collaboration among different sectors and stakeholders involved in the exploration and exploitation of the seabed and ocean floor beyond national jurisdiction, such as States Parties, contractors, the Enterprise, the United Nations and its specialised agencies, and other international and non-governmental organizations. This coordination is structured under the General Principles section of Part XI of the UNCLOS, specifically in Articles 156-185 (https://www.un.org/Depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11.htm). The ISA has established three principal organs: the Assembly, the Council, and the Secretariat, as well as two subsidiary organs: the Economic Planning Commission and the Legal and Technical Commission, to carry out its functions and responsibilities under the Convention (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/struct-funct.pdf). The ISA also has an organ for carrying out activities in the Area directly: the Enterprise, and all States Parties are ipso facto members of the Authority (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). The ISA adopts and applies rules, regulations  and procedures for the management of activities in the Area, taking into account the protection of the marine environment, the equitable sharing of benefits, and the promotion of international cooperation ((https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba_25_c_wp1-e_0.pdf)). The ISA cooperates with other relevant international organizations and facilitates the exchange of scientific and technical information on activities in the Area (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/struct-funct.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNDP involves working with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through alignment, integration, and coherence for SDG implementation and review. This is structured under the Institutional and Coordination Mechanisms guidance note, which provides information on how countries have adapted their existing institutional and coordination frameworks or established new ones in order to implement the SDGs (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/publications/Institutional_Coordination_Mechanisms_GuidanceNote.pdf). The UNDP operates through the Executive Board of 36 members, which oversees and supports the activities of UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS, and UN Women. The UNDP also has a leadership team headed by an Administrator, who is the third highest-ranking official of the United Nations after the United Nations Secretary-General and Deputy Secretary-General (https://www.undp.org/organizational-chart). The UNDP leadership team consists of an Associate Administrator, five Assistant Administrators, a Director of the Bureau of External Relations and Advocacy, a Director of the Bureau of Management Services, and a Chief of Staff (https://www.undp.org/organizational-chart). It has six regional bureaus, each led by a Regional Director, who works closely with the Administrator and the leadership team to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the organization (https://www.undp.org/organizational-chart). There is also the UN Development Group (UNDG), which unites the 40 UN funds, programmes, specialized agencies, departments, and offices that play a role in development (https://unsceb.org/united-nations-development-group-undg). The UNDG is led by the UNDG Chair, who is the UNDP Administrator, and supported by the UNDG secretariat, which is hosted by UNDP. The UNDG ensures coordination and coherence among the UN entities at the global, regional, and country levels, and supports the Resident Coordinators and UN Country Teams in delivering effective and efficient support to countries (https://unsceb.org/about). The UNDP also has country offices and technical experts that support the UNDP's work in promoting sustainable development, democratic governance, and peacebuilding in 170 countries and territories (https://www.undp.org/acceleratorlabs/our-locations). Additionally, the UNDP hosts the UN Office for South-South Cooperation, which promotes and facilitates South-South and triangular cooperation among countries across the world (https://data.undp.org/insights/south-south-cooperation).

matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNDP involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, foundations, the academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that sustainable development goals are achieved in all activities and policies. matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNCTAD involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with Other Institutions within the United Nations System section of the General Assembly resolution 1995 (XIX), specifically in section II, paragraph 3 d (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf). UNCTAD also has a Trade and Development Board of 55 members, a secretariat headed by a Secretary-General, and various commissions, committees, and intergovernmental groups (section IV, paragraphs 32-40) (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/dtltlb2016d1_en.pdf). UNCTAD supports the implementation of the UN development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, offering research and analysis, technical assistance, intergovernmental consensus-building, and policy advice for developing countries (section II, paragraph 3 c) (https://elearning.unctad.org/pluginfile.php/34150/mod_page/content/12/UNCTAD_Competition_Consumer_Policies_short_course_part1.pdf). UNCTAD also leads the UN Inter-Agency Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity, involving 15 UN agencies, providing a mechanism for the coordination of trade and development operations at the national and regional levels within the UN system, as endorsed by the UN Chief Executives Board for Coordination (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/dom20092rev1_en.pdf). UNCTAD also cooperates with other international and regional organizations, such as WTO, OECD, World Bank, ILO, and CITES, addressing common trade and development challenges (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N16/459/44/PDF/N1645944.pdf?OpenElement).
decision_rationale: Relationship mechanism confirmed; retained with provenance metadata.

The UNIDO provides technical assistance, policy advice, and capacity-building services to its Member States, and supports the development, transfer and adaptation of industrial technology. The UNIDO gives due regard to the specific needs and priorities of the least developed countries, as well as to the principle of equitable geographical distribution (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2019-09/Upscaling%20TC_Sept%202019.pdf).

source_title: International Telecommunication Union (ITU) — Vertical Coordination evidence
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within ITU involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relations with the United Nations and Other International Organizations section of the ITU Constitution, specifically in Articles 48-50 (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU operates through the Plenipotentiary Conference of all the members, the Council of 48 members, and a secretariat headed by a Secretary-General (Articles 8-10) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU also has three Sectors: Radiocommunication, Telecommunication Standardization, and Telecommunication Development, each with its own conference, assembly, and bureau (Articles 11-13) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU assists members in the implementation of its standards, regulations, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (Article 14) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). ITU's work is organized around five strategic goals: Growth, Inclusiveness, Sustainability, Innovation, and Partnership, each overseen by a Deputy Secretary-General or an Assistant Secretary-General (https://sdgs.un.org/un-system-sdg-implementation/international-telecommunication-union-itu-24522). excerpt_<=50w: member Executive Board made up entirely of government representatives ([URI]).
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNICEF involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through delegation of authority, directing, and controlling. The body responsible for guiding UNICEF’s global work is a 36-member Executive Board made up entirely of government representatives (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/14411/file/2023-EB-Informal_Guide_2023-EN-2022.12.19.pdf). The executive board is responsible for establishing policies, approving new programmes, and making key decisions on administrative and financial plans. The Office of the Secretary of the Executive Board (OSEB) is responsible for maintaining an effective relationship between the Executive Board and the UNICEF secretariat 9https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/board-secretariat). UNICEF operates through its country offices that are responsible for carrying out the organization’s mission through a programme of cooperation developed in partnership with the host government (https://www.unicef.org/where-we-work). These programs are planned and delivered in five-year stints, and they are designed to focus on practical ways to improve the rights and prospects of women and children in that country (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/country-programme-documents). Regional Offices within host countries are responsible for guiding the delivery of this work, and they report and provide technical assistance to country offices when needed. There are also a range of specialized offices dotted around the world, such as UNICEF’s Supply Division which is responsible for procuring and delivering most of life-saving vaccines that UNICEF delivers in developing countries (https://www.unicef.org/supply/). The overall management and administration of UNICEF as a global organization takes place at its headquarters in New York, USA, where UNICEF’s global policy on children is formed under the supervision of the UNICEF executive team. UNICEF’s operational framework aims to help UNICEF staff and partners develop programmes across the social ecological model and the mental health continuum of prevention, promotion and treatment to improve the mental health and psychosocial wellbeing of children, adolescents and their caregivers globally, working together with a broad range of partners at the country, regional and global levels (https://www.unicef.org/reports/global-multisectoral-operational-framework).
