matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within ITC involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through strategic supervision, strategic management, and executive management. ITC is headed by an Executive Director who reports to the Secretary-General of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the Director-General of the World Trade Organization (WTO) (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). The ITC operates through the Joint Advisory Group of all the members, the Consultative Committee of the ITC Trust Fund, and a secretariat headed by the Executive Director (https://intracen.org/about-us/governance). ITC also has advisory bodies, such as the Global Network of Trade Promotion Organizations and the Global Network of Trade and Investment Support Institutions (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). ITC’s work is organised around four divisions, each overseen by a Director who works closely with the Executive Director to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). There is also the Senior Management Committee, consisting of the Executive Director, the Deputy Executive Director, the Directors of the four divisions, and the Chief of Staff, providing strategic and internal policy advice to the Executive Director on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of ITC and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). Additionally, a network of country offices and technical experts supports ITC’s work in promoting trade and private sector development as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.intracen.org/about-us/where-we-work). In addition, ITC coordinates with the United Nations and its agencies and is a partner of the Enhanced Integrated Framework, the Aid for Trade Initiative, and the Standards and Trade Development Facility (https://www.intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/partnerships).

matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within ITC involves working with different sectors and stakeholders within the trade and development domain, such as MSMEs, BSOs, governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN agencies to ensure that trade contributes to inclusive, sustainable and prosperous economies (https://intracen.org/our-work/partnerships). There is also the Management and Coordination Unit providing strategic and internal policy advice to the Executive Secretary. matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNU involves collaboration with affiliated institutions, such as the UN General Assembly and UNESCO. This is achieved through reporting, approving, devising, and implementing the principles, policies, budget, and work programme of the University as structured in Articles III-IX of the UNU Charter (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf). The UNU operates through the UNU Council of 12 appointed members, the UNU Rector, and three ex officio members (the UN Secretary-General, the UNESCO Director-General and the UNITAR Executive Director) (Articles III-VI). The UNU Council is responsible for devising the principles and policies that govern the University’s operations, and for considering and approving the UNU budget and work programme (Article IV). The UNU Council reports annually to the UN General Assembly, the UN Economic and Social Council, and the Executive Board of UNESCO (Article IV). The UNU Rector is the chief academic and administrative officer of the University and is appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations in consultation with the Director-General of UNESCO (Article V). The UNU Rector exercises the powers delegated to him or her by the UNU Council and is accountable to the UNU Council for the discharge of his or her functions (Article V). The UNU institutes and programmes are the operational units of the University and are established by the UNU Council in accordance with the principles and policies laid down by the Council (Article VII). The UNU institutes and programmes are headed by directors who are appointed by the UNU Rector in consultation with the UNU Council and are responsible to the UNU Rector for the academic and administrative management of their respective units (Article VII, paragraph 2). The UNU institutes and programmes carry out research, teaching, training, and capacity development activities in line with the UNU strategic plan and the UNU Council-approved work programme and budget (Article IX).

For example, UNU consults with the education sector to provide topical, timely and relevant postgraduate training and degree programmes (https://unu.edu/learning), with the social sector to promote human rights and peace (https://unu.edu/topics/human-rights), with the economic sector to foster innovation and sustainable development (https://unu.edu/topics/innovation), and with the environmental sector to protect the environment and natural resources (https://unu.edu/topics/natural-resources). matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within Ramsar Secretariat involves working with the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the Conference of the Contracting Parties (COP), the Standing Committee, the Scientific and Technical Review Panel (STRP), and the Contracting Parties to the Convention. This is achieved through organizing, supporting, and implementing the decisions and resolutions of the Convention's governing bodies. This is structured under the Secretariat section of the Convention text, specifically in Articles 8 and 9 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf). The Ramsar Secretariat is based at the headquarters of the IUCN in Gland, Switzerland, and follows IUCN procedures and policies on staffing and recruitment (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat is headed by a Secretary General, who is appointed by the Standing Committee with the approval of the COP, and reports to the Standing Committee. The Secretariat also consists of a Deputy Secretary General, a Senior Advisor on Environment and Development, and other staff members organized into five teams: Administrative and Financial Management, Communications, Convention and Policy Support, Regional Affairs, and Scientific and Technical Support (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/hr_org_chart_20230601.pdf). The Secretariat's main functions are to maintain the List of Wetlands of International Importance, help convene and organize the meetings of the COP, the Standing Committee, and the STRP, provide administrative and communications support to the STRP, provide administrative, scientific, and technical support to Contracting Parties, organize Ramsar Advisory Missions, develop cooperation with other conventions and institutions, and administer funding programmes (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat also works closely with the six International Organization Partners of the Convention: BirdLife International, International Water Management Institute, IUCN, Wetlands International, WWF International, and Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships/international-organization-partners).

source_title: Ramsar Convention on Wetlands Secretariat (Ramsar)  — Horizontal Coordination evidence
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the Ramsar Secretariat involves working with different partners and actors within the wetland domain, such as other global and regional conventions and agencies, national and local governments, civil society, private sector, and scientific and academic institutions to ensure that wetlands are conserved, wisely used, restored and valued by all. This coordination is supported by the Convention’s Strategic Plan 2016-2024 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/4th_strategic_plan_2016_2024_e.pdf). For example, the Ramsar Secretariat works with the biodiversity sector to support the implementation of other biodiversity-related conventions, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) or the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS), with the water sector to promote the integration of wetlands into water resources management, such as the Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) or the Water Framework Directive (WFD), with the climate change sector to enhance the role of wetlands in climate change mitigation and adaptation, such as the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) or the Paris Agreement, or with the disaster risk reduction sector to highlight the importance of wetlands in reducing disaster risks, such as the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction or the Hyogo Framework for Action (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships/partnerships-other-conventions). Horizontal coordination within the Ramsar Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other partners and actors, such as the Ramsar Regional Initiatives (https://www.ramsar.org/activity/ramsar-regional-initiatives) or the Wetlands for the Future Fund (https://www.ramsar.org/wetlands-future), (2) Participation in intergovernmental and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Biodiversity Liaison Group (https://www.cbd.int/blg/) or the Global Partnership for Plant Conservation (https://www.plants2020.net/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for wetland sector engagement with other partners and actors, such as the Ramsar Handbooks (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/pdf/lib/hbk4-18.pdf) or the Ramsar Advisory Missions (https://www.ramsar.org/activity/ramsar-advisory-missions), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for wetland issues and policies among other partners and actors, such as the World Wetlands Day (https://www.worldwetlandsday.org/) or the Ramsar Awards (https://www.ramsar.org/our-work/activities/ramsar-awards).

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within the Minamata Convention Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), other specialized agencies, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through delegation of authority, directing, and controlling (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/secretariat). The Secretariat operates under the leadership of the Executive Secretary, supported by a team of officers responsible for programme management, coordination, administration, communications, and knowledge management (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/secretariat). The Secretariat cooperates with the secretariats of the Basel, Rotterdam, and Stockholm conventions in areas of relevance to these conventions (https://minamataconvention.org/en/documents/cooperation-and-coordination-between-secretariats-minamata-convention-mercury-and-basel). It also facilitates assistance to Parties, particularly developing country Parties and Parties with economies in transition, on request, in the implementation of the Convention (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/43171/Minamata.pdf). The Secretariat's work is organized around key operational articles under the Minamata Convention, each overseen by a Programme Management Officer who works closely with the Executive Secretary to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/2021-07/Key%20control%20measures%20under%20the%20Minamata%20Convention_05%2016_EN.pdf). There is also a network of country offices and technical experts supporting the Secretariat's work in promoting health and well-being as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/secretariat). In addition, the Secretariat coordinates with the Global Environment Facility and the Special Programme to support capacity-building and technical assistance (https://minamataconvention.org/en/documents/international-cooperation-and-coordination).

matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the Minamata Convention Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the mercury domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to protect human health and the environment from the adverse effects of mercury. This coordination is guided by Article 24 of the Minamata Convention on Mercury (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf) as part of the functions of the Secretariat. matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNOOSA involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations and other specialised agencies, as well as regional and sub-regional organisations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through providing secretariat services, implementing decisions and recommendations, and facilitating partnerships and dialogue. UNOOSA operates through the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) of all the members, the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee and the Legal Subcommittee of 92 members, and a secretariat headed by a Director (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html). It also has working groups, expert groups, and other subsidiary bodies. The Office of the Director oversees and coordinates the strategic direction and operational priorities of UNOOSA (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/director.html); The Committee, Policy and Legal Affairs Section (CPLA) provides substantive, secretariat, organisational and administrative support to the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), its Scientific and Technical Subcommittee (STSC) and its Legal Subcommittee (LSC); The Space Applications Section (SAS) plans and implements the United Nations Programme on Space Applications to build national capability in the areas of basic sciences; The United Nations Platform for Space-based Information for Disaster Management and Emergency Response (UN-SPIDER) helps all countries access and use space-based information in all phases of the disaster management cycle, including prevention, preparedness, early warning, response and reconstruction; and the International Committee on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (ICG) brings together all global navigation satellite system (GNSS) providers to improve their uses for sustainable development and their compatibility (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html). The Director of UNOOSA is supported by the Senior Advisor on Space Science and Education, who provides expert advice and supports research relating to the activities and programmes carried out by the Office. The Senior Advisor also works closely with the Regional Centres for Space Science and Technology Education, affiliated to the United Nations (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html). UNOOSA also collaborates with space agencies and intergovernmental and non-governmental organisations involved in space-related activities (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/partnerships.html). In addition, UNOOSA maintains, on behalf of the United Nations Secretary-General, the Register of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/spaceobjectregister/index.html) and discharges the responsibilities of the Secretary-General under the UN treaties and principles on outer space.

The CND is responsible for deciding the scope of control of substances under the international drug control conventions, while the CCPCJ acts as a preparatory and implementing body for the United Nations Congress on Crime prevention and Criminal Justice (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/commissions/index.html).There is also the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) which is an independent and quasi-judicial monitoring body for the implementation of the United Nations international drug control conventions (https://www.incb.org/). UNODC's operational systems are based on the UNODC Strategy 2021-2025, which aims to equip UNODC to deliver effectively, efficiently, and with accountability, elevating support to Member States to build just, inclusive, and resilient societies. source_title: United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) — Horizontal Coordination evidence
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNODC involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the drug, crime, corruption and terrorism domains, such as governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN entities to ensure that the world is safer from these threats and that human rights, development and the rule of law are upheld in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by the UNODC Strategy 2021-2025 (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Advocacy-Section/UNODC-Strategy-WEB.pdf). For example, UNODC works with the health sector to address the world drug problem and provide prevention and treatment services (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/drug-prevention-and-treatment/index.html), with the justice sector to prevent and counter organized crime and terrorism and strengthen criminal justice systems (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/organized-crime/index.html, https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/terrorism/index.html, https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/justice-and-prison-reform/index.html), with the environment sector to combat crimes that affect the environment and biodiversity (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/wildlife-and-forest-crime/index.html), or with the education sector to promote a culture of lawfulness and prevent violence and crime among youth (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/). Horizontal coordination within UNODC can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Programme for Combating Wildlife and Forest Crime (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Wildlife/Annual_Report_GPWLFC2021.pdf) or the Global Maritime Crime Programme (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/piracy/index.html), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Coordination Group against Trafficking in Persons (https://icat.un.org/) or the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Coordination Compact (https://www.un.org/counterterrorism/global-ct-compact), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for drug, crime, corruption and terrorism sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Standards for the Treatment of Drug Use Disorders (https://www.unodc.org/documents/drug-prevention-and-treatment/UNODC-WHO_International_Standards_Treatment_Drug_Use_Disorders_April_2020.pdf) or the Global Judicial Integrity Network (https://www.unodc.org/ji/en/index.html), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for drug, crime, corruption and terrorism issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Drug Report (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/world-drug-report-2023.html) or the Education for Justice initiative (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/en/index.html).

For example, UNODC works with the health sector to address the world drug problem and provide prevention and treatment services (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/drug-prevention-and-treatment/index.html), with the justice sector to prevent and counter organized crime and terrorism and strengthen criminal justice systems (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/organized-crime/index.html, https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/terrorism/index.html, https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/justice-and-prison-reform/index.html), with the environment sector to combat crimes that affect the environment and biodiversity (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/wildlife-and-forest-crime/index.html), or with the education sector to promote a culture of lawfulness and prevent violence and crime among youth (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/). Horizontal coordination within UNODC can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Programme for Combating Wildlife and Forest Crime (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Wildlife/Annual_Report_GPWLFC2021.pdf) or the Global Maritime Crime Programme (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/piracy/index.html), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Coordination Group against Trafficking in Persons (https://icat.un.org/) or the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Coordination Compact (https://www.un.org/counterterrorism/global-ct-compact), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for drug, crime, corruption and terrorism sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Standards for the Treatment of Drug Use Disorders (https://www.unodc.org/documents/drug-prevention-and-treatment/UNODC-WHO_International_Standards_Treatment_Drug_Use_Disorders_April_2020.pdf) or the Global Judicial Integrity Network (https://www.unodc.org/ji/en/index.html), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for drug, crime, corruption and terrorism issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Drug Report (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/world-drug-report-2023.html) or the Education for Justice initiative (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/en/index.html).

source_title: Climate Change Secretariat — Horizontal Coordination evidence
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the UNFCCC involves collaboration across various sectors and stakeholders in the climate change arena, including governments, institutions, civil society, the private sector, and the scientific community. This coordination is structured under the Institutional and Financial Arrangements section of the Convention, specifically outlined in Articles 7-11 (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf). The UNFCCC has established the Conference of the Parties (COP) as its supreme decision-making body, which adopts decisions and protocols for implementing the Convention's objectives and principles. It also has set up two subsidiary bodies: the Subsidiary Body for Scientific and Technological Advice (SBSTA) and the Subsidiary Body for Implementation (SBI), to support the COP (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf). Furthermore, the UNFCCC defines a financial mechanism to aid developing countries and a mechanism for resolving questions about Convention implementation (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf). It also collaborates with the IPCC to ensure scientific coherence, with the GEF (https://ccsr.aori.u-tokyo.ac.jp/old/unfccc4/pdfs/unfccc.int/resource/docs/cop2/15a01.pdf) and GCF (https://www.ciesin.columbia.edu/repository/entri/docs/cop/FCCC_COP17_dec03.pdf) for financial resources and with the Technology Mechanism for climate technology development and transfer, as detailed in various decisions decision 1/CP.16 (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/2010/cop16/eng/07a01.pdf). This structure facilitates information exchange and communication on actions addressing climate change and its impacts.

matrix_cell_text_full: The UNFCCC Secretariat maintains collaborative relationships with various UN agencies and international organizations to advance climate action and sustainable development (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/sbsta2022_inf01pdf.pdf). This collaboration includes working with the UN Development Programme (UNDP) on implementing NDCs under the Paris Agreement, with UNESCO to promote climate change education and research, and with the WHO and WMO to address health risks and improve climate data related to climate change (https://unfccc.int/documents/628347). Additionally, the Secretariat aligns with the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) as part of the Rio Conventions from the 1992 Earth Summit. They focus on tackling climate change, desertification, and biodiversity loss through initiatives like land degradation neutrality and sustainable management. Strengthened by a 2023 memorandum of understanding, their cooperation is guided by the Joint Liaison Group (JLG), established to enhance synergy and coordination among the Rio Conventions (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/publications/adaptation_eng.pdf).

excerpt_<=50w: Strategies: instrument portfolio and governance tools used to pursue objectives (e.g., standards, MRV, compliance, capacity building).
matrix_cell_text_full: The UNFCCC Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a six-year Strategic Plan, revised biennially by the Conference of the Parties, which establishes the secretariat's vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. This plan, applicable for 2020-2025, aligns with the Paris Agreement and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, detailed in decision 18/CP.25. Secondly, a biennial programme budget and workplan, devised by the secretariat and ratified by the Conference of the Parties, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/sbi2021_04E.pdf). The current budget and workplan for 2022-2023 are tailored to the Parties' needs and stakeholders' priorities, as outlined in decision FCCC/SBI/2021/4/Add (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/sbi2022_inf03.pdf). It also maintains the registry for Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) established under the Paris Agreement, a key aspect of the implementation of the Paris Agreement (https://www4.unfccc.int/sites/ndcstaging/Pages/Home.aspx?_gl=1*ewhacw*_ga*MjAxOTI0NTk2NC4xNzAxOTkxOTI3*_ga_7ZZWT14N79*MTcwMTk5MTkyOC4xLjEuMTcwMTk5ODIxNC4wLjAuMA..). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Convention, the Kyoto Protocol, and the Paris Agreement, addressing adaptation, mitigation, finance, technology, transparency, and capacity-building, with key instruments listed here (https://sdg.iisd.org/news/unfccc-closes-2020-with-28-long-term-low-emission-development-strategies/).

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNFCCC involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with Other Bodies section of the Convention, specifically in Articles 7, 8, 11, and 16. The UNFCCC operates through a Conference of the Parties (COP) of all the members, a Bureau of 11 members, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Secretary (Articles 7 and 8). The UNFCCC also has two subsidiary bodies for scientific and technological advice (SBSTA) and for implementation (SBI), as well as other subsidiary bodies and mechanisms as needed (Articles 9 and 10). The UNFCCC facilitates the provision of financial resources and the transfer of technology to developing country Parties, through a financial mechanism operated by an entity or entities designated by the COP (Article 11). The UNFCCC also adopts and amends annexes to the Convention, which may include lists of Parties with different commitments or responsibilities in accordance with the rules of procedure and the principles of the Convention (Article 16). (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf)

excerpt_<=50w: Defined objectives: stated institutional purposes/goals expressed in founding and/or strategic texts.
matrix_cell_text_full: OHCHR, as mandated by General Assembly Resolution 48/141, aims to promote and protect all human rights. Its objectives include promoting all civil, cultural, economic, political, and social rights (paragraph 4 a), carrying out tasks assigned by UN bodies in human rights and making recommendations (paragraph 4 b), promoting the right to development and enhancing support from UN bodies (paragraph 4 c), providing advisory services and technical and financial assistance to support human rights actions and programs (paragraph 4 d), coordinating UN education and public information programmes in human rights (paragraph 4 e), actively working to remove obstacles and prevent human rights violations (paragraph 4 f), engaging in dialogue with governments for human rights implementation (paragraph 4 g), enhancing international cooperation for human rights promotion and protection (paragraph 4 h), coordinating human rights activities across the UN system (paragraph 4 i), streamlining the UN human rights machinery for improved efficiency (paragraph 4 j), and overseeing the Centre for Human Rights (paragraph 4 k). These roles establish the OHCHR as the key UN entity responsible for human rights activities under the Secretary-General's direction. (https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/atf/cf/%7B65BFCF9B-6D27-4E9C-8CD3-CF6E4FF96FF9%7D/a_res_48_141.pdf)

source_title: This coordination is guided by the mandate of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, as established in the
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within OHCHR involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the human rights domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that human rights are respected, protected, and fulfilled in all policies and that human rights policies are consistent with other sectoral policies. This coordination is guided by the mandate of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, as established in the General Assembly resolution 48/141 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). For example, OHCHR works with the justice sector to promote the rule of law and access to justice for all (https://unsceb.org/sites/default/files/imported_files/Annex2Activitiesfinal7June_0.pdf), with the development sector to integrate human rights into the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.ohchr.org/en/sdgs/ohchrs-work-2030-agenda-sustainable-developmentx), or with the peace and security sector to prevent and respond to human rights violations in conflict and post-conflict situations (https://peacemaker.un.org/sites/peacemaker.un.org/files/DPPA-OHCHR-Joint-Practice-Note.pdf). Horizontal coordination within OHCHR can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UN Common Country Analysis (https://procurement-notices.undp.org/view_file.cfm?doc_id=194928) and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework with UNCTs (https://unsdg.un.org/2030-agenda/cooperation-framework), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral mechanisms, networks, and platforms, such as the Human Rights Council or the UN Human Rights Treaty Bodies (https://www.ohchr.org/EN/HRBodies/Pages/HumanRightsBodies.aspx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for human rights mainstreaming and engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Human Rights Indicators (https://www.ohchr.org/EN/Issues/Indicators/Pages/HRIndicatorsIndex.aspx) or the Human Rights Based Approach to Development Cooperation (https://www.ohchr.org/Documents/Publications/FAQen.pdf), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for human rights issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Human Rights Day (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us/human-rights-day) or the Annual Report of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/publications/ohchr-reports/ohchr-report-2022.pdf). The OHCHR provides leadership and coordination on matters related to human rights, supports the development and implementation of human rights norms and standards, provides technical assistance and capacity-building to States and other actors, and monitors and reports on human rights situations (https://www.ohchr.org/EN/AboutUs/Pages/WhatWeDo.aspx). OHCHR facilitates the participation of various actors in the human rights sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on human rights matters (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/OHCHRreport2022/documents/UN-Human-Rights-at-headquarters-.pdf).

excerpt_<=50w: Inter‑institutional relationships: formalised cooperation with other bodies (e.g., MoUs, joint programmes, agreements; partner type × mechanism × year).
matrix_cell_text_full: OHCHR collaborates with various organizations to promote and protect human rights (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us/what-we-do). It works with the Human Rights Council (HRC), established in 2006 by resolution 60/251, serving as the main intergovernmental body responsible for human rights issues (https://www.dfat.gov.au/sites/default/files/ohchr-assessment.pdf) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N05/502/66/PDF/N0550266.pdf?OpenElement). As the secretariat of the HRC, OHCHR's relationship with the Council is based on resolution 48/141, paragraph 4 (b), which entrusts the High Commissioner with the task of making recommendations to the competent bodies of the UN system in the field of human rights (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, OHCHR supports the treaty bodies and special procedures, providing substantive and technical assistance for the monitoring and implementation of international human rights instruments and standards, as mandated by resolution 48/141, paragraph 4 (a) and (d) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). It also cooperates with UN agencies, funds and programmes, as well as regional and national human rights institutions, civil society organizations, and other actors, to enhance coordination and effectiveness of human rights activities throughout the UN system, as stipulated by resolution 48/141, paragraph 4 (h) and (i) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). Moreover, OHCHR participates in the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), offering technical and logistical support for the peer review mechanism of the human rights situation of all UN Member States, as established by resolution 60/251, paragraph 5 (e) (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/hrcouncil/docs/a.res.60.251_en.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: OHCHR collaborates with various organizations to promote and protect human rights (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us/what-we-do). It works with the Human Rights Council (HRC), established in 2006 by resolution 60/251, serving as the main intergovernmental body responsible for human rights issues (https://www.dfat.gov.au/sites/default/files/ohchr-assessment.pdf) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N05/502/66/PDF/N0550266.pdf?OpenElement). As the secretariat of the HRC, OHCHR's relationship with the Council is based on resolution 48/141, paragraph 4 (b), which entrusts the High Commissioner with the task of making recommendations to the competent bodies of the UN system in the field of human rights (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, OHCHR supports the treaty bodies and special procedures, providing substantive and technical assistance for the monitoring and implementation of international human rights instruments and standards, as mandated by resolution 48/141, paragraph 4 (a) and (d) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). It also cooperates with UN agencies, funds and programmes, as well as regional and national human rights institutions, civil society organizations, and other actors, to enhance coordination and effectiveness of human rights activities throughout the UN system, as stipulated by resolution 48/141, paragraph 4 (h) and (i) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). Moreover, OHCHR participates in the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), offering technical and logistical support for the peer review mechanism of the human rights situation of all UN Member States, as established by resolution 60/251, paragraph 5 (e) (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/hrcouncil/docs/a.res.60.251_en.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: OHCHR derives its mandate from the Charter of the United Nations, which establishes the promotion and protection of human rights as one of the purposes and principles of the UN, particularly chapter 1 (article 1), chapter 3 (article 13), chapter 9 (article 53),  chapter 10 (article 62 & 68), chapter 12 (article 76) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/publication/ctc/uncharter.pdf). Resolution A/RES/48/141 adopted by the UN General Assembly established the post of High Commissioner for the promotion and protection of all human rights and outlined the mandate, functions, and responsibilities of the High Commissioner, as well as the location and resources of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/atf/cf/%7B65BFCF9B-6D27-4E9C-8CD3-CF6E4FF96FF9%7D/a_res_48_141.pdf). Additionally, OHCHR's jurisdiction is influenced by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2021/03/udhr.pdf) and the international human rights treaties (https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/human-rights), which confer legal form on inherent human rights and develop the body of international human rights law. The treaties, particularly the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/ccpr.pdf) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/cescr.pdf), outline the obligations and duties of States to respect, protect and fulfil human rights. OHCHR also supports the implementation of the UN's human rights mechanisms and procedures, such as the Human Rights Council, the treaty bodies, the special procedures, and the Universal Periodic Review, which provide further legal frameworks for OHCHR's jurisdiction over specific human rights issues and situations (https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-and-mechanisms/international-human-rights-law).

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within OHCHR involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through dialogue, cooperation, and assistance (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/english/planaction.pdf). This is structured under the Establishment of the post of High Commissioner for the promotion and protection of all human rights section of the General Assembly Resolution 48/141, specifically in paragraphs 2-5 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). The OHCHR operates under the direction and authority of the Secretary-General, and reports annually to the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council (paragraph 2). The OHCHR also works with the Human Rights Council, the treaty bodies, and the special procedures, providing substantive and technical support for the monitoring and implementation of international human rights standards (paragraph 4 a and d). The OHCHR cooperates with UN agencies, funds and programmes, as well as regional and national human rights institutions, civil society organizations, and other actors, to enhance coordination and effectiveness of human rights activities throughout the UN system (paragraph 4 h and i). OHCHR's work is organized around seven regions, each overseen by a Regional Representative who works closely with the High Commissioner to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Office (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us/where-we-work). There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the High Commissioner, Deputy High Commissioner, Assistant Secretary-General, and Directors of the thematic and geographic divisions) providing strategic and operational guidance to the High Commissioner on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of OHCHR; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Office and the governing bodies (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/OHCHRreport2021/documents/OHCHR_AR-2021_Management.pdf). Also, a network of country offices and human rights advisers supports the OHCHR's work in promoting and protecting human rights as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.ohchr.org/EN/Countries/Pages/WorkInField.aspx). Additionally, OHCHR participates in the Universal Periodic Review, offering technical and logistical support for the peer review mechanism of the human rights situation of all UN Member States, as established by resolution 60/251, paragraph 5 (e) (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/hrcouncil/docs/a.res.60.251_en.pdf).

excerpt_full: Vertical coordination within OHCHR involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through dialogue, cooperation, and assistance (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/english/planaction.pdf). This is structured under the Establishment of the post of High Commissioner for the promotion and protection of all human rights section of the General Assembly Resolution 48/141, specifically in paragraphs 2-5 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N94/012/56/PDF/N9401256.pdf?OpenElement). The OHCHR operates under the direction and authority of the Secretary-General, and reports annually to the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council (paragraph 2). The OHCHR also works with the Human Rights Council, the treaty bodies, and the special procedures, providing substantive and technical support for the monitoring and implementation of international human rights standards (paragraph 4 a and d). The OHCHR cooperates with UN agencies, funds and programmes, as well as regional and national human rights institutions, civil society organizations, and other actors, to enhance coordination and effectiveness of human rights activities throughout the UN system (paragraph 4 h and i). OHCHR's work is organized around seven regions, each overseen by a Regional Representative who works closely with the High Commissioner to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Office (https://www.ohchr.org/en/about-us/where-we-work). There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the High Commissioner, Deputy High Commissioner, Assistant Secretary-General, and Directors of the thematic and geographic divisions) providing strategic and operational guidance to the High Commissioner on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of OHCHR; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Office and the governing bodies (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/OHCHRreport2021/documents/OHCHR_AR-2021_Management.pdf). Also, a network of country offices and human rights advisers supports the OHCHR's work in promoting and protecting human rights as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.ohchr.org/EN/Countries/Pages/WorkInField.aspx). Additionally, OHCHR participates in the Universal Periodic Review, offering technical and logistical support for the peer review mechanism of the human rights situation of all UN Member States, as established by resolution 60/251, paragraph 5 (e) (https://www2.ohchr.org/english/bodies/hrcouncil/docs/a.res.60.251_en.pdf).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the IMO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the maritime domain, such as governments, the shipping industry, port authorities, maritime training institutions, and other UN agencies to ensure that maritime safety, security, and environmental protection are integrated into all policies (https://www.un.org/en/chronicle/article/role-international-maritime-organization-preventing-pollution-worlds-oceans-ships-and-shipping). This coordination is guided by Articles 25 and 66 of the Convention on the International Maritime Organization (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf). For example, the IMO works with the education sector to promote maritime training and capacity building through institutions like the World Maritime University (WMU) and the International Maritime Law Institute (IMLI) (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/WMUandIMLI.aspx), with the environmental sector to address issues like biofouling and greenhouse gas emissions through initiatives like the GloFouling Partnerships project (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/PartnershipsProjects/Pages/GloFouling-Project.aspx), or with the development sector to enhance maritime capabilities in regions like Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean through its Integrated Technical Cooperation Programme (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/ITCP.aspx). Horizontal coordination within the IMO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global SAR Plan (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Safety/Pages/GlobalSARPlan.aspx), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Global Integrated Shipping Information System (https://gisis.imo.org/Public/Default.aspx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for maritime sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) COde (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Security/Pages/SOLAS-XI-2%20ISPS%20Code.aspx) , (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for maritime issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Day of the Seafarer (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Events/Pages/Day-of-the-Seafarer-2024.aspx). The IMO provides leadership and direction on matters critical to maritime safety and security, shapes the maritime research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses maritime trends (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/Geo-Coverage.aspx). The IMO facilitates the participation of various actors in the maritime sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on maritime matters (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/TechnicalCooperation/Pages/Geo-Coverage.aspx)

matrix_cell_text_full: The IMO collaborates with a diverse array of organizations to support its maritime governance objectives. It maintains formal relations with 66 intergovernmental organizations, as governed by Articles 25 and 66 of the Convention on the International Maritime Organization (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf), and detailed in resolution A.1168(32) adopted by the IMO Assembly on 15 December 20211 (https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/KnowledgeCentre/IndexofIMOResolutions/AssemblyDocuments/A.1168(32).pdf). This includes cooperation with the United Nations (UN), with the relationship between the IMO and the UN outlined in Part XV of the IMO Convention, specifically Article 592 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf). The IMO also engages with non-governmental international organizations that contribute expert advice to IMO Member States on their respective areas of work, with formal relations established as per the provisions contained in the Rules and Guidelines for Consultative Status (https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/OurWork/ERO/Documents/RULES%20AND%20GUIDELINES%20FOR%20CONSULTATIVE%20STATUS%20-%20December%202019.pdf). Additionally, the IMO supports the implementation of the UN Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development, collaborating with various stakeholders to enhance ocean governance3. These relationships enable the IMO to fulfill its mandate, ensuring the safety, security, and environmental performance of international shipping, and facilitating global maritime cooperation1. The IMO collborates with the  IOC inl research efforts to understand and address human impacts on the ocean’s ecosystems (The IOC coordinates global research efforts to understand and address human impacts on the ocean’s ecosystems, where the IMO contributes with its expertise on maritime aspects1.),  including the  Global Ocean Oxygen Decade  (GOOD) (https://www.ioc.unesco.org/en/global-ocean-oxygen-decade). IMO collabortes with the IOC, IAEA, UNEP, WMO, and others on the  GESAMP Working Group 45 on Climate Change and Greenhouse Gas Related Impacts on Contaminants in the Ocean (http://www.gesamp.org/work/groups/wg-45-ghg-impacts-on-contaminants-in-the-ocean). IMO als collaboration with GEF and UNDP to protect marine biodiversity by preventing the transfer of invasive aquatic species through the GloFouling Partnership project (https://www.google.com/search?client=safari&rls=en&q=GloFouling+Partnerships&ie=UTF-8&oe=UTF-8) .

excerpt_<=50w: Strategies: instrument portfolio and governance tools used to pursue objectives (e.g., standards, MRV, compliance, capacity building).
matrix_cell_text_full: IMO implements its objectives and mandates through various strategies, such as a six-year Strategic Plan adopted by the IMO Assembly every two years that defines the mission, vision, principles, directions, indicators, and outputs of the Organization. The current plan for the six-year period 2024 to 2029 is aligned with the UN Sustainable Development Goals and detailed in [resolution A.1149 (32)] (https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/PressBriefings/pages/IMO-Assembly-adopts-budget,-strategic-plan.aspx). Another strategy is a biennial budget and work program which is prepared by the IMO Council and approved by the IMO Assembly, and outlines the resources, accomplishments, and achievements for each output of the Strategic Plan (https://www.imo.org/en/MediaCentre/PressBriefings/pages/IMO-Assembly-adopts-budget,-strategic-plan.aspx). The current program reflects the needs and priorities of the members and the industry and detailed in [resolution A.1150 (32)]. Thirdly, the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships sets a vision to reduce GHG emissions from international shipping and phase them out as soon as possible, with specific targets for carbon intensity reduction and the uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies (https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/OurWork/Environment/Documents/annex/MEPC%2080/Annex%2015.pdf). Additionally, the IMO maintains various regulatory frameworks, such as the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) and the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), which are periodically updated to meet new challenges and technologies in maritime transport (https://www.un.org/depts/los/consultative_process/mar_sec_submissions/imo.pdf).

excerpt_<=50w: Source of jurisdiction: formal legal basis enabling authority (treaty/charter article(s) or constitutive resolution reference).
matrix_cell_text_full: The IMO's jurisdiction is established by the Convention for the creation of the International Maritime Organization (IMO), adopted at a diplomatic conference held in Geneva in 1948 under the auspices of the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf). The Convention, which entered into force on 17 March 1958, defines the IMO's mandate, particularly in Article 1, which outlines its purposes, including cooperation among governments in the field of governmental regulation and practices relating to technical matters of all kinds affecting shipping engaged in international trade (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf). Furthermore, the IMO's role in implementing regulations is reinforced by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), specifically Article 94, which mandates states to effectively exercise jurisdiction and control over ships flying their flag (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/unclos_e.pdf). This includes the duty of the flag State to implement regulations recognized as IMO shipping rules and standards (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/unclos_e.pdf). Furthermore, various IMO conventions such as SOLAS 1974, MARPOL, STCW 1978, and others influences IMO's mandate, under which administrations are responsible for implementing laws and regulations to ensure maritime safety and environmental protection (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/IIIS/Pages/default.aspx). In addtion several Protocols, Amendments, Recommendations, codes and roslutios of the IMOenabling it to function as a global standard-setter for maritime safety, security, and environmental performance. (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/Environment/Pages/International-Conventions,-Protocols-and-Codes.aspx)

source_title: committees, Legal Committee, Technical Cooperation Committe, Facilitation Committee and the Secretariat that address various aspects of maritime safety,
excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within IMO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with Other Organizations section of the IMCO Convention, specifically in Articles 45-48. The IMO operates through an Assembly of all the members, a Council of 40 members, and a Secretary-General (Articles 12-18 of the Convention) The IMO operates through its Assembly, Council, and a series of committees and sub-committees, Legal Committee, Technical Cooperation Committe, Facilitation Committee and the Secretariat that address various aspects of maritime safety, security, and environmental protection (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/Structure.aspx). It also works closely with Member States to implement and enforce international maritime conventions and standards (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%201276/volume-1276-I-4214-English.pdf).  . The IMO also has committees, sub-committees, and other subsidiary bodies (Articles 19-24). The IMO assists members in the implementation of its conventions, codes, standards, and guidelines, and provides technical assistance and capacity building upon request (Articles 25-26).  This coordination is also structured under the IMO’s framework for cooperation with intergovernmental organizations, as established in resolution A.1168(32) adopted by the IMO Assembly (https://wwwcdn.imo.org/localresources/en/KnowledgeCentre/IndexofIMOResolutions/AssemblyDocuments/A.1168(32).pdf).  The World Maritime University (WMU) and the IMO International Maritime Law Institute (IMLI) are key educational pillars of the IMO, fostering expertise and knowledge in maritime law and policy (https://www.imo.org/en/About/Pages/WMUandIMLI.aspx). There are also some affliated bodies to the IMO including  the Global MTCC Network (GMN)  focusing on improving energy efficiency in the maritime sector and supports developing regions in moving towards maritime decarbonization (https://www.imo.org/en/OurWork/PartnershipsProjects/Pages/IMO-EuropeanUnionProject.aspx) . IMO has regional coordinators/advisors for technical cooperation activities, in Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, Kenya, Philippines and Trinidad and Tobago (https://www.imo.org/en/about/pages/structure.aspx#9). The IMO operates a network of regional centers, including NOWPAP MERRAC, REMPEITC-Caribe, MEMAC, ROPME, REMPEC, PEMSEA, and PERSGA, which play crucial roles in regional maritime safety, security, and environmental protection efforts

matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within DOALOS involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the ocean domain, such as fisheries, environment, security, trade, science, private sector, civil society, and other UN agencies to ensure that ocean affairs and the law of the sea are integrated into all policies (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). This is structured under the section 9.5 of the document, which outlines the inter-agency cooperation and coordination of the Division (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en).  This coordination is guided by the mandate of DOALOS to promote the uniform and consistent application of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and related agreements (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). The DOALOS participates in the inter-agency mechanism UN-Oceans, which seeks to enhance the coordination, coherence and effectiveness of competent organizations of the United Nations system and the International Seabed Authority on ocean issues (https://www.un.org/depts/los/coop_coor/un_oceans.htm). The DOALOS also liaises with other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, non-governmental organizations, and academic institutions on matters related to ocean affairs and the law of the sea (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/). DOALOS conducts consultations with regional intergovernmental organizations and others in Africa, Asia-Pacific, and Latin America/Caribben to gain insight in ongoing regional programmes and activities on ocean governance and to identify capacity-building needs and priorities in the region (https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/consultations).  The DOALOS facilitates the exchange of information and best practices among governments and other interested parties on issues under its consideration. For example, DOALOS works with the scientific community to support marine scientific research and with environmental sectors to address marine biodiversity conservation (https://www.un.org/depts/los/general_assembly/general_assembly.htm). Horizontal coordination within DOALOS can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders (https://www.un.org/depts/los/biodiversity/prepcom.htm), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as UN-Oceans, the inter-agency coordination mechanism on ocean and coastal issues (https://www.un.org/depts/los/consultative_process/consultative_process.htm), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for engagement with other sectors and stakeholders (https://www.un.org/depts/los/), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for ocean issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/5214236EGM%20Report%20on%20Oceans.pdf). DOALOS provides leadership and direction on matters critical to oceans and the law of the sea, shapes the ocean governance research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses trends related to oceans and maritime affairs (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos). DOALOS facilitates the participation of various actors in the ocean sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on ocean matters (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos).

matrix_cell_text_full: DOALOS collaborates with key organizations to support ocean governance. It liaises with the International Seabed Authority (ISA), implementing a relationship agreement effective since 25 July 1996, as per UNCLOS Annex III Article 4 and the 1994 Agreement Article 177, detailed in resolution 48/263 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n94/332/98/pdf/n9433298.pdf?token=YhD8GNV5K9pWhEpVuW&fe=true). Similarly, DOALOS maintains a relationship with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), providing administrative support based on an agreement aligned with the Tribunal's Statute Article 5 (https://www.itlos.org/fileadmin/itlos/documents/basic_texts/statute_en.pdf) and the 1994 Agreement Article 178, detailed in resolution 51/204 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n97/769/51/pdf/n9776951.pdf?token=FFhG7JOPZn4wAkSphS&fe=true). Additionally, DOALOS supports the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS) by providing technical assistance and facilities, aiding developing states in their submissions, with its functions detailed in CLCS Rules of Procedure and Annex II of UNCLOS (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n08/309/23/pdf/n0830923.pdf?token=KvJ2MrzDVqwVV4OiQU&fe=true). It also services the Informal Consultative Process (ICP) on Oceans and the Law of the Sea, preparing related reports, with its mandate in resolution 54/33 (http://www.worldlii.org/int/other/UNGA/1999/71.pdf). Moreover, DOALOS facilitates the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, established in 2002, to enhance scientific understanding and decision-making, involving a Group of Experts and a Working Group, with terms detailed in resolution 57/141 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf). Moreover, DOALOS provides capacity-building assistance to developing countries in the field of ocean affairs and the law of the sea, through training, fellowships, technical assistance, and financial support (https://www.un.org/ola/en/content/div-doalos).

matrix_cell_text_full: DOALOS engages in vertical coordination with various levels of institutions, including the United Nations, specialized agencies, regional bodies, national governments, and local authorities, as outlined in section 9.2 of its governing document.  The structure of this coordination is outlined in the Secretary-General's Bulletin ST/SGB/2021/1, which organizes the Office of Legal Affairs and details the functions of DOALOS (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en). It maintains liaison with entities like the International Seabed Authority and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, and provides support to the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, the General Assembly, and the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, incuding Socioeconomic Aspects (section 9.5) (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en). DOALOS's work is structured to ensure the consistent application of the Convention across various levels of governance, supporting the development of maritime policies that align with international law (https://www.un.org/depts/los/doalos_activities/about_doalos.htm). The Division also engages with the International Seabed Authority and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, maintaining liaison and providing administrative support as necessary¹. excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full:
Horizontal coordination within the FAO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the food and agriculture domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that food security and nutrition are considered in all policies and that agricultural policies are aligned with other sectoral policies (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/en/). This coordination is guided by Article 1 of the Constitution of the FAO (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf). For example, FAO works with the environmental sector to address climate change impacts on food security (https://www.fao.org/3/i5188e/I5188E.pdf), or with the economic sector to enhance rural development and livelihoods (https://www.fao.org/agrifood-economics/areas-of-work/en/), and with the ocean sector  to enhance underwater food systems and ensure sustainable aquatic food production for the growing global population (https://news.un.org/en/story/2022/06/1121602). Horizontal coordination within FAO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Action Programme on Food Security and Nutrition in Small Island States (https://www.fao.org/3/i7297e/i7297e.pdf), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, such as the Committee on World Food Security (https://www.fao.org/sustainable-development-goals-helpdesk/champion/article-detail/committee-on-world-food-security/en), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, such as the Voluntary Guidelines on Food Systems and Nutrition (https://www.fao.org/cfs/vgfsn/en/),
(4) Advocacy campaigns like World Food Day (https://www.fao.org/newsroom/detail/world-food-day--global-ceremony-highlights-water-s-role-against-troubled-backdrop/en) or The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report (https://www.fao.org/publications/home/fao-flagship-publications/the-state-of-food-security-and-nutrition-in-the-world/en). The FAO provides leadership on global food security, shapes the agricultural research agenda, sets standards, offers evidence-based policy options, provides technical support, and monitors food and nutrition trends (https://www.fao.org/3/cb7099en/cb7099en.pdf). It facilitates the participation of diverse actors in the agricultural sector and enhances cooperation within the UN system on food and agriculture matters (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/en/)

igo: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
source_title: constitution, the FAO maintains relations with the United Nations as a specialized agency (Article XII), and with other international, regional, and national organizations and authorities related to food and agriculture (Article XIII)
excerpt_<=50w: Inter‑institutional relationships: formalised cooperation with other bodies (e.g., MoUs, joint programmes, agreements; partner type × mechanism × year).
matrix_cell_text_full:
As stated in its constitution, the FAO maintains relations with the United Nations as a specialized agency (Article XII), and with other international, regional, and national organizations and authorities related to food and agriculture (Article XIII). The FAO may also enter into agreements with Member Nations for the establishment of international institutions dealing with food and agriculture (Article XV) (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf). The FAO engages with a diverse array of institutions to advance its mission. It partners with Member States and various stakeholders, including civil society, the private sector, academia, and research centers, to combat food insecurity and malnutrition (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/en/). The FAO’s collaboration with academia and research institutions is crucial for mobilizing knowledge and innovations, as well as for providing evidence-based solutions to policy processes (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/academia/en/). 
Furthermore, the FAO works closely with international organizations to facilitate partnerships for food and nutrition security, agriculture, and rural development3. For instance, the FAO’s Strategy for Private Sector Engagement aims to strengthen strategic engagement with the private sector towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (https://doi.org/10.4060/cb3352en). In addition, the FAO is involved in South-South Cooperation, which is a key instrument for delivering on its mandate and achieving the SDGs (https://www.fao.org/3/i5163e/i5163e.pdf). This cooperation is facilitated through the FAO’s Partnerships and UN Collaboration Division, which develops strategic cooperation with non-state actors (https://www.fao.org/3/cc7997en/cc7997en.pdf).

source_title: It also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies that assist members in implementing standards, policies, and programmes,
excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full:
The FAO’s vertical coordination involves collaboration with various levels of governance and institutions, including the United Nations, specialized agencies, regional and intergovernmental organizations, national governments, and local authorities. The FAO operates through the Conference of all the members, the Council, and a secretariat headed by a Director-General  (Articles III, IV, V, and VII). It also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies that assist members in implementing standards, policies, and programmes, providing technical cooperation and assistance upon request (https://www.fao.org/3/k8024e/k8024e.pdf)
The FAO’s work is organized around five major programme areas, each overseen by a Deputy Director-General who works closely with the Director-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.fao.org/3/ne576en/ne576en.pdf). The Senior Management Team, consisting of the Director-General and Deputy Directors-General, provides strategic and operational guidance to ensure coherence and alignment between the different departments and divisions of the Organization and the governing bodies https://www.fao.org/about/org-chart/en/). Furthermore, the FAO’s structure includes Regional, Liaison, and Country Offices, Subregional Offices, and Partnership and Liaison Offices, which facilitate the FAO’s work on the ground, ensuring that its global mandates are translated into local action (https://www.fao.org/about/who-we-are/worldwide-offices/en/). The Governing Bodies, such as the Conference, Council, Regional Conferences, Committee on World Food Security, Council Committees, and Technical Committees (https://www.fao.org/unfao/govbodies/home/en/) and the Statutory Bodies (https://www.fao.org/unfao/govbodies/gsb-subject-matter/subject-matter/en/) , play a pivotal role in decision-making and oversight. The Oversight Advisory Committee further supports this structure by providing independent advice on issues related to governance, risk management, and internal control https://www.fao.org/about/oversight-advisory-committee/en/). In alignment with the UN Development System reform, the FAO leverages the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework and UN Common Country Analysis to integrate food security and agrifood systems transformation within the broader UN support to national governments (https://www.fao.org/partnerships/fao-un-system/en). This approach ensures that the FAO’s efforts are harmonized with the UN’s overarching goals and contribute effectively to sustainable development initiatives globally.

As defined in Paragraph 2 of Resolution 4 (EC-XL) of the WMO Executive Council (https://archive.ipcc.ch/docs/WMO_resolution4_on_IPCC_1988.pdf), the IPCC's objectives include the following main tasks:
(1) Assessing the scientific information that is related to the various components of the climate change issue, such as emissions of major greenhouse gases and modification of the Earth's radiation balance resulting therefrom, and the environmental and socio-economic consequences of climate change; (2) Formulating realistic response strategies for the management of the climate change issue; (3) Providing scientific and socio-economic information and advice, initially for the development and negotiations of a UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and after its entry into force, to continue to work closely with the UNFCCC and provide scientific, technical and socio-economic information and advice; and (4) Reporting on its activities to the governing bodies of WMO and UNEP and communicating the results of the assessments broadly. These tasks enable the IPCC to fulfil its role as an intergovernmental panel on climate change that provides authoritative and comprehensive assessments of the current state of knowledge on climate change and its potential impacts.

This coordination is guided by the Principles Governing IPCC Work (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/09/ipcc-principles.pdf). For example, IPCC works with the energy sector to assess the mitigation potential and costs of different energy sources and technologies (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/renewable-energy-sources-and-climate-change-mitigation/), with the agriculture sector to evaluate the impacts of climate change on food security and land use (https://www.ipcc.ch/srccl/), the ocean sector to examine the changes in the ocean and cryosphere and their implications for ecosystems and human well-being (https://www.ipcc.ch/srocc/), or with the health sector to analyse the risks and opportunities for health adaptation and mitigation (https://www.ipcc.ch/report/ar6/wg2/chapter/chapter-7/). Horizontal coordination within IPCC can take various forms, such as (1) Joint preparation and approval of assessment reports and special reports with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Sixth Assessment Report (https://www.ipcc.ch/assessment-report/ar6/) or the Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5°C (https://www.ipcc.ch/sr15/), (2) Participation in intergovernmental and multisectoral panels, working groups, and task forces, such as the IPCC Bureau (https://www.ipcc.ch/bureau/) or the Task Force on National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/), (3)Development and dissemination of guidelines, methodologies, and data for climate change research and policy, such as the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories (https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/2006gl/) or the IPCC Data Distribution Centre (https://www.ipcc-data.org/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for climate change issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the IPCC Outreach Programme (https://www.ipcc.ch/outreach/) and IPCC Communication Strategy (https://archive.ipcc.ch/meetings/session35/IAC_CommunicationStrategy.pdf). In addition, the IPCC provides scientific assessments of the state of knowledge on climate change, its causes, potential impacts and response options, informs the negotiations under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), engages with a wide range of interested parties at various levels, and ensures the quality and transparency of its work (https://www.ipcc.ch/about/).

matrix_cell_text_full: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) collaborates with key organizations to support climate change governance. It liaises with the United Nations (UN), implementing a relationship agreement effective since its establishment in 1988 (https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2021/07/AR6_FS_What_is_IPCC.pdf), as per the UN's mandate to provide policymakers with regular assessments of the scientific basis of climate change, its impacts, future risks, and adaptation and mitigation options. Similarly, IPCC maintains a relationship with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), providing vital scientific information to limit climate change and establish a strong link between sustainable economic development, climate change, and vulnerability (https://www.undp.org/blog/five-key-takeaways-latest-ipcc-report). Additionally, IPCC supports the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) by assessing the scientific literature and providing vital scientific information to the climate change process (https://unfccc.int/topics/science/workstreams/cooperation-with-the-ipcc/background-cooperation-with-the-ipcc). It also services the Conference of the Parties (COP) and the Subsidiary Body for Scientific and Technological Advice (SBSTA) (https://unfccc.int/process/bodies/subsidiary-bodies/sbsta), by preparing related reports within its mandate. Moreover, IPCC facilitates the assessment process through its Task Force on Greenhouse Gas Inventories, carrying out important work on methodologies for estimating and reporting GHG emissions (https://www.ipcc.ch/working-group/tfi/).

The IPCC divides the world into 10 regions for its interactive atlas (https://interactive-atlas.ipcc.ch/regional-information/guidance), which shows the projected changes and impacts of climate change for each region based on different scenarios and models.
