excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within IOM involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the migration domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN agencies to ensure that migration is humane, orderly, and beneficial for migrants and society. This coordination is guided by Article 8 of the IOM Constitution (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf). For example, IOM works with the health sector to promote the well-being of migrants and public health (https://www.iom.int/migration-health), with the development sector to enhance the contribution of migration to sustainable development (https://www.iom.int/migration-and-development), the humanitarian sector to provide assistance and protection to migrants in crisis situations (https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/migrated_files/What-We-Do/docs/Assisting-migrants-caught-in-crisis-IOM-activities-2012.pdf) or with the human rights sector to uphold the rights and dignity of migrants (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/migrants_human_rights.pdf). Horizontal coordination within IOM can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Migration Governance Framework (https://www.iom.int/sites/default/files/about-iom/migof_brochure_a4_en.pdf) or the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration (https://www.iom.int/global-compact-migration), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Global Migration Group (https://www.ohchr.org/en/migration/global-migration-group) or the Platform on Disaster Displacement (https://disasterdisplacement.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for migration sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Handbook of Migration and Development (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/booklet_migration_and_development_series_1mar2018.pdf) or the Migration Crisis Operational Framework (https://www.iom.int/mcof), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for migration issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Dialogue on Migration (https://www.iom.int/idm) or the World Migration Report (https://worldmigrationreport.iom.int/).

matrix_cell_text_full: IOM cooperates with various partners to advance migration governance and, in particular, achieve the 2030 Agenda. It engages with the United Nations (UN), implementing a relationship agreement (https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/about-iom/IOM-UN-Agreement-Sept19-2016.pdf) effective since 19 September 2016, as per the UN General Assembly Resolution 70/296. matrix_cell_text_full: The IOM executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a five-year Strategic Plan (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/pub2023-159-r_-_strategic_plan_2024-2028-en_0.pdf), revised annually by the Council, establishes the IOM's vision, mission, strategic objectives, enablers, and cross-cutting priorities. The current plan, applicable for 2024-2028, aligns with the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration and the United Nations Secretary-General’s Action Agenda on Internal Displacement. Secondly, an annual budget and work plan, devised by the IOM and approved by the Council, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current budget and work plan for 2024 is tailored to the Member States' needs and stakeholders' priorities (https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/developmentfund/iom-development-fund-financial-guidelines-2024.pdf). Thirdly, an IOM Development fund with a strategic plan applicable for 2022-2027 (https://www.iom.int/sites/g/files/tmzbdl486/files/documents/2023-05/iom-development-fund-strategic-plan-2022-2027_6.pdf) aimed at providing Member States with accountable and effective seed funding for innovative migration-related initiatives that align with national, regional, and global development strategies and priorities, as well as supporting the development and strengthening of the capacities of Member States to achieve effective and sustainable migration governance that benefits migrants and society. The IOM also maintains the Migration Data Portal (https://migrationdataportal.org/), a key aspect of the implementation of the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration. Finally, various strategies, frameworks, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the IOM's mandate, addressing migration, environment, and climate change, governance, resilience, and mobility (https://publications.iom.int/books/institutional-strategy-migration-environment-and-climate-change-2021-2030).

excerpt_<=50w: Source of jurisdiction: formal legal basis enabling authority (treaty/charter article(s) or constitutive resolution reference).
matrix_cell_text_full: IOM derives its mandate from the Constitution of the International Organization for Migration (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf), which established IOM as an intergovernmental organization in the field of migration. The present Constitution is an incoporation of the Constitution of 19 October 1953 of the Intergovernmental Committee for European Migration (former designation of the Organization), which entered into force on 30 November 1954, the amendments adopted on 20 May 1987 by the 55th Session of the Council (Resolution no. 724), which entered into force on 14 November 1989, the amendments adopted on 24 November 1998 by the 76th Session of the Council (Resolution No. 997), which entered into force on 21 November 2013 and the amendments adopted on 28 October 2020 by the Fourth Special Session of the Council (Resolution No.1385), which entered into force on 28 October 2020 (https://publications.iom.int/books/constitution-and-basic-texts). Specifically, Article 1 of the Constitution defines the purposes and functions of IOM, and Article 2 outlines the procedures of membership. Articles IV-VIII of the Constitution establish procedures for Council, Administration, Headquarters, Finance, and Legal Status respectively. IOM's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Council, the Executive Committee, and the Standing Committee on Programmes and Finance (https://governingbodies.iom.int/standing-committee-programmes-and-finance). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for IOM's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. IOM's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration 9https://refugeesmigrants.un.org/sites/default/files/180711_final_draft_0.pdf), the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol (https://www.unhcr.org/sites/default/files/legacy-pdf/4ec262df9.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for IOM's jurisdiction over specific migration issues and domains.

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within IOM involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other international organizations, Member States, regional and subregional bodies, and local actors. This is achieved through consultation, information sharing, and joint action. This is structured under Chapter III (Organs), Chapter IV (Council), Chapter V (Administration), and Chapter VI (Headquarters) of the IOM Constitution (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf), specifically in Articles 5-18. The IOM operates through the Council of all the Member States, the Administration headed by a Director General, and two Deputy Directors General. The Council may also set up subsidiary bodies as required (Article 10). IOM is present in 171 countries and has 9 regional offices worldwide (https://www.iom.int/iom-organizational-structure), and its work in each region led by a Regional Director who reports to the Director General and coordinates with the Headquarters and the Country Offices to implement policies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.iom.int/where-we-work). There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the Director General, the Deputy Directors General, the Chief of Staff, the Regional Directors, and the Directors of Departments) providing strategic guidance and oversight to the Director General on matters related to the operational and managerial work of IOM; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://www.iom.int/senior-management). Moreover, a network of 550 country offices and field locations supports IOM's work in delivering migration services and assistance to migrants, governments, and other stakeholders (https://www.iom.int/countries). Additionally, IOM operates Global Administrative Centres and Special Liaison Offices (https://www.iom.int/iom-organizational-structure).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to Part XI, Section 4 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the International Seabed Authority's objectives encompass several key functions: organizing and controlling activities in the Area, particularly with a view to administering the resources of the Area (Article 157, paragraph 1); establishing specific policies for the Authority in conformity with the Convention and the general policies established by the Assembly (Article 162, paragraph 1); adopting and applying provisionally the rules, regulations and procedures of the Authority relating to prospecting, exploration and exploitation in the Area, as well as the financial management and internal administration of the Authority (Article 162, paragraph 2 o); supervising and coordinating the implementation of the provisions of Part XI and inviting the attention of the Assembly to cases of non-compliance (Article 162, paragraph 2 a); exercising control over activities in the Area in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 4, and the rules, regulations and procedures of the Authority (Article 162, paragraph 2 l); and ensuring the equitable sharing of financial and other economic benefits derived from activities in the Area, taking into account the interests and needs of developing States and peoples who have not attained full independence or other self-governing status (Article 160, paragraph 2 f and g; Article 162, paragraph 2 g). These functions enable the Authority to fulfil its role as the organization through which States Parties shall carry out their rights and obligations under the Convention with respect to activities in the Area (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm).

source_title: International Seabed Authority — Horizontal Coordination evidence
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the ISA involves collaboration among different sectors and stakeholders involved in the exploration and exploitation of the seabed and ocean floor beyond national jurisdiction, such as States Parties, contractors, the Enterprise, the United Nations and its specialised agencies, and other international and non-governmental organizations. This coordination is structured under the General Principles section of Part XI of the UNCLOS, specifically in Articles 156-185 (https://www.un.org/Depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11.htm). The ISA has established three principal organs: the Assembly, the Council, and the Secretariat, as well as two subsidiary organs: the Economic Planning Commission and the Legal and Technical Commission, to carry out its functions and responsibilities under the Convention (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/struct-funct.pdf). The ISA also has an organ for carrying out activities in the Area directly: the Enterprise, and all States Parties are ipso facto members of the Authority (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). The ISA adopts and applies rules, regulations  and procedures for the management of activities in the Area, taking into account the protection of the marine environment, the equitable sharing of benefits, and the promotion of international cooperation ((https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba_25_c_wp1-e_0.pdf)). The ISA also establishes a system of compensation or other measures of economic adjustment assistance for developing States that may be adversely affected by activities in the Area according to article 160 (10), Part XI of UNCLOS (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). The ISA cooperates with other relevant international organizations and facilitates the exchange of scientific and technical information on activities in the Area (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/struct-funct.pdf).

excerpt_<=50w: Inter‑institutional relationships: formalised cooperation with other bodies (e.g., MoUs, joint programmes, agreements; partner type × mechanism × year).
matrix_cell_text_full: The ISA cooperates with various organizations to achieve its objectives and mandates. It maintains a relationship with the United Nations (UN), as an observer to the UN General Assembly, based on an agreement in accordance with UNCLOS Article 156, paragraph 2, and the 1994 Agreement Article 169 (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/UN-ISA-Agrmnt-1.pdf). Similarly, it maintains a relationship with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), as the principal judicial organ for the settlement of disputes relating to the activities in the Area, based on an agreement in accordance with UNCLOS Article 187 and the 1994 Agreement Article 178, detailed in resolution 51/205. Additionally, it consults and collaborates with the relevant specialized agencies of the UN, such as the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), and the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission (IOC), as well as other international and regional organizations, such as the International Maritime Organization (IMO), the International Hydrographic Organization (IHO), and the regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs), on matters of common interest, in accordance with UNCLOS Article 156, paragraph 3, and the 1994 Agreement Article 170 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/publication/CTC/Ch_XXI_6_english_p.pdf). It also participates in the Informal Consultative Process (ICP) on Oceans and the Law of the Sea, providing inputs and updates on its activities, with its role recognized in resolution 54/33 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N00/237/93/PDF/N0023793.pdf?OpenElement). Moreover, it contributes to the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, providing data and information on the environmental aspects of the activities in the Area, with its involvement encouraged in resolution 57/141 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The International Seabed Authority (ISA) fulfills its objectives through diverse strategies: firstly, a five-year Strategic Plan (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Strategic_Plan_Booklet.pdf), adopted in 2018 by the ISA Assembly (https://www.isa.org.jm/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/isba24_a10-en.pdf), aligns with UNCLOS, the 1994 Agreement (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). matrix_cell_text_full: ISA derives its mandate from the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which established the ISA as an autonomous international organization. Specifically, Part XI of UNCLOS ((https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm) and Annexes III (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/annex3.htm) and IV (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/annex4.htm) of UNCLOS provide the legal framework for the ISA’s jurisdiction over the international seabed area and its mineral resources (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm). Additionally, ISA’s jurisdiction is influenced by the Agreement relating to the Implementation of Part XI of UNCLOS (http://www2.ecolex.org/server2neu.php/libcat/docs/TRE/Full/En/TRE-001196.pdf). The Agreement, particularly Section 5 and Annexes, ooutlinesthe procedures and mechanisms for the ISA’s administration of the international seabed area and its environmental protection (http://www2.ecolex.org/server2neu.php/libcat/docs/TRE/Full/En/TRE-001196.pdf).

These objectives establish ITU as the UN's specialized agency for telecommunications, contributing to global information society development.

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within ITU involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the telecommunication domain, such as radiocommunication, telecommunication standardization, telecommunication development, and other related fields (https://www.itu.int/en/about/Pages/whatwedo.aspx). This coordination is structured under the Structure of the Union section of the ITU Constitution, specifically in Articles 7-24 (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU, in particular, to "maintain and extend international cooperation among all the Member States of the Union for the improvement and rational use of telecommunications of all kinds", as defined in its mission according to  Article 1 of the ITU Constitution (https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-R/information/Pages/mission-statement.aspx#:~:text=This%20mission%20lies%20within%20the,of%20telecommunications%20of%20all%20kinds%22.) The ITU also allocates radio-frequency spectrum and satellite orbits, coordinates efforts to eliminate harmful interference, fosters the development of technical facilities and services, promotes the extension of the benefits of new technologies to all the world's inhabitants, and harmonizes the actions of its members and partners in the attainment of its purposes (https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-r/oth/0A/0E/R0A0E0000010001PDFE.pdf). The ITU cooperates with other international organizations and facilitates the participation of concerned entities in its activities (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: ITU collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It engages with 193 Member States and over 900 Sector Members and Associates through the Plenipotentiary Conference, the supreme organ of the ITU, established by Article 8 of the Constitution of the ITU (https://www.itu.int/en/about/Pages/default.aspx). As the specialized agency of the United Nations for telecommunications, information and communication technologies, ITU's relationship with the UN is based on the Agreement between the United Nations and the International Telecommunication Union, signed in 1947 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/212014/files/E_RES_90%28V%29-EN.pdf?ln=en). Additionally, ITU supports the implementation of the World Summit on the Information Society (WSIS) outcomes and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, providing a platform for multi-stakeholder dialogue and action on the role of ICTs in development, as recognized by resolution 70/125 of the UN General Assembly³. It also cooperates with other UN specialized agencies, such as UNESCO, WHO, and WMO, and other organizations, such as WTO, OECD, and ICANN, addressing common ICT issues and challenges (https://www.itu.int/net/wsis/review/inc/docs/phase6/v/r/wsis10-5-3.pdf). Moreover, ITU collaborated with the WMO and UNESCO-IOCJoint on the Joint Task Force on SMART Submarine repeaters equipped with scientific sensors for climate monitoring and disaster risk reduction (tsunami warnings) (https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-t/oth/0b/11/T0B110000203302PDFE.pdf).

It also cooperates with other UN specialized agencies, such as UNESCO, WHO, and WMO, and other organizations, such as WTO, OECD, and ICANN, addressing common ICT issues and challenges (https://www.itu.int/net/wsis/review/inc/docs/phase6/v/r/wsis10-5-3.pdf). Moreover, ITU collaborated with the WMO and UNESCO-IOCJoint on the Joint Task Force on SMART Submarine repeaters equipped with scientific sensors for climate monitoring and disaster risk reduction (tsunami warnings) (https://www.itu.int/dms_pub/itu-t/oth/0b/11/T0B110000203302PDFE.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: ITU derives its mandate from the Constitution (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf) and the Convention of the International Telecommunication Union, which is an international treaty signed and ratified by almost all countries of the world (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Convention-E.pdf). The treaty is the founding document of the ITU, a specialized agency of the United Nations (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). Specifically, Article 1 of the Constitution defines the purposes and functions of the ITU, which include maintaining and extending international cooperation among all its Member States for the improvement and rational use of telecommunications of all kinds, promoting the development and efficient operation of technical facilities, and harmonizing the actions of Member States and Sector Members (https://www.itu.int/en/history/Pages/ConstitutionAndConvention.aspx). Additionally, ITU's jurisdiction is influenced by the resolutions and decisions of the Plenipotentiary Conference (https://search.itu.int/history/HistoryDigitalCollectionDocLibrary/5.23.61.en.100.pdf), which is the supreme organ of the ITU and has the power to amend the Constitution and the Convention (Article 8 of the Constitution). ITU also adopts and supervises the Administrative Regulations, such as the Radio Regulations and the International Telecommunication Regulations, which are binding on all ITU Member States and provide the legal framework for ITU's jurisdiction over the use of the radio-frequency spectrum, satellite orbits, and international telecommunication services (Article 4 of the Constitution). Also, The ITU Constitution and Convention are complemented by the Administrative Regulations, which comprise the ITU International Telecommunication Regulations and ITU Radio Regulations, and are binding on all ITU member states as well (https://www.itu.int/en/history/Pages/RegulationsCollection.aspx#:~:text=ITU's%20Administrative%20Regulations%20contain%20provisions,operation%20of%20international%20telecommunication%20services).

source_title: International Telecommunication Union (ITU) — Vertical Coordination evidence
excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within ITU involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relations with the United Nations and Other International Organizations section of the ITU Constitution, specifically in Articles 48-50 (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU operates through the Plenipotentiary Conference of all the members, the Council of 48 members, and a secretariat headed by a Secretary-General (Articles 8-10) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU also has three Sectors: Radiocommunication, Telecommunication Standardization, and Telecommunication Development, each with its own conference, assembly, and bureau (Articles 11-13) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). The ITU assists members in the implementation of its standards, regulations, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (Article 14) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). ITU's work is organized around five strategic goals: Growth, Inclusiveness, Sustainability, Innovation, and Partnership, each overseen by a Deputy Secretary-General or an Assistant Secretary-General (https://sdgs.un.org/un-system-sdg-implementation/international-telecommunication-union-itu-24522). Also, a network of regional and area offices and technical specialists supports the ITU's work in promoting the Connect 2030 Agenda as an integral part of regional and global development policies, in line with ITU RES 135 (https://www.itu.int/net4/proposals/PP18/Main/GetDocument?idProposal=49237&isSub=true&codeLang=E).

matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within ITC involves working with different sectors and stakeholders within the trade and development domain, such as MSMEs, BSOs, governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN agencies to ensure that trade contributes to inclusive, sustainable and prosperous economies (https://intracen.org/our-work/partnerships). This coordination is currently guided by its Strategic Plan for 2022-2025 (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). For example, ITC works with the MSME sector to improve their competitiveness and access to markets, with the BSO sector to strengthen their capacity and service delivery, with the government sector to create conducive policy and regulatory environments, and with the civil society and private sector to foster partnerships and innovation (https://intracen.org/our-work/partnerships). Horizontal coordination within ITC can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint design and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the SheTrades Initiative (https://www.shetrades.com/en) or the Trade for Sustainable Development Programme (https://intracen.org/our-work/projects/trade-for-sustainable-development-t4sd), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the UN Inter-Agency Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity (https://unctad.org/projects/UN-Inter-agency-Cluster#:~:text=and%20Productive%20Capacity-,United%20Nations%20Inter%2DAgency%20Cluster%20on%20Trade%20and%20Productive%20Capacity,levels%20within%20the%20UN%20system.) or the Enhanced Integrated Framework (https://www.enhancedif.org/en), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for trade sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the SME Competitiveness Outlook (https://intracen.org/resources/publications/sme-competitiveness-outlook) or the Market Access Map (https://www.macmap.org/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for trade issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Export Development Forum (https://intracen.org/news-and-events/events/world-export-development-forum-wedf) or the Trade Promotion Organization Network World Conference and Awards (https://intracen.org/news-and-events/events/world-trade-promotion-organizations-conference-and-awards-wtpo2024). The ITC provides leadership and direction on matters related to trade and development, shapes the trade and MSME agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses trade trends (https://intracen.org/about-us/governance/corporate-documents/itc-strategic-plan).

matrix_cell_text_full: ITC works with various institutions to achieve its goals of trade promotion and development. It is a joint agency of the WTO and the UN, operating under the guidance of the UN General Assembly and the WTO General Council (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are). It also cooperates with the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the UN Development Programme (UNDP), and other UN specialized agencies and programmes, as well as regional and intergovernmental organizations, to implement trade-related technical assistance and capacity-building activities (https://intracen.org/our-work/partnerships). Furthermore, ITC collaborates with the International Trade Centre Trust Fund (ITF), which is a multi-donor trust fund that supports ITC’s projects and programmes. Additionally, ITC maintains relations with other trade-related institutions, such as the Codex Alimentarius Commission, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), and the World Health Organization (WHO), to address various aspects of trade and development, as well as with the private sector, Governments, civil societies and philanthropic foundations, multilateral partners, academia, training and research partners, business support organizations, and regional partners (https://intracen.org/our-work/partnerships).

matrix_cell_text_full: ITC executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Joint Advisory Group, establishes ITC's vision, mission, strategic goals, core services, and impact areas. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its mandates (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). The plan also articulates ITC's vision of a world where trade builds inclusive, sustainable and prosperous economies, one where the recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic creates resilience and ensures a green transition. Secondly, an annual Operational Plan, devised by ITC and approved by the Consultative Committee of the ITC Trust Fund, details activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current Operational Plan for 2023 is tailored to the clients' needs and partners' priorities (https://intracen.org/file/operationalplan2023pdf). It also maintains the Trade Map, a key aspect of the provision of trade intelligence to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) (https://intracen.org/resources/tools/trade-map). The plan also specifies how ITC will assist MSMEs in creating jobs through entrepreneurship and value chain development, with a focus on women, youth, people with disabilities, and those in vulnerable situations. ITC operates on an annual budget for its work programmes, and the 2024 budget is aligned with the ITC Strategic Plan 2022-2025 and the Operational Plan 2023, which focus on the 5 'Ps' of the Global Agenda - prosperity, people, planet, peace, and partnership 9https://intracen.org/file/proposedprogrammebudgetfor2024pdf). ITC’s Regular Budget (RB) is funded in equal parts by the UN and the WTO. Its extra budgetary resources (XB) consist of pledges from donor governments, governmental organizations, other international organizations and civil society, including NGOs, the business sector and a variety of foundations. These commitments often extend over multiyear periods (https://intracen.org/about-us/funding). In addition, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing ITC's vision, mission, and principles, addressing trade competitiveness, inclusiveness, sustainability, and digitalization (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). Finally, ITC Annual Report offers a comprehensive review of the organization’s activities and detailed information on the results and effectiveness of its work. The latest report for 2022 (https://intracen.org/file/itcannualreport2022eng-interactive20junepdf) showcases how ITC delivered above and beyond the call of duty to set the Sustainable Development Goals back on track and help small enterprises continue finding new pathways to prosperity through trade, despite the challenges posed by the ‘four Cs’ – COVID, climate, conflict and cost-of-living. The report also presents results from the first year of ITC’s Strategic Plan 2022–2025, which pushes its value proposition further than before, laying out a bold roadmap for creating trade that is sustainable, inclusive and transformative.

matrix_cell_text_full: ITC derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly Resolution 2297 (XXII) (https://documents.un.org/doc/resolution/gen/nr0/236/32/pdf/nr023632.pdf?token=KPeCl92Q67Vpf1B3TZ&fe=true), which established The International Trade Centre as a joint subsidiary organ of the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the United Nations (UN) through the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) in accordance with the recommendations of the 1964 Global Agreement on Tariff and Trade (GATT) (https://docs.wto.org/gattdocs/q/GG/SPEC/64-151.pdf). The Resolution defined the objectives and functions of ITC and also outlined the governance and administrative arrangements. Additionally, ITC is subject to the relevant provisions of the UN Charter, the WTO Agreement, and the UNCTAD resolutions ((https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/wto_itc_e.htm).). ITC's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations of its governing bodies, such as the Joint Advisory Group (JAG), the Consultative Committee of ITC Trust Fund (CCITF), and the parent organizations (WTO and UNCTAD) (https://intracen.org/about-us/governance). These decisions and recommendations provide strategic direction and oversight the for ITC's activities and programmes, as well as resource mobilization and partnership development (https://intracen.org/file/itcstrategicplan2022-2025pdf). Furthermore, ITC's mandate is supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and the Aid for Trade Initiative, which provide further legal frameworks for ITC's jurisdiction over specific trade and development issues and domains (https://intracen.org/file/operationalplan2023pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within ITC involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, the World Trade Organization, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through strategic supervision, strategic management, and executive management. ITC is headed by an Executive Director who reports to the Secretary-General of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the Director-General of the World Trade Organization (WTO) (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). The ITC operates through the Joint Advisory Group of all the members, the Consultative Committee of the ITC Trust Fund, and a secretariat headed by the Executive Director (https://intracen.org/about-us/governance). ITC also has advisory bodies, such as the Global Network of Trade Promotion Organizations and the Global Network of Trade and Investment Support Institutions (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). ITC’s work is organised around four divisions, each overseen by a Director who works closely with the Executive Director to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). There is also the Senior Management Committee, consisting of the Executive Director, the Deputy Executive Director, the Directors of the four divisions, and the Chief of Staff, providing strategic and internal policy advice to the Executive Director on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of ITC and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/structure-and-management). Additionally, a network of country offices and technical experts supports ITC’s work in promoting trade and private sector development as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.intracen.org/about-us/where-we-work). In addition, ITC coordinates with the United Nations and its agencies and is a partner of the Enhanced Integrated Framework, the Aid for Trade Initiative, and the Standards and Trade Development Facility (https://www.intracen.org/about-us/who-we-are/partnerships).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the Minamata Convention Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the mercury domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to protect human health and the environment from the adverse effects of mercury. This coordination is guided by Article 24 of the Minamata Convention on Mercury (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf) as part of the functions of the Secretariat. For example, the Secretariat works with the health sector to support the phase-out of mercury in medical devices and dental amalgam (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health#:~:text=A%20significant%20example%20of%20mercury,included%20high%20concentrations%20of%20methylmercury.), with the mining sector to promote the reduction and elimination of mercury use in artisanal and small-scale gold mining (https://2009-2017.state.gov/e/oes/eqt/chemicalpollution/mercury/245187.htm), with the waste sector to ensure the environmentally sound management and transportation of mercury wastes (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/submission_from_government/%28JPN%29Article11.pdf), or with the trade sector to regulate the import and export of mercury and mercury compounds (https://minamataconvention.org/en/news/minamata-online-article-3-trade-mercury). Horizontal coordination within the Minamata Convention Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Environment Facility (https://www.thegef.org/topics/chemicals-and-waste) or the Special Programme on Institutional Strengthening (https://www.unep.org/explore-topics/chemicals-waste/what-we-do/special-programme/goal-special-programme), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Organization Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (https://partnership.who.int/iomc) or the Global Mercury Partnership (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/partners/global-mercury-partnership#:~:text=Initiated%20in%202005%20by%20a,legally%2Dbinding%20instrument%20on%20mercury.), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for mercury sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Minamata Initial Assessments (https://minamataconvention.org/en/parties/minamata-initial-assessments) or the Mercury Inventory Toolkit (https://www.unep.org/topics/chemicals-and-pollution-action/pollution-and-health/heavy-metals/mercury/mercury-inventory), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for mercury issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Conference on Mercury as a Global Pollutant (https://minamataconvention.org/en/news/icmgp-2022-reducing-mercury-emissions-achieve-greener-world) or the Minamata Online E-Learning Platform (https://minamataconvention.org/en/resources/e-learning).

For example, the Secretariat works with the health sector to support the phase-out of mercury in medical devices and dental amalgam (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mercury-and-health#:~:text=A%20significant%20example%20of%20mercury,included%20high%20concentrations%20of%20methylmercury.), with the mining sector to promote the reduction and elimination of mercury use in artisanal and small-scale gold mining (https://2009-2017.state.gov/e/oes/eqt/chemicalpollution/mercury/245187.htm), with the waste sector to ensure the environmentally sound management and transportation of mercury wastes (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/submission_from_government/%28JPN%29Article11.pdf), or with the trade sector to regulate the import and export of mercury and mercury compounds (https://minamataconvention.org/en/news/minamata-online-article-3-trade-mercury). Horizontal coordination within the Minamata Convention Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Environment Facility (https://www.thegef.org/topics/chemicals-and-waste) or the Special Programme on Institutional Strengthening (https://www.unep.org/explore-topics/chemicals-waste/what-we-do/special-programme/goal-special-programme), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Organization Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (https://partnership.who.int/iomc) or the Global Mercury Partnership (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/partners/global-mercury-partnership#:~:text=Initiated%20in%202005%20by%20a,legally%2Dbinding%20instrument%20on%20mercury.), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for mercury sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Minamata Initial Assessments (https://minamataconvention.org/en/parties/minamata-initial-assessments) or the Mercury Inventory Toolkit (https://www.unep.org/topics/chemicals-and-pollution-action/pollution-and-health/heavy-metals/mercury/mercury-inventory), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for mercury issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Conference on Mercury as a Global Pollutant (https://minamataconvention.org/en/news/icmgp-2022-reducing-mercury-emissions-achieve-greener-world) or the Minamata Online E-Learning Platform (https://minamataconvention.org/en/resources/e-learning).

matrix_cell_text_full: The Minamata Convention is responsible for protecting human health and the environment from the adverse effects of mercury and mercury compounds (https://minamataconvention.org/en). This includes regulating the entire life cycle of mercury, such as its mining, trade, use, emission, release, storage, and disposal. The Minamata Convention also provides controls over a range of products and processes that contain or use mercury, and requires parties to phase down or eliminate them by 2020 or later (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about). The Minamata Convention also supports the identification and management of contaminated sites, the monitoring and assessment of mercury levels, and the provision of information and public awareness on mercury risks (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about). Furthermore, the Minamata Convention facilitates technical and financial assistance, capacity-building, and cooperation among parties and stakeholders for the effective implementation of the treaty (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about).

excerpt_<=50w: Strategies: instrument portfolio and governance tools used to pursue objectives (e.g., standards, MRV, compliance, capacity building).
matrix_cell_text_full: The Minamata Convention Secretariat executes its objectives through specific strategies. Firstly, the Secreatariat develops a programme of work and budget for each biennium, which is approved by the Conference of the Parties. The programme of work and budget, applicable for 2024-2025 (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/2024-01/Programme_work_budget_for_2024-2025.pdf), outlines the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources for implementing the Convention based on the needs and priorities of the Parties and other stakeholders, as reflected in COP-5 decision document (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/documents/information_document/UNEP-MC-COP.5-INF36-POWB-Fact-sheets_English.pdf). Secondly, various mechanisms and tools provide technical and financial support to the Parties, especially developing countries and countries with economies in transition, to assist them in fulfilling their obligations under the Convention. These include the Implementation and Compliance Committee (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/implementation-and-compliance-committee), the Specific International Programme (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/specific-international-programme), the Global Environment Facility (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/gef), the Special Programme (https://minamataconvention.org/en/implementation/special-programme), the Global Mercury Partnership (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/partners/global-mercury-partnership), and the Minamata Online platform (https://minamataconvention.org/es/node/3136). The main sources of funding for the Minamata Convention are the Global Environment Facility Trust Fund (GEF) and the Specific International Programme (SIP) to support capacity-building and technical assistance (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about/financial-mechanism). The GEF has pledged $265 million for the four-year cycle starting in July 2022 (https://www.thegef.org/newsroom/news/minamata-convention-receives-increased-funding-pledge-global-environment-facility). Finally, various partnerships, initiatives, and platforms provide a framework for cooperation and information exchange among Parties, scientific communities, civil society, and other relevant stakeholders, on issues such as mercury supply and trade, mercury-added products, mercury waste, health and environmental impacts of mercury, and mercury-free technologies and alternatives (https://minamataconvention.org/en/resources/partnerships).

matrix_cell_text_full:
The Minamata Convention derives its mandate from the Minamata Convention on Mercury, which established the Convention as an international treaty to protect human health and the environment from mercury and mercury compounds (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf). Article 1 of the Convention defines the objective of the Convention, and Article 15 lays out the mechanism for Implementation and Compliance Committee to promote implementation 
of, and review compliance with, all provisions of the Convention. Similarly Article 23 establishes the Conference of Parties to the Convention while Article 24 outlines the functions of the Convention's Secretariat. Additionally, the Convention's articles and annexes, which were adopted by the Conference of Plenipotentiaries on 10 October 2013 (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf), specify the obligations and commitments of the Parties to the Convention, such as regulating the sources and trade of mercury, controlling the emissions and releases of mercury, managing the mercury waste and contaminated sites, providing information and public awareness, and facilitating technical and financial assistance and cooperation. The Convention's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and resolutions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Conference of the Parties, the Implementation and Compliance Committee, and the Secretariat (https://minamataconvention.org/en/meeting-documents?f%5B0%5D=document_type_2%3A307). These decisions and resolutions provide guidance and direction for the Convention's implementation and review, as well as cooperation and coordination with other relevant organisations and stakeholders. The Convention's mandate is also supported by the participation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and their Disposal (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2019.English.pdf), the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf), and the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for the Convention's jurisdiction over specific mercury-related issues and domains.

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the OECD involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the economic and social domains, such as governments, civil society, private sector, academic community, and other international organisations to ensure that economic co-operation and development are considered in all policies and that OECD policies are aligned with other sectoral policies (https://www.oecd.org/about/). This coordination is guided by Article 2 of the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). For example, the OECD works with the education sector to improve learning outcomes and skills development (https://www.oecd.org/education/), with the transport sector to enhance mobility and environmental performance (https://www.oecd.org/transport/), or with the ocean sector to promote sustainable management and use of marine resources (https://www.oecd.org/ocean/OECD-work-in-support-of-a-sustainable-ocean.pdf). Horizontal coordination within the OECD can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the OECD Action Plan on the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.oecd.org/dac/Better%20Policies%20for%202030.pdf) or the OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting Project (https://www.oecd.org/tax/beps/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the OECD Development Assistance Committee (https://www.oecd.org/dac/development-assistance-committee/) or the OECD Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes (https://www.oecd.org/tax/transparency/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for OECD sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the OECD Principles on Artificial Intelligence (https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/instruments/OECD-LEGAL-0449) or the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Business Conduct (https://www.oecd.org/investment/due-diligence-guidance-for-responsible-business-conduct.htm), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for economic co-operation and development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the OECD Forum (https://www.oecd.org/forum/) or the OECD Economic Outlook (https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/economics/oecd-economic-outlook_16097408). The OECD provides policy analysis and advice, based on its multidisciplinary expertise, peer learning and dialogue, and policy coherence for sustainable development (https://www.oecd.org/about/how-we-work/).

matrix_cell_text_full: OECD collaborates with various organizations to promote economic co-operation and development. It maintains relations with the European Communities, established by the Treaties of Paris and Rome of 18th April, 1951, and 25th March, 1957, as defined in Supplementary Protocol No. 1 to the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD Convention), article 13 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). It also enters into agreements with Members, non-member States and international organizations, as provided for in OECD Convention, article 5 (c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Additionally, OECD participates in the activities of other international organizations or institutions, such as the UN, the World Bank, the IMF, and the WTO, in a manner consistent with its obligations, as stated in OECD Convention, article 1 (c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). It also contributes to the economic development of both Member and non-member countries in the process of economic development, by appropriate means and, in particular, by the flow of capital to those countries, as agreed in OECD Convention, article 2 (e) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Moreover, OECD supports the further expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis, as one of the most important factors favouring the economic development of countries and the improvement of international economic relations, as affirmed in OECD Convention, article 1 (c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The OECD derives its mandate from the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which established OECD as an intergovernmental organisation with 38 member countries, to stimulate economic progress and world tradem (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Specifically, Article 1 of the Convention defines the aims and objectives of OECD, and Article 2 outlines the functions and activities of OECD (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). Additionally, OECD’s rules of procedure, rule 18 on the functions of the OECD secretariat, states that the secretariat shall assist the Council and its subsidiary bodies in carrying out their work and shall perform any other tasks entrusted to it by the Council (https://www.oecd.org/legal/Rules%20of%20Procedure%20OECD%20Oct%202013.pdf). OECD’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions, agreements, recommendations, etc adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Council, the Ministerial Council, and the committees (https://legalinstruments.oecd.org/en/). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for OECD’s work and policy advice, as well as the cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. OECD’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international standards and frameworks, such as the Common Reporting Standard (https://www.oecd.org/tax/automatic-exchange/common-reporting-standard/), the Base erosion and profit shifting (BEPS) (https://www.oecd.org/tax/beps/about/), which provide further legal and technical frameworks for the OECD.

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination connected to the OECD involves downward coordination into subsidiary bodies of OECD and receipt of governance input from member states. This is achieved through reporting, cooperation, and assistance (https://www.oecd.org/effective-public-investment-toolkit/Improving-coordination.pdf). This is structured under the Relations with the European Communities and Agreements with Members, non-member States and international organisations sections of the OECD Convention, specifically in Articles 13-15 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). The OECD operates through the Council of all the members, the Ministerial Council of ministers from member countries and the European Union, and a secretariat headed by a Secretary-General (Articles 3-8) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). The OECD also has committees, working parties, and other subsidiary bodies (Article 9) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). The OECD assists members and non-members in the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes, and provides policy analysis and advice upon request (Article 2) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). The OECD's work is organised around 14 major substantive directorates, each overseen by Directors who works closely with the Secretary-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organisation (https://www.oecd.org/about/document/list-of-departments-and-special-bodies.htm). There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the Secretary-General and Deputy Secretaries-General) providing strategic and operational guidance to the Secretary-General on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of the OECD; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the different directorates and divisions of the Organisation and the governing bodies (https://www.oecd.org/about/document/list-of-departments-and-special-bodies.htm). Moreover, the OECD operates various centres, networks, and initiatives that facilitate dialogue, knowledge sharing, and policy innovation among its members and partners, such as the Development Centre (https://www.oecd.org/dev/), the Centre for Entrepreneurship, SMEs, Regions and Cities (https://www.oecd.org/cfe/), the Global Relations Secretariat (https://www.oecd.org/global-relations/), the Sahel and West Africa Club Secretariat (https://www.oecd.org/swac/), the OECD Eurasia Competitiveness Platform (https://www.oecd.org/eurasia/), the OECD Latin America and the Caribbean Regional Programme (https://www.oecd.org/latin-america/regional-programme/), the OECD Southeast Asia Regional Programme (https://www.oecd.org/southeast-asia/regional-programme/), the OECD Korea Policy Centre, the OECD Tokyo Centre, the OECD Mexico Centre for Latin America, the OECD Istanbul Centre, the OECD Brazil Centre, the OECD China Centre, the OECD India Centre, the OECD Eurasia Centre (https://www.oecd.org/general/oecdcentres.htm), the OECD Global Forum on Transparency and Exchange of Information for Tax Purposes (https://www.oecd.org/tax/transparency/), the OECD International Network on Financial Education (https://www.oecd.org/financial/education/oecd-international-network-on-financial-education.htm), the OECD International Transport Forum (https://www.itf-oecd.org/), and the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency (https://www.oecd-nea.org/), the OECD Partnership in Statistics for Development in the 21st Century (https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/docserver/078f091a-en.pdf?expires=1704549733&id=id&accname=guest&checksum=1A5600A8424B7AA33B844179E9EE8441).

source_title: Ramsar Convention on Wetlands Secretariat (Ramsar)  — Horizontal Coordination evidence
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the Ramsar Secretariat involves working with different partners and actors within the wetland domain, such as other global and regional conventions and agencies, national and local governments, civil society, private sector, and scientific and academic institutions to ensure that wetlands are conserved, wisely used, restored and valued by all. This coordination is supported by the Convention’s Strategic Plan 2016-2024 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/4th_strategic_plan_2016_2024_e.pdf). For example, the Ramsar Secretariat works with the biodiversity sector to support the implementation of other biodiversity-related conventions, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) or the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS), with the water sector to promote the integration of wetlands into water resources management, such as the Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) or the Water Framework Directive (WFD), with the climate change sector to enhance the role of wetlands in climate change mitigation and adaptation, such as the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) or the Paris Agreement, or with the disaster risk reduction sector to highlight the importance of wetlands in reducing disaster risks, such as the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction or the Hyogo Framework for Action (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships/partnerships-other-conventions). Horizontal coordination within the Ramsar Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other partners and actors, such as the Ramsar Regional Initiatives (https://www.ramsar.org/activity/ramsar-regional-initiatives) or the Wetlands for the Future Fund (https://www.ramsar.org/wetlands-future), (2) Participation in intergovernmental and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Biodiversity Liaison Group (https://www.cbd.int/blg/) or the Global Partnership for Plant Conservation (https://www.plants2020.net/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for wetland sector engagement with other partners and actors, such as the Ramsar Handbooks (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/pdf/lib/hbk4-18.pdf) or the Ramsar Advisory Missions (https://www.ramsar.org/activity/ramsar-advisory-missions), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for wetland issues and policies among other partners and actors, such as the World Wetlands Day (https://www.worldwetlandsday.org/) or the Ramsar Awards (https://www.ramsar.org/our-work/activities/ramsar-awards).

matrix_cell_text_full: The Ramsar Secretariat's jurisdiction is based on the Convention on Wetlands, which applies to all wetlands within the territories of its 163 Contracting Parties (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat), and includes a wide variety of habitats such as marshes, peatlands, floodplains, rivers and lakes, and coastal areas such as saltmarshes, mangroves, and seagrass beds, but also coral reefs and other marine areas no deeper than six metres at low tide, as well as human-made wetlands such as waste-water treatment ponds and reservoirs (https://leap.unep.org/sites/default/files/2020-09/manual6-2013-e.pdf). The Secretariat has authority over the conservation and wise use of these wetlands, as well as their designation for inclusion in the Ramsar List of Wetlands of International Importance (https://leap.unep.org/sites/default/files/2020-09/manual6-2013-e.pdf). The Secretariat does not have jurisdiction over the entire ocean space or maritime zones of its Contracting Parties, but only over the wetlands that fall within the definition of the Convention.

matrix_cell_text_full: The Ramsar Secretariat is responsible for coordinating the implementation of the Convention on Wetlands, which aims to conserve and wisely use all wetlands within the territories of its 163 Contracting Parties (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Convention covers all aspects of wetland conservation and wise use, such as maintaining the ecological character of wetlands, promoting their sustainable use, enhancing their biodiversity, and ensuring their resilience to climate change (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/manual6-2013-e.pdf). The Convention also identifies wetlands of international importance, especially those providing waterfowl habitat, and encourages international cooperation and information exchange on wetland issues (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/pdf/lib/hbk4-17.pdf). The Secretariat provides administrative, scientific, and technical support to Contracting Parties, as well as funding programmes for wetland conservation and management projects, focusing on a wide variety of wetland habitats, such as marshes, peatlands, rivers, lakes, coastal and marine areas, and human-made wetlands (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat).

matrix_cell_text_full: The Ramsar Secretariat executes its defined objectives following certain strategies, including its fourth strategic plan which spans from 2016-2024 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/4th_strategic_plan_2022_update_e.pdf). This plan has three strategic goals: 1) address the drivers of wetland loss and degradation; 2) effectively conserve and manage the Ramsar Site Network; and 3) wisely use all wetlands. The Secretariat also has a Workplan that is structured around the seven core functions of the Secretariat and sets out principal activities and corresponding annual and triennial indicators for each, together with indicative lead responsibilities and principal funding source. The most recent Workplan is applicable for 2023-2025 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/2023-09/secretariat_workplan_2023_2025_e.pdf). Ramsar Secretariat's core funding is based on contributions from Contracting Parties to the Convention 9https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat also prepares an annual core budget which is approved by the Conference of the Contracting Parties. The core budget for 2022 was presented in Annex 1 of Resolution ExCOP3.2 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/excop3_2_financial_budgetary_matters_e.pdf). Finally, the Secretariat develops cooperation with other conventions, intergovernmental institutions, and national and international NGOs (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships). It also organizes Ramsar Advisory Missions at the request of Contracting Parties and contributes to the follow-up of RAM reports (https://www.ramsar.org/our-work/activities/ramsar-advisory-missions). These strategies and mechanisms provide an operational framework for implementing the Convention's mission of conservation and wise use of all wetlands through local and national actions and international cooperation.

matrix_cell_text_full: The Ramsar Secretariat derives its mandate from the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance especially as Waterfowl Habitat, also known as the Ramsar Convention, which was signed in Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, entered into force in 1975, and ammended in 1994 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf). Specifically, Article 8 of the Convention assigned bureau duties to the International Union for the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources as a body to carry out the day-to-day coordination of the Convention's activities, as detailed in Paragraph 2 of article 8. Additionally, Rule 27 of the Convention's Rules of Procedure (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/ramsar_rules_of_procedure_e_0.pdf) defines the functions of the Secretariat, which include performing all other work that the Conference of the Parties requires and directs (Rule 27 g), and Rule 26 states the duties of the Secretary General. The Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by the COP, the Standing Committee, and the STRP, which provide guidance and direction for the Secretariat's work, as well as cooperation and coordination with other conventions, intergovernmental institutions, and national and international NGOs (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/2023-07/list_resolutions_recommendations_e_1.pdf). The Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Convention on Migratory Species, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, and the UN Convention to Combat Desertification, which provide further legal frameworks for the Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific wetland-related issues and domains (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships/partnerships-other-conventions).

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within Ramsar Secretariat involves working with the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the Conference of the Contracting Parties (COP), the Standing Committee, the Scientific and Technical Review Panel (STRP), and the Contracting Parties to the Convention. This is achieved through organizing, supporting, and implementing the decisions and resolutions of the Convention's governing bodies. This is structured under the Secretariat section of the Convention text, specifically in Articles 8 and 9 (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf). The Ramsar Secretariat is based at the headquarters of the IUCN in Gland, Switzerland, and follows IUCN procedures and policies on staffing and recruitment (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat is headed by a Secretary General, who is appointed by the Standing Committee with the approval of the COP, and reports to the Standing Committee. The Secretariat also consists of a Deputy Secretary General, a Senior Advisor on Environment and Development, and other staff members organized into five teams: Administrative and Financial Management, Communications, Convention and Policy Support, Regional Affairs, and Scientific and Technical Support (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/hr_org_chart_20230601.pdf). The Secretariat's main functions are to maintain the List of Wetlands of International Importance, help convene and organize the meetings of the COP, the Standing Committee, and the STRP, provide administrative and communications support to the STRP, provide administrative, scientific, and technical support to Contracting Parties, organize Ramsar Advisory Missions, develop cooperation with other conventions and institutions, and administer funding programmes (https://www.ramsar.org/about/bodies/secretariat). The Secretariat also works closely with the six International Organization Partners of the Convention: BirdLife International, International Water Management Institute, IUCN, Wetlands International, WWF International, and Wildfowl & Wetlands Trust (https://www.ramsar.org/about/partnerships/international-organization-partners).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full:
Horizontal coordination within BRS Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the chemicals and waste domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that the sound management of chemicals and waste is achieved and that human health and the environment are protected from their adverse effects. This coordination is guided by the preambles and the objectives of the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). For example, the BRS Secretariat works with the health sector to prevent and reduce the exposure to hazardous chemicals and waste (such as mercury, lead, asbestos, and pesticides) and to promote the implementation of the health-related provisions of the conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Vision/Vision201819/tabid/7862/language/en-US/Default.aspx), with the agriculture sector to support the environmentally sound management of pesticides and other chemicals used in agriculture and to promote alternatives to hazardous pesticides (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx), the trade sector to facilitate the exchange of information and the prior informed consent procedure for certain hazardous chemicals and waste in international trade or with the climate change sector to address the linkages between chemicals (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx), waste and climate change and to promote low-carbon and circular economy approaches (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Horizontal coordination within BRS Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Special Programme on Institutional Strengthening for Chemicals and Waste Management or the Global Environment Facility (GEF) projects on persistent organic pollutants (POPs), mercury and integrated chemicals and waste management (https://www.brsmeas.org/Decisionmaking/COPsandExCOPs/20212022COPs/MeetingDocuments/tabid/8810/ctl/Download/mid/24689/language/en-GB/Default.aspx?id=111&ObjID=29473), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Organization Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (IOMC) (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/IGOs/IOMC/tabid/4094/language/en-US/Default.aspx) or the Environmental Network for Optimizing Regulatory Compliance on Illegal Traffic (ENFORCE) (https://www.basel.int/Implementation/LegalMatters/IllegalTraffic/Meetings/ENFORCE8Brussels2024/tabid/9702/Default.aspx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for chemicals and waste sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the technical guidelines for the environmentally sound management of waste or the guidance on best available techniques and best environmental practices for POPs 9https://www.brsmeas.org/Resources/Shared/scripts/appPubKit/docs/06a-StockholmConvention-GuidelinesBATBEP.English.pdf), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for chemicals and waste issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Triple COPs (https://enb.iisd.org/basel-rotterdam-stockholm-conventions-brs-cops-2023) or the online briefings and webinars. The BRS Secretariat provides leadership and direction on matters related to chemicals and waste management, shapes the policy agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to parties, and monitors and assesses chemicals and waste trends (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx).

Horizontal coordination within BRS Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the chemicals and waste domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that the sound management of chemicals and waste is achieved and that human health and the environment are protected from their adverse effects. This coordination is guided by the preambles and the objectives of the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). For example, the BRS Secretariat works with the health sector to prevent and reduce the exposure to hazardous chemicals and waste (such as mercury, lead, asbestos, and pesticides) and to promote the implementation of the health-related provisions of the conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Vision/Vision201819/tabid/7862/language/en-US/Default.aspx), with the agriculture sector to support the environmentally sound management of pesticides and other chemicals used in agriculture and to promote alternatives to hazardous pesticides (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx), the trade sector to facilitate the exchange of information and the prior informed consent procedure for certain hazardous chemicals and waste in international trade or with the climate change sector to address the linkages between chemicals (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx), waste and climate change and to promote low-carbon and circular economy approaches (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Horizontal coordination within BRS Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Special Programme on Institutional Strengthening for Chemicals and Waste Management or the Global Environment Facility (GEF) projects on persistent organic pollutants (POPs), mercury and integrated chemicals and waste management (https://www.brsmeas.org/Decisionmaking/COPsandExCOPs/20212022COPs/MeetingDocuments/tabid/8810/ctl/Download/mid/24689/language/en-GB/Default.aspx?id=111&ObjID=29473), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Organization Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (IOMC) (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/IGOs/IOMC/tabid/4094/language/en-US/Default.aspx) or the Environmental Network for Optimizing Regulatory Compliance on Illegal Traffic (ENFORCE) (https://www.basel.int/Implementation/LegalMatters/IllegalTraffic/Meetings/ENFORCE8Brussels2024/tabid/9702/Default.aspx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for chemicals and waste sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the technical guidelines for the environmentally sound management of waste or the guidance on best available techniques and best environmental practices for POPs 9https://www.brsmeas.org/Resources/Shared/scripts/appPubKit/docs/06a-StockholmConvention-GuidelinesBATBEP.English.pdf), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for chemicals and waste issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Triple COPs (https://enb.iisd.org/basel-rotterdam-stockholm-conventions-brs-cops-2023) or the online briefings and webinars. The BRS Secretariat provides leadership and direction on matters related to chemicals and waste management, shapes the policy agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to parties, and monitors and assesses chemicals and waste trends (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx).

Source: Conversation with Bing, 2/15/2024
