matrix_cell_text_full: The BRS Secretariat cooperates with key entities to support the sound management of chemicals and waste. It is administered by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), as per Article 16 of the Basel Convention (https://www.basel.int/Portals/4/Basel%20Convention/docs/text/BaselConventionText-e.pdf), Article 19 of the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf) and Article 20 of the Stockholm Convention (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf). It also implements memoranda of understanding with UNEP and FAO, clarifying the institutional relationship and responsibilities of the entities (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners2/CooperationWithPartners/tabid/2841/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Furthermore, the BRS Secretariat coordinates with other international bodies, such as the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM), the Minamata Convention on Mercury, the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, and the World Health Organization (WHO), to promote synergies and avoid duplication of efforts (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/MEAs/MinamataConvention/tabid/4083/language/en-US/Default.aspx). It also engages with various stakeholders, such as industry, civil society, academia and media, to raise awareness and mobilize resources for the implementation of the conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners2/CooperationWithPartners/tabid/2841/language/en-US/Default.aspx). It also coordinates with the International Seabed Authority (ISA), the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS), the Informal Consultative Process (ICP) on Oceans and the Law of the Sea, and the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/TechnicalAssistance/Partnerships/tabid/4900/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Furthermore, the BRS Secretariat engages with stakeholders, such as regional centres, non-governmental organizations, industry associations, and scientific institutions, to provide technical assistance, capacity building, and information exchange (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners2/CooperationWithPartners/tabid/2841/language/en-US/Default.aspx).

matrix_cell_text_full: The BRS Secretariat is responsible for facilitating the implementation of the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions, which aim to protect human health and the environment from hazardous chemicals and wastes (https://www.un.org/depts/los//general_assembly/contributions_2020/SecretariatBRS.pdf). This includes providing administrative, technical and legal support to the parties and their subsidiary bodies, as well as receiving and conveying information from and to the parties. The BRS Secretariat also coordinates with other international bodies and stakeholders, and delivers capacity-building, awareness-raising and outreach activities for the sound management of chemicals and wastes, in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The BRS Secretariat contributes to the protection of the marine environment and the law of the sea by preventing and combating illegal traffic in hazardous wastes and other wastes, including through transboundary movements at sea. The Secretariat also supports the parties in reducing direct discharge or land runoff of hazardous pollutants or wastes into the marine and coastal environments, which can harm marine biodiversity and ecosystems (https://www.un.org/depts/los//general_assembly/contributions_2020/SecretariatBRS.pdf). The BRS Secretariat works closely with other relevant UN agencies, such as the International Maritime Organization and the Division for Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea, to ensure coherence and synergies in addressing these issues (https://www.un.org/depts/los/general_assembly/contributions_2014_2/BRS_Conventions.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The Secretariats of the Basel and Stockholm conventions (BRS) execute their objectives via several strategies: Firstly, as laid out in Article 16 of the Basel Convention (https://www.basel.int/Portals/4/Basel%20Convention/docs/text/BaselConventionText-e.pdf), Article 19 of the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf) and Article 20 of the Stockholm Convention (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf), The budget of the Secretariats and their staffing are determined by the conferences of the parties and are funded by contributions from parties, based on the United Nations scale of assessment (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The Secretariat also develop biennium work plans for how to implement the programmes of work of the Basel, Rotterdam, and Stockholm conventions. The work plans for the biennium 2024-2025 (https://www.brsmeas.org/Portals/4/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-CHW-RC-POPS-MNGMT-REP-BRSWorkplan-2024-2025.English.xlsx) include 36 programme of work activities. In addition various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Conventions. The strategies that the BRS secretariat use to achieve its objectives and mandates include (1) Establishing and facilitating the work of small intersessional working groups, expert working groups, and project groups, composed of representatives of Parties and observers, to carry out the activities under the work programmes, (2) Providing information, best practices, lessons learned, and recommendations on various aspects of the environmentally sound management of hazardous wastes and other wastes, through the development and dissemination of briefs, reports, and other materials, (3) Organizing and conducting capacity-building activities, such as regional workshops, webinars, and online courses, to assist Parties and other stakeholders in implementing the provisions and obligations of the Convention, and (4) Strengthening the communication and outreach with potential partners and other initiatives, such as the regional centres, other multilateral environmental agreements, and relevant organizations and networks, to promote information sharing and collaboration on hazardous chemicals and wastes issues (https://www.brsmeas.org/Portals/4/download.aspx?d=UNEP-CHW.16-INF-46-Rev.1.English.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The Secretariats of the Basel and Stockholm conventions (BRS) execute their objectives via several strategies: Firstly, as laid out in Article 16 of the Basel Convention (https://www.basel.int/Portals/4/Basel%20Convention/docs/text/BaselConventionText-e.pdf), Article 19 of the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf) and Article 20 of the Stockholm Convention (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf), The budget of the Secretariats and their staffing are determined by the conferences of the parties and are funded by contributions from parties, based on the United Nations scale of assessment (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The Secretariat also develop biennium work plans for how to implement the programmes of work of the Basel, Rotterdam, and Stockholm conventions. The work plans for the biennium 2024-2025 (https://www.brsmeas.org/Portals/4/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-CHW-RC-POPS-MNGMT-REP-BRSWorkplan-2024-2025.English.xlsx) include 36 programme of work activities. In addition various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Conventions. The strategies that the BRS secretariat use to achieve its objectives and mandates include (1) Establishing and facilitating the work of small intersessional working groups, expert working groups, and project groups, composed of representatives of Parties and observers, to carry out the activities under the work programmes, (2) Providing information, best practices, lessons learned, and recommendations on various aspects of the environmentally sound management of hazardous wastes and other wastes, through the development and dissemination of briefs, reports, and other materials, (3) Organizing and conducting capacity-building activities, such as regional workshops, webinars, and online courses, to assist Parties and other stakeholders in implementing the provisions and obligations of the Convention, and (4) Strengthening the communication and outreach with potential partners and other initiatives, such as the regional centres, other multilateral environmental agreements, and relevant organizations and networks, to promote information sharing and collaboration on hazardous chemicals and wastes issues (https://www.brsmeas.org/Portals/4/download.aspx?d=UNEP-CHW.16-INF-46-Rev.1.English.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The BRS Secretariat derives its mandate from the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm conventions, which established the BRS Secretariat as a joint secretariat serving the three conventions (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). Specifically, Article 16 of the Basel Convention (https://www.basel.int/Portals/4/Basel%20Convention/docs/text/BaselConventionText-e.pdf), Article 19 of the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/ConventionText/UNEP-FAO-RC-CONVTEXT-2017.English.pdf) and Article 20 of the Stockholm Convention (https://chm.pops.int/portals/0/repository/convention_text/unep-pops-cop-convtext-full.english.pdf) define the functions and responsibilities of the BRS Secretariat, which include providing administrative, technical and legal support to the parties and their subsidiary bodies, as well as receiving and conveying information from and to the parties. Additionally, the memoranda of understanding between the conferences of the parties and the entities administering the secretariats of the conventions, namely the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) (https://www.pic.int/Portals/5/download.aspx?d=UNEP-FAO-RC-COP.9-RC-9-14.En.pdf), clarify the institutional relationship between the parties and UNEP/FAO, including the delegation of authority, financial matters, reporting and programmatic cooperation. The BRS Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and resolutions adopted by the conferences of the parties and their subsidiary bodies, such as the Conference of the Parties serving as the meeting of the Parties to the Basel Convention, the Conference of the Parties to the Rotterdam Convention, and the Conference of the Parties to the Stockholm Convention (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/History/tabid/2690/language/en-US/Default.aspx). These decisions and resolutions provide guidance and direction for the BRS Secretariat's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other international bodies and stakeholders. The BRS Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.brsmeas.org/Implementation/ProgrammeofWork/SustainableDevelopmentGoals/Overview/tabid/8490/language/en-US/Default.aspx), the Minamata Convention on Mercury (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/MEAs/MinamataConvention/tabid/4083/language/en-US/Default.aspx), and the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM (https://www.brsmeas.org/Partners/UNEP/SAICM/tabid/4073/language/en-US/Default.aspx), which provide further legal frameworks for the BRS Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific issues and domains related to the sound management of chemicals and wastes.

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full:
Vertical coordination within BRS Secretariat involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as UNEP, the FAO, the conferences of the parties (COPs) and the subsidiary bodies of the three conventions, as well as the national focal points and regional centres of the parties. This is achieved through memoranda of understanding, reporting, and programmatic collaboration. The BRS Secretariat operates under the guidance of the COPs and their subsidiary bodies, such as the Chemical Review Committee (CRC) and the Persistent Organic Pollutants Review Committee (POPRC), and provides administrative and technical support to them (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The BRS Secretariat is headed by an Executive Secretary, who is assisted by two Deputy Executive Secretaries, one for the Basel and Stockholm conventions and one for the Rotterdam Convention (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Structure/OurTeam/tabid/2641/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The BRS Secretariat also has a matrix structure with four units: the Legal and Policy Unit, the Policy and Strategy Unit, the Programme Resources and Oversight Unit, and the Technical Assistance Unit (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Structure/OurTeam/tabid/2641/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The BRS Secretariat assists parties in the implementation of the conventions, provides information and guidance, facilitates technical assistance and capacity building, and coordinates with other international bodies. The BRS Secretariat works closely with the UNEP and FAO, which jointly serve the Rotterdam Convention Secretariat, and reports to the UNEP Executive Director and FAO Director General on administrative and financial matters (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Overview/tabid/3609/language/en-US/Default.aspx). The BRS Secretariat also cooperates with the regional offices of UNEP and FAO, as well as the regional centres designated under the Basel and Stockholm conventions, to deliver regional and national activities and services. There is also the Environmental Network for Optimizing Regulatory Compliance on Illegal Traffic (ENFORCE), which is a network of experts and practitioners that aims to enhance the implementation and enforcement of the Basel Convention and prevent and combat illegal traffic and trade in hazardous wastes (https://www.basel.int/Implementation/TechnicalAssistance/Partnerships/ENFORCE/Overview/tabid/4526/Default.aspx). Additionally, the BRS Secretariat engages with other relevant stakeholders, such as civil society, industry, academia, and media, to raise awareness and promote the sound management of chemicals and waste.

Source: Conversation with Bing, 2/15/2024

matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the CBD's objectives are to pursue the following goals in accordance with its relevant provisions: (1) Conservation of biological diversity: to protect and maintain the variability among living organisms and the ecological systems they form, as well as their intrinsic and instrumental values for humanity (preamble; Article 1), (2) Sustainable use of its components: to use the components of biological diversity, such as genetic resources, species and ecosystems, in a way and at a rate that does not lead to their long-term decline, thereby maintaining their potential to meet the needs and aspirations of present and future generations (preamble; Article 1), and (3) Fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources: to ensure that the benefits derived from the access to and exploitation of genetic resources, such as scientific, technological, economic and social benefits, are shared in a fair and equitable way with the countries and communities that provide such resources, as well as with the holders of traditional knowledge, innovations and practices relevant to the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity (preamble; Article 1; Article 8 j; Article 15; Article 16; Article 19). This objective also includes the provision of appropriate access to genetic resources and the transfer of relevant technologies, taking into account all rights over those resources and technologies (Article 1; Article 15; Article 16).

excerpt_full: According to the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the CBD's objectives are to pursue the following goals in accordance with its relevant provisions: (1) Conservation of biological diversity: to protect and maintain the variability among living organisms and the ecological systems they form, as well as their intrinsic and instrumental values for humanity (preamble; Article 1), (2) Sustainable use of its components: to use the components of biological diversity, such as genetic resources, species and ecosystems, in a way and at a rate that does not lead to their long-term decline, thereby maintaining their potential to meet the needs and aspirations of present and future generations (preamble; Article 1), and (3) Fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources: to ensure that the benefits derived from the access to and exploitation of genetic resources, such as scientific, technological, economic and social benefits, are shared in a fair and equitable way with the countries and communities that provide such resources, as well as with the holders of traditional knowledge, innovations and practices relevant to the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity (preamble; Article 1; Article 8 j; Article 15; Article 16; Article 19). This objective also includes the provision of appropriate access to genetic resources and the transfer of relevant technologies, taking into account all rights over those resources and technologies (Article 1; Article 15; Article 16).

Horizontal coordination within the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the biodiversity domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, indigenous and local communities, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that biodiversity is conserved, sustainably used, and equitably shared in all activities and policies. This coordination is led by the Secretariat according to Article 24 of the Convention (https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles/?a=cbd-24). For example, CBD works with the agriculture sector to promote the conservation and sustainable use of agricultural biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/agro/), with the health sector to enhance the linkages between biodiversity and human health (https://www.cbd.int/health/), with the ocean sector to protect and restore marine and coastal biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/marine/), or with the climate change sector to address the impacts of climate change on biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.cbd.int/climate/). Horizontal coordination within CBD can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Programme of Work on Island Biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/island/pow.shtml) or the Global Taxonomy Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/gti/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Biodiversity Liaison Group (https://www.cbd.int/blg/) or the Collaborative Partnership on Forests (https://www.cpfweb.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for biodiversity sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Ecosystem Approach (https://www.cbd.int/ecosystem/) or the Access and Benefit-sharing Clearing-House (https://absch.cbd.int/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for biodiversity issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Day for Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/idb/) or the Global Biodiversity Outlook (https://www.cbd.int/gbo/).
The CBD Secretariat provides leadership and direction on matters related to biodiversity, science and technology, shapes the biodiversity research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses biodiversity trends (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/).

It is institutionally linked to UN Environment, its host institution, as per decision II/19 (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/role.shtml). The Secretariat also liaises with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) to host the NBSAP Forum, through generous funding provided by the Global Environmental Facility (GEF) (https://www.undp.org/nature/our-flagship-initiatives/gbf-action-nbsap-support). matrix_cell_text_full: The CBD's jurisdiction is based on the principle of national sovereignty over biological diversity, meaning that the CBD applies to the components of biological diversity in areas within the limits of each Contracting Party's national jurisdiction, and to the processes and activities carried out under its jurisdiction or control, regardless of where their effects occur (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf). The CBD does not have authority over oceans and maritime zones beyond the limits of national jurisdiction, except for the responsibility to prevent or minimize damage to the environment of other States or of areas beyond the limits of national jurisdiction (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf). Therefore, the CBD's jurisdiction varies depending on the extent of each Contracting Party's national jurisdiction, which may include exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial waters, contiguous zones, inland waters, and coastal areas.

matrix_cell_text_full: The CBD Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a post-2020 global biodiversity framework, adopted by the Conference of the Parties at its fifteenth meeting, provide the vision, mission, goals and targets for biodiversity conservation and sustainable use for the next decade, aligning with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Paris Agreement (https://www.cbd.int/doc/strategic-plan/Post2020/Bubb.pdf). This framework, based on extensive consultations and inputs from various stakeholders, build on the achievements and lessons learned from the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011-2020 and the Aichi Biodiversity Targets (https://www.cbd.int/doc/strategic-plan/2011-2020/Aichi-Targets-EN.pdf), as well as the current state of knowledge and science on biodiversity and ecosystem services. Secondly, a four-year medium-term programme of work, approved by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the activities, expected outcomes, indicators and budget of the Secretariat for the period of interest, in support of the implementation of the Convention and its Protocols (https://www.cbd.int/information/adm-fin). This programme of work is structured around six core functions of the Secretariat, namely: servicing meetings of the governing bodies and subsidiary bodies; facilitating implementation; providing policy advice and support; fostering communication, outreach and partnerships; managing information and knowledge; and ensuring sound management and administration, as detailed in Article 24 of the Convention document (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf). The programme of work also includes a results-based management framework and a resource mobilization strategy. The major source of funding for the CBD Secretariat is the General Trust Fund for the Convention on Biological Diversity (BY Trust Fund), which is funded from the assessed contributions of Parties to the CBD, based on the United Nations scales of assessment (https://www.cbd.int/convention/parties/contributions.shtml). In addition, various mechanisms, initiatives and partnerships provide a platform for cooperation and coordination among Parties, other Governments, international organizations, civil society, indigenous peoples and local communities, and the private sector, on various thematic and cross-cutting issues related to biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/programmes). Some of these include: the Clearing-House Mechanism (https://www.cbd.int/chm), which facilitates the exchange of information and technical and scientific cooperation; the Global Taxonomy Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/gti/default.shtml), which enhances taxonomic knowledge and capacity; the LifeWeb Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/undb/media/factsheets/undb-factsheet-lifeweb-en.pdf), which supports the establishment and management of protected areas; the Bio-Bridge Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/biobridge/), which fosters technical and scientific collaboration among Parties; the Global Partnership for Plant Conservation, which supports the implementation of the Global Strategy for Plant Conservation (https://www.cbd.int/gspc/default.shtml); and the Biodiversity for Development Initiative ( Biodiversity for Development Initiative), which promotes the integration of biodiversity into development policies and plans.

This framework, based on extensive consultations and inputs from various stakeholders, build on the achievements and lessons learned from the Strategic Plan for Biodiversity 2011-2020 and the Aichi Biodiversity Targets (https://www.cbd.int/doc/strategic-plan/2011-2020/Aichi-Targets-EN.pdf), as well as the current state of knowledge and science on biodiversity and ecosystem services. Secondly, a four-year medium-term programme of work, approved by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the activities, expected outcomes, indicators and budget of the Secretariat for the period of interest, in support of the implementation of the Convention and its Protocols (https://www.cbd.int/information/adm-fin). This programme of work is structured around six core functions of the Secretariat, namely: servicing meetings of the governing bodies and subsidiary bodies; facilitating implementation; providing policy advice and support; fostering communication, outreach and partnerships; managing information and knowledge; and ensuring sound management and administration, as detailed in Article 24 of the Convention document (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf). The programme of work also includes a results-based management framework and a resource mobilization strategy. The major source of funding for the CBD Secretariat is the General Trust Fund for the Convention on Biological Diversity (BY Trust Fund), which is funded from the assessed contributions of Parties to the CBD, based on the United Nations scales of assessment (https://www.cbd.int/convention/parties/contributions.shtml). In addition, various mechanisms, initiatives and partnerships provide a platform for cooperation and coordination among Parties, other Governments, international organizations, civil society, indigenous peoples and local communities, and the private sector, on various thematic and cross-cutting issues related to biodiversity (https://www.cbd.int/programmes). Some of these include: the Clearing-House Mechanism (https://www.cbd.int/chm), which facilitates the exchange of information and technical and scientific cooperation; the Global Taxonomy Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/gti/default.shtml), which enhances taxonomic knowledge and capacity; the LifeWeb Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/undb/media/factsheets/undb-factsheet-lifeweb-en.pdf), which supports the establishment and management of protected areas; the Bio-Bridge Initiative (https://www.cbd.int/biobridge/), which fosters technical and scientific collaboration among Parties; the Global Partnership for Plant Conservation, which supports the implementation of the Global Strategy for Plant Conservation (https://www.cbd.int/gspc/default.shtml); and the Biodiversity for Development Initiative ( Biodiversity for Development Initiative), which promotes the integration of biodiversity into development policies and plans.

matrix_cell_text_full: The CBD derives its mandate from the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), which is the international legal instrument for "the conservation of biological diversity, the sustainable use of its components and the fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the utilization of genetic resources" that has been ratified by 196 nations (https://www.un.org/en/observances/biological-diversity-day/convention). Specifically, Article 1 of the Convention states the objectives of CBD, which are to conserve biological diversity, to use its components sustainably, and to share the benefits of genetic resources fairly and equitably; Article 23 establishes a Conference of the Parties, which shall be the supreme body of the convention and shall keep under review the implementation of the convention. It also specifies the functions, procedures and frequency of the meetings of the Conference of the Parties, and the participation of observers; Article 24 establishes the CBD Secretariat, which shall arrange for and service the meetings of the Conference of the Parties and perform other functions assigned to it by the convention or by any protocol. It also requires the Conference of the Parties to designate the secretariat from among the existing competent international organizations that have signified their willingness to carry out the secretariat functions; and Article 25 establishes a subsidiary body on scientific, technical and technological advice, which shall provide the Conference of the Parties and its other subsidiary bodies with timely advice relating to the implementation of the convention. The CBD's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations adopted by its governing bodies, including the Conference of the Parties (https://www.cbd.int/cop), the Subsidiary Body on Scientific, Technical and Technological Advice (https://www.cbd.int/sbstta), and the Subsidiary Body on Implementation (https://www.cbd.int/sbi). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for the CBD's work programmes and thematic areas, as well as cooperation and coordination with other conventions and organisations. The CBD's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various protocols and frameworks, such as the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (https://bch.cbd.int/protocol/#:~:text=The%20Cartagena%20Protocol%20on%20Biosafety%20to%20the%20Convention%20on%20Biological,diversity%2C%20taking%20also%20into%20account), the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-sharing (https://www.cbd.int/abs#:~:text=The%20Nagoya%20Protocol%20on%20Access%20to%20Genetic%20Resources%20and%20the,a%20fair%20and%20equitable%20way.), and the Post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/409e/19ae/369752b245f05e88f760aeb3/wg2020-05-l-02-en.pdf), which provide further legal instruments and targets for the CBD's jurisdiction over specific biodiversity issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within the CBD Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other international organizations, member governments, and local communities. This is achieved through organizing meetings, preparing reports, assisting member governments in the implementation of various programmes of work, coordinating with other international organizations, and collecting and disseminating information (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat). The CBD Secretariat, based in Montreal, Canada, operates under the guidance of the Executive Secretary, who is appointed by the United Nations Secretary-General 9https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/executive-secretary). The Executive Secretary leads the strategic and planning activities of the Secretariat, as well as the intergovernmental processes and activities under the Convention and its two protocols, guided by Article 32 of the Convention (https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles/default.shtml?a=cbd-32). The Secretariat is accountable to the Conference of the Parties (COP) and its subsidiary bodies as detailed in Article 23 (https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles.shtml?a=cbd-23) and Article 25 (https://www.cbd.int/convention/articles.shtml?a=cbd-25) of the Convention respectively (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/role.shtml). There are various divisions within the Secretariat, each focusing on different aspects of the CBD's mandate (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/staff/default.shtml). In addition, the CBD Secretariat collaborates with key organizations such as UN Environment, its host institution, and liaises with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) to host the NBSAP Forum (https://www.cbd.int/secretariat/role.shtml).

 — Horizontal Coordination evidence
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full:
Horizontal coordination within the CITES Secretariat involves collaboration with different organizations, instruments and processes that are relevant to the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity and wildlife trade, such as other biodiversity-related conventions, international organizations, enforcement agencies, scientific bodies, and civil society. This coordination is reflected in Goal 5 of the CITES Strategic Vision: 2021-2030 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/reports/Implementation/E-SV-indicators.pdf), specifically under Indicators 5.14, and 5.15, as well as Objectives 5.2 and 5.3. For example, CITES works with the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) to align its objectives and actions with the post-2020 global biodiversity framework (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-CoP19-Inf-11.pdf), with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) to ensure the sustainable management of marine and tree species (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/com/sc/62/E62-14-04-A1.pdf), with the World Health Organization (WHO) to address the links between wildlife trade and zoonotic diseases (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-CoP19-23-02_0.pdf), or with the World Customs Organization (WCO) to enhance the capacity and effectiveness of customs officers in combating illegal wildlife trade (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/sec/CITES-WCO.pdf). Horizontal coordination within the CITES Secretariat can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other organizations and processes, such as the International Consortium on Combating Wildlife Crime (ICCWC) (https://cites.org/eng/prog/iccwc.php) or the Joint CITES-CMS African Carnivores Initiative (https://cites.org/eng/node/55702), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, groups, and platforms, such as the Biodiversity Liaison Group (BLG) (https://www.cbd.int/blg/) or the Environment Management Group (EMG) (https://unemg.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for CITES implementation and cooperation with other organizations and processes, such as the CITES guidelines for developing legislation (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/prog/Legislation/guidelines_legislation.pdf) or the CITES Trade Database (https://trade.cites.org/), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for CITES issues and policies among other organizations and processes, such as the World Wildlife Day (https://www.wildlifeday.org/) or the CITES Newsletter (https://cites.org/eng/news/newsletter.php). The CITES Secretariat provides administrative and technical support to the Parties, facilitates the implementation and enforcement of the Convention, coordinates with other organizations and processes, and promotes the objectives and principles of CITES (https://cites.org/eng/disc/sec/index.php).

excerpt_<=50w: Strategies: instrument portfolio and governance tools used to pursue objectives (e.g., standards, MRV, compliance, capacity building).
matrix_cell_text_full: The CITES Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a ten-year Strategic Vision, adopted by the Conference of the Parties, outlines the Convention’s direction for the 2021-2030 timeframe in fulfilment of its mandate (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/reports/Implementation/E-SV-indicators.pdf). This vision, annexed to Resolution Conf. 18.3 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-18-03.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its Sustainable Development Goals, as well as the post-2020 Global Biodiversity Framework (https://www.cbd.int/doc/c/409e/19ae/369752b245f05e88f760aeb3/wg2020-05-l-02-en.pdf) being developed by Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It also recognizes the importance of global cooperation to address the threats posed by illegal trade in wildlife, as acknowledged by the United Nations General Assembly. The vision sets five broad goals and corresponding objectives and indicators to measure progress and performance. Secondly, a triennial budget and work programme, proposed by the Secretariat and approved by the Conference of the Parties, details the activities, outputs, and resources required to implement the Convention and the decisions of the Parties. The current budget and work programme for 2023-2025 is based on the priorities identified by the Parties and the Secretariat, as well as the expected income from the Trust Fund and external sources, as specified in Resolution Conf. 19.1 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/COP/19/resolution/E-Res-19-01.pdf). Thirdly various resolutions, decisions, agreements, and partnerships provide guidance and support for the implementation and enforcement of the Convention at the national, regional, and international levels, addressing legal and sustainable trade, compliance and enforcement, capacity-building, cooperation and collaboration, and awareness-raising, with key instruments listed here (https://cites.org/eng/res/index.php). The Convention is financed by core and external funds. The core funding, known as the CITES Trust Fund (CTL), finances the administrative costs of the Secretariat, the Conference of the Parties and its subsidiary bodies, the Standing Committee and other permanent committees. The CITES Trust Fund is replenished from contributions of the Parties to the Convention based on the United Nations scale of assessment, adjusted to take account of the fact that not all members of the United Nations are Parties to the Convention. The external funds, known as the CITES External Trust Fund (QTL) funds the voluntary programmes/projects activities costs. The CITES External Trust Fund consists of extrabudgetary contributions from Parties and other entities on a purely voluntary basis. Each offer of funding to the CITES External Trust Fund is negotiated and vetted by the Secretariat (https://cites.org/eng/disc/fund.php).

matrix_cell_text_full: The CITES Secretariat derives its mandate from the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES-Convention-EN.pdf), which established CITES as an international agreement between governments to regulate wildlife trade. Specifically, Article XII of the Convention defines the functions of the Secretariat, which include arranging and servicing meetings of the Parties and the committees, communicating with the Parties and other relevant organizations, preparing reports and studies, and providing advice and assistance to the Parties. Additionally, the CITES guidelines for developing legislation (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/prog/Legislation/guidelines_legislation.pdf), which were adopted by the Conference of the Parties in Resolution Conf. 8.4 (Rev. CoP15) (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-Res-08-04-R15_0.pdf), state that the Secretariat has the authority to review and assess the national legislation of the Parties and to provide them with recommendations and assistance to ensure compliance with the Convention. excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within the CITES Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions. This is achieved through the overall leadership and management of the Secretariat, strategic planning and policy matters of the Secretariat, Depositary Government and Parties’ liaison, resource mobilization, high level relationships with partner organizations, and relationships with UNEP Executive and Deputy (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The CITES Secretariat operates through various units such as the Governing Bodies Unit, Office of the Secretary-General, Outreach and Projects Unit, Science Unit, Administration & Finance Unit, Legal Unit, and Enforcement Unit. Each unit has specific roles and responsibilities that contribute to the overall functioning of the Secretariat (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The Office of the Secretary-General provides overall leadership and management of the Secretariat, leads on strategic planning and policy matters of the Secretariat, Depositary Government and Parties’ liaison, resource mobilization, leads on high level relationships with partner organizations, leads on the relationships with UNEP Executive and Deputy (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The Secretary-General serves serves as the chief executive officer of the Convention and reports to the Conference of the Parties (https://cites.org/eng/disc/cop.php). The CITES Secretariat’s work is organized around various units, each overseen by a unit head who works closely with the Secretary-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The Enforcement Unit provides enforcement support, relationships with international organizations combatting wildlife crime (i.e. ICCWC partners), wildlife crime and illegal wildlife trade advice (anti-smuggling, anti-fraud, combatting organized crime, money laundering and illegal wildlife trade, etc.), national reporting on illegal wildlife trade, and capacity building for enforcement (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). The Legal Unit provides support for compliance to Parties, National Legislation Project, legal and trade advice (legislation, annotations, etc), regulatory support to CoP and Committees, socio-economic / livelihoods issues, major groups liaison, relationships with international trade organizations and industry, national reporting, NIAPs, inter-agency affairs, legal advice on legal instruments and to the SG, and capacity building for legal/compliance matters (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES_Functional_Stucture_Oct2021.pdf). There are also committees that facilitate knowledge-sharing within the Secretariat. The Standing Committee provides policy guidance to the Secretariat and oversees the management of the budget. It also coordinates and oversees the work of other committees and working groups, and carries out tasks given to it by the Conference of the Parties (https://cites.org/disc/sc.php). The Animals Committee provides scientific advice and guidance to the Secretariat and the Parties on all matters relating to the international trade in animal specimens. It also reviews the implementation of the Convention and the effectiveness of its resolutions for animals (https://cites.org/disc/ac_pc.php). The Plants Committee performs similar functions as the Animals Committee, but for plant specimens. It also cooperates with the Animals Committee on matters of common interest (https://cites.org/disc/ac_pc.php). Additionally, the CITES Secretariat operates through various projects and programmes such as the Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants programme (MIKE), the CITES Tree Species Programme (CTSP), and others. The CITES Secretariat also underwent a restructuring as of September 2020 (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/documents/E-Annual%20Report%202020-2021.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to Article IX of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), the CMS Secretariat's objectives include several key functions: arranging for and servicing meetings of the Conference of the Parties, the Scientific Council and the Standing Committee (paragraph 4 a); maintaining liaison with and promoting liaison between the Parties, the standing bodies set up under AGREEMENTS and other international organizations concerned with migratory species (paragraph 4 b); obtaining from any appropriate source reports and other information which will further the objectives and implementation of this Convention and arranging for the appropriate dissemination of such information (paragraph 4 c); inviting the attention of the Conference of the Parties to any matter pertaining to the objectives of this Convention (paragraph 4 d); preparing for the Conference of the Parties reports on the work of the Secretariat and on the implementation of this Convention (paragraph 4 e); maintaining and publishing a list of Range States of all migratory species included in Appendices I and II (paragraph 4 f); promoting, under the direction of the Conference of the Parties, the conclusion of AGREEMENTS (paragraph 4 g); maintaining and making available to the Parties a list of AGREEMENTS and, if so required by the Conference of the Parties, providing any information on such AGREEMENTS (paragraph 4 h); maintaining and publishing a list of the recommendations made by the Conference of the Parties pursuant to subparagraphs (e), (f) and (g) of paragraph 5 of Article VII or of decisions made pursuant to sub-paragraph (h) of that paragraph (paragraph 4 i); providing for the general public information concerning this Convention and its objectives (paragraph 4 j); and performing any other function entrusted to it under this Convention or by the Conference of the Parties (paragraph 4 k). These functions enable the Secretariat to fulfil its role as the Convention's coordinating body.

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the CMS Secretariat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the wildlife conservation domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that migratory species are protected and their habitats are conserved in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by Article IX of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF). For example, CMS works with the aquatic species sector to promote the conservation and management of marine mammals, fish, and turtles (https://www.cms.int/iosea-turtles/en/page/mou-text-cmp), with the avian species sector to enhance the conservation and management of migratory birds (https://www.cms.int/en/publication/review-migratory-bird-flyways-and-priorities-management-0), the terrestrial species sector to develop the conservation and management of migratory land mammals and bats (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/Doc_13_Bats_Study_combined_E_0.pdf) or with the cross-cutting conservation issues sector to address common threats and challenges to migratory species, such as climate change, illegal killing, and renewable energy (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_scc-sc5_crp.3_e_cross-cutting-conservation-issues_e.pdf). matrix_cell_text_full: The CMS Secretariat works with various partners to implement the Convention and conserve migratory species. It cooperates with the secretariats of other biodiversity-related MEAs, such as CBD, CITES, Ramsar, and UNCCD, to harmonize policies and activities (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships), as per Paragraph 4(b) of Article IX of the Convention (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF) and resolution 11.10 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop12_res.11.10%28rev.cop12%29_e.pdf). It also collaborates with other inter-governmental bodies, such as UNESCO, IWC, and ITTO, to promote joint initiatives and projects on specific species or habitats, as per resolution 12.7 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop13_res.12.7_rev.cop13_e.pdf). It engages with non-governmental organizations, such as IUCN, BLI, OceanCare, and IFAW, to support scientific research, conservation action, and public awarenes (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships). It partners with the private sector, such as TUI AG, to raise funds and foster corporate social responsibility, following a code of conduct (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/basic_page_documents/code_of_conduct.pdf) adopted in resolution 10.21 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/10_21_synergies_e_0_0.pdf). It participates in the IPBES as an observer and contributes to its assessments and work programme (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/Doc_04_1_IPBES_E.pdf). It also supports the development and implementation of regional and thematic agreements and initiatives under the Convention, such as EAAFP, WHMSI, and SCF, as per Article IV and V of the Convention and Paragraph 6 of resolution 12.3 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop12_res.12.3_manila-declaration_e_1.pdf).

excerpt_<=50w: Strategies: instrument portfolio and governance tools used to pursue objectives (e.g., standards, MRV, compliance, capacity building).
matrix_cell_text_full:
The CMS Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies:
Firstly, the CMS Secretariat has a Strategic Plan. This plan, proposed for 2024-2032, aligns with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, as stated in the draft resolution UNEP/CMS/COP14/CRP14.2 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop14_crp14.2_spms_e.docx). The plan is revised periodically, with the latest revision published in February, 2024. The Strategic Plan outlines the Secretariat’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. It aligns with the Convention’s mandate to conserve migratory species of wild animals. Secondly, the CMS operates on triennium budgets to fulfill its strategic plans, but may also operate interim budgets as deemed fit. The interim budget for 2024 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/036_Interim%20Budget%20for%202024_ExCOP1%20%281%29_2.pdf) provides for the same funding levels as the 2023 budget that was approved by COP13. The budget period covers the calendar year, from January 1 to December 31 and details activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. In February 2024, the CMS COP14 will adopt a budget for the triennium 2024-2026, which will supersede the interim budget for 2024 (https://www.cms.int/en/news/2023028-process-adoption-interim-cms-budget-2024-through-silence-procedure-and-convening). Thirdly, the CMS Secretariat promotes and supports the development of Agreements. These agreements are designed to address the conservation needs of specific groups of migratory species or specific migratory species that have an unfavorable conservation status (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/agreements). The CMS Secretariat engages closely with UNEP through various mechanisms to enhance cooperation and policy coherence between UNEP and the multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs). This includes periodic meetings with UNEP Executive Director and the Director of Law Division and the MEAs Focal Points Network coordinated by Law Division (https://www.cms.int/en/news/cms-and-unep-strengthen-mea-coordination). The Secretariat also collaborates with a number of organizations outside the framework of formal agreements (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships). The CMS Secretariat crafts different action and strategic plans for different programs with varying cycles based on the decisions and resolutions of the Conference of the Parties (COP), the Scientific Council (ScC) and the Standing Committee (StC), while also accepting inputs from other environmental treaties and organizations (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/action-plans). It also supports the implementation of CMS instruments, such as Memoranda of Understanding (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/mou), Action Plans (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/action-plans) and Concerted Actions (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/concerted-actions), which provide cooperative frameworks for the conservation and management of migratory species, as listed here (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments). Finally, various partnerships, mechanisms, platforms and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Convention and its instruments, addressing threats, habitats, knowledge, governance and synergies, with key examples listed here (https://www.cms.int/en/partnerships).

matrix_cell_text_full:
The CMS Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies:
Firstly, the CMS Secretariat has a Strategic Plan. This plan, proposed for 2024-2032, aligns with the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, as stated in the draft resolution UNEP/CMS/COP14/CRP14.2 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/document/cms_cop14_crp14.2_spms_e.docx). The plan is revised periodically, with the latest revision published in February, 2024. The Strategic Plan outlines the Secretariat’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. It aligns with the Convention’s mandate to conserve migratory species of wild animals. Secondly, the CMS operates on triennium budgets to fulfill its strategic plans, but may also operate interim budgets as deemed fit. The interim budget for 2024 (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/036_Interim%20Budget%20for%202024_ExCOP1%20%281%29_2.pdf) provides for the same funding levels as the 2023 budget that was approved by COP13. The budget period covers the calendar year, from January 1 to December 31 and details activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. In February 2024, the CMS COP14 will adopt a budget for the triennium 2024-2026, which will supersede the interim budget for 2024 (https://www.cms.int/en/news/2023028-process-adoption-interim-cms-budget-2024-through-silence-procedure-and-convening). Thirdly, the CMS Secretariat promotes and supports the development of Agreements. These agreements are designed to address the conservation needs of specific groups of migratory species or specific migratory species that have an unfavorable conservation status (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/agreements). The CMS Secretariat engages closely with UNEP through various mechanisms to enhance cooperation and policy coherence between UNEP and the multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs). This includes periodic meetings with UNEP Executive Director and the Director of Law Division and the MEAs Focal Points Network coordinated by Law Division (https://www.cms.int/en/news/cms-and-unep-strengthen-mea-coordination). The Secretariat also collaborates with a number of organizations outside the framework of formal agreements (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships). The CMS Secretariat crafts different action and strategic plans for different programs with varying cycles based on the decisions and resolutions of the Conference of the Parties (COP), the Scientific Council (ScC) and the Standing Committee (StC), while also accepting inputs from other environmental treaties and organizations (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/action-plans). It also supports the implementation of CMS instruments, such as Memoranda of Understanding (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/mou), Action Plans (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/action-plans) and Concerted Actions (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/concerted-actions), which provide cooperative frameworks for the conservation and management of migratory species, as listed here (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments). Finally, various partnerships, mechanisms, platforms and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the Convention and its instruments, addressing threats, habitats, knowledge, governance and synergies, with key examples listed here (https://www.cms.int/en/partnerships).

matrix_cell_text_full: The CMS Secretariat derives its mandate from the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), which established CMS as an environmental treaty that aims to protect and conserve terrestrial, aquatic and avian migratory animals and their habitats (https://www.cms.int/en/convention-bodies/secretariat). Specifically, Article IX of the Convention defines the functions of the CMS Secretariat, which include organizing and servicing meetings of the Conference of the Parties, the Scientific Council and the Standing Committee, promoting and supporting the development of Agreements, stimulating and supervising research and conservation projects, promoting the exchange of information between the Parties and liaising with international governmental and non-governmental organizations. The CMS Secretariat is provided and administered by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) (https://www.cms.int/en/convention-bodies/secretariat). The CMS Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by the Conference of the Parties, the Scientific Council and the Standing Committee, which provide guidance and direction for the CMS Secretariat's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders 9https://www.cms.int/en/documents/cop-resolutions). The CMS Secretariat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/int_exp_regs_part1_1_e.pdf), and the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for the CMS Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific migratory species and issues.

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within the CMS Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), other multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs), regional and sub-regional organisations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through reporting, advising, and supporting. This is guided by Articles VII-IX of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF) as well as by the three Rules of Procedures for the Convention (https://www.cms.int/en/documents/rules-procedures). The CMS operates through the Conference of the Parties (COP) of all the members, the Standing Committee (StC) of 10 members, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Secretary (Article VII). It also has a Scientific Council (ScC) and other subsidiary bodies (Article VIII). The CMS Secretariat develops and promotes Agreements, services meetings, supports and supervises research and conservation projects and co-operates with governments and partner organizations (Article IX). The CMS Secretariat is provided by UNEP and is based in Bonn, Germany and has an out-posted office in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (https://www.cms.int/en/about/structure). Also, a network of focal points and experts supports the CMS's work in promoting the conservation and sustainable use of migratory species across their range states (https://www.cms.int/en/page/focal-points). Additionally, CMS operates 21 Agreements and Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) covering more than 500 species of migratory animals (https://www.cms.int/en/cms-instruments/agreements). Besides the Executive Secretary, at the CMS Secretariat, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of a Deputy Executive Secretary and 5 Unit Coordinators with portfolios focusing on different aspects of the CMS's mandate (https://www.cms.int/en/convention-bodies/cms-organizational-structure). In addition, CMS Secretariat coordinates with other MEAs and their secretariats, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, and the Convention on the Conservation of European Wildlife and Natural Habitats (Bern Convention) (https://www.cms.int/en/about/partnerships).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the UNCCD Secretariat involves collaboration with different regions and stakeholders within the land degradation domain, such as affected countries, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that desertification, land degradation and drought are addressed effectively and efficiently in all activities and policies. Thirdly, the Secretariat supports countries that want to achieve national/regional land degradation neutrality, identify how land and soil are critical for climate change adaptation and mitigation, implement land management practices, design programmes and projects that transform communities, and provide science and research needed to take informed decisions (https://www.unccd.int/convention/secretariat). Finally, the Secretariat has been granted additional mandates to play a leading role with regards to operational objectives on advocacy, awareness raising and education, policy framework, and science, technology, and knowledge, as well as a support role in other operational objectives on capacity building and financing and technology transfer (https://knowledge.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/The%20secretariat.pdf). matrix_cell_text_full: The UNCCD Secretariat derives its mandate from the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), which established the UNCCD as a legally binding framework to address desertification and the effects of drought (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf). Specifically, Article 23 of the Convention defines the functions and location of the Secretariat, Article 22 establishes modalities for the Conference of Parties, and Articles 20-21 outline the financial resources and funding mechanism of the Secretariat. Additionally, the UNCCD 2018-2030 Strategic Framework, adopted by the Conference of the Parties (COP) in 2017, specifies the vision, mission, strategic objectives, and expected impacts of the UNCCD for the period 2018-2030 (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/ICCD_COP%2813%29_L.18-1716078E_0.pdf). The Strategic Framework also defines the roles and responsibilities of the Secretariat, the COP, and its subsidiary bodies, as well as the affected country Parties and other stakeholders. The UNCCD Secretariat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and recommendations adopted by the COP and its subsidiary bodies, such as the Committee for the Review of the Implementation of the Convention (CRIC) and the Committee on Science and Technology (CST) (https://www.unccd.int/convention/governance/cric). These decisions and recommendations provide guidance and direction for the implementation of the Convention and the Strategic Framework, as well as cooperation and coordination with other relevant international bodies and conventions. Furthermore, UNCCD Secretariat's mandate is supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and the African Union Agenda 2063, which provide further legal frameworks for the UNCCD Secretariat's jurisdiction over specific land and soil-related issues and domains (https://www.unccd.int/land-and-life/sdgs/unccd-cbd-and-unfccc-joint-liaison-group).

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNCCD Secretariat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other environmental agreements, regional and sub-regional organisations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under Articles 8, 22, 23, and 24 of the UNCCD Convention (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf). The UNCCD operates through the Conference of the Parties, the Committee on Science and Technology, and the Committee for the Review of the Implementation of the Convention as subsidiary bodies, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Secretary (Articles 22-24). Other UNCDD subsidiary bodies include intergovernmental working groups, regional coordination units, and Global Mechanism groups (https://www.unccd.int/convention/governance). UNCCD's work is organised around five regional implementation annexes, each overseen by a Regional Coordinator (https://www.unccd.int/convention/governance). There is also the Management and Coordination Unit providing strategic and internal policy advice to the Executive Secretary. A network of regional coordination units and technical experts supports the UNCCD's work in promoting land degradation neutrality and sustainable land management (https://www.unccd.int/resources/reports/2019-evaluation-regional-coordination-units-august-2019).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within IPBES involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the biodiversity and ecosystem services domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that biodiversity and ecosystem services are conserved, restored and used sustainably for human well-being and nature's balance. This coordination is guided by the Functions, Operating Principles and Institutional Arrangements of IPBES document (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2675). IPBES works with the conservation sector to assess the status and trends of biodiversity and ecosystem services and their values (https://www.ipbes.net/assessment-reports), with the development sector to identify policy options and actions for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals and other global targets (https://www.ipbes.net/global-assessment), with the education sector to enhance capacity-building and knowledge generation and sharing (https://www.ipbes.net/capacity-building), or with the indigenous and local communities sector to recognize and respect their diverse knowledge systems and practices (https://www.ipbes.net/deliverables/1c-ilk). Horizontal coordination within IPBES can take various forms, such as (1) Joint planning and implementation of assessments and other deliverables with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the regional assessments of biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/regional-assessments) or the thematic assessment of land degradation and restoration (https://www.ipbes.net/assessment-reports/ldr) with FAO, UNCCD and other partners, (2) Participation in intergovernmental and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel (https://www.ipbes.net/multidisciplinary-expert-panel) or the Stakeholder Engagement Network (https://www.ipbes.net/stakeholders) (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for biodiversity and ecosystem services sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework) or the IPBES guide on the production and integration of assessments from and across all scales (https://www.ipbes.net/guide-production-and-integration-assessments-all-scales), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for biodiversity and ecosystem services issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the IPBES #PledgeToAct campaign (https://www.ipbes.net/pledgeact) or the IPBES media centre (https://www.ipbes.net/media-centre).

matrix_cell_text_full: IPBES collaborates with key organisations to support biodiversity and ecosystem services. It has an institutional link with the United Nations Environment Programme, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the United Nations Development Programme, based on a collaborative partnership arrangement approved by the Plenary in its decision IPBES-2/8 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/4911) . Similarly, IPBES has memoranda of understanding with several strategic partners, such as Future Earth, the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, the Inter-American Institute for Global Change Research, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature, as requested by the Plenary in its decision IPBES-4/4 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/5979) . Additionally, IPBES engages with various multilateral environmental agreements related to biodiversity and ecosystem services, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, the Convention on Migratory Species, the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, and the World Heritage Convention, as reported by the Executive Secretary in document IPBES/5/INF/16 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/7303). It also involves a large number of NGOs, organizations, conventions and civil society groupings as observers in the formal IPBES process, with several thousand individual stakeholders contributing to and benefiting from its work (https://www.ipbes.net/about). Moreover, IPBES supports the recognition and engagement of Indigenous peoples and local communities and their knowledge systems in its activities, as outlined in its approach adopted by the Plenary in its decision IPBES-4/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/5976).

matrix_cell_text_full: The IPBES Secretariat executes its defined objectives and functions via several strategies: firstly, a rolling work programme up to 2030 backed by Decision IPBES-7/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/27458) and based on requests, inputs and suggestions from relevant bodies under multilateral environmental agreements as well as governments and other stakeholders. The rolling work program aims to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, long-term human well-being and sustainable development. This work programme corresponds to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, including the Sustainable Development Goals (http://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/sustainable-development-goals/), the biodiversity-related conventions and other biodiversity and ecosystem service processes (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). It initially focuses on three topics: the interlinkages between biodiversity and other relevant issues reflected in the 2030 Agenda, the determinants of transformative change, and the tools and solutions for conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). Secondly, a biennial budget and work programme, approved by the Plenary, detail the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each deliverable of the work programme (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme). The current budget and work programme for 2022-2023 is based on the priorities identified by the Plenary and the available resources, as outlined in decision IPBES-8/1 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/102793). It also supports the development and use of policy support tools and methodologies, such as the IPBES online catalogue of policy support tools and methodologies (https://www.ipbes.net/catalogue-policy-support-tools-and-methodologies), the IPBES guide on the production and integration of assessments from and across all scales (https://www.ipbes.net/guide-production-assessments), and the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework). Finally, various assessments, task forces, expert groups, and platforms provide an evidence base for informing policy and decision-making, addressing the state of knowledge on the interactions between human societies and the natural world, the drivers and impacts of biodiversity change, and the options and pathways for achieving conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/104403). Some of the key assessments include the global assessment report on biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/global-assessment), the assessment report on invasive alien species (https://www.ipbes.net/ias), the assessment report on the sustainable use of wild species (https://www.ipbes.net/sustainable-use-assessment), and the assessment report on the diverse conceptualization of multiple values of nature and its benefits (https://files.ipbes.net/ipbes-web-prod-public-files/downloads/IPBES-4-INF-13_EN.pdf).

indicator_label: Enabling legal instrument and mandate clauses
source_title: resolution 65/162 on 20 December 2010 and Decision 26/4
excerpt_<=50w: Source of jurisdiction: formal legal basis enabling authority (treaty/charter article(s) or constitutive resolution reference).
matrix_cell_text_full:
IPBES derives its mandate from the 2010 Busan Outcome document (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/3115), which was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly resolution 65/162 on 20 December 2010 and Decision 26/4 
of 24 February 2011. The first session of Plenary convened in Nairobi in 2011 to determine modalities 
and institutional arrangements for IPBES (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/3377) and a second session of Plenary in Panama in 2012 established IPBES as an independent intergovernmental body to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services (https://www.ipbes.net/history-establishment). Specifically, paragraph 4 of the Busan Outcome defines the objectives and functions of IPBES, and paragraph 5 outlines the operating principles and modalities of IPBES. Additionally, the IPBES rules of procedure, rule 2 on the functions of the IPBES secretariat (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2675), states the duties of the secretariat in servicing and supporting the sessions of the Plenary and other subsidiary bodies, and in performing other tasks entrusted to it by the Plenary. IPBES's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its Plenary, such as the IPBES work programme (https://www.ipbes.net/work-programme), the IPBES conceptual framework (https://www.ipbes.net/conceptual-framework), and the IPBES assessment process (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/18538#:~:text=An%20IPBES%20assessment%20is%20a,ensure%20legitimacy%2C%20relevance%20and%20credibility.). These resolutions and provisional documents provide guidance and direction for IPBES's activities and deliverables, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/24663). IPBES's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the Convention on Migratory Species (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for IPBES's jurisdiction over specific biodiversity and ecosystem services issues and domains.
