excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full:
Vertical coordination within IPBES involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other multilateral environmental agreements, intergovernmental and non-governmental organizations, scientific and academic institutions, indigenous peoples and local communities, and other stakeholders. This is achieved through the establishment of partnerships, the provision of policy support, the facilitation of knowledge generation and the enhancement of capacity-building. This is structured under the Operating Principles and Procedures of the Platform section of the IPBES document (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2675), specifically in paragraphs 9-14. The IPBES operates through the Plenary, which is the decision-making body of the Platform and consists of all the members, the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel, which provides scientific and technical guidance to the Plenary, and the secretariat, which is responsible for the day-to-day operations of the Platform (paragraphs 9-12). The IPBES also has task forces, expert groups and other subsidiary bodies to carry out specific tasks and functions (https://www.ipbes.net/about). The IPBES supports the implementation of its work programme and the delivery of its products and services by engaging with various partners and stakeholders at different levels, such as the United Nations Environment Programme, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations and the United Nations Development Programme, which provide administrative and technical support to the Platform (paragraph 21). The IPBES also collaborates with other relevant international initiatives and processes, such as the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the Global Biodiversity Information Facility and the International Union for Conservation of Nature, to ensure coherence and avoid duplication of efforts (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/102783). Lastly, the IPBES promotes the involvement of a wide range of stakeholders, such as scientific and academic institutions, civil society organizations, the private sector and the media, in its activities and processes, and encourages the establishment of national, subregional and regional platforms and networks to support its work (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/102793).

matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UN-Women involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the gender equality and women's empowerment domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that gender equality and women's rights are promoted and protected in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by the General Assembly resolution 64/289 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/64/289) that established UN-Women as a composite entity with a dual mandate of normative support and operational activities. For example, UN-Women works with the human rights sector to support the implementation of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.unwomen.org/en/csw), with the peace and security sector to advance the women, peace and security agenda (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/ending-violence-against-women), with the development sector to promote women's economic empowerment and social protection (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/economic-empowerment), or with the humanitarian sector to ensure that women and girls are protected and empowered in crisis situations (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/economic-empowerment). Horizontal coordination within UN-Women can take various forms, such as: (1) UN System Coordination: UN-Women leads and coordinates the efforts of the UN system to ensure that commitments on gender equality and gender mainstreaming translate into action. It provides substantive and technical support to UN intergovernmental bodies, such as the Commission on the Status of Women, the Economic and Social Council, the General Assembly and the Security Council. It also works with the UN System Chief Executives Board for Coordination, the regional directors teams and the resident coordinator system to enhance coherence and accountability for gender equality across the UN system (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/un-system-coordination), (2) Regional and country coordination: UN-Women has a staff presence in six regional offices and more than 80 countries, where it works as a member of the UN country teams and the regional coordination mechanisms. It provides policy advice, technical support, capacity development and advocacy to national and regional partners, as well as innovative and catalytic programming to address the needs and priorities of women and girls. It also leads the UN gender theme groups and supports the development and implementation of the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/un-system-coordination/regional-and-country-coordination), (3) Strategic partnerships: UN-Women engages in policy dialogue, fosters knowledge exchange, and supports joint initiatives and campaigns to advance gender equality and women's empowerment. It also participates in various interagency and multisectoral platforms and networks, such as the Generation Equality Forum, the Spotlight Initiative, the Action Coalition on Economic Justice and Rights, and the UN Girls' Education Initiative (https://www.unwomen.org/en/partnerships), and (4) Advocacy and communication: UN-Women communicates and disseminates information on the achievements, challenges and opportunities for gender equality, using various media channels and tools, such as WomenWatch, UN Women Data Hub, UN Women Annual Report, and UN-Women social media accounts (https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/in-focus/strengthening-womens-access-to-justice/un-women-events).

matrix_cell_text_full: UN-Women collaborates with key institutions to advance gender equality and women's empowerment. It supports UN Member States as they set global standards for achieving gender equality, and works with governments and civil society to design laws, policies, programmes and services needed to ensure that the standards are effectively implemented and truly benefit women and girls worldwide (https://www.unwomen.org/en/about-us/about-un-women). Similarly, UN-Women liaises with the UN Development Programme (UNDP), implementing a relationship agreement effective since 1 January 2011, as per General Assembly resolution 64/289 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Executive%20Board/GA-Res-64-289-en-Adopted%20by%20the%20General%20Assembly%20on%202%20July%202010%20pdf.pdf), which established UN Women as a composite entity of the UN system, comprising the Division for the Advancement of Women, the International Research and Training Institute for the Advancement of Women, the Office of the Special Adviser on Gender Issues and Advancement of Women, and the United Nations Development Fund for Women (Paragraph 53). Additionally, UN-Women facilitates linkages and influences between women’s lived experiences and efforts with regional intergovernmental policy and programme processes, and leverages spaces for women leaders to directly engage regional institutions, participate in mediation and other conflict resolution and peace initiatives (https://africa.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/peace-and-security_africa). It also services the Commission on the Status of Women (CSW) (https://www.unwomen.org/en/csw#:~:text=The%20Commission%20on%20the%20Status,II)%20of%2021%20June%201946.) with its mandate in Economic and Social Council resolution 11(II) of 21 June 1946(https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3845514/files/E_2ndsess-_Resolutions-EN.pdf?ln=en) by preparing related reports. Moreover, UN-Women maintains a relationship with the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) (https://www.ohchr.org/en/treaty-bodies/cedaw#:~:text=The%20Committee%20on%20the%20Elimination,rights%20from%20around%20the%20world.), providing substantive support and servicing its sessions, with its functions detailed in the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/Documents/ProfessionalInterest/cedaw.pdf) and its Optional Protocol.

source_title: Un Women Strategic Plan 2022 2025).
excerpt_<=50w: Strategies: instrument portfolio and governance tools used to pursue objectives (e.g., standards, MRV, compliance, capacity building).
matrix_cell_text_full: UN-Women executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the organization’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets (https://www.unwomen.org/en/un-women-strategic-plan-2022-2025). This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2021/UN-Women-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025-brochure-en.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/CSW/PFA_E_Final_WEB.pdf). Secondly, an integrated results and resources framework (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2021-02/irrf_updated%20on%2028%20may.pdf), devised by UN-Women and approved by the Executive Board, details the specific results that UN Women aims to achieve and their respective set of indicators and resources. The current framework for 2022-2025 is based on the needs and priorities of women and girls worldwide, as outlined in the Annex I of the UN Women Strategic Plan 2022–2025. It also monitors and reports on the progress and challenges of achieving gender equality and the empowerment of all women and girls, a key aspect of the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwomen.org/en/news/in-focus/women-and-the-sdgs). Thirdly, a biennial Integrated Budget and work plan, devised by the entity and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current Budget for 2024-2025 (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/2023-05/Integrated%20Budget%202024-2025%20final.pdf) is tailored to the needs and priorities of the countries and regions where UN-Women operates, as outlined in the integrated results and resources framework. It also maintains the Women Count programme (https://data.unwomen.org/women-count), a global initiative to improve the production, accessibility and use of gender data for evidence-based advocacy and policy-making. Finally, various partnerships, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the UN-Women Strategic Plan, addressing governance and participation in public life, women’s economic empowerment, ending violence against women and girls, and women, peace and security, humanitarian action, and disaster risk reduction (https://www.unwomen.org/en/partnerships/businesses-and-foundations/why-un-women).

excerpt_<=50w: Source of jurisdiction: formal legal basis enabling authority (treaty/charter article(s) or constitutive resolution reference).
matrix_cell_text_full: UN-Women derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly resolution 64/289 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/64/289), which established UN-Women as a multi-tiered intergovernmental governance structure. Specifically, Paragraphs 48-56 define the Purpose and General Principles of UN-Women, Paragraphs 57-67 outline the structure of Governance of the Entity, Paragraphs 68-74 define the provisions for Administration and Human Resources, Paragraphs 75-80 define Financing operations, and 81-89 describe Transitional arrangements and Review of Implementation. Additionally, UN-Women's strategic plan (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2021/UN-Women-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025-brochure-en.pdf), which is approved by the Executive Board, states the vision, goals, and outcomes of UN-Women, and guides its operational activities and resource allocation. UN-Women's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Commission on the Status of Women (https://www.unwomen.org/en/csw), the Economic and Social Council (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/intergovernmental-support/economic-and-social-council#:~:text=The%20UN%20Economic%20and%20Social,bodies%2C%20particularly%20its%20functional%20commissions.), and the General Assembly (https://www.un.org/womenwatch/ianwge/resolutions/ga_res_by_topic.htm). These resolutions and decisions provide policy guidance and recommendations for UN-Women's work on gender equality and women's empowerment, as well as cooperation and coordination with other UN entities and stakeholders. UN Women's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2016/CEDAW-for-Youth.pdf), the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/CSW/PFA_E_Final_WEB.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwomen.org/en/what-we-do/2030-agenda-for-sustainable-development), which provide further legal frameworks for UN Women's jurisdiction over specific gender issues and domains.

source_title: Women involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the General Assembly, the Economic and Social
excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UN-Women involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council, the Commission on the Status of Women, the Executive Board, regional and country offices, and national partners (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/un-system-coordination). This is achieved through reporting, oversight, guidance, support, and partnership. This is structured under the Organizational arrangements section of the Comprehensive Proposal for the Composite Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of women (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n10/202/88/pdf/n1020288.pdf?token=g8uLB3qijkKMoS6hAv&fe=true), specifically under Article III (Functions and Structure), Subarticle E (Organization Chart and structure), as well as under Article IV (Organizational Arrangements), Subarticle B (Governance). The UN-Women is a subsidiary organ of the General Assembly and reports to the General Assembly through the Economic and Social Council. The Commission on the Status of Women is the principal global policymaking body on gender equality and provides recommendations to guide the activities and operations of UN-Women. The Executive Board oversees the operational activities of UN-Women and applies the overall policy guidance of the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council. The UN-Women is led by an Executive Director at the Under-Secretary-General level, who has full authority in financial and administrative matters and delegated authority from the Secretary-General. The UN-Women has three main divisions at the Headquarters level: the Intergovernmental Support and Strategic Partnerships Division, the Programme and Policy Division, and the Operations Division. The UN-Women also has regional divisions and subregional and country offices to provide technical support, oversight, and guidance to its country-level staff and to work with the United Nations country teams and national partners (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Executive%20Board/EB-2012-S2-UNW-2012-10-RegionalArchitecture-en.pdf). The UN-Women works as a full member of the resident coordinator system at the country level and as a leader of the United Nations gender theme group. The UN-Women also develops strategic partnerships with multilateral and regional organizations, civil society and women's organizations, and other relevant actors, fostering strong linkages between the normative and the operational aspects of gender equality and women's empowerment at all levels (https://www.unwomen.org/en/partnerships).

excerpt_full: Vertical coordination within UN-Women involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council, the Commission on the Status of Women, the Executive Board, regional and country offices, and national partners (https://www.unwomen.org/en/how-we-work/un-system-coordination). This is achieved through reporting, oversight, guidance, support, and partnership. This is structured under the Organizational arrangements section of the Comprehensive Proposal for the Composite Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of women (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n10/202/88/pdf/n1020288.pdf?token=g8uLB3qijkKMoS6hAv&fe=true), specifically under Article III (Functions and Structure), Subarticle E (Organization Chart and structure), as well as under Article IV (Organizational Arrangements), Subarticle B (Governance). The UN-Women is a subsidiary organ of the General Assembly and reports to the General Assembly through the Economic and Social Council. The Commission on the Status of Women is the principal global policymaking body on gender equality and provides recommendations to guide the activities and operations of UN-Women. The Executive Board oversees the operational activities of UN-Women and applies the overall policy guidance of the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council. The UN-Women is led by an Executive Director at the Under-Secretary-General level, who has full authority in financial and administrative matters and delegated authority from the Secretary-General. The UN-Women has three main divisions at the Headquarters level: the Intergovernmental Support and Strategic Partnerships Division, the Programme and Policy Division, and the Operations Division. The UN-Women also has regional divisions and subregional and country offices to provide technical support, oversight, and guidance to its country-level staff and to work with the United Nations country teams and national partners (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Executive%20Board/EB-2012-S2-UNW-2012-10-RegionalArchitecture-en.pdf). The UN-Women works as a full member of the resident coordinator system at the country level and as a leader of the United Nations gender theme group. The UN-Women also develops strategic partnerships with multilateral and regional organizations, civil society and women's organizations, and other relevant actors, fostering strong linkages between the normative and the operational aspects of gender equality and women's empowerment at all levels (https://www.unwomen.org/en/partnerships).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the UN Global Compact involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the sustainable development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that the core values and principles of the UN are respected and supported by all partners and that the partnerships are aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/un-business-agenda). This coordination is guided by the Guidelines on a Principle-based Approach to the Cooperation between the United Nations and the Business Sector (https://www.un.org/en/ethics/assets/pdfs/Guidelines-on-Cooperation-with-the-Business-Sector.pdf). For example, the UN Global Compact works with the human rights sector to promote the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (https://www.ohchr.org/documents/publications/GuidingprinciplesBusinesshr_eN.pdf), with the labour sector to provide guidance and support to strengthen business respect for labour standards by embedding and implementing the UN Global Compact labour principles (Principles 3, 4, 5 and 6) (https://unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc/our-work/labour#:~:text=The%20UN%20Global%20Compact%20provides,decent%20work%20for%20all%20workers.), or with the environment sector to foster climate action and circular economy (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/action/climate). Horizontal coordination within the UN Global Compact can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Action Platform for Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions (https://d306pr3pise04h.cloudfront.net/docs/publications%2FActionPlatform_Launch_Flyer.pdf) with UNDP, UNODC and OHCHR, (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the UN Global Compact Action Platform (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/action/globalallianceforsdgfinance) or the UN Global Compact Network (https://www.unglobalcompact.org/engage-locally), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for partnership engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UN-Business Partnership Guidebook (https://d306pr3pise04h.cloudfront.net/docs/issues_doc%2Fun_business_partnerships%2FUNBusinessPartnershipHandbook.pdf) or the SDG Compass (https://sdgcompass.org/), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for sustainable development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UN Global Compact Leaders Summit (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/events/2137-un-global-compact-leaders-summit) or the UN Global Compact Annual Report (https://ungc-communications-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/docs/publications/UN%20GLOBAL%20COMPACT_2022%20ANNUAL%20REPORT.pdf). The UN Global Compact provides a framework and a platform for businesses to align their strategies and operations with the UN values and principles, to engage in collective action for sustainable development, and to report on their progress and impact (https://www.unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc). The UN Global Compact facilitates the participation of various actors in the sustainable development sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on partnership matters (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/partnerships), (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/un-business-agenda).

matrix_cell_text_full: The UN Global Compact cooperates with various organizations to achieve its objectives. It works with the UN Secretary-General and the UN Global Compact Board, which provide strategic guidance and oversight for the initiative, as per resolution 73/254, paragraph 15 ([1](https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement). As a voluntary platform for businesses to align with the UN values and principles, the UN Global Compact's relationship with the UN is based on resolution 55/215, which endorsed the initiative in 2000 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N00/572/05/PDF/N0057205.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, the UN Global Compact supports the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, providing a framework for business action and partnerships, as affirmed in resolution 70/1, paragraph 67 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_70_1_E.pdf). It also partners with UN specialized agencies, funds and programmes, such as UNDP, UNICEF, UN Women, and UNEP, as well as other organizations such as the International Labour Organization, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, addressing relevant issues and sectors (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/un-business-agenda). Moreover, the UN Global Compact engages with its participants and stakeholders, including over 13,000 companies and 3,800 non-business signatories from 160 countries, through its Local Networks, platforms, programmes, and initiatives (https://unglobalcompact.org/participation/join/benefits), as outlined in resolution 73/254, paragraph 16 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement).

The UN Global Compact Office derives its mandate from the UN Secretary-General, who launched the initiative in 1999 as a voluntary platform for businesses to adopt sustainable and socially responsible policies and practices (https://unglobalcompact.org/take-action/20th-anniversary-campaign#:~:text=Launched%20in%202000%20by%20former,face%20to%20the%20global%20market.). Additionally, the UN Global Compact's jurisdiction is influenced by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (https://www.un.org/en/udhrbook/pdf/udhr_booklet_en_web.pdf), the International Labour Organization's Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_norm/---declaration/documents/publication/wcms_467653.pdf), the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_CONF.151_26_Vol.I_Declaration.pdf), and the United Nations Convention Against Corruption (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/UNCAC/Publications/Convention/08-50026_E.pdf), which provide the basis for its ten principles on human rights, labour, environment and anti-corruption (https://unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc/mission/principles). The UN Global Compact also supports the implementation of the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, which provide further guidance for its participants and stakeholders on advancing societal goals with an emphasis on collaboration and innovation (https://unglobalcompact.org/what-is-gc/mission).

Furthermore, the UN Global Compact's jurisdiction is endorsed by the UN General Assembly, which has adopted several resolutions and a decision that recognize its role and activities, encourage its expansion and participation, and call for its strengthening and alignment with the UN's values and principles. These include resolutions 55/215 of 21 December 2000, 56/76 of 11 December 2001, 58/129 of 19 December 2003, 60/215 of 22 December 2005, 62/211 of 19 December 2007, 64/223 of 21 December 2009, 66/223 of 22 December 2011, 68/234 of 20 December 2013 and 70/224 of 22 December 2015, as well as decision 72/543 of 20 December 2017 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N18/463/65/PDF/N1846365.pdf?OpenElement). These resolutions and decision reflect the support and recognition of the UN General Assembly for the UN Global Compact as a strategic partner and a leading initiative for corporate sustainability and social responsibility.

matrix_cell_text_full:
Vertical coordination within the UN Global Compact involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions such as the  UN Secretary-General, the UN Global Compact Board, the Global Compact Office, Local Networks, and participating entities (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/un-business-agenda) (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/governance). This is achieved through strategic guidance, oversight, coordination, implementation, and reporting, structured under the Governance section of the UN Global Compact Strategy 2021-2023 (https://ungc-communications-assets.s3.amazonaws.com/docs/about_the_gc/UN-GLOBAL-COMPACT-STRATEGY-2021-2023.pdf). The Global Compact Office, managed by an Executive Director, coordinates overall initiative management and upholds integrity measures (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/governance).
The Global Network Council, a joint committee of Local Network representatives and Global Compact Office chiefs, advises the Executive Director. Additionally, Regional Network Councils offer platforms for Local Networks to collaborate and provide systematic recommendations. Local Networks, business-led multi-stakeholder platforms, assist businesses in implementing the Ten Principles and advancing Sustainable Development Goals, adapting to national contexts (https://unglobalcompact.org/engage-locally/about-local-networks). With 69 Local Networks globally, each network is led by a Local Board and Representative, working closely with the Global Compact Office and Regional Teams (https://unglobalcompact.org/engage-locally/about-local-networks). There is also the Communication on Progress (COP) policy, which requires participating companies to report annually on their progress in implementing the Ten Principles and contributing to the Global Goals, a key aspect of the accountability and transparency of the UN Global Compact (https://unglobalcompact.org/participation/report/cop). Additionally, the Global Network Council, with regionally elected Local Network representatives, advises the Executive Director. Also, the Regional Network Councils in five regions collaborate and share best practices, electing a chair to join the Global Network Council (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/governance/local-network-advisory-group). UN Global Compact engages with its Local Networks, which are clusters of participants and stakeholders who work together to promote the UN Global Compact and its principles at the country level, as well as to support local learning, dialogue, and partnerships (https://unglobalcompact.org/about/governance).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNFPA involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the population and development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that sexual and reproductive health and rights, gender equality and empowerment of women, and population data and analysis are integrated in all activities and policies. matrix_cell_text_full: The UNFPA executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the UNFPA's vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 as detailed in document DP/FPA/2021/8 (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/DP.FPA_.2021.8_-_UNFPA_strategic_plan_2022-2025_-_FINAL_-_14Jul21_-_Corrected_19Jul21.pdf), aligns with the Programme of Action of the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD) (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/pub-pdf/programme_of_action_Web%20ENGLISH.pdf), the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Resolution_A_RES_70_1_EN.pdf), and the United Nations reforms. Secondly, an Integrated Budget, devised by the UNFPA and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each strategic objective. The current Integrated Budget for 2022-2025 is tailored to the needs of people left furthest behind and the priorities of stakeholders, as outlined in document DP/FPA/2021/9 (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/ENG_DP.FPA_.2021.9_-_Integrated_budget_2022-2025.pdf). It also maintains the Data for Development Platform, a key aspect of the implementation of the ICPD agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.unfpa.org/data). UNFPA evaluation is a key function that supports accountability, evidence-based decision-making and learning for the organization (https://www.unfpa.org/evaluation). It helps UNFPA become more agile and adaptive amid changing contexts, to reach the furthest behind first. UNFPA evaluation is governed by the evaluation policy, approved by the Executive Board, and implemented by the Independent Evaluation Office (IEO), which reports directly to the Executive Board. UNFPA evaluation covers various topics and levels, such as population dynamics, sexual and reproductive health, gender equality, humanitarian action, and organizational effectiveness. UNFPA evaluation also engages with various stakeholders, such as UNFPA staff, partners, donors, governments, civil society, and youth, to ensure relevance, quality, and use of evaluation findings and recommendations.

matrix_cell_text_full: UNFPA derives its mandate from the United Nations General Assembly, which established UNFPA as a subsidiary organ of the United Nations (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-un-system). UNFPA receives overall policy guidance from the General Assembly and the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC). It reports to its governing body, the UNDP/UNFPA Executive Board, on administrative, financial and programme matters (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-un-system). UNFPA's jurisdiction is also influenced by the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD), which was convened by the General Assembly in 1994 and adopted the Programme of Action 9https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/event-pdf/icpd_eng_2.pdf). excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNFPA involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other funds and programmes, regional and subregional offices, country and territory offices, and implementing partners (https://www.unfpa.org/unfpa-un-system). This is achieved through consultative strategic planning, clear organizational structure, robust contractual framework, and solid oversight functions. The UNFPA operates under the guidance and oversight of the Executive Board of the United Nations Development Programme, the United Nations Population Fund and the United Nations Office for Project Services, which consists of 36 members elected by the Economic and Social Council (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/resource-pdf/Background_Document_on_the_Population_Programme_of_the_UN.pdf). The UNFPA also engages with other United Nations entities through the United Nations Sustainable Development Group and the United Nations Development Coordination Office (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/UNFPA%20Information%20Note%20on%20UNDS%20reform%20-%20FINAL%20-%2020May2022.pdf). The UNFPA has a well-defined organizational structure, with its headquarters in New York, consisting of 14 divisions, offices, services and units, with some headquarters functions located in Geneva (humanitarian) and Copenhagen (supply chain) (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/Management%20Response%20-%20JIU%20MAR%20-%20FINAL%20-%20FINAL%20-%2026Apr23%20_0.pdf). Furthermore, UNFPA has six regional offices, eight representational offices, three subregional offices, and 121 country and territory offices (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/Management%20Response%20-%20JIU%20MAR%20-%20FINAL%20-%20FINAL%20-%2026Apr23%20_0.pdf). The UNFPA supports the implementation of its strategic plan and the achievement of its three transformative results through various modalities, such as country programme documents, intergovernmental and inter-agency processes, global and regional initiatives, and thematic funds (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/ENG_DP.FPA_.2021.8_-_UNFPA_strategic_plan_2022-2025_-_FINAL_-_14Jul21.pdf). The UNFPA has established a solid oversight framework for its activities, consisting of the Office of Audit and Investigation Services, the Evaluation Office, and the Ethics Office (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/Management%20Response%20-%20JIU%20MAR%20-%20FINAL%20-%20FINAL%20-%2026Apr23%20.pdf). The oversight structure is supplemented by external oversight provided by the Oversight Advisory Committee, the Board of Auditors and the Joint Inspection Unit (https://www.unfpa.org/sites/default/files/board-documents/main-document/Management%20Response%20-%20JIU%20MAR%20-%20FINAL%20-%2025Apr23-updated.pdf).

source_title: UN Research Institute for Social Development (UNRISD) — Horizontal Coordination evidence
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNRISD involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the social development domain, such as governments, civil society, academia, the private sector, and other UN agencies to ensure that social equity, inclusion and justice are central to development thinking, policy and practice. This coordination is currently guided by the UNRISD Strategy 2021-2025 (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4A1D94EBE95DA31A802586D8004198E8/UNRISD-Strategy-2021-2025.pdf). For example, UNRISD works with the social policy sector to promote transformative social policy for inclusive and sustainable development (https://www.unrisd.org/en/research/programme-areas/social-policy-and-development-2000-2009), with the gender sector to advance gender justice and development (https://www.unrisd.org/en/research/programme-areas/gender-justice-and-development), with the economy sector to explore alternative economies for transformation (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4E6DACF58A13FA328025870B0047E2B3/AE4T---A5-Prospectus-UNRISD-Programme.pdf), and with the environment sector to foster environmental and climate justice (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/CACDA014C224E6978025870B0047F8BF/Climate---A5-Prospectus-UNRISD-Programme.pdf). Horizontal coordination within UNRISD can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint research and policy analysis with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the project on Politics of Domestic Resource Mobilization for Social Development with UNDP, UNICEF and the International Policy Centre for Inclusive Growth (https://www.unrisd.org/pdrm) or the project on Sustainable Development Performance Indicators with the Bertelsmann Stiftung (https://www.unrisd.org/sdpi), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral networks and platforms, such as the Social Protection Inter-Agency Cooperation Board (https://www.social-protection.org/gimi/ShowWiki.action?id=62) or the UN Inter-Agency Task Force on Social and Solidarity Economy (https://unsse.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of knowledge products and tools for social development engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the flagship report on Overcoming Inequalities in a Fractured World: Between Elite Power and Social Mobilization (http://213.219.61.110/unrisd/website/projects.nsf/(httpProjects)/259326031472FE1BC125834C0038A3B9?OpenDocument), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for social development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UNRISD Conference on Overcoming Inequalities in a Fractured World (https://geneva.fes.de/fileadmin/user_upload/documents/2018/Booklet---UNRISD-Conference-2018.pdf) or the UNRISD Podcast Series on New Directions in Social Policy (https://www.unrisd.org/en/library/podcasts).

matrix_cell_text_full: The UNRISD pursues its objectives and mandates through several strategies: firstly, a five-year institutional strategy, developed through consultation with its stakeholders, defines the Institute’s vision, mission, research programmes, and expected results. The current strategy, applicable for 2021-2025 (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4A1D94EBE95DA31A802586D8004198E8/UNRISD-Strategy-2021-2025.pdf), focuses on overcoming inequalities and achieving a new eco-social contract. This plan aligns with the UN's Sustainable Development Goals and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The present strategy sets out five research programmes: Transformative Social Policy, Gender Justice and Development, Alternative Economies for Transformation, Environmental and Climate Justice, and Translating Research into Policy and Practice—Bonn Programme. UNRISD engages with its network and partners through a co-production process (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/about/outreach-unrisd-2023.pdf). The Institute is committed to comprehensive consultation with its stakeholders on where its research activities are directed, as well as how UNRISD conducts and communicates about its research (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/C393FC7BBDCA9A1B8025859D00490220/UNRISD-Institutional-Strategy-2021-2025-Consultation-Document-V1.2.pdf).  It also maintains the UNRISD Flagship Report, a key publication that synthesizes the Institute’s research and policy analysis on the social dimensions of contemporary development issues (https://www.un-ilibrary.org/content/books/9789290851332#:~:text=This%20UNRISD%20Flagship%20Report%20shows,are%20built%20in%20by%20design.). UNRISD receives no funding from the regular budget of the United Nations but depends entirely on voluntary contributions from national governments, multilateral donors, foundations and other sources and must fully mobilize all the financial resources necessary to cover the institutional and staff costs required to implement the UNRISD Strategy 2021–2025 ((https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/4A1D94EBE95DA31A802586D8004198E8/UNRISD-Strategy-2021-2025.pdf). The underlying assumption in terms of delivering results, therefore, is that UNRISD will design and successfully implement a fundraising strategy that will diversify the Institute’s funding sources, and generate predictable, stable and increased revenues. Various institutional initiatives, collaborations, and regulatory mechanisms also provide an operational framework for implementing the Institute's objectives. For instance, the work programme of the UNRISD Bonn office aims to create new interagency collaborations and enhance synergies between research and learning activities (https://www.unbonn.org/UNRISD#:~:text=The%20work%20programme%20of%20the,and%20contributing%20to%20training%20and). The Institute also organises regular Seminar Series to provide a space for open, informed, and insightful conversation around contemporary issues of concern to social development research and policy (https://www.unrisd.org/en/activities/events).

source_title: Statutes of UNRISD (https://documents
excerpt_<=50w: Source of jurisdiction: formal legal basis enabling authority (treaty/charter article(s) or constitutive resolution reference).
matrix_cell_text_full: UNRISD derives its mandate from the Statutes of UNRISD (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n63/166/83/pdf/n6316683.pdf?token=yYyPtTVGKo5T95bmTP&fe=true), which established UNRISD as an autonomous research institute within the United Nations that undertakes multidisciplinary research and policy analysis on the social dimensions of contemporary development issues. Specifically, the Statutes defines the Purposes and general organization of the Institute (Articles 1-3); Administrative and financial arrangements (Articles 4-9); and Personnel arrangements (Articles 10-14). Articles 2 and 3 specify that the Institute is supervised by a Board composed of five members nominated by the Social Commission, a representative of the Secretary-General, the Directors of the regional planning institutes, the representatives of two specialized agencies, and the Director of the Institute. The Board lays down general rules, approves work programmes and budgets, and reports to the Social Commission. UNRISD's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its Board, which is composed of eminent social scientists and representatives of the United Nations and its specialized agencies (https://www.unrisd.org/en/about/our-team). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNRISD's research agenda and activities, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. UNRISD's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unrisd.org/en/research/projects/2030-agenda-for-sustainable-development), the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (https://cdn.unrisd.org/assets/legacy-files/301-info-files/ED0B565D0ADD38A1C125804F00333F7E/Flagship2016_Ch5.pdf), and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/2051AAAA_Outcome.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for UNRISD's jurisdiction over specific social development issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Preamble and Part I of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the objectives of the UNICEF have been mandated to fulfil, as specified in this document, include several key functions: promoting and protecting the rights of every child, in accordance with the principles proclaimed in the Charter of the United Nations and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Preamble, paragraph 2); ensuring that each child enjoys a full and decent life, in conditions that ensure dignity, promote self-reliance and facilitate the child's active participation in the community (Article 23, paragraph 1); providing appropriate assistance and protection to children who are living in exceptionally difficult conditions, such as those affected by armed conflict, disability, displacement, exploitation, abuse or neglect (Preamble, paragraph 9; Article 22, 23, 32, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39); respecting the responsibilities, rights and duties of parents or other persons legally responsible for the child, and providing them with the necessary support for the child's well-being and development (Article 5, 18, 27); and fostering international cooperation for improving the living conditions of children in every country, in particular in the developing countries (Preamble, paragraph 10; Article 4, 17, 23, 24, 28, 29, 45) (https://www.unicef.org/media/52626/file). These functions enable the UNICEF to fulfil its role as the United Nations Children's Fund, which is responsible for providing humanitarian and developmental aid to children worldwide (https://www.unicef.org/what-we-do).

matrix_cell_text_full:
Horizontal coordination within UNICEF involves working with different sectors and stakeholders within the child rights domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, foundations, philanthropists, and other UN agencies to ensure that every child survives, thrives, learns, is protected, has a voice, and lives in a safe and clean environment. This coordination is guided by the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.unicef.org/media/52626/file) and the UNICEF Strategic Plan (2022-2025) (https://www.unicef.org/sites/default/files/2022-02/UNICEF-strategic-plan-2022-2025-publication-EN.pdf). For example, UNICEF works with the health sector to provide immunization, nutrition, and maternal and newborn care services (https://www.unicef.org/health), with the education sector to ensure quality and inclusive learning opportunities for all children (https://www.unicef.org/education), with the humanitarian sector to prevent and respond to violence, abuse, and exploitation of children (https://www.unicef.org/protection), or with the environment sector to address the impacts of climate change and environmental degradation on children (https://www.unicef.org/environment-and-climate-change). Horizontal coordination within UNICEF can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Partnership to End Violence Against Children (https://www.end-violence.org/) or the Generation Unlimited initiative (https://www.generationunlimited.org/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (https://interagencystandingcommittee.org/) or the Scaling Up Nutrition Movement (https://scalingupnutrition.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for child rights sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Core Commitments for Children in Humanitarian Action (https://www.corecommitments.unicef.org/) or the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (https://mics.unicef.org/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for child rights issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the State of the World’s Children report (https://www.unicef.org/reports/state-of-worlds-children) or the World Children’s Day (https://www.unicef.org/world-childrens-day)
Through its coordination, UNICEF provides leadership and direction on matters related to child rights, while shaping the child rights agenda, setting standards, articulating evidence-based policy options, providing technical support to countries, and monitoringand assessesing child rights trends (https://www.unicef.org/about/what-we-do).

excerpt_<=50w: Strategies: instrument portfolio and governance tools used to pursue objectives (e.g., standards, MRV, compliance, capacity building).
matrix_cell_text_full: UNICEF implements its objectives through several key strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan (2022-2025), revised by the Executive Board, outlining UNICEF’s vision, mission, and goals aligned with the Convention on the Rights of the Child and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (https://www.unicef.org/sites/default/files/2022-02/UNICEF-strategic-plan-2022-2025-publication-EN.pdf), detailed in document E/ICEF/2021/11 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N21/108/01/PDF/N2110801.pdf?OpenElement). Secondly, a biennial Integrated Results and Resources Framework (2022-2025) specifies expected results, indicators, and resources for each Strategic Plan outcome, based on a theory of change and results-based management (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/7426/file/2021-25-Add1-Strategic_Plan_2022-2025-IRRF-EN-ODS.pdf), as outlined in document E/ICEF/2021/12 (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/5316/file/2021-12-Draft_Strategic_Plan_2022-2025-EN-2021.05.04.pdf). UNICEF also focuses on monitoring the implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (https://www.unicef.org/child-rights-convention/unicef-role). Additionally, UNICEF's Data for Children Strategic Framework sets principles for data work, including action, innovation, and trust, with strategic objectives like improving data quality and fostering data partnerships (https://data.unicef.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Data-for-Children-Strategic-Framework-UNICEF.pdf). The UNICEF Disability Inclusion Policy and Strategy (DIPAS) 2022-2030 aligns with the CRPD, CRC, and UNDIS, setting priorities for disability-inclusive services and participation (https://www.unicef.org/media/134511/file/An%20inclusive%20world,%20starts%20with%20me,%20with%20you,%20with%20all%20of%20us.pdf). Finally, the UNICEF 2021-2030 Child Protection Strategy aligns with the CRC and SDGs, focusing on strengthening child protection systems, addressing harmful social norms, leveraging partnerships, and enhancing evidence for child protection (https://www.unicef.org/media/104416/file/Child-Protection-Strategy-2021.pdf). These comprehensive strategies enable UNICEF to deliver results for children globally, including in humanitarian and fragile contexts.

excerpt_<=50w: Source of jurisdiction: formal legal basis enabling authority (treaty/charter article(s) or constitutive resolution reference).
matrix_cell_text_full: UNICEF derives its mandate from the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), establishing it as the leading global child rights authority within the United Nations system (https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/children). Specifically, Resolution 57/60 of the UNGA provides the legal basis for UNICEF's jurisdiction over the protection and promotion of the rights of every child, everywhere (http://www.worldlii.org/int/other/UNGA/2002/125.pdf). Additionally, UNICEF's jurisdiction is guided by the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), which is the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history (https://www.unicef.org/media/52626/file). UNICEF also supports the implementation of other international and regional instruments and mechanisms that advance the rights and well-being of children and young people, such as the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW) (https://www.unwomen.org/sites/default/files/Headquarters/Attachments/Sections/Library/Publications/2016/CEDAW-for-Youth.pdf), the African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACRWC) (https://au.int/sites/default/files/treaties/36804-treaty-african_charter_on_rights_welfare_of_the_child.pdf), and the Committee on the Rights of the Child (CRC Committee) (https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/legal-standards-and-guidelines/crcc156-guidelines-regarding-implementation-optional).

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNICEF involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through delegation of authority, directing, and controlling. The body responsible for guiding UNICEF’s global work is a 36-member Executive Board made up entirely of government representatives (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/media/14411/file/2023-EB-Informal_Guide_2023-EN-2022.12.19.pdf). The executive board is responsible for establishing policies, approving new programmes, and making key decisions on administrative and financial plans. The Office of the Secretary of the Executive Board (OSEB) is responsible for maintaining an effective relationship between the Executive Board and the UNICEF secretariat 9https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/board-secretariat). UNICEF operates through its country offices that are responsible for carrying out the organization’s mission through a programme of cooperation developed in partnership with the host government (https://www.unicef.org/where-we-work). These programs are planned and delivered in five-year stints, and they are designed to focus on practical ways to improve the rights and prospects of women and children in that country (https://www.unicef.org/executiveboard/country-programme-documents). Regional Offices within host countries are responsible for guiding the delivery of this work, and they report and provide technical assistance to country offices when needed. There are also a range of specialized offices dotted around the world, such as UNICEF’s Supply Division which is responsible for procuring and delivering most of life-saving vaccines that UNICEF delivers in developing countries (https://www.unicef.org/supply/). The overall management and administration of UNICEF as a global organization takes place at its headquarters in New York, USA, where UNICEF’s global policy on children is formed under the supervision of the UNICEF executive team. UNICEF’s operational framework aims to help UNICEF staff and partners develop programmes across the social ecological model and the mental health continuum of prevention, promotion and treatment to improve the mental health and psychosocial wellbeing of children, adolescents and their caregivers globally, working together with a broad range of partners at the country, regional and global levels (https://www.unicef.org/reports/global-multisectoral-operational-framework).

source_title: resolution 1995 (XIX) of 30 December 1964 (https://unctad
excerpt_<=50w: Defined objectives: stated institutional purposes/goals expressed in founding and/or strategic texts.
matrix_cell_text_full: As per the  General Assembly resolution 1995 (XIX) of 30 December 1964 (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf),  Key objectives of UNCTAD include promoting international trade, especially to accelerate economic development, and enhancing trade between countries at varied development stages, including developing countries and those with different economic systems (section II, paragraph 3 a). It formulates principles and policies on international trade and economic development (section II, paragraph 3 b), proposes effective implementation strategies, considering economic system diversity and development stages (section II, paragraph 3 c). UNCTAD reviews and coordinates United Nations system activities in international trade and economic development, collaborating with the General Assembly and Economic and Social Council (section II, paragraph 3 d). It initiates actions for negotiating and adopting multilateral trade legal instruments (section II, paragraph 3 e), harmonizes trade and development policies of governments and regional groups (section II, paragraph 3 f), and addresses other relevant matters (section II, paragraph 3 g). Additionally, UNCTAD evaluates and recommends institutional arrangement improvements, including comprehensive organization establishment within the UN system (section III, paragraphs 30 and 31). Additionally, UNCTAD's jurisdiction is influenced by the outcomes of its quadrennial conferences, which set the priorities and work programme of the organization (https://investmentpolicy.unctad.org/investment-dispute-settlement). UNCTAD also supports the implementation of the UN's development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals including the ocean ((https://unctad.org/news/conservation-and-sustainable-use-marine-biodiversity-areas-beyond-national-jurisdiction-recent)), which provide further legal frameworks for UNCTAD's jurisdiction over specific trade and development issues and regions (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/iteiit16_en.pdf)

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNCTAD involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with Other Institutions within the United Nations System section of the General Assembly resolution 1995 (XIX), specifically in section II, paragraph 3 d (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf). UNCTAD also has a Trade and Development Board of 55 members, a secretariat headed by a Secretary-General, and various commissions, committees, and intergovernmental groups (section IV, paragraphs 32-40) (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/dtltlb2016d1_en.pdf). UNCTAD supports the implementation of the UN development agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, offering research and analysis, technical assistance, intergovernmental consensus-building, and policy advice for developing countries (section II, paragraph 3 c) (https://elearning.unctad.org/pluginfile.php/34150/mod_page/content/12/UNCTAD_Competition_Consumer_Policies_short_course_part1.pdf). UNCTAD also leads the UN Inter-Agency Cluster on Trade and Productive Capacity, involving 15 UN agencies, providing a mechanism for the coordination of trade and development operations at the national and regional levels within the UN system, as endorsed by the UN Chief Executives Board for Coordination (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/dom20092rev1_en.pdf). UNCTAD also cooperates with other international and regional organizations, such as WTO, OECD, World Bank, ILO, and CITES, addressing common trade and development challenges (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/UNDOC/GEN/N16/459/44/PDF/N1645944.pdf?OpenElement).

source_title: United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) — Horizontal Coordination evidence
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNDP involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, foundations, the academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that sustainable development goals are achieved in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by the UNDP Strategic Plan (2022 - 2025) (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2021-09/UNDP-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025_1.pdf). For example, UNDP works with the governance sector to promote democratic institutions and human rights (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2022-07/Renewed%20Governance%20and%20Peacebuilding%20Framework%20for%20Africa%202022-2025_Summarised%20Document_0.pdf), with the environment sector to address climate change and biodiversity loss (https://www.undp.org/nature/our-work-areas/biodiversity-conservation), with the crisis prevention and recovery sector to support peacebuilding and resilience (https://www.undp.org/tag/crisis-response), or with the poverty reduction and inclusive growth sector to reduce inequalities and enhance social protection (https://www.undp.org/tag/poverty-reduction-and-inequality). Horizontal coordination within UNDP can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UNDP-UNEP Poverty-Environment Action for Sustainable Development Goals (https://www.undp.org/policy-centre/nairobi/poverty-environment-action-sdgs#:~:text=Poverty%2DEnvironment%20Action%20aims%20at,and%20private%20finance%20and%20investment.), the UNDP-UN Women Joint Programme on Electoral Assistance (https://www.undp.org/publications/preventing-violence-against-women-elections-programming-guide) or the UNDP-UNICEF-UNFPA Joint Programme on Local Governance and Decentralized Service Delivery (http://web.undp.org/evaluation/evaluations/documents/decentralization_final_Report.PDF), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the UN Sustainable Development Group (https://unsdg.un.org/about) or the Global Partnership for Effective Development Cooperation (http://effectivecooperation.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for development sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Human Development Report (http://hdr.undp.org/en) or the Socio-Economic Impact Assessment (https://www.undp.org/coronavirus/socio-economic-impact-covid-19), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the UNDP Goodwill Ambassadors and Advocates (https://www.undp.org/goodwill-ambassadors-and-advocates) or the UNDP Shop (https://shop.undp.org/).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNDP collaborates with various partners to advance sustainable development. It works with governments, providing policy advice, technical assistance, and financial support, based on the UN Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) and the Country Programme Documents (CPDs) that outline the country-specific priorities and results (https://www.undp.org/our-partners). It coordinates with the UN development system, ensuring coherent and effective support to countries, with its Administrator as the Vice-Chair of the UN Sustainable Development Group, which unites the 40 UN entities that contribute to the attainment of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development at the country level (https://popp.undp.org/policy-page/managing-partnerships). Furthermore, UNDP partners with international financial institutions, mobilizing non-core funding and implementing joint projects, such as the World Bank, the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, with whom UNDP has formal agreements (https://www.undp.org/our-partners). It likewise collaborates with other UN entities, such as the UN Environment Programme, the UN Human Settlements Programme, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, and the UN Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women, on various thematic areas and initiatives, while also engaging with the private sector to foster innovation and entrepreneurship, and with foundations, civil society organizations, and goodwill ambassadors, leveraging their knowledge, networks, and resources, through various platforms and initiatives like the SDG Philanthropy Platform, the Business Call to Action, and the UNDP Innovation Facility (http://web.undp.org/evaluation/documents/directors-desk/papers/UNDPs_partnership_with_private_sector-12_2017.pdf). These partnerships are essential for UNDP to fulfill its strategic plan and contribute to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

matrix_cell_text_full: The UNDP executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised annually by the Executive Board, establishes the UNDP's vision, mission, directions of change, signature solutions, and enablers. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2021-09/UNDP-Strategic-Plan-2022-2025_1.pdf), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Paris Agreement, and is structured around “3x6x3” - 3 directions of change, 6 signature solutions, and 3 enablers - to help countries expand human capabilities and development choices, build a more equitable world, and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The three directions of change are structural transformation, leaving no one behind, and resilience. The six signature solutions are poverty and inequality, governance, resilience, environment, energy, and gender equality. The three enablers are strategic innovation, digitalization, and development financing. Secondly, an annual integrated budget and workplan, devised by the UNDP and ratified by the Executive Board, detail activities, outputs, indicators, and resources corresponding to each signature solution. The budget and workplan for 2024 is tailored to the countries' needs and stakeholders' priorities (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2023-12/dp2024-CRP1_3.pdf). The UNDP also maintains the SDG Accelerator Lab Network, a key aspect of the innovation and digitalisation of the UNDP (https://www.undp.org/acceleratorlabs). UNDP proposes a total budget of $5.4 billion for 2022-2025, comprising $1.4 billion for institutional effectiveness and $4 billion for development activities based on projected income and in alignment with the strategic plan outcomes and outputs. In order to achieve its mandate, UNDP relies entirely on voluntary contributions from UN Member States, multilateral organizations, private sector and other sources, in the form of unrestricted regular resources (core), and contributions earmarked for a specific theme, programme or project (https://www.undp.org/funding). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the UNDAF, the UNDP Strategic Plan, and the SDGs, addressing poverty and inequality, governance, resilience, environment, energy, and gender equality (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/2022-07/UNDP%20Strategic%20Plan%202022-2025.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNDP derives its mandate from the United Nation's General Assembly resolution 2029 (XX), establishing it in 1965 as a merger of two previous programmes, the United Nations Expanded Programme of Technical Assistance (EPTA) (1949) and the United Nations Special Fund (1958) to provide technical assistance to developing countries and to be responsible for the coordination of development activities on the country level, as well as the monitoring and reporting of the progress made in achieving the development goals (UNDP-MX-SpecialFundandTechnicalAssistanceMX.pdf). Specifically, Paragraph 4 of the Resolution states that a single inter-governmental committee of thirty-seven members, to be known as the Governing Council of the UNDP, shall be established to perform the funtions previously exercised by the Governing Council of the Special Fund and the Technical Assistance Committee, including the consideration and approval of projects and programmes and the allocation of funds, and Paragraph 5 requests the Economic and Social Council to elect the members of the Governing Council from among States Members of the United Nations or members of the specialized agencies or of the International Atomic Energy Agency, providing for equitable and balanced representation. Similarly, Paragraph 6 of the Resolution establishes the Inter-Agency Consultative Board of the UNDP to meet under the chairmanship of the Administrator or Co-Administrator. UNDP’s mandate is also influenced by the quadrennial comprehensive policy review of operational activities for development of the United Nations system (QCPR), which provides guidance and direction for UNDP and other UN development agencies (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/dp2022-17_Annex%203.docx). Its mandate is likewise supported by its Financial Regulations Rules (https://popp.undp.org/document/undp-financial-regulations-and-rules) and by its Programme and Operations Policies and Procedures (https://popp.undp.org/). In addition, the UNDP's mandate is influenced by the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.undp.org/sustainable-development-goals/life-on-land?gad_source=1&gclid=CjwKCAiA_tuuBhAUEiwAvxkgTs0LJirFb70iqfh78qtj276maQH96QDdTQEyrmw-FYYh6IPHZd3pDxoCO5IQAvD_BwE).

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNDP involves working with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through alignment, integration, and coherence for SDG implementation and review. This is structured under the Institutional and Coordination Mechanisms guidance note, which provides information on how countries have adapted their existing institutional and coordination frameworks or established new ones in order to implement the SDGs (https://www.undp.org/sites/g/files/zskgke326/files/publications/Institutional_Coordination_Mechanisms_GuidanceNote.pdf). The UNDP operates through the Executive Board of 36 members, which oversees and supports the activities of UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS, and UN Women. The UNDP also has a leadership team headed by an Administrator, who is the third highest-ranking official of the United Nations after the United Nations Secretary-General and Deputy Secretary-General (https://www.undp.org/organizational-chart). The UNDP leadership team consists of an Associate Administrator, five Assistant Administrators, a Director of the Bureau of External Relations and Advocacy, a Director of the Bureau of Management Services, and a Chief of Staff (https://www.undp.org/organizational-chart). It has six regional bureaus, each led by a Regional Director, who works closely with the Administrator and the leadership team to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the organization (https://www.undp.org/organizational-chart). There is also the UN Development Group (UNDG), which unites the 40 UN funds, programmes, specialized agencies, departments, and offices that play a role in development (https://unsceb.org/united-nations-development-group-undg). The UNDG is led by the UNDG Chair, who is the UNDP Administrator, and supported by the UNDG secretariat, which is hosted by UNDP. The UNDG ensures coordination and coherence among the UN entities at the global, regional, and country levels, and supports the Resident Coordinators and UN Country Teams in delivering effective and efficient support to countries (https://unsceb.org/about). The UNDP also has country offices and technical experts that support the UNDP's work in promoting sustainable development, democratic governance, and peacebuilding in 170 countries and territories (https://www.undp.org/acceleratorlabs/our-locations). Additionally, the UNDP hosts the UN Office for South-South Cooperation, which promotes and facilitates South-South and triangular cooperation among countries across the world (https://data.undp.org/insights/south-south-cooperation).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNEP collaborates with a wide range of organizations to fulfill its objectives. It engages with 193 Member States and various stakeholders through the UN Environment Assembly (UNEA), established in 2013 by resolution 67/251, serving as the highest-level environmental decision-making body (https://undocs.org/A/Res/67/251). As the primary environmental authority within the UN system, UNEP's relationship with the UN is grounded in resolution 2997 (XXVII), which established UNEP in 1972 (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/RESOLUTION/GEN/NR0/270/27/IMG/NR027027.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, UNEP supports multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans, providing legal and operational frameworks for specific environmental issues and regions, as stipulated in resolution 2997 (XXVII), paragraph 2 c (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/RESOLUTION/GEN/NR0/270/27/IMG/NR027027.pdf?OpenElement), and resolution 58/240, paragraph 4 of the UN General Assembly (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_58_240.pdf). It also collaborates with UN specialized agencies like FAO, IMO, and IOC, and other organizations such as ISA, ITLOS, and RFMOs, addressing shared environmental concerns. Moreover, UNEP contributes to the Regular Process for Global Reporting and Assessment of the Marine Environment, offering data on marine environmental conditions, as recognized in resolution 57/141, paragraph 6 (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_57_141.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNEP fulfills its objectives through diverse strategies: firstly, a four-year Medium-Term Strategy (MTS) for the period 2022–2025 set by and adopted by the UN Environmental Assembly (UNEA), adopted in 2021 (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/35162/Doc3%20Reve1%20EnglishK2100501.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y), aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Stockholm Declaration on the Human Environment, and the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development. The MTS defines UNEP’s vision, mission, strategic objectives, core functions, subprogrammes and indicators for measuring progress (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/policies-and-strategies). Secondly, a biennial Programme of Work and Budget 2022-2023, based on the MTS, devised by UNEP and ratified by UNEA, details the activities, outputs, resources, and partnerships corresponding to each subprogramme (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/38040/MTS_PoW2022.pdf?sequence=3&isAllowed=y). UNEP also supports the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans, which provide legal frameworks and operational mechanisms for addressing specific environmental issues and regions (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/why-does-un-environment-matter/secretariats-and-conventions). Furthermore, UNEP's work is guided by a number of over-arching strategies, policies and guidelines for ensuring access to information, preventing and responding to misconduct and fraud, enhancing sustainability, and engaging with civil society and the private sector, etc. (https://www.unep.org/about-un-environment/policies-and-strategies). Every two years, UNEA also adopts resolutions and decisions on various environmental topics, which guide UNEP’s implementation of its objectives and mandates (https://www.unep.org/news-and-stories/story/what-you-need-know-about-un-environment-assembly). These strategies collectively ensure effective coordination and promotion of environmental action within the United Nations system and beyond.

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNEP involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with the United Nations and Inter-Agency Cooperation section of the Governing Council decision 2/1, specifically in paragraphs 3-5. UNEP operates through the UN Environment Assembly (UNEA) of all the members, a Committee of Permanent Representatives of 58 members, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Director (paragraphs 6-8) (http://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/17307/K1607113_UNEPEA2_RES1E.docx?sequence=5&isAllowed=y). UNEP also has six regional offices and various thematic divisions and centres (paragraph 9) (http://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/17307/K1607113_UNEPEA2_RES1E.docx?sequence=5&isAllowed=y). UNEP supports the implementation of multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs) and regional seas conventions and action plans, which provide legal frameworks and operational mechanisms for addressing specific environmental issues and regions (paragraph 10) (http://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/17307/K1607113_UNEPEA2_RES1E.docx?sequence=5&isAllowed=y).
