source_title: United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat) — Horizontal Coordination evidence
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UN-Habitat involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the urban development and human settlements domain, such as national and local governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN agencies to ensure sustainable urbanization. This coordination is presently guided by the UN-Habitat Strategic Plan for 2020-2023 (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/documents/2019-09/strategic_plan_2020-2023.pdf). For example, UN-Habitat works with the housing sector to promote adequate and affordable housing for all (https://unhabitat.org/5-housing-and-slum-upgrading), with the transport sector to enhance urban mobility and accessibility (https://unhabitat.org/topic/mobility-and-transport), with the health sector to support urban health and well-being (https://unhabitat.org/topic/urban-health), or with the environment sector to strengthen climate action and improve urban environment (https://unhabitat.org/climate-action). Horizontal coordination within UN-Habitat can take various forms, such as: (1) Global flagship programmes, which are integrated and multisectoral programmes that aim to achieve impact at scale in the four domains of change of UN-Habitat, namely spatial inequality and poverty, shared prosperity, climate action and urban environment, and urban crisis prevention and response. They are designed and implemented in partnership with other sectors and stakeholders, such as UNDP, UNEP, UNICEF, WHO, World Bank, and others. Examples of global flagship programmes are the Global Public Space Programme (https://unhabitat.org/programme/global-public-space-programme) or the Participatory Slum Upgrading Programme (https://unhabitat.org/programme/the-participatory-slum-upgrading-programme-psup), (2) Interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, which are mechanisms that facilitate coordination, information exchange, and joint action among different sectors and stakeholders on urban issues and policies. UN-Habitat participates in and leads several of these mechanisms, such as the UN Sustainable Development Group (https://unsdg.un.org/about), or the UN Task Team on the New Urban Agenda (https://habitat3.org/the-new-urban-agenda/preparatory-process/united-nations-task-team/), (3) Guidelines, standards, and tools for urban sector engagement through products that provide evidence-based guidance, technical norms, and practical solutions for urban sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Guidelines on Urban and Territorial Planning (https://unhabitat.org/international-guidelines-on-urban-and-territorial-planning) or the City Prosperity Initiative (https://unhabitat.org/knowledge/city-prosperity-initiative), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for urban issues and policies through activities that aim to influence and inform other sectors and stakeholders about the importance and potential of sustainable urbanization and human settlements, such as the World Habitat Day (https://unhabitat.org/world-habitat-day) or the World’s Cities Report (https://unhabitat.org/wcr/).

source_title: Partnerships At Un Habitat
excerpt_<=50w: Inter‑institutional relationships: formalised cooperation with other bodies (e.g., MoUs, joint programmes, agreements; partner type × mechanism × year).
matrix_cell_text_full: UN-Habitat establishes and strengthens strategic relationships with a diverse range of partners at national, regional, and international levels, including political actors, civil society, professional organizations, and the private sector (https://unhabitat.org/partnerships-at-un-habitat). It works with partners through the World Urban Forum (https://wuf.unhabitat.org/), multi-stakeholder thematic partnerships, and advisory boards. These partnerships include the Cities and Climate Change Initiative (https://unhabitat.org/initiative/cities-and-climate-change-initiative), Gender Equality Network (https://unhabitat.org/network/gender-equality-network), Global Alliance for Urban Crisis (https://unhabitat.org/network/global-alliance-for-urban-crises#:~:text=The%20Global%20Alliance%20for%20Urban,humanitarian%20crises%20in%20urban%20settings.), Global Housing Strategy Platform (https://unhabitat.org/programme/global-housing-strategy-making-housing-affordable-for-all), Global Land Tool Network (GLTN), (https://unhabitat.org/programme/global-land-tool-network-gltn) and others. UN-Habitat also services the World Urban Campaign, an advocacy and partnership platform to raise awareness about positive urban change (https://unhabitat.org/partnerships-at-un-habitat). Furthermore, UN-Habitat partners with sister agencies across the UN, such as UNDESA, UNDP, and UNRCOs, as well as with a large network of local and national partners across the globe to advance SDG localization (https://sdgs.un.org/un-system-sdg-implementation/united-nations-habitat-un-habitat-44150).

matrix_cell_text_full: The UN-Habitat executes its objectives via several strategies. Its programmes and initiatives are currently guided by a four-year Strategic Plan (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/documents/2019-09/strategic_plan_2020-2023.pdf), endorsed by the Committee of Permanent Representatives and approved by the UN-Habitat Assembly, which sets out the vision, mission, objective, domains of change, drivers of change, and organizational performance enablers of the organization. This plan, applicable for 2020-2023, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the New Urban Agenda, and other global frameworks (https://unhabitat.org/about-us/our-strategy). Some of the specific strategies in place for UN-Habitat to achieve its objectives and mandates according to the Strategic Plan include: (1) Refocusing its niche as the thought leader and go-to agency that sets the global discourse and agenda on sustainable urban development, (2) Aligning its work with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the New Urban Agenda, and other relevant global frameworks and commitments, (3) Delivering four domain-specific goals that address the key challenges and opportunities of urbanization: reduced spatial inequality and poverty, enhanced shared prosperity, strengthened climate action, and effective urban crises prevention and response, (4) Integrating cross-cutting themes such as social inclusion, resilience, and safety throughout its programmes and projects, (5) Strengthening its partnerships with various stakeholders, including national and local governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and media, and (6) Improving its organizational effectiveness by enhancing its governance, accountability, transparency, innovation, and resource mobilization.  According to the document, the estimated budget for the strategic plan for 2020-2023 is $1.2 billion, of which $500 million is expected to come from the regular budget and $700 million from extrabudgetary sources. The budget is based on the projected resource requirements for the implementation of the four domains of change, the drivers of change and the organizational performance enablers.

matrix_cell_text_full:
UN-Habitat derives its mandate from several UN General Assembly resolutions, which established UN-Habitat as the focal point for all urbanization and human settlement matters within the UN system. Specifically, resolution 3327 (XXIX) of 1975 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/3327(XXIX)) created the United Nations Habitat and Human Settlements Foundation (UNHHSF), the first official UN body dedicated to urbanization. Resolution 32/162 of 1977 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/32/162) transformed the Committee on Housing, Building, and Planning into the Commission on Human Settlements, an intergovernmental body serviced by the Centre for Human Settlements (also known as “Habitat”). Resolution 56/206 of 2002 (https://undocs.org/en/A/RES/56/206) merged the UNHHSF, the Commission on Human Settlements, and Habitat into UN-Habitat, a fully-fledged UN programme managed by its own secretariat and headed by its own Executive Director. UN-Habitat's mandate is also shaped by the outcomes of the three UN conferences on human settlements: Habitat I in Vancouver (1976), Habitat II in Istanbul (1996), and Habitat III in Quito (2016). These conferences resulted in the adoption of the Vancouver Declaration on Human Settlements (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/1396335538wpdm_Vancouver_Declaration_EN.pdf), the Istanbul Declaration on Human Settlements (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/Istanbul_Declaration_EN.pdf) and the Habitat Agenda (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/Habitat_Agenda_EN.pdf), and the New Urban Agenda (https://unhabitat.org/sites/default/files/download-manager-files/The%20New%20Urban%20Agenda%20_%20Revised%20Low%20Res.pdf), respectively. These documents define the global standards and principles for achieving sustainable urban development and adequate shelter for all. UN-Habitat's jurisdiction is also influenced by the alignment of its work with other internationally agreed upon development goals, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (2015) (https://unhabitat.org/sustainable-development-goals), and the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (2015) (https://unhabitat.org/climate-change). These goals provide further legal frameworks and targets for UN-Habitat's jurisdiction over specific urban issues and domains. UN-Habitat's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Framework Convention on Climate Change (https://unfccc.int/files/essential_background/background_publications_htmlpdf/application/pdf/conveng.pdf), the Vienna Convention on the Protection of the Ozone Layer (https://ozone.unep.org/sites/default/files/2019-12/The%20Ozone%20Treaties%20EN%20-%20WEB_final.pdf), and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/resource/UNDRR%20Presentation_Sendai%20Framework-GGA6%20%281%29.pdf).

Source: Conversation with Bing, 2/14/2024

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UN-Habitat involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council, other UN agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through policy guidance, oversight, reporting, and partnership. Multilevel governance of UN-Habitat is structured under the resolution A/RES/56/206, specifically in Article IA (paragraphs 1-8) and Article 1B  (paragraphs 1-4). UN-Habitat is structured in three main bodies: (1) The Governing Council (GC), whose role is to set the major strategic and policy directions for UN-Habitat and approve its programmes and budget. It is composed of 58 member states that are elected by the UN General Assembly's Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC) (https://unhabitat.org/governing-council). The Governing Council meets every two years, (2) The UN-Habitat Secretariat, whose task is to ensure the execution of the Governing Council’s decisions and to translate these into specific strategies, programmes and initiatives. The Secretariat is the executive body of the organization. Headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya, it acts as the focal point for all urban and human settlement matters within the United Nations system (https://unhabitat.org/our-secretariat), and (3) The Committee of Permanent Representatives (CPR), which ensures that the Governing Council’s decisions are enacted by the Secretariat within the set framework. It has a supervising role and represents the Governing Council at the Secretariat to address issues arising between the biennial Governing Council meetings. The CPR is composed of ambassadors or foreign envoys of member states accredited to UN-Habitat (https://unhabitat.org/governance/committee-of-permanent-representatives).The UN-Habitat operates through the Governing Council of 58 members, elected by the Economic and Social Council, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Director, elected by the General Assembly . excerpt_<=50w: Defined objectives: stated institutional purposes/goals expressed in founding and/or strategic texts.
matrix_cell_text_full: According to Chapter I of the Constitution of the UNIDO, the Organization's objectives are to promote and accelerate industrial development in the developing countries, with a view to assisting in the establishment of a new international economic order, and to promote industrial development and cooperation on global, regional and national, as well as on sectoral levels (Article 1). To fulfil these objectives, the Organization shall perform various functions, such as encouraging and assisting the developing countries in their industrialization efforts, initiating and coordinating the activities of the United Nations system in the field of industrial development, creating and developing new concepts and approaches for industrial development, providing a forum and an instrument for international cooperation and dialogue on industrial matters, serving as a clearing-house for industrial information, promoting and encouraging the development, transfer and use of industrial technology, organizing and supporting industrial training programmes, assisting in the exploitation, conservation and transformation of natural resources, developing special measures for the least-developed and other disadvantaged developing countries, and assisting in obtaining external financing for industrial projects (Article 2). These functions enable the Organization to play the central role in and be responsible for reviewing and promoting the coordination of all activities of the United Nations system in the field of industrial development, in conformity with the responsibilities of the Economic and Social Council under the Charter of the United Nations and with the applicable relationship agreements (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNIDO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the industrial development domain, such as governments, private sector, civil society, academia, and other UN agencies. This coordination is structured under the Objectives and Functions section of the UNIDO Constitution, specifically in Articles 1-2 (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf). The UNIDO promotes and accelerates inclusive and sustainable industrial development in developing countries and economies in transition, with a view to assisting in the establishment of a new international economic order (https://sdgs.un.org/sites/default/files/publications/2021Introduction%20to%20UNIDO-%20Inclusive%20and%20Sustainable%20Industrial%20Development.pdf). The UNIDO also initiates, coordinates and follows up the activities of the UN system in the field of industrial development, and acts as a forum and instrument for industrial cooperation and partnership (https://sdgs.un.org/sites/default/files/publications/2021Introduction%20to%20UNIDO-%20Inclusive%20and%20Sustainable%20Industrial%20Development.pdf). The UNIDO provides technical assistance, policy advice, and capacity-building services to its Member States, and supports the development, transfer and adaptation of industrial technology. The UNIDO gives due regard to the specific needs and priorities of the least developed countries, as well as to the principle of equitable geographical distribution (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2019-09/Upscaling%20TC_Sept%202019.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNIDO collaborates with various organizations to achieve its objectives and mandates. It works with 170 Member States and various stakeholders through the General Conference, the Industrial Development Board, and the Programme and Budget Committee, which are the policymaking organs of the Organization, as stipulated in Chapter III of the Constitution of UNIDO (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf). As a specialized agency of the UN, UNIDO's relationship with the UN is based on the Agreement between the United Nations and the United Nations Industrial Development Organization, which entered into force in 1985, as detailed in resolution 40/180 of the UN General Assembly (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/2010-10/UN-UNIDO%20Relationship%20Agreement_1985_CP-2_0.pdf?OpenElement). It also partners with other UN entities, such as FAO, IAEA, ILO, UNCTAD, UNDP, UNEP, UNESCO, UNFCCC, and WHO (https://www.unido.org/our-focus/cross-cutting-services/partnerships-prosperity/partnerships-international-development-organizations).)  international financial institutions, such as the African Development Bank, the European Investment Bank and the World Bank (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2018-03/FDI25_Web_15March.pdf), as well as other intergovernmental organizations, such as the African Union, the European Union, the Organization of American States, and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, addressing common industrial challenges and opportunities (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2021-06/PFC%20Newsletter%2010_31May2021.pdf). Moreover, UNIDO engages with the private sector, civil society, academia, and media, fostering inclusive and sustainable industrialization (https://www.unido.org/search?keys=private+sector+partnership).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNIDO derives its mandate from its own Constitution, which entered into force in 1985 (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf). The Constitution provides the legal basis for UNIDO’s jurisdiction over the industrial development of its member states and regions, as well as the promotion and acceleration of industrial cooperation among these states. Additionally, UNIDO’s jurisdiction is influenced by the 2013 Lima Declaration (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2018-12/UNIDO_GC15_Lima_Declaration.pdf) and the 2019 Abu Dhabi Declaration (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2019-11/UNIDO_Abu_Dhabi_Declaration_1.pdf), which reaffirm UNIDO’s role as the specialized agency of the UN for inclusive and sustainable industrial development. UNIDO also supports the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals, which provide further frameworks for UNIDO’s jurisdiction over specific industrial sectors and issues (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/2017-05/IDB.45_12_E_UNIDO_and_the_2030_Agenda_for_Sustainable_Development_V1702655_0.pdf).

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNIDO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is structured under the Relationship with the United Nations section of the Constitution of UNIDO, specifically in Article 9. UNIDO operates through the General Conference of all the members, the Industrial Development Board of 53 members, and the Secretariat headed by a Director General (Articles 5-8) (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf). In various countries and regions, UNIDO operates  30 field officers, 19 Regional Hub, 4  Liaison Offices, 10 Investment and Technology Promotion Offices, and 2 Project Offices (https://www.unido.org/who-we-are/unido-worldwide). UNIDO supports the implementation of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals, which provide the global framework and targets for addressing development challenges and opportunities (https://www.unido.org/our-focus-advancing-economic-competitiveness/achieving-sdgs). UNIDO also partners with other UN entities, such as FAO, IAEA, ILO, UNCTAD, UNDP, UNEP, UNESCO, UNFCCC, and WHO, as well as other intergovernmental organizations, such as the African Union, the European Union, the Organization of American States, and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, addressing common industrial challenges and opportunities (https://www.unido.org/our-focus/cross-cutting-services/partnerships-prosperity/partnerships-international-development-organizations).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) has been mandated to fulfil several objectives (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..), such as: supporting the implementation, follow-up and review of the Framework, including through the development of coherent and actionable guidance for its implementation (paragraph 48 a); supporting the coordination of disaster risk reduction in the United Nations system (paragraph 48 b); supporting the coherence of the disaster risk reduction and climate change agendas (paragraph 48 c); convening the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction and supporting the organization of regional platforms for disaster risk reduction (paragraph 48 d); supporting the development of national and local disaster risk reduction strategies and plans, and facilitating their integration into relevant development and sectoral plans and policies (paragraph 48 e); supporting the development and strengthening of national and local mechanisms and capacities for monitoring and reviewing progress and levels of implementation of the Framework (paragraph 48 f); and supporting the development of indicators and methodologies for the assessment of disaster risk and disaster risk reduction (paragraph 48 g). These objectives enable the UNDRR to fulfil its role as the focal point in the United Nations system for the coordination of disaster risk reduction and the implementation of the Framework (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_69_283.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNDRR collaborates with various organizations to implement the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/partners-and-stakeholders/multistakeholder-initiatives-and-partnershipsf). It works with the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), and the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) to provide technical support and guidance to Member States and other stakeholders on disaster risk reduction, as stated in paragraph 48 (a) of the Sendai Framework (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..). matrix_cell_text_full: The UNDRR executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a four-year Strategic Framework, revised annually by the General Assembly, which establishes the UNDRR's vision, mission, strategic objectives, expected accomplishments, and indicators of achievement (https://www.undrr.org/media/49267/download?startDownload=true). This framework, applicable for 2022-2025, aligns with the Sendai Framework and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, detailed in document A/76/6 (Sect. 23) (https://undocs.org/en/A/76/6(Sect.23)). Secondly, a biennial programme plan and budget, devised by the secretariat and approved by the General Assembly, detail activities, outputs, resources, and performance information corresponding to each strategic objective. The current programme plan and budget for 2022-2023 are tailored to the Member States' needs and stakeholders' priorities, as outlined in document A/76/6/Add.1 (https://undocs.org/en/A/76/6/Add.1). It also maintains the Sendai Framework Monitor, a key tool for the monitoring and review of the Sendai Framework and the disaster risk reduction-related Sustainable Development Goals (https://sendaimonitor.undrr.org/). Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for coordinating and guiding disaster risk reduction across the United Nations system and beyond, addressing governance, resilience, preparedness, recovery, and financing, with key instruments listed here (https://www.undrr.org/what-we-do)." Through the revised United Nations plan of action on disaster risk reduction for resilience, the UNDRR executes its commitments to the implementation of the Sendai Framework and integrated approach to the achievement of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/49076_unplanofaction.pdf).

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNDRR involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/partners-and-stakeholders/un-system). This is achieved through coordination, guidance, and support. This is structured under the Institutional Arrangements section of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, specifically in paragraphs 48-48 (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..). The UNDRR operates through the General Assembly of all the members, the Economic and Social Council, and a secretariat headed by a Special Representative of the Secretary-General (paragraph 48). The UNDRR also has regional and sub-regional offices, thematic platforms, and a Scientific and Technical Advisory Group (paragraph 48). The UNDRR assists members in the development and implementation of national and local disaster risk reduction strategies and plans, and provides technical support and guidance upon request (paragraph 48 e and f). UNDRR's work is organized around five regions, each overseen by a Regional Director who works closely with the Special Representative of the Secretary-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.undrr.org/about-undrr/where-we-work). There are also the Regional Platforms, multi-stakeholder forums that reflect the commitment of governments to improve coordination and implementation of disaster risk reduction activities while linking to international and national efforts (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/regional-platforms), and National Platforms, serving as mechanisms for coordination and policy guidance on disaster risk reduction that are multisectoral and interdisciplinary in nature, with public, private and civil society participation involving all concerned entities within a country (https://www.undrr.org/terminology/national-platform-disaster-risk-reduction). A  "UNDRR Stakeholder Engagement Mechanism" (UNDRR-SEM) has been setup to  leverage the convening and advocacy powers of the  Major Groups and other stakeholders (MGoS) and server as the main interloculator betwwen the UNDRR and other stakeholder groups for the integration of disaster risk reduction into the broader 2030 Agenda (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/partners-and-stakeholders/stakeholder-engagement-mechanism). Likewise, UNDRR coordinates two mechanisms related to the UN Plan of Action: the high-level UN Senior Leadership Group on Disaster Risk Reduction for Resilience and the UN Disaster Risk Reduction Focal Points Group at the working level (https://www.undrr.org/implementing-sendai-framework/partners-and-stakeholders/un-system). Also, a network of country offices and technical experts supports the UNDRR's work in coordinating and guiding disaster risk reduction as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.undrr.org/where-we-work). Additionally, UNDRR operates the Global Education and Training Institute in Incheon, Republic of Korea, and the Kobe Office in Japan (https://www.undrr.org/who-we-are). Besides the Special Representative of the Secretary-General, at the UNDRR headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of a Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General and 7 Directors with portfolios focusing on different aspects in accordance with the UNDRR's mandate (https://www.undrr.org/who-we-are). In addition, UNDRR coordinates with the European Union and its agencies and is the host organization and partner of the Making Cities Resilient 2030 initiative (https://www.undrr.org/news/making-cities-resilient-campaign-2030).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to Part A, Section III of UNOOSA's working document "The 'Space2030' Agenda: Space as a Driver of Sustainable Development" (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf), the United Nations UNOOSA has been mandated to fulfil the following objectives: Enhance space-derived economic benefits and strengthen the role of the space sector as a major driver of sustainable development (Overarching objective 1); Harness the potential of space to solve everyday challenges and leverage space-related innovation to improve the quality of life (Overarching objective 2); Improve access to space for all and ensure that all countries can benefit socioeconomically from space science and technology applications and space-based data, information and products, thereby supporting the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (Overarching objective 3); and Build partnerships and strengthen international cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space and in the global governance of outer space activities (Overarching objective 4). excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNOOSA involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the space domain, including its Member States, United Nations entities, intergovernmental and non-governmental organizations, and industry and private sector entities, to promote and facilitate the peaceful uses of outer space and the use of space science and technology for sustainable development. matrix_cell_text_full: UNOOSA cooperates with various organisations to promote and facilitate peaceful international cooperation in outer space. It works closely with the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), providing substantive secretariat services and implementing its decisions and recommendations, as per General Assembly resolution 1472 (XIV) of 12 December 1959 (https://www.unoosa.org/pdf/gares/ARES_14_1472E.pdf). The budget is mainly funded by the regular budget of the United Nations, but also relies on voluntary contributions from Member States and other entities for some of its activities.

matrix_cell_text_full: UNOOSA derives its mandate from the UN General Assembly resolution 1472 (XIV) of 12 December 1959, which established the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) and its secretariat, later renamed as UNOOSA (https://www.unoosa.org/pdf/gares/ARES_14_1472E.pdf). Specifically, paragraph 1 of the resolution defines the objectives and functions of COPUOS. Additionally, UNOOSA's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and principles, such as the five treaties and five declarations on outer space, which provide the legal framework for UNOOSA's jurisdiction over the exploration and use of outer space for peaceful purposes (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties.html). The five treaties on outer space are: (1) The Outer Space Treaty (1967) on the Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introouterspacetreaty.html), (2) The Rescue Agreement (1968) on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introrescueagreement.html), (3) The Liability Convention (1972) on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introliability-convention.html), (4) The Registration Convention (1976) on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/introregistration-convention.html), and (5) The Moon Agreement (1984) governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/intromoon-agreement.html). UNOOSA's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by COPUOS and the General Assembly, such as the Space2030 Agenda and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, which provide guidance and direction for UNOOSA's activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/resolutions.html).

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNOOSA involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations and other specialised agencies, as well as regional and sub-regional organisations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through providing secretariat services, implementing decisions and recommendations, and facilitating partnerships and dialogue. UNOOSA operates through the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS) of all the members, the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee and the Legal Subcommittee of 92 members, and a secretariat headed by a Director (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html). It also has working groups, expert groups, and other subsidiary bodies. The Office of the Director oversees and coordinates the strategic direction and operational priorities of UNOOSA (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/director.html); The Committee, Policy and Legal Affairs Section (CPLA) provides substantive, secretariat, organisational and administrative support to the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space (COPUOS), its Scientific and Technical Subcommittee (STSC) and its Legal Subcommittee (LSC); The Space Applications Section (SAS) plans and implements the United Nations Programme on Space Applications to build national capability in the areas of basic sciences; The United Nations Platform for Space-based Information for Disaster Management and Emergency Response (UN-SPIDER) helps all countries access and use space-based information in all phases of the disaster management cycle, including prevention, preparedness, early warning, response and reconstruction; and the International Committee on Global Navigation Satellite Systems (ICG) brings together all global navigation satellite system (GNSS) providers to improve their uses for sustainable development and their compatibility (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html). The Director of UNOOSA is supported by the Senior Advisor on Space Science and Education, who provides expert advice and supports research relating to the activities and programmes carried out by the Office. The Senior Advisor also works closely with the Regional Centres for Space Science and Technology Education, affiliated to the United Nations (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/structure.html). UNOOSA also collaborates with space agencies and intergovernmental and non-governmental organisations involved in space-related activities (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/aboutus/partnerships.html). In addition, UNOOSA maintains, on behalf of the United Nations Secretary-General, the Register of Objects Launched into Outer Space (https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/spaceobjectregister/index.html) and discharges the responsibilities of the Secretary-General under the UN treaties and principles on outer space.

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNOPS involves working with different sectors and partners within the development, humanitarian and peacebuilding domains, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the UN system, and other international organizations to ensure that projects, infrastructure and procurement are delivered in a sustainable and efficient manner. This coordination is currently guided by the UNOPS Strategic Plan 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en) and the UNOPS sustainability policy (https://www.unops.org/about/our-story/sustainable-development-goals#:~:text=Sustainability%20at%20UNOPS,-We%20are%20committed&text=Working%20closely%20with%20government%20partners,achieve%20long%2Dterm%20sustainable%20development.). For example, UNOPS works with the health sector to support the COVID-19 response and recovery (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/news/standing-together-to-tackle-covid-19#:~:text=CORONAVIRUS%20GLOBAL%20HEALTH%20EMERGENCY&text=Last%20year%2C%20UNOPS%20delivered%20around,term%20impacts%20of%20the%20pandemic.), with the transport sector to improve road safety and connectivity (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/news/developing-inclusive-transport-infrastructure), with the water sector to enhance access to clean water and sanitation (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/stories/sustainable-water-supply-for-towns-in-darfur) or with the environment sector to promote climate action and resilience (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/stories/advancing-climate-action-building-resilience). Horizontal coordination within UNOPS can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint delivery and implementation of projects and programmes with other sectors and partners, such as the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria (https://www.theglobalfund.org/en/) or the European Union (https://www.unops.org/about/our-story/partnerships), (2) Participation in intersectoral and multi-stakeholder platforms and initiatives, such as the Global Infrastructure Hub (https://content.unops.org/publications/Infrastructure_underpining_sustainable_development_EN.pdf) or the UN Road Safety Fund (https://roadsafetyfund.un.org/), (3) Development and application of standards and tools for sustainable project management, infrastructure and procurement, such as the Infrastructure Sustainability Rating Tool (https://sustainable.unops.org/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilize support for sustainable development goals and policies among other sectors and partners, such as the UNOPS Possibilities Portal (https://www.unops.org/business-opportunities/unops-possibilities/unops-possibilities-portal) or the UNOPS Annual Report (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3971697/files/DP_OPS_2022_5-EN.pdf?ln=en).

matrix_cell_text_full: The United Nations Office for Project Services (UNOPS) executes its objectives via several strategies: Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan, revised as needed, establishes the organization's vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/strategic-plan). This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en), aligns with the Sustainable Development Goals (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf). It underscores UNOPS commitment to expanding the capacity and resource base for countries to achieve these goals (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/strategic-plan). The plan was agreed in June 2023 following UNOPS management reforms. The budget for the 2022-2025 strategic plan as presented in the document estimates the total delivery of $8.5 billion and the total expenditure of $1.1 billion for the four-year period. Secondly, UNOPS operates in accordance with a strict legislative framework comprised of Directives and Instructions (https://www.unops.org/policies). These are organization-wide policies that govern actions within UNOPS and its external relations. They explain procedures and business processes for the implementation of Directives, as well as United Nations legislation applicable to UNOPS. Futhermore, UNOPS's flagship publication, the Annual Statistical Report on United Nations Procurement keeps track of the combined spending on goods and services of 39 UN organizations, a record number of reporting organizations (https://www.unops.org/news-and-stories/news/what-did-the-united-nations-buy-last-year). Finally, to advance the 2030 Agenda, UNOPS aims to engage in collaborative partnerships with a focus on sharing its expertise in infrastructure, procurement, project management, human resources, and financial services (https://www.unops.org/about/our-story/partnerships). UNOPS works with a variety of partners, from the UN family to governments, non-governmental organizations, academia, and the private sector. The organization also hosts several entities under its agreements, grouped by theme (https://www.unops.org/about).

excerpt_<=50w: Source of jurisdiction: formal legal basis enabling authority (treaty/charter article(s) or constitutive resolution reference).
matrix_cell_text_full: UNOPS derives its mandate from the 2010 General Assembly resolution 65/176 (https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n10/523/10/pdf/n1052310.pdf?token=YpwFrn88GVoLxo0p9e&fe=true) and Executive Board Decisions (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/executive-board/executive-board-documents) which reaffirmed the role of UNOPS as a central resource for the United Nations system in procurement and contracts management as well as in civil works and physical infrastructure development, including the related capacity development activities. The resolution also recognized the operational capacity of UNOPS to implement projects in support of peacebuilding, humanitarian and development operations. Specifically, paragraph 1 of the resolution defines the vision and mission of UNOPS, and paragraph 2 outlines the core values and principles of UNOPS. Additionally, UNOPS’s financial regulations and rules (https://content.unops.org/documents/libraries/policies-2020/executive-office-directives-and-instructions/financial-regulations-and-rules/en/EOD.ED-Financial-Regulations-and-Rules.pdf), regulation 1.01 on the scope and applicability, states that UNOPS shall operate in accordance with the policies and procedures established by the Executive Director in consultation with the Executive Board. UNOPS’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the decisions and directives adopted by its Executive Board, such as the strategic plan 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en), the organizational structure (https://content.unops.org/documents/libraries/policies-2020/executive-office-directives-and-instructions/organizational-principles-and-governance-model/en/EOI.ED-Organisational-Structure.pdf), and the anti-bribery and anti-corruption policy (https://content.unops.org/publications/EB-for-docs-not-going-in-library/UNOPS-Anti-Bribery-and-Anti-Corruption-Policy-December-2023.pdf). UNOPS’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/content/documents/21252030%20Agenda%20for%20Sustainable%20Development%20web.pdf), the Paris Agreement on Climate Change (https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/english_paris_agreement.pdf), and the New Urban Agenda (https://habitat3.org/wp-content/uploads/NUA-English.pdf), which provide further legal frameworks for UNOPS’s jurisdiction over specific development issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNOPS involves working with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through strategic coordination and advice, operational partnerships and collaboration, and service delivery and support. This is structured under the UNOPS Organizational Principles and Governance Model (https://content.unops.org/documents/libraries/policies-2020/executive-office-directives-and-instructions/organizational-principles-and-governance-model/en/EOD.ED-Organizational-Principles-and-Governance-Model.pdf). UNOPS operates under the oversight and guidance of the UNDP/UNFPA/UNOPS Executive Board, which consists of 36 members representing the five regional groups of the United Nations (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/executive-board). The Executive Director of UNOPS is the head of the organization and reports to the Executive Board and the Secretary-General of the United Nations. The Executive Director is supported by a Deputy Executive Director/Chief Operating Officer and a senior management team comprising the leads of four core management groups (Finance, People and Change, Procurement, and Infrastructure and Project Management) and other functional groups (Legal, Corporate Support, Partnerships and Communications, Business Improvement, Ethics, Audit and Investigations). UNOPS also has an Audit Advisory Committee and an Investment Advisory Committee that provide independent advice to the Executive Director on various aspects of the organization's management and performance (https://www.unops.org/about/governance/accountability/coordination-and-advice). UNOPS work is organized around five regions, each headed by a Regional Director who reports to the Executive Director. The regions are: Asia, Africa, Europe and Central Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Middle East. Each region has a Regional Office that coordinates and supports the delivery of the regional portfolio and implements the corporate improvement agenda. The regions also have Operational Hubs, Operations Centres, Project Centres, and Clusters that manage and deliver services to partners and clients at the country or thematic level (https://www.unops.org/about/our-structure).

strengthening regional and international cooperation in preventing and combating transnational crime, in particular organized and economic crime, money-laundering, illicit trafficking in women and children, financial crimes and terrorism in all its forms; and promoting effective and fair administration of justice, with due respect for the rights of all those affected by crime or involved in the criminal justice system (Section 2.3 a); Promoting adherence to the international treaties on drug control, crime prevention and terrorism and their effective implementation by States (Section 6.2 f); and Providing assistance to Member States in the implementation of relevant General Assembly resolutions and declarations related to action against terrorism (Section 6.2 g).

source_title: United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) — Horizontal Coordination evidence
excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNODC involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the drug, crime, corruption and terrorism domains, such as governments, civil society, private sector, academia, and other UN entities to ensure that the world is safer from these threats and that human rights, development and the rule of law are upheld in all activities and policies. This coordination is guided by the UNODC Strategy 2021-2025 (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Advocacy-Section/UNODC-Strategy-WEB.pdf). For example, UNODC works with the health sector to address the world drug problem and provide prevention and treatment services (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/drug-prevention-and-treatment/index.html), with the justice sector to prevent and counter organized crime and terrorism and strengthen criminal justice systems (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/organized-crime/index.html, https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/terrorism/index.html, https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/justice-and-prison-reform/index.html), with the environment sector to combat crimes that affect the environment and biodiversity (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/wildlife-and-forest-crime/index.html), or with the education sector to promote a culture of lawfulness and prevent violence and crime among youth (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/). Horizontal coordination within UNODC can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Programme for Combating Wildlife and Forest Crime (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Wildlife/Annual_Report_GPWLFC2021.pdf) or the Global Maritime Crime Programme (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/piracy/index.html), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Coordination Group against Trafficking in Persons (https://icat.un.org/) or the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Coordination Compact (https://www.un.org/counterterrorism/global-ct-compact), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for drug, crime, corruption and terrorism sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Standards for the Treatment of Drug Use Disorders (https://www.unodc.org/documents/drug-prevention-and-treatment/UNODC-WHO_International_Standards_Treatment_Drug_Use_Disorders_April_2020.pdf) or the Global Judicial Integrity Network (https://www.unodc.org/ji/en/index.html), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for drug, crime, corruption and terrorism issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Drug Report (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/world-drug-report-2023.html) or the Education for Justice initiative (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/en/index.html).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNODC's jurisdiction is not limited to a specific geographical area, but rather to the offences established in accordance with the Organized Crime Convention and other relevant treaties. This means that UNODC can assist states in preventing and combating transnational organized crime, corruption, terrorism, drug trafficking, money laundering, cybercrime, and other related issues, regardless of where they occur (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/en/organized-crime/module-8/key-issues/jurisdictions.html). However, UNODC respects the sovereignty and jurisdiction of each state party, and encourages cooperation and coordination among states to avoid jurisdictional gaps or conflicts (https://www.unodc.org/e4j/en/cybercrime/module-7/key-issues/sovereignty-and-jurisdiction.html). UNODC also has field offices in various regions and countries, which provide technical assistance and support to the local authorities (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/corruption/country-profile/index.html). UNODC does not have a specific jurisdiction over ocean spaces and maritime zones, but rather works with states and other international organizations to address various crimes and threats that occur at sea, in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea³ and other relevant treaties (https://www.un.org/Depts/los/general_assembly/contributions_2019/UNODC.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNODC is a global leader in the fight against illicit drugs and international crime and is mandated to assist member states in their struggle against illicit drugs, crime, and terrorism. In the area of criminal justice, UNODC’s work covers the entire criminal justice chain (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/justice-and-prison-reform/cpcj-home.html). This includes comprehensive crime prevention strategies, legal and institutional reforms, improving crime investigation capacities, promoting humane prison management systems, facilitating international cooperation in legal matters, and addressing specific issues of human trafficking, money laundering, organized crime, cybercrime, and corruption (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Advocacy-Section/UNODC-at-a-glance_PRINT.pdf). In terms of drug prevention, treatment, and care, UNODC supports countries to develop and implement comprehensive drug demand reduction interventions based on scientific evidence (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/drug-prevention-and-treatment/index.html). This includes addressing drug use disorders as any other health disorder, and ensuring access to health-based drug prevention, treatment, care, and rehabilitation services (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/drug-prevention-and-treatment/index.html). Furthermore, UNODC plays a crucial role in addressing HIV/AIDS, particularly in vulnerable populations such as people who use drugs and those in prisons (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/hiv-aids/new/Our_HIV_work.html). It promotes comprehensive, evidence-informed interventions that reduce the risk of HIV, including harm reduction services like needle and syringe programs and opioid substitution therapy (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/hiv-aids/new/Our_HIV_work.html).

excerpt_<=50w: Strategies: instrument portfolio and governance tools used to pursue objectives (e.g., standards, MRV, compliance, capacity building).
matrix_cell_text_full: UNODC executes its objectives and mandates by having Strategic Plans and work programs supported by annual or biennial integrated budgets. it's most recent five-year Strategic Plan, applicable for 2021-2025, guides its vision, mission, values, and expected accomplishments, and is aligned with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the United Nations reform agenda (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Advocacy-Section/UNODC-Strategy-WEB.pdf). The plan focuses on five thematic areas: world drug problem, organized crime, corruption and economic crime, terrorism, and criminal prevention and criminal justice (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/strategy/index.html). In addition, a proposed annual programme plan and budget, applicable for 2024, specifies the activities, outputs, indicators, and resources for each strategic objective, based on the results and lessons learned from the 2022 budget perfomance evaluation, as well as the priorities and needs of Member States (https://www.unodc.org/documents/commissions/CND/CND_Sessions/CND_65Reconvened/ECN72022_CRP16_ECN152022_CRP9_2221350A.pdf). The international conventions and protocols on drug control, crime prevention and terrorism also provide UNODC with the legal frameworks for its jurisdiction and mandate, and which UNODC serves as the guardian and the secretariat, supporting their implementation by Member States (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1961_en.pdf). In addition, UNODC work programmes and budgets are influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Commission on Narcotic Drugs, the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, and the Economic and Social Council, which also provide guidance and direction for UNODC's cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/treaties/CTOC/resolutions-and-decisions-conference-of-the-parties-to-the-united-nations-convention-against-transnational-organized-crime.html#COP11). UNODC is funded mainly by voluntary contributions from various sources, but faces challenges in securing predictable and adequate funding to address the growing demands of Member States and to support the 2030 Agenda. UNODC aims to diversify its funding sources by expanding its partnership base, exploring new donors and engaging with the private sector and foundations. UNODC also seeks to increase the availability of non-earmarked resources to enhance its programme and results-based management, research, policy guidance and strategic direction (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/donors/index.html).

excerpt_<=50w: Source of jurisdiction: formal legal basis enabling authority (treaty/charter article(s) or constitutive resolution reference).
matrix_cell_text_full: UNODC derives its jurisdiction from several legal, conventional, and executive bases. The major conventions that underpin its defined objectives, operations, and strategic frameworks include the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime and the Protocols Thereto, 2000 (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/UNTOC/Publications/TOC%20Convention/TOCebook-e.pdf); the United Nations Convention against Corruption, 2003 (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/UNCAC/Publications/Convention/08-50026_E.pdf); the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961 as amended by the 1972 Protocol (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1961_en.pdf); the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, 1971 (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1971_en.pdf); the United Nations Convention against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, 1988 (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1988_en.pdf); and  several ant-terrorism conventions (https://sherloc.unodc.org/cld/v3/sherloc/treaties/search.jspx#?mv=treaties&c=%7B%22filters%22:%5B%7B%22fieldName%22:%22treaty.type_s1%22,%22value%22:%22International%22%7D,%7B%22fieldName%22:%22treaty.topics.topic_s%22,%22value%22:%22Terrorism%22%7D%5D,%22match%22:%22%22,%22startAt%22:20,%22sortings%22:%22%22%7D). UNODC’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by the Conference of the Parties (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/treaties/CTOC/resolutions-and-decisions-conference-of-the-parties-to-the-united-nations-convention-against-transnational-organized-crime.html#COP11), as well as by the Commission on Narcotic Drugs and the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, which are the policy-making bodies of UNODC (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/commissions/Secretariat/index.html). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNODC’s activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. UNODC’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as several international drug control conventions (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/commissions/CND/Mandate_Functions/Scheduling.html), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/sustainable-development-goals/index.html), which provide further legal frameworks for UNODC’s jurisdiction over specific issues and domains related to drugs, crime, corruption, terrorism, and justice.

The major conventions that underpin its defined objectives, operations, and strategic frameworks include the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime and the Protocols Thereto, 2000 (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/UNTOC/Publications/TOC%20Convention/TOCebook-e.pdf); the United Nations Convention against Corruption, 2003 (https://www.unodc.org/documents/treaties/UNCAC/Publications/Convention/08-50026_E.pdf); the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961 as amended by the 1972 Protocol (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1961_en.pdf); the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, 1971 (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1971_en.pdf); the United Nations Convention against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances, 1988 (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/convention_1988_en.pdf); and  several ant-terrorism conventions (https://sherloc.unodc.org/cld/v3/sherloc/treaties/search.jspx#?mv=treaties&c=%7B%22filters%22:%5B%7B%22fieldName%22:%22treaty.type_s1%22,%22value%22:%22International%22%7D,%7B%22fieldName%22:%22treaty.topics.topic_s%22,%22value%22:%22Terrorism%22%7D%5D,%22match%22:%22%22,%22startAt%22:20,%22sortings%22:%22%22%7D). UNODC’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by the Conference of the Parties (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/treaties/CTOC/resolutions-and-decisions-conference-of-the-parties-to-the-united-nations-convention-against-transnational-organized-crime.html#COP11), as well as by the Commission on Narcotic Drugs and the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice, which are the policy-making bodies of UNODC (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/commissions/Secretariat/index.html). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNODC’s activities and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. UNODC’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as several international drug control conventions (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/commissions/CND/Mandate_Functions/Scheduling.html), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/sustainable-development-goals/index.html), which provide further legal frameworks for UNODC’s jurisdiction over specific issues and domains related to drugs, crime, corruption, terrorism, and justice.

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNODC involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. UNODC operates through the Office of the Executive Director (OED), Division for Operations (DO), Division for Treaty Affairs (DTA), Independent Evaluation Section (IES), and Division for Policy Analysis and Public Affairs (DPA), among others. The UNODC also has various regional sections and field offices (https://www.unodc.org/documents/evaluation/UNODC_OrganizationalChart.pdf). UNODC's work is organized around five thematic focus areas identified alongside a streamlining of processes designed to build a more agile, fit-for-purpose organization . The Commission on Narcotic Drugs (CND) and the Commission on Crime Prevention and Criminal Justice (CCPCJ) are policymaking bodies within the United Nations system and act as governing bodies to UNODC, guiding its international action against drugs and crime. The CND is responsible for deciding the scope of control of substances under the international drug control conventions, while the CCPCJ acts as a preparatory and implementing body for the United Nations Congress on Crime prevention and Criminal Justice (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/commissions/index.html).There is also the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) which is an independent and quasi-judicial monitoring body for the implementation of the United Nations international drug control conventions (https://www.incb.org/).  In addition, UNODC's field offices supports UNODC's work in promoting peace and security, human rights, and development by making the world safer from drugs, crime, corruption, and terrorism (https://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/field-offices.html). UNODC's operational systems are based on the UNODC Strategy 2021-2025, which aims to equip UNODC to deliver effectively, efficiently, and with accountability, elevating support to Member States to build just, inclusive, and resilient societies. The operational systems are also guided by the UN standards and norms in crime prevention and criminal justice, which promote human rights (https://www.unodc.org/documents/Advocacy-Section/UNODC-Strategy-WEB.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Charter of the United Nations University (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf), the University's objectives are as follows: (1) To contribute, through collaborative research and education, to efforts to resolve the pressing global problems of human survival, development, and welfare that are the concern of the United Nations, its Peoples, and Member States (Article I, paragraph 1); (2) To disseminate the knowledge gained in its activities to the United Nations and its agencies, to scholars and to the public, in order to increase dynamic interaction in the worldwide community of learning and research (Article I, paragraph 4), (3) To assist in the development of vigorous academic and scientific communities everywhere and particularly in the developing countries, devoted to their vital needs in the fields of learning and research within the framework of the aims assigned to those centres and programmes in the present Charter (Article I, paragraph 6); and (4) To grant and confer master’s degrees and doctorates, diplomas, certificates and other academic distinctions under conditions laid down for that purpose in the statutes by the Council of the University (Article I, paragraph 8). These objectives reflect the University's mission as an international community of scholars, engaged in research, postgraduate training and dissemination of knowledge in furtherance of the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations (Article I, paragraph 1).

matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the United Nations University (UNU) involves collaboration with different academic and research institutions, UN agencies, governments, civil society, and other stakeholders to address the pressing global problems of human survival, development and welfare. This coordination is guided by Article I of the UNU Charter, (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf), as well as by the UNU 2020-2024 Strategic Plan (https://i.unu.edu/media/unu.edu/attachment/100694/UNU-Strategic-Plan-2020-2024.pdf). For example, UNU consults with the education sector to provide topical, timely and relevant postgraduate training and degree programmes (https://unu.edu/learning), with the social sector to promote human rights and peace (https://unu.edu/topics/human-rights), with the economic sector to foster innovation and sustainable development (https://unu.edu/topics/innovation), and with the environmental sector to protect the environment and natural resources (https://unu.edu/topics/natural-resources). Horizontal coordination within UNU can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint research and training projects and programmes with other academic and research institutions, UN agencies, and other stakeholders, such as the UNU Institute for Integrated Management of Material Fluxes and of Resources (https://flores.unu.edu/en) or the UNU Institute for the Advanced Study of Sustainability (https://ias.unu.edu/en), (2) Participation in academic and policy networks, platforms, and partnerships, such as the Academic Council on the United Nations System (https://acuns.org) or the Sustainable Development Solutions Network (https://www.unsdsn.org), (3) Development and dissemination of publications, reports, and policy briefs for academic and policy audiences, such as the UNU Policy Brief Series (https://unu.edu/ias/unu-ias-policy-brief-series#:~:text=Our%20policy%20briefs%20present%20analysis,global%2C%20national%20and%20local%20levels.) or the UNU World Institute for Development Economics Research Working Paper Series (WIDER) (https://www.wider.unu.edu/publications), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for the UNU's vision, mission, and activities among academic and policy communities, such as the UNU Conversation Series (https://unu.edu/events/unu-conversation-series) or the UNU Annual Report (https://unu.edu/about/annual-reports).

It also coordinates its activities with the UN and its agencies, such as UNITAR (Article VI, paragraph 1 f), UNIDO, as well as as as well as regional and national bodies, such as the European Union, the African Development Bank, and the Japanese Government. It may receive voluntary contributions and assistance from governments, organizations, and individuals, and mobilizes resources from various donors and funding agencies, such as the German Government, the World Bank, and the International Climate Initiative, to support its academic projects and core operations (Article IX, paragraphs 1-2). Additionally, the UNU designates certain institutions and centres, particularly in developing countries, as associated institutions of the UNU, on terms and conditions decided by the Council (https://unu.edu/unu-system). Moreover, UNU partners with academic institutions and networks around the world, such as Maastricht University, the University of Tokyo, and the International Partnership for the Satoyama Initiative, to conduct joint research, education, and training programmes (https://unu.edu/about).

matrix_cell_text_full: The United Nations University (UNU) implements its objectives and mandates through a variety of strategies: (1) The UNU has a strategic plan that guides the development and implementation of the institute’s research, policy development, teaching, and capacity-building initiatives. The current strategic plan spans from 2020 to 2024 (https://i.unu.edu/media/unu.edu/attachment/100694/UNU-Strategic-Plan-2020-2024.pdf). This plan is closely aligned with the overall strategic direction of the UNU (https://unu.edu/ias/about-unu-ias/strategic-plan). It was produced through an inclusive process of internal stocktaking and dialogue, reflecting the outcomes of a comprehensive external evaluation of UNU-IAS conducted in 2020 (https://unu.edu/ias/about-unu-ias/strategic-plan), (2) The UNU Council is responsible for considering and approving the UNU budget and work programme. The Work Program and budget estimate for the biennium 2022-2023 is designed to support the United Nations University’s (UNU) vision of promoting sustainable human development and its mission to contribute, through research and capacity building, to efforts to resolve the pressing global problems that are the concern of the United Nations, its Peoples and Member States. The budget of USD 124.8 million, a 10.9% increase from the previous biennium, is funded through various sources including project fundraising, institutional fundraising, income from the endowment fund, cumulative surplus carried forward, and other income (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-01/Approved-UNU-Work-Programme-and-Budget-Estimates-for-the-2022-2023-Biennium.pdf), (3) The UNU has established the UNU SDG–Universities Platform through the UNU-IAS in 2020, which provides opportunities for Japanese universities to proactively collaborate with different stakeholders to promote research and educational activities advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (https://unu.edu/ias/unu-sdg-universities-platform), and (5) The UNU Council devises the principles and policies that govern the University’s operations. The Council holds two regular sessions per year (https://unu.edu/about/unu-council). Finally, the UNU has 13 institutes located in 12 countries around the world, each contributing to the mission of the UNU through their specific programmes of work. The global UNU system is coordinated by UNU Headquarters in Tokyo (https://unu.edu/unu-system).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNU derives its mandate from the Charter of the United Nations University, which established UNU as an international community of scholars and a think tank of the United Nations (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf). Specifically, Article I of the Charter defines the purposes and structure of UNU, and Article II affirms its academic freedom and autonomy. Additionally, the Charter outlines the organization (Article III), personnel (Article VIII), finance and budget (Article IX), location (Article X), and the status and authority (Article XI) of UNU. UNU's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing board, the Council of UNU, which is composed of 12 members appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations with the concurrence of the Director-General of UNESCO (https://unu.edu/about/unu-council). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNU's research, postgraduate training, and dissemination of knowledge, as well as cooperation and coordination with other academic institutions and policymakers around the world (Article IV, Paragraph 4). UNU's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the 2030 Agenda and the Sustainable Development Goals, which provide further thematic frameworks for UNU's jurisdiction over specific sustainability issues and domains (https://unu.edu/topics/sdg-partnerships).

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNU involves collaboration with affiliated institutions, such as the UN General Assembly and UNESCO. This is achieved through reporting, approving, devising, and implementing the principles, policies, budget, and work programme of the University as structured in Articles III-IX of the UNU Charter (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf). The UNU operates through the UNU Council of 12 appointed members, the UNU Rector, and three ex officio members (the UN Secretary-General, the UNESCO Director-General and the UNITAR Executive Director) (Articles III-VI). The UNU Council is responsible for devising the principles and policies that govern the University’s operations, and for considering and approving the UNU budget and work programme (Article IV). The UNU Council reports annually to the UN General Assembly, the UN Economic and Social Council, and the Executive Board of UNESCO (Article IV). The UNU Rector is the chief academic and administrative officer of the University and is appointed by the Secretary-General of the United Nations in consultation with the Director-General of UNESCO (Article V). The UNU Rector exercises the powers delegated to him or her by the UNU Council and is accountable to the UNU Council for the discharge of his or her functions (Article V). The UNU institutes and programmes are the operational units of the University and are established by the UNU Council in accordance with the principles and policies laid down by the Council (Article VII). The UNU institutes and programmes are headed by directors who are appointed by the UNU Rector in consultation with the UNU Council and are responsible to the UNU Rector for the academic and administrative management of their respective units (Article VII, paragraph 2). The UNU institutes and programmes carry out research, teaching, training, and capacity development activities in line with the UNU strategic plan and the UNU Council-approved work programme and budget (Article IX).

matrix_cell_text_full: The objectives of the WBG are established in the Articles of Agreement and Conventions of its constituent institutions (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). The IBRD Articles of Agreement (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/722361541184234501/IBRDArticlesOfAgreement-English.pdf) state that the WBG through IBRD aims to assist in the reconstruction and development of territories of members by facilitating the investment of capital for productive purposes, promoting private foreign investment by means of guarantees or participations in loans and other investments, and supplementing private investment by providing finance for productive purposes out of its own capital, funds raised by it and its other resources (Article I, Section 1). As specified in the IDA Articles of Agreement (https://ida.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/ida-articlesofagreement.pdf), the WBG through IDA aims to promote economic development, increase productivity and thus raise standards of living in the less-developed areas of the world by providing finance to projects and programs that contribute to the economic or social development of the members whose per capita income is low, and to those members in the opinion of the Association are not able to borrow from the IBRD on suitable terms (Article I, Section 1). The WBG through the IFC Articles of Agreement (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/6a4a091b83577eb35e881dbf9016c5c3-0330032020/original/IFCArticlesOfAgreement.pdf) aims to further economic development by encouraging the growth of productive private enterprise in member countries, particularly in the less-developed areas, by assisting in financing the establishment, improvement and expansion of private productive enterprises, and by stimulating and helping to create conditions conducive to the flow of private capital, domestic and foreign, into productive investment in member countries (Article I, Section 1). According to the MIGA Convention (https://www.miga.org/sites/default/files/archive/Documents/miga_convention_november_2010.pdf), the WBG through MIGA aims to encourage the flow of investments for productive purposes among member countries, and in particular to developing member countries, by providing guarantees against non-commercial risks in respect of investments in member countries, by establishing and operating a trust fund to provide technical assistance to member countries in connection with the promotion of foreign investment, and by exercising such other incidental powers as shall be necessary or desirable in the furtherance of its objective (Article 2, Section 1). Lastly, the WBG through the ICSID Convention (https://icsid.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/ICSID%20Convention%20English.pdf) aims to provide facilities for conciliation and arbitration of investment disputes between contracting states and nationals of other contracting states, and to bring together parties who have agreed to use such facilities, in order to facilitate the settlement of such disputes and to contribute to the development of international law on investments (Article 1, Section 2).
