matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the World Bank Group (WBG) involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the development domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other multilateral institutions to help countries end extreme poverty and promote shared prosperity in a sustainable manner. This coordination is guided by the World Bank Group Strategy (https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/e3804a75-62f2-5348-8d04-6f8ec14212fb/content), which outlines how the WBG will work in partnership to fulfill its mandate. For example, the WBG works with the health sector to improve health outcomes and strengthen health systems (https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/health), with the education sector to ensure quality and inclusive learning for all (https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/education), with the energy sector to increase access to affordable, reliable, and sustainable energy (https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/energy), or with the environment sector to address climate change and environmental challenges (https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/environment). Horizontal coordination within the WBG can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Global Practice Groups (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#global-practice-groups) or the Country Partnership Frameworks (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#country-partnership-frameworks), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the G-20 (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#g20), the UN Development System (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#un-development-system), or the Multilateral Development Banks (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement#multilateral-development-banks), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for development sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World bank group evaluation Principles (https://ieg.worldbankgroup.org/sites/default/files/Data/reports/WorldBankEvaluationPrinciples.pdf) or the Business Ready (B-READY) platform (https://www.worldbank.org/en/businessready), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for development issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Human Capital Project (https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/human-capital) or the World Development Report (https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/wdr/wdr-archive).

matrix_cell_text_full: The World Bank Group executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a World Bank Group Strategy adopted in 2013, based on the principles of country ownership, evidence-based solutions, and global and regional integration (https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/16093/32824_ebook.pdf?sequence=4&isAllowed=y). Secondly, a World Bank Group Evolution Roadmap that outlines the key actions and reforms to implement the WBG Strategy and enhance the WBG's effectiveness and efficiency (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/evolution-roadmap). This roadmap, endorsed by the Board of Governors in 2020, focuses on four pillars: (i) strengthening country platforms and partnerships, (ii) enhancing the WBG's financial and operational capacity, (iii) improving the WBG's business model and internal processes, and (iv) fostering a culture of innovation and learning. Thirdly, a set of thematic and sector strategies that provide the strategic framework and guidance for the WBG's engagement in specific areas of development, such as gender, climate change, fragility and conflict, human capital, infrastructure, and private sector development. These strategies are aligned with the WBG Strategy and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and are informed by global knowledge and evidence (https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/sdgs-2030-agenda). In addition, the WBG prepares Country Partnership Frameworks (CPFs) and Regional Partnership Frameworks (RPFs) that define the WBG's support to individual countries and regions, based on their development priorities, challenges, and opportunities. These frameworks are developed in consultation with the governments, civil society, and other stakeholders, and are aligned with the WBG Strategy and the country's own development strategy (https://www.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/country-strategies). The WBG also maintains various initiatives, platforms, and funds that provide the operational and financial instruments for addressing specific development challenges and opportunities (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/what-we-do/brief/initiatives-platforms-and-funds) while engaging in partnerships, coalitions, and networks that provide the collaborative framework for enhancing the impact and effectiveness of the WBG's interventions, leveraging the comparative advantages and resources of different actors, and addressing cross-cutting issues such as governance, data, and innovation (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/partners).

This roadmap, endorsed by the Board of Governors in 2020, focuses on four pillars: (i) strengthening country platforms and partnerships, (ii) enhancing the WBG's financial and operational capacity, (iii) improving the WBG's business model and internal processes, and (iv) fostering a culture of innovation and learning. Thirdly, a set of thematic and sector strategies that provide the strategic framework and guidance for the WBG's engagement in specific areas of development, such as gender, climate change, fragility and conflict, human capital, infrastructure, and private sector development. These strategies are aligned with the WBG Strategy and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and are informed by global knowledge and evidence (https://www.worldbank.org/en/programs/sdgs-2030-agenda). In addition, the WBG prepares Country Partnership Frameworks (CPFs) and Regional Partnership Frameworks (RPFs) that define the WBG's support to individual countries and regions, based on their development priorities, challenges, and opportunities. These frameworks are developed in consultation with the governments, civil society, and other stakeholders, and are aligned with the WBG Strategy and the country's own development strategy (https://www.worldbank.org/en/projects-operations/country-strategies). The WBG also maintains various initiatives, platforms, and funds that provide the operational and financial instruments for addressing specific development challenges and opportunities (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/what-we-do/brief/initiatives-platforms-and-funds) while engaging in partnerships, coalitions, and networks that provide the collaborative framework for enhancing the impact and effectiveness of the WBG's interventions, leveraging the comparative advantages and resources of different actors, and addressing cross-cutting issues such as governance, data, and innovation (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/partners).

The WBG derives its mandate from the Articles of Agreement, Conventions, or equivalent governance documents of its five constituent institutions: the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), the International Development Association (IDA), the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), and the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). These documents outline the conditions of membership, the general principles of organization, management, and operations, and the status, immunities, and privileges of each organization ((https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). The IBRD Articles of Agreement (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/722361541184234501/IBRDArticlesOfAgreement-English.pdf), which came into effect on December 27, 1945, define the purposes and functions of the IBRD, the capital stock and voting power of the members, the loans and guarantees of the IBRD, the operations and transactions of the IBRD, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IBRD. Similarly, the IDA Articles of Agreement (https://ida.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/ida-articlesofagreement.pdf), which came into effect on September 24, 1960, define the purposes and functions of the IDA, the resources and management of the IDA, the terms and conditions of financing by the IDA, the operations and transactions of the IDA, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IDA. The IFC Articles of Agreement (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/6a4a091b83577eb35e881dbf9016c5c3-0330032020/original/IFCArticlesOfAgreement.pdf), which came into effect on July 20, 1956, define the purposes and functions of the IFC, the capital stock and voting power of the members, the loans, guarantees, and other operations of the IFC, the operations and transactions of the IFC, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the IFC. The MIGA Convention (https://www.miga.org/sites/default/files/archive/Documents/miga_convention_november_2010.pdf), which came into force on April 12, 1988, defines the purposes and functions of the MIGA, the membership and capital of the MIGA, the guarantees and other operations of the MIGA, the relations with other international organizations, the withdrawal and suspension of membership, and the status, immunities, and privileges of the MIGA. Lastly, the ICSID Convention (https://icsid.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/ICSID%20Convention%20English.pdf), which entered into force on October 14, 1966, defines the purposes and functions of the ICSID, the jurisdiction of the ICSID, the recognition and enforcement of awards, the administrative and financial provisions of the ICSID, the amendment and interpretation of the ICSID Convention, and the final provisions of the ICSID Convention.
The WBG’s jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the Boards of Governors, the Boards of Executive Directors, and the Council of Governors (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/leadership). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for the WBG’s activities and programs, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. The WBG’s mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Sustainable Development Goals (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/259801562965232326/2030Agenda-2019-final-web.pdf), the Paris Agreement on Climate Change ((https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/english_paris_agreement.pdf), and the Addis Ababa Action Agenda on Financing for Development (https://sustainabledevelopment.un.org/frameworks/addisababaactionagenda), which provide further legal frameworks for the WBG’s jurisdiction over specific development issues and domains.

Vertical coordination within the WBG involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other international organizations, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through consultation, cooperation, and partnership (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/collaboration-engagement) and structured under the Articles of Agreement and Conventions of the World Bank’s constituent institutions: IBRD, IDA, IFC, MIGA, and ICSID (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). The WBG operates through the Board of Governors, the Board of Executive Directors, and the President and staff. The Board of Governors consists of one governor and one alternate governor appointed by each member country (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/leadership/governors). The Board of Executive Directors consists of 25 executive directors who represent the member countries or groups of countries. The President is the chief of the operating staff of the WBG and conducts its ordinary business under the direction of the Board of Executive Directors (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/leadership/directors).
The WBG also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies that assist in its work. The Development Committee advises the Board of Governors on development issues and the transfer of resources to developing countries (https://www.devcommittee.org/en/devcommittee/home); the Inspection Panel investigates complaints from people who believe they have been harmed by a World Bank-funded project (https://www.inspectionpanel.org/); and the Independent Evaluation Group assesses the performance and impact of the World Bank Group’s activities (https://ieg.worldbankgroup.org/evaluations). The WBG’s work is organized around six regions, each overseen by a Vice President who works closely with the President and the Board of Executive Directors to implement the World Bank Group’s agenda across all levels of the organization (https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/922161468339057329/pdf/384810ADR1Manu1l1Mediation01PUBLIC1.pdf). There is also the Global Practices and Cross-Cutting Solutions Areas, which provide technical expertise and knowledge on various sectors and themes; and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), and the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), which are separate legal entities within the World Bank Group that focus on private sector development, investment guarantees, and dispute resolution, respectively (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/annual-report/our-organization). With 189 member countries and staff from more than 170 countries, the WBG operates offices and technical centers in more than 130 countries, where it works with governments, civil society, and other partners to support its mission of ending extreme poverty and promoting shared prosperity (https://www.worldbank.org/en/who-we-are). In addition, the WBG coordinates with other international organizations and agencies, such as the United Nations, the International Monetary Fund, the World Trade Organization, and the regional development banks, to enhance global cooperation and effectiveness in addressing development challenges (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/partners).

matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within WFP involves working with different actors and sectors within the food security and nutrition domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that food assistance is delivered effectively and efficiently to the people in need and that food systems are transformed to support the achievement of zero hunger. This coordination is guided by Article III of the General Regulations of WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150). For example, WFP works with the health sector to address malnutrition and micronutrient deficiencies (https://www.wfp.org/nutrition), with the education sector to provide school feeding and improve learning outcomes (https://www.wfp.org/school-meals), with the social protection sector to strengthen national safety nets and resilience (https://www.wfp.org/social-protection), or with the climate change sector to reduce the risks and impacts of climate shocks on food security (https://www.wfp.org/climate-action). Horizontal coordination within WFP can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and activities with other actors and sectors, such as the Country Strategic Plans (https://www.wfp.org/country-strategic-planning) or the Emergency Response Preparedness Plan (https://www.wfp.org/emergency-preparedness-and-response#:~:text=Emergency%20preparedness%20and%20response%20is,and%20timely%20when%20crises%20erupt.) with OCHA, UNICEF and WHO; (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral mechanisms and platforms, such as the Food Security Cluster (https://www.wfp.org/food-security-cluster) or the Scaling Up Nutrition Movement (https://scalingupnutrition.org/); (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for food security and nutrition sector engagement with other actors and sectors, such as the Food Security and Nutrition Analysis (https://www.wfp.org/food-security-analysis) or the Fill the Nutrient Gap (https://www.wfp.org/publications/fill-nutrient-gap); and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for food security and nutrition issues and policies among other actors and sectors, such as the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (https://www.wfp.org/publications/2021-state-food-security-and-nutrition-world-report-and-inbrief) or the Global Report on Food Crises (https://www.wfp.org/publications/global-report-food-crises-2023).

matrix_cell_text_full: WFP cooperates with various institutions to achieve its goals and objectives of eradicating hunger and malnutrition. It works closely with other UN agencies and international organizations, as stated in Article III of the General Regulations of the WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150). It has a special relationship with the other two Rome-based UN agencies – FAO and IFAD – with which it shares a common vision of promoting food security. It also has a strong operational partnership with UNHCR for providing food assistance to refugees and internally displaced people. Moreover, WFP collaborates with UNDP and other development partners to support countries' self-defined priorities and accelerate climate action, as part of the UN Development Assistance Framework. Furthermore, WFP engages with other international and regional organizations, such as ECHO, OAS and ICRC, to deliver humanitarian aid and enhance resilience. Additionally, WFP partners with UNV and Online Volunteers to support its work to achieve Zero Hunger (https://www.unv.org/Success-stories/un-volunteers-wfp-road-zero-hunger).

matrix_cell_text_full: The World Food Programme (WFP) executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a four-year Strategic Plan establishes the organization’s vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets. This plan, applicable for 2022-2025 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000132205), outlines the many ways for WFP, working in synergy with others, to most efficiently and effectively save and change lives. It is grounded within renewed global commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its associated Sustainable Development Goals 9https://www.wfp.org/publications/wfp-strategic-plan-2022-25). Secondly, a biennial Management Plan, presented to the Executive Board, details the projected operational needs, the provisional global implementation plan, the programme support and business operations budget, and the use of reserves and general fund. The current Management Plan for 2024-2026 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000151658) highlights the corporate budget required to implement WFP’s programme of work, based on the funding forecasts and prioritization criteria. It also outlines WFP’s key drivers of hunger, such as conflict, climate change, and economic shocks, and how WFP responds to them through various programmes, operations, and platforms (https://www.wfp.org/publications/wfp-management-plan-2024-2026). Thirdly, the Corporate Results Framework (CRF) 2022-2025 (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000136871) guides the planning, implementation, monitoring, and reporting of WFP’s programmes towards the objectives identified in the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan. The CRF, supplemented by the policy on country strategic plans (CSPs) (https://www.wfp.org/publications/policy-country-strategic-plans), provides a performance and accountability framework that enables WFP to measure and demonstrate its response to humanitarian needs. In addition, the WFP has over 32 policies in effect under the 2022-2025 Strategic Plan. An update of the portfolio of policies is submitted annually and can be found as the “Compendium of Policies” on the Executive Board website (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000151657). Finally, various policies, frameworks, agreements, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the WFP Strategic Plan, addressing food security, nutrition, resilience, capacity strengthening, social protection, and innovation (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000132607).

matrix_cell_text_full: The World Food Programme (WFP) derives its mandate from the General Assembly Resolution 2095 (XX) of 20 December 1965 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/2095(XX)), which extended the WFP on a continuing basis for as long as multilateral food aid is feasible and desirable, Resolution 1714 (XVI) of 19 December 1961 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/1714(XVI)), which established WFP as an experimental programme, and Resolution 3404 (XXX) of 28 November 1975 (http://undocs.org/en/A/RES/3404(XXX)), which named Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes oversight of WFP. In addition, pursuant to Resolution 50/8 of 1 November 1995 (https://documents.un.org/doc/resolution/gen/n95/257/30/img/n9525730.pdf?token=lBOUzh2cYTpOtGNhBZ&fe=true), the Committee on Food Aid Policies and Programmes (CFA) was reconstituted as the WFP Executive Board with effect from 1 Jan. 1996. The General Assembly Resolutions 1714 (XVI) and 2095 (XX) define the objectives and scope of WFP, and Resolution 50/8 outlines the structure and membership of the United Nations/FAO Intergovernmental Committee of the WFP, which is the governing body of the programme. matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within WFP involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, FAO, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through consultation, guidance, supervision, and direction of the activities of WFP in accordance with the overall policy guidance of the United Nations and FAO as structured under Article III-VIII of the General Regulations of WFP (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000141150), which establish that WFP shall consult with and seek advice and cooperation from the United Nations and FAO, and coordinate and operate in close liaison with appropriate United Nations agencies and operating programmes, bilateral assistance programmes, and other relevant organizations. WFP operates through the Executive Board of 36 members, jointly established by the United Nations and FAO, and a secretariat headed by an Executive Director (Article V, paragraph 1). The Executive Board is responsible for providing intergovernmental support and specific policy direction to and supervision of the activities of WFP, and ensuring that WFP is responsive to the needs and priorities of recipient countries (Article VI, paragraph 1). The Executive Director is responsible and accountable to the Board for the administration of WFP and for the implementation of WFP programmes, projects and other activities (Article VII, paragraph 1). The Executive Director also represents WFP and performs functions conferred by the agreements concluded by the United Nations and FAO on behalf of WFP with States or intergovernmental organizations (Article VIII, paragraph 1). WFP's work is organised around five regions, each overseen by a Regional Director who works closely with the Executive Director to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization. There is also the Senior Management Group (consisting of the Executive Director, Deputy Executive Directors, Assistant Executive Directors, Regional Directors, Chief of Staff, Inspector General and Director of Legal Services) providing strategic and operational guidance to the Executive Director on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of WFP; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://www.wfp.org/governance-and-leadership). Additionally, a network of country offices and technical experts supports WFP's work in providing food assistance and enhancing food security and nutrition as an integral part of regional and national development policies. Besides the Executive Director, at the WFP headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of Deputy Executive Directors and Assistant Executive Directors with portfolios focusing on different aspects of WFP's mandate. In addition, WFP coordinates with the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) and other humanitarian partners through the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) and the cluster system to ensure effective and principled humanitarian action (https://executiveboard.wfp.org/document_download/WFP-0000138085). WFP also collaborates with the Committee on World Food Security (CFS) (https://www.fao.org/sustainable-development-goals-helpdesk/champion/article-detail/committee-on-world-food-security/en#:~:text=The%20Committee%20on%20World%20Food,security%20and%20nutrition%20for%20all.), the Global Network Against Food Crises (GNAFC) (https://www.fightfoodcrises.net/#:~:text=The%20Global%20Network%20Against%20Food,based%20responses%20and%20collective%20efforts), the Scaling Up Nutrition (SUN) Movement 9https://sunbusinessnetwork.org/about-us/#:~:text=The%20Scaling%20Up%20Nutrition%20(SUN,to%20scaling%20up%20nutrition%20action.), and other platforms and initiatives to promote global food security and nutrition.

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full:
Horizontal coordination within WHO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the health domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that health is considered in all policies and that health policies are aligned with other sectoral policies. This coordination is guided by Article 2 of the Constitution of the World Health Organization (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). For example, WHO works with the education sector to promote health literacy and school health programmes (https://www.who.int/teams/health-promotion/enhanced-wellbeing/ninth-global-conference/health-literacy), with the transport sector to reduce road traffic injuries and air pollution (https://www.who.int/teams/environment-climate-change-and-health/healthy-urban-environments/transport), or with the ocean sector to enhance the health in coastal areas particularly during natural disasters (https://www.who.int/health-topics/tropical-cyclones#tab=tab_1). Horizontal coordination within WHO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the One Health Joint Plan of Action (2022 - 2026) with FAO, UNEP and WOAH (https://wedocs.unep.org/bitstream/handle/20.500.11822/40843/one_health.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y),
(2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Standing Committee or the UN Interagency Task Force on the Prevention and Control of Noncommunicable Diseases (https://uniatf.who.int/about-us/what-we-do), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for health sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Health in All Policies Framework for Country Action (https://www.afro.who.int/sites/default/files/2017-06/140120HPRHiAPFramework.pdf) or the Health Impact Assessment Toolkit (https://www.who.int/tools/health-impact-assessments), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for health issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Health Day (https://www.who.int/campaigns/world-health-day) or the World Health SStatisticsReport (https://www.who.int/data/gho/publications/world-health-statistics). The WHO provides leadership and direction on matters critical to health, shapes the health research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses health trends (https://www.who.int/about/what-we-do). WHO facilitates the participation of various actors in the health sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on health matters (https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/WHA75/A75_39-en.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The WHO executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a five-year General Programme of Work, approved by the World Health Assembly, which sets the strategic direction, priorities, and budget of the organization (https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/EB152/B152_28-en.pdf). This plan, applicable for 2019-2025, aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the triple billion targets of achieving universal health coverage, addressing health emergencies, and promoting healthier populations. (https://www.who.int/data/triple-billion-dashboard) Secondly, a biennial Programme Budget, proposed by the Director-General and adopted by the World Health Assembly, which details the expected results, indicators, and resources for each strategic priority and programme area (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/346071/9789240036109-eng.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y). The current budget for 2022-2023 is based on the Thirteenth General Programme of Work and reflects the needs and priorities of member states and partners (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/346071/9789240036109-eng.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y). Thirdly, various global health sector strategies, developed in consultation with member states and stakeholders, which provide a comprehensive and coherent approach to address specific health issues, such as HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections. These strategies, applicable for 2022-2030, propose a common vision, goals, and strategic directions for ending epidemics and advancing universal health coverage, primary health care, and health security (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/360348/9789240053779-eng.pdf?sequence=1). Finally, various resolutions, decisions, and recommendations, adopted by the World Health Assembly and the Executive Board, which provide policy guidance and oversight for the implementation of the WHO's objectives and mandates. These include addressing health emergencies, communicable and non-communicable diseases, health systems, health promotion, and health governance, with key instruments listed here (https://www.who.int/teams/integrated-health-services/patient-safety/policy/resolutions).

The Constitution defines the objective, functions, and principles of WHO, as well as the rights and obligations of its member states (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf) Additionally, WHO's jurisdiction is influenced by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2021/03/udhr.pdf) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1976/01/19760103%2009-57%20PM/Ch_IV_03.pdf), which recognize the right to health as a fundamental human right. WHO also supports the implementation of various health-related conventions and treaties, such as the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/42811/9241591013.pdf?sequence=1) and the International Health Regulations (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/246107/9789241580496-eng.pdf?sequence=1), which provide further legal frameworks for WHO's jurisdiction over specific health issues and situations.

The Constitution defines the objective, functions, and principles of WHO, as well as the rights and obligations of its member states (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf) Additionally, WHO's jurisdiction is influenced by the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (https://www.un.org/sites/un2.un.org/files/2021/03/udhr.pdf) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1976/01/19760103%2009-57%20PM/Ch_IV_03.pdf), which recognize the right to health as a fundamental human right. WHO also supports the implementation of various health-related conventions and treaties, such as the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/42811/9241591013.pdf?sequence=1) and the International Health Regulations (https://iris.who.int/bitstream/handle/10665/246107/9789241580496-eng.pdf?sequence=1), which provide further legal frameworks for WHO's jurisdiction over specific health issues and situations.

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within WHO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities.  This is achieved through delegation of authority, directing, and controlling. This is structured under the Relationship with the United Nations and Other International Organizations section of the WHO Constitution, specifically in Articles 69-70 (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). The WHO operates through the World Health Assembly of all the members, the Executive Board of 34 members, and a secretariat headed by a Director-General (Articles 18-26) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). The WHO also has committees, commissions, and other subsidiary bodies (Articles 27-28). The WHO assists members in the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (Articles 23-24) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf). WHO's work is organized around six regions, each overseen by a Regional Director who works closely with the Director-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.who.int/about/who-we-are). There is also the Global Policy Group (consisting of the Director-General, Deputy Director-General, Regional Directors and the Executive Director of the WHO Emergencies Programme) providing strategic and internal policy advice to the Director-General on matters related to the programmatic and managerial work of WHO; and ensuring coherence and alignment between the three levels of the Organization and the governing bodies (https://www.who.int/director-general/global-policy-group). Also, a network of country offices and technical experts supports the WHO's work in promoting health and well-being as an integral part of regional and national development policies (https://www.who.int/countries/en/). Additionally, WHO operates 7 technical centres and in-country offices in 30 Member States (https://www.who.int/europe/about-us/about-who-europe/technical-centres). Besides the director General,  at the WHO headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of an Executive Director and 9 Assistant Director-GeneraI with portfolios focusing on different aspects in accordance with the WHO's mandate (https://www.who.int/director-general/who-headquarters-leadership-team). In addition, WHO/Europe coordinates with the European Union and its agencies and is the host organisation and partner of the European Observatory on Health Systems and Policies (https://www.who.int/europe/about-us/about-who-europe/technical-centres).

excerpt_<=50w: Defined objectives: stated institutional purposes/goals expressed in founding and/or strategic texts.
matrix_cell_text_full: According to the Convention Establishing the World Intellectual Property Organization (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833), WIPO's objectives encompass two main aspects: promoting the protection of intellectual property throughout the world (Article 3(i)) and ensuring administrative cooperation among the Unions (Article 3(ii)). To achieve these objectives, the Organization, through its appropriate organs, has several functions, such as: developing measures to facilitate the efficient protection of intellectual property and to harmonize national legislation in this field (Article 4(i)); performing the administrative tasks of the Paris Union, the Berne Union, and other international agreements related to intellectual property (Article 4(ii)); encouraging the conclusion of international agreements to promote the protection of intellectual property; offering legal-technical assistance to States requesting it (Article 4(iv)); assembling and disseminating information concerning the protection of intellectual property (Article 4(vi)); maintaining services facilitating the international protection of intellectual property (Article 4(vii)); and taking all other appropriate action in relation to the stated objectives (Article 4(viii)). These objectives and functions enable WIPO to contribute to better understanding and cooperation among States for their mutual benefit on the basis of respect for their sovereignty and equality, and to encourage creative activity in the industrial, scientific, literary or artistic fields (Preamble).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within WIPO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the intellectual property domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the scientific community, and other UN agencies to promote and protect intellectual property rights and foster innovation and creativity. This coordination is guided by Article 13 of the WIPO Convention (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833). For example, WIPO works with the culture sector to safeguard the diversity of cultural expressions and support the creative industries (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/tk/913/wipo_pub_913.pdf), with the health sector to facilitate access to medicines and medical technologies (https://tind.wipo.int/record/28688/files/wipo_pub_628.pdf), the education sector to enhance the quality and availability of educational resources (https://welc.wipo.int/) or with the environment sector to address climate change and biodiversity issues (https://www.wipo.int/policy/en/climate_change/). Horizontal coordination within WIPO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programs and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the WIPO Development Agenda (https://www.wipo.int/ip-development/en/agenda/), the WIPO Re:Search initiative with WHO and BIO Ventures for Global Health (https://www.wipo.int/research/en/), or the WIPO GREEN platform with UNEP and other partners (https://www3.wipo.int/wipogreen/en/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the UN Inter-Agency Task Force on Financing for Development (https://financing.desa.un.org/iatf/home/) or the Accessible Books Consortium (https://www.accessiblebooksconsortium.org/en/web/abc/about/index), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for intellectual property sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the WIPO Standards (https://www.wipo.int/standards/en/) or the WIPO IP Portal (https://ipportal.wipo.int/), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilize support for intellectual property issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Intellectual Property Day (https://www.wipo.int/ip-outreach/en/ipday/) or the WIPO Magazine (https://www.wipo.int/wipo_magazine/en/).

It works closely with the World Trade Organization (WTO), implementing the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/500864), which sets minimum standards for IP protection and enforcement, as per the WIPO-WTO Cooperation Agreement of 1995 (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/wo_ga_24/wo_ga_24_5_rev-annex1.doc#:~:text=The%20WIPO%2DWTO%20Agreement%20of,technical%20assistance%20to%20developing%20countries.). Similarly, WIPO maintains a relationship with the United Nations (UN) and its specialised agencies, such as the UN Development Programme (UNDP), the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), to align its strategies and objectives with the UN's 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, as per the WIPO General Assembly Resolution of 2016 (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/305623). Additionally, WIPO supports the WIPO Intergovernmental Committee on Intellectual Property and Genetic Resources, Traditional Knowledge and Folklore (IGC) (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo-pub-rn2023-5-2-en-the-wipo-intergovernmental-committee-on-intellectual-property-and-genetic-resources-traditional-knowledge-and-folklore.pdf), which aims to reach an agreement on the protection of these forms of IP, with its mandate and work program detailed in Item 20 of the WIPO General Assembly Decision of 2019 (https://www.wipo.int/export/sites/www/about-wipo/ja/assemblies/pdf/2019_decisions.pdf). It also services the WIPO Standing Committee on the Law of Trademarks, Industrial Designs and Geographical Indications (SCT) (https://www.wipo.int/policy/en/sct/#:~:text=The%20SCT%20was%20created%20in,of%20national%20laws%20and%20procedures.), which deals with the development of international norms and standards in these areas.

matrix_cell_text_full: The WIPO executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, a five-year Medium-Term Strategic Plan (MTSP), prepared by the Secretariat and noted by the Assemblies of WIPO, provides high-level strategic guidance for the corresponding Program and Budgets covered by the MTSP. This plan, applicable for 2022-2026 (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/wo_pbc_32/wo_pbc_32_3.pdf), outlines WIPO's vision, mission, strategic pillars, and foundation. Secondly, a biennial Program of Work and Budget, approved by the Assemblies of WIPO, details the expected results, performance indicators, and resources for each program and strategic goal. The current Program of Work and Budget for 2022-2023 (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo_pub_360_pb22_23.pdf) is based on the MTSP and reflects the priorities and needs of the Member States and stakeholders (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/wo_pbc_32/wo_pbc_32_3.pdf). It also supports the implementation of the WIPO Development Agenda, which consists of 45 recommendations to enhance the development dimension of WIPO's activities (https://www.wipo.int/export/sites/www/ip-development/en/agenda/docs/recommendations.pdf). Finally, various initiatives, platforms, and projects provide an operational framework for delivering WIPO's services and advancing its goals, such as WIPO Re:Search (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo_pub_gc_18.pdf), which facilitates research and development for neglected tropical diseases, malaria, and tuberculosis; WIPO IP and Gender Action Plan (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/pubdocs/en/wipo-pub-rn2023-1-en-wipo-intellectual-property-ip-and-gender-action-plan-the-role-of-ip-in-support-of-women-and-girls.pdf), which aims to promote gender equality and women's empowerment in the IP ecosystem; and WIPO GREEN (https://www3.wipo.int/wipogreen/en/), which connects providers and seekers of green technologies and fosters innovation and diffusion of environmentally sound solutions.

matrix_cell_text_full: WIPO derives its mandate from the Convention Establishing the World Intellectual Property Organization (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833), which established WIPO as a specialized agency of the United Nations. Specifically, Article 3 of the Convention states the objectives of the Organization; Article 4 lists the functions of the Organization; Article 5 specifies the conditions for membership in the Organization, which are open to any State that is a member of any of the Unions, or a member of the United Nations or related agencies, or invited by the General Assembly; Article 6 defines the composition, functions, voting, and procedures of the General Assembly, which is the supreme organ of the Organization consisting of the States party to this Convention that are members of any of the Unions; Article 8 defines the composition, functions, voting, and procedures of the Coordination Committee, which is an organ of the Organization consisting of the States party to this Convention that are members of the Executive Committees of the Paris Union and the Berne Union, or both; Article 11 outlines the sources and management of the finances of the Organization; Article 12 grants the Organization the legal capacity necessary for the fulfillment of its objectives and the exercise of its functions; and Artice 13 authorizes the Organization to establish working relations and cooperate with other intergovernmental organizations, and to make suitable arrangements for consultation and cooperation with international and national non-governmental organizations, in matters within its competence. WIPO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the General Assembly, the Coordination Committee (https://www.wipo.int/meetings/en/topic.jsp?group_id=104), and the Assemblies of the Unions (https://www.wipo.int/about-wipo/en/assemblies/#:~:text=Assemblies%20of%20WIPO%20%E2%80%93%202024,July%209%20to%2017%2C%202024.). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for WIPO's activities and programs, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. WIPO's mandate is also supported by the administration of various international treaties and agreements, such as the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/287556), the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283693), and the Marrakesh Treaty to Facilitate Access to Published Works for Persons Who Are Blind, Visually Impaired or Otherwise Print Disabled (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/301019), which provide further legal frameworks for WIPO's jurisdiction over specific intellectual property issues and domains.

matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within WIPO involves cooperation with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and non-governmental organizations. This is achieved through working relations, consultation, and collaboration. This is structured under the Relations with Other Organizations section of the WIPO Convention (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833), specifically in Article 8 (Coordination Committee), Article 9 (International Bureau), and Article 13 (Relations with Other Organizations). The WIPO operates through the General Assembly of all the members, the Conference of all the parties to the Convention, the Coordination Committee of the members of the Executive Committees of the Paris and Berne Unions, and a secretariat headed by a Director General. The WIPO also has permanent committees, standing committees, and other subsidiary bodies. WIPO assists members in the protection of intellectual property throughout the world and provides legal-technical assistance upon request. WIPO's work is organized around six sectors, each overseen by a Deputy Director General who works closely with the Director General to implement strategies and programs across all levels of the Organization (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/a_32/a_32_inf_2-main1.doc). There is also the Senior Management Team (consisting of the Director General, Deputy Directors General, Assistant Directors General, and the Legal Counsel) providing strategic direction and oversight to the Organization and ensuring coherence and alignment between the different sectors and the governing bodies (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/a_32/a_32_inf_2-main1.doc). Additionally, WIPO operates external offices in 7 countries (https://www.wipo.int/about-wipo/en/offices/).

The WIPO operates through the General Assembly of all the members, the Conference of all the parties to the Convention, the Coordination Committee of the members of the Executive Committees of the Paris and Berne Unions, and a secretariat headed by a Director General. WIPO assists members in the protection of intellectual property throughout the world and provides legal-technical assistance upon request. WIPO's work is organized around six sectors, each overseen by a Deputy Director General who works closely with the Director General to implement strategies and programs across all levels of the Organization (https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/govbody/en/a_32/a_32_inf_2-main1.doc). matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within WMO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the meteorological domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, scientific community, and other UN agencies to ensure that meteorological considerations are integrated into all policies and that meteorological policies are aligned with other sectoral policies (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/public-private-partnerships). This coordination is guided by the WMO Unified Data Policy (https://wmo.int/wmo-unified-data-policy-resolution-res1#:~:text=The%20WMO%20Unified%20Policy%20for,States%20and%20Territories%20of%20WMO.). For example, WMO works with the disaster risk reduction sector to support humanitarian activities (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/wmo-coordination-mechanism-wcm), with the climate sector to provide weather, water, and climate information (https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/climate-change-bad-health-climate-services-save-lives), or with the ocean sector to enhance the meteorological services in coastal areas (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/Marine/JCOMM/Overview). Horizontal coordination within WMO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the WMO Coordination Mechanism (WCM) to support humanitarian activities (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/wmo-coordination-mechanism-wcm), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Inter-Agency Standing Committee (https://meetings.wmo.int/EC-76/English/2.%20PROVISIONAL%20REPORT%20%28Approved%20documents%29/EC-76-d03-1%2813%29-WMO-COORDINATION-MECHANISM-IMPLEMENTATION-PLAN-approved_en.docx), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for meteorological sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the WMO Technical Regulations (https://wmo.int/about-us/governance/technical-commissions/standards-and-recommended-practices#:~:text=WMO%20Technical%20Regulations%2C%20an%20international,universal%20application%20by%20all%20Members.) or the WMO Unified Data Policy (https://wmo.int/wmo-unified-data-policy-resolution-res1#:~:text=The%20WMO%20Unified%20Policy%20for,States%20and%20Territories%20of%20WMO.), (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for meteorological issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, as documented in the WMO Strategic Plan 2024-2027 (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/68578/download?file=1336_WMO-Strategic-Plan-2024-2027_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). The WMO provides leadership and direction on matters critical to meteorology, shapes the meteorological research agenda, sets norms and standards, articulates evidence-based policy options, provides technical support to countries, and monitors and assesses meteorological trends (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/our-mandate). WMO facilitates the participation of various actors in the meteorological sector and enhances cooperation and coordination within the UN system on meteorological matters (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/our-mandate).

matrix_cell_text_full:
The WMO collaborates with key organizations to fulfill its objectives. It engages with 193 Member States and various stakeholders through the World Meteorological Congress, serving as the highest-level meteorological decision-making body (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/overview). As the primary meteorological authority within the UN system, WMO's relationship with the UN is grounded in Part XII, Article 25 of the Convention of the World Meteorological Organization (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1), pursuant to Article 57 of the Charter of the United Nations (https://www.un.org/en/about-us/un-charter/full-text). 
Additionally, WMO supports National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs) and advances the application of meteorology and hydrology in many societal and economic areas (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/overview). Pursuant to Part XIII, Article 26 of its convention, WMO collaborates with UN specialized agencies, multilateral development banks, climate funds and others, addressing shared meteorological concerns (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). 
Moreover, WMO contributes to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/partnerships).
Furthermore, WMO maintains a relationship with the public, private, and academic sectors operating in the global weather arena through its Public-Private Engagement (PPE) initiative (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/public-private-partnerships). This initiative encourages and enables Members to pursue mutually beneficial partnerships and engagement with all sectors and stakeholders in order to enhance weather, climate, and water services for businesses, individuals, and society as a whole (https://community.wmo.int/en/activity-areas/public-private-partnerships). 
Finally, WMO facilitates the Voluntary Cooperation Programme (VCP), which focuses on meeting urgent needs of Members through direct financing, small grants and transfer of expertise and technology (https://old.wmo.int/extranet/pages/prog/dra/vcp_en.php).

The WMO Secretariat executes its objectives via several strategies: firstly, a Strategic Plan, revised every four years by the World Meteorological Congress, which establishes the secretariat's vision, mission, strategic goals, core functions, and targets (https://community.wmo.int/en/planning-and-monitoring/strategic-planning#:~:text=The%20process&text=The%20WMO%20Strategic%20Plan%20articulates,the%202020%2D2023%20financial%20period). The current plan, applicable for 2024-2027, aligns with the WMO's mandate to advance meteorological, climatological, hydrological, and related environmental services (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/68578/download?file=1336_WMO-Strategic-Plan-2024-2027_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). Secondly, a  Results-based Budget, devised by the secretariat and ratified by the World Meteorological Congress, detail resources for implementation of the Strategic Plan, including the functioning of constituent bodies and the Secretariat (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/56690?medianame=1236_en_#page=33&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q=).  
Finally, various agreements, mechanisms, platforms, and initiatives provide an operational framework for implementing the WMO's mandate, addressing meteorology, hydrology, climatology, and related environmental disciplines (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/55618/download?file=1196_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). These regulatory provisions make it possible to operate the 24/7/365 global systems for observations, data exchange and management, forecasting and provision of authoritative scientific assessments and standardized service products to a variety of users in each WMO Member State and Member Territory (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/55618/download?file=EC-69_Progress_report_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). 
The WMO also has a Competency Framework that helps Members design their services for effective delivery, assist in staffing decisions, guide the performance assessment of staff members, and offer recommended learning outcomes to use in planning training programmes (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/56877/download?file=1209_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1).  In addition to these, the WMO has Resolutions, Decisions and Recommendations adopted by the Congress, Executive Council, Regional Associations and Technical Commissions in force (https://tools.wmo.int/wmo-resolutions/). These resolutions and decisions guide the overall progress towards achieving departmental targets and organizational objectives and goals.

matrix_cell_text_full: WMO derives its mandate from the Convention of the World Meteorological Organization, which established WMO as a specialized agency of the United Nations (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). Specifically, Article 2 of the Convention defines the purposes and functions of WMO, and Article 3 outlines the structure and membership of WMO (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). Additionally, WMO's general regulations, regulation 154 on the general function of the WMO secretariat, states that the secretariat shall execute the decisions of the constituent bodies and provide them with the necessary services (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). WMO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its constituent bodies, such as the World Meteorological Congress, the Executive Council, and the regional associations (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/35722/download?file=48-I_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for WMO's activities and programmes, as well as the cooperation and coordination with other organizations and stakeholders. WMO's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Vienna Convention on the Protection of the Ozone Layer, and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, which provide further legal frameworks for WMO's jurisdiction over specific meteorological issues and domains.

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full:
Vertical coordination within the WMO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and intergovernmental organizations, national governments, and local authorities⁵. This is achieved through reporting, cooperation, and assistance⁶. This is structured under the Convention of the World Meteorological Organization⁵. The WMO operates through the World Meteorological Congress, the supreme body of the Organization, which determines policy (https://public-old.wmo.int/en/about-us/governance#:~:text=The%20World%20Meteorological%20Congress%20is,activities%20within%20their%20respective%20Regions.). Each member state and territory is represented by a Permanent Representative with WMO when Congress meets every four years (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance). The Executive Council (EC) implements Congress decisions⁴. The Secretariat is an eight-department organization with a staff of 200 headed by a Secretary-General, who can serve a maximum of two four-year terms (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance).  Six regional associations are responsible for the coordination of meteorological, hydrological and related activities within their respective Regions, while technical commissions consisting of technical experts study technical matters and make recommendations to Congress and the Executive Council (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance). 
The Officers of WMO are a President and three Vice-Presidents, who are also chair and vice-chairs of Congress and the Executive Council (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance). The Secretary-General oversees the functioning of the Secretariat, headquartered in Geneva (https://wmo.int/about-wmo/governance). There is also The Bureau (the Bureau consists of the President, the three Vice-Presidents and the Secretary-General), an informal consultative mechanism to advise the President and facilitate the discharge of his mandate and coordinate the work of Congress and the Executive Council. WMO, in addition to constituent bodies (Executive Council, regional associations and technical commissions), establishes additional bodies to advise on specific subjects. Currently, these include: Research Board on Weather, Climate, Water and the Environment (Research Board), acting as the primary conduit to engage the international research community in the work of WMO; Scientific Advisory Panel (SAP), advising on WMO research strategies and the optimal scientific directions to support the evolution of its mandate in weather, climate, water and related environmental and social sciences; Joint WMO-IOC Collaborative Board (JCB), an interagency body with the Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO to coordinate on ocean matters of common interest; Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), created in 1988 by WMO and UNEP, is the United Nations body for assessing the science related to climate change; the  Financial Advisory Committee (FINAC) provides advice from WMO Members on financial matters and the affordability, sustainability and implementation of the results-based budget to Congress and the Executive Council.
The WMO assists members in the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes, and provides technical cooperation and assistance upon request (https://wmo.int/about-us/governance/technical-commissions/standards-and-recommended-practices).  Also the WMO Liaison Offices represent the scientific and technical work and priorities of WMO Members in international processes at their location and the wider region (https://wmo.int/about-us/liaison-offices). WMO currently has some 38 institutions acting as 26 Regional Training Centres (RTC), offering short and long-term training to staff of WMO Member National Hydrological and Meteorological Services (https://public-old.wmo.int/en/resources/meteoworld/wmo-regional-training-centres). Additionally, the WMO operates the Education and Training Programme (ETRP) that aims at ensuring the National Meteorological and hydrological Services (NMHSs) and their associated institutions are competent to deliver required services and play other relevant roles in national socioeconomic development, by making available the necessary policy, guidance, resources and training (https://wmo.int/activities/education-and-training-programme).

excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within UNWTO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the tourism domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other UN agencies to ensure that tourism is a driver of economic growth, social inclusion, environmental sustainability, and cultural diversity (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-at-fitur-2024-investments-sustainable-tourism-and-collaboration). For example, UNWTO works with the health sector to support the safe and responsible recovery of tourism from the COVID-19 pandemic (https://www.unwto.org/covid-19-oneplanet-responsible-recovery), with the education sector to enhance the quality and relevance of tourism education and training (https://www.unwto.org/un-tourism-academy), with the culture sector to foster the preservation and promotion of cultural heritage and diversity (https://www.unwto.org/tourism-and-culture), or with the environment sector to advance the transition to a low-carbon and circular economy in tourism (https://www.unwto.org/sustainable-development/one-planet). Horizontal coordination within UNWTO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Technical Cooperation Programme (https://www.unwto.org/technical-cooperation) or the Global Tourism Plastics Initiative with UNEP and the Ellen MacArthur Foundation (https://www.unwto.org/sustainable-development/global-tourism-plastics-initiative), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Committee on Tourism and Competitiveness (https://www.unwto.org/competitiveness-commitee-ctc#:~:text=The%20Committee%20on%20Tourism%20and%20Competitiveness%20(CTC)%20is%20one%20of,DEC%2F7(XCV).) or the UN Inter-Agency Task Force on Social and Solidarity Economy (https://unsse.org/), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for tourism sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the International Recommendations for Tourism Statistics (https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publication/Seriesm/SeriesM_83rev1e.pdf) or the Tourism Satellite Account (https://unstats.un.org/unsd/publication/Seriesf/SeriesF_80rev1e.pdf), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for tourism issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the World Tourism Day (https://www.unwto.org/world-tourism-day) or the Tourism for SDGs Platform (https://tourism4sdgs.org/).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNWTO cooperates with various institutions to promote sustainable and responsible tourism (https://www.unwto.org/sustainable-development). It partners with the European Union (EU), implementing a framework agreement signed in Brussels on 28 February 2018, (https://www.unwto.org/europe/press-release/2018-02-28/unwto-deepens-tourism-cooperation-european-union). Likewise, UNWTO maintains a relationship with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), collaborating on projects related to rural development and food security, based on a memorandum of understanding signed in 2020 (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-and-fao-to-work-together-on-developing-tourism-for-rural-development). Furthermore, UNWTO supports the World Trade Organization (WTO), contributing to the trade and development agenda and the Aid for Trade initiative (https://www.unwto.org/global/news/2019-07-15/tourism-world-trade-organization-wto-aid-trade-global-review-2019). It also engages with the UN system, participating in the UN System Chief Executives Board for Coordination (UNCEB) (https://www.unwto.org/archive/global/press-release/2013-04-04/unwto-hosts-meeting-un-chief-executives-board) and the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) (https://www.unwto.org/archive/africa/press-release/2017-07-07/unwto-hosts-presentation-unctad-report-tourism-driver-transformative-and-in), preparing joint reports and recommendations. Additionally, UNWTO facilitates the Partnerships in Education (https://www.unwto.org/partnerships-in-education) to enhance education and training capabilities in tourism, involving certified programmes and affiliate members.

matrix_cell_text_full: The United Nations World Tourism Organization (UNWTO) executes its objectives via several strategies. Firstly, the UNWTO has a strategic plan that is directed towards governments of UNWTO Member States and aims to support and strengthen the capacity of National, regional, and local tourism Administrations (https://www.unwto.org/UNWTO-strategy). This strategic plan involves a sectorial analysis of tourism education and training, identifying weaknesses in the system as well as gaps between the educational offering and the real needs of the sector. The final product of this action is a strategic document containing plans and programmes in education and training at the national or regional level (https://www.unwto.org/UNWTO-strategy). Secondly, the UNWTO has a Programme of Work for 2024-2025, which is a wide-reaching plan built around clear priorities, including key pillars and landmarks (https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2023-10/A25_4_c_Draft_Programme_Work_2024_2025_rev1_En.pdf?VersionId=f87QHlfdEF31lDDrbrms82gFO2NCQZu5). This plan is aimed at restoring tourist confidence by developing and harmonizing minimum international standards, and providing sufficient guarantees for the protection of international tourists in the post COVID-19 world (https://www.unwto.org/international-code-for-the-protection-of-tourists). Thirdly, the UNWTO has established policy frameworks to effectively support the tourism sector at different levels: national, regional, and local (https://www.unwto.org/policy-destination-management). These policies focus on tourism policy and strategic planning, governance and vertical cooperation, and public-private partnerships. Finally, the UNWTO has instituted several collaborative initiatives. For example, it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the African Civil Aviation Commission (AFCAC) to promote sustainable tourism and the implementation of the Single African Air Transport Market (SAATM) (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-and-afcac-partner-around-air-connectivity-in-africa). It also has a partnership with Google to lead global tourism’s recovery through innovation, education, and market intelligence (https://www.unwto.org/news/unwto-and-google-launch-global-partnership-to-lead-tourism-recovery). The UNWTO's strategic plans and initiatives are typically aligned with global agendas such as the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, indicating a long-term perspective (https://www.unwto.org/reports/from-crisis-to-transformation/agenda-2030.html). The UNWTO also works with its members and partners on an ongoing basis to achieve its objectives (https://www.unwto.org/europe/partnerships).

matrix_cell_text_full: UNWTO derives its mandate from the Statutes of the World Tourism Organization (https://webunwto.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/imported_images/51970/unwtostatuteseng.pdf), which established UNWTO as a specialized agency of the United Nations. Specifically, Article 3 of the Statutes defines the aims and objectives of UNWTO, Articles 4-7 outlines the provisions for membership of the UNWTO, Article 8-24 define organizational structure and governance, and Articles 25-26 describe budgets and expenditures. Additionally, the General Rules of Procedure of UNWTO ((https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2019-11/130718basicdocumentsenweb.pdf) also govern the functioning and decision-making of UNWTO's governing bodies, namely the General Assembly, the Executive Council, and the regional commissions. The rules of procedure specify the composition, powers, duties, sessions, agenda, voting, languages, and other aspects of these bodies, as well as the role and responsibilities of the UNWTO secretariat. The rules of procedure are based on the Statutes of UNWTO, and can be amended by the General Assembly or the Executive Council, as appropriate. The rules of procedure also provide for the participation of other UNWTO members, such as associate members and affiliate members, as well as observers and guests, in the meetings and activities of UNWTO. UNWTO's jurisdiction is also influenced by the resolutions and decisions adopted by its governing bodies, such as the General Assembly, the Executive Council, and the regional commissions (https://www.unwto.org/unwto-general-assembly). These resolutions and decisions provide guidance and direction for UNWTO's policies and programmes, as well as cooperation and coordination with other organisations and stakeholders. UNWTO's mandate is also supported by the implementation of various international agreements and frameworks, such as the Global Code of Ethics for Tourism (https://webunwto.s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2019-10/gcetpassportglobalcodeen.pdf), the Convention on the Protection of Tourists (https://webunwto.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/imported_images/47266/6_report_on_the_convention_of_tourists_en_0.pdf), and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development (https://www.unwto.org/tourism-in-2030-agenda), which provide further legal frameworks for UNWTO's jurisdiction over specific tourism issues and domains.

excerpt_<=50w: Vertical coordination: linkages across governance levels (global–regional–national) such as focal points, reporting lines, subsidiary bodies.
matrix_cell_text_full: Vertical coordination within UNWTO involves collaboration with higher and lower level institutions, such as the United Nations, other specialized agencies, regional and sub-regional organizations, national governments, and local authorities. This is achieved through policy and governance models, strategic leadership, effective implementation, and efficient governance. This is structured under the Statutes of the World Tourism Organization (https://webunwto.s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/imported_images/51970/unwtostatuteseng.pdf) under the Sections Headquarters (Article 2), Organs (Article 8), General Assembly (Articles 9-13), Executive Council (Articles 14-20), Secretariat (Articles 21-24), Budget and Expenditure (Articles 25-26), Quorum (Article 27), Voting (Articles 28-30), Legal Personality, Privileges and Immunities (Articles 31-32), and Amendments (Article 33). The UNWTO operates through the General Assembly of all the Full Members, the Executive Council of elected Full Members, and a Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General. The UNWTO also has technical or regional bodies that may be established by the Assembly and assists Members in the development and management of tourism destinations, the promotion and development of tourism, and the implementation of its standards, policies, and programmes. UNWTO's work is organised around five regions, each overseen by a Regional Director who works closely with the Secretary-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.unwto.org/regional-departments). There is also the Global Tourism Crisis Committee, composed of the Secretary-General, the Regional Directors, the Chairs of the Executive Council and the Committee of Affiliate Members, and representatives of the United Nations and other international organizations, which provides guidance and recommendations on the response of the tourism sector to the COVID-19 crisis and the recovery measures (https://www.unwto.org/news/global-tourism-crisis-committee-meets-again-to-explore-safe-travel-in-age-of-vaccines). In addition, the Affiliate Members of UNWTO are a network of over 500 entities from the private sector, including companies, educational and research institutions, destinations, and NGOs. They collaborate with UNWTO and its Member States to promote sustainable tourism development. By joining the Affiliate Members, entities gain benefits such as global visibility, competitiveness, innovation, and access to UNWTO resources and events. The Affiliate Members have an exclusive online platform, AMConnected+, where they can communicate, share information, and build relationships within the network and with UNWTO. The strategic direction and activities of the Affiliate Members are overseen by the Board of Affiliate Members, which is composed of 12 elected representatives and liaises with UNWTO (https://www.unwto.org/affiliate-members).

matrix_cell_text_full: According to Article III of the Marrakesh Agreement Establishing the World Trade Organization (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf), the WTO's objectives encompass several key functions: facilitating the implementation, administration and operation of the WTO agreements and providing a framework for their further negotiation (paragraph 1); providing a forum for trade negotiations and a framework for their implementation (paragraph 2); administering the dispute settlement mechanism and ensuring the prompt and effective resolution of trade disputes (paragraph 3); administering the trade policy review mechanism and enhancing the transparency of trade policies (paragraph 4); cooperating with other international organizations and ensuring greater coherence in global economic policy-making (paragraph 5); and helping developing countries, especially the least-developed ones, to benefit from the multilateral trading system and to achieve their trade and development objectives. These functions enable the WTO to fulfil its role as the common institutional framework for the conduct of trade relations among its members in matters related to the WTO agreements (Article II, paragraph 1).
