excerpt_<=50w: Horizontal coordination: coordination with peers at similar levels (inter‑agency platforms, joint workplans, cross‑sector coordination).
matrix_cell_text_full: Horizontal coordination within the WTO involves collaboration with different sectors and stakeholders within the trade domain, such as governments, civil society, private sector, the academic community, and other international organizations to ensure that trade flows smoothly, predictably and freely as possible and that trade policies are consistent with the multilateral trading system. This coordination is guided by Article V of the WTO Agreement (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf). For example, the WTO works with the agriculture sector to reduce trade barriers and distortions in agricultural markets (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/agric_e/agric_e.htm), with the services sector to facilitate the expansion and liberalization of trade in services (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/serv_e/serv_e.htm), the environment sector to address the linkages between trade and environmental policies (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/envir_e/envir_e.htm) or with the development sector to assist developing and least-developed countries to benefit from the global trading system (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/devel_e/devel_e.htm). Horizontal coordination within the WTO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Aid for Trade initiative (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/devel_e/a4t_e/aid4trade_e.htm) or the Trade Facilitation Agreement Facility (https://www.tfafacility.org/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Committee on Trade and Environment (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/envir_e/cte00_e.htm) or the Enhanced Integrated Framework (https://www.enhancedif.org/en), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for trade sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Trade Policy Review Mechanism (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/tpr_e/tpr_e.htm) or the Trade Monitoring Database (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/tpr_e/trade_monitoring_e.htm), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for trade issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Public Forum (https://www.wto.org/english/forums_e/public_forum_e/public_forum_e.htm) or the World Trade Report (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/publications_e/world_trade_report_e.htm).

For example, the WTO works with the agriculture sector to reduce trade barriers and distortions in agricultural markets (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/agric_e/agric_e.htm), with the services sector to facilitate the expansion and liberalization of trade in services (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/serv_e/serv_e.htm), the environment sector to address the linkages between trade and environmental policies (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/envir_e/envir_e.htm) or with the development sector to assist developing and least-developed countries to benefit from the global trading system (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/devel_e/devel_e.htm). Horizontal coordination within the WTO can take various forms, such as: (1) Joint planning and implementation of programmes and projects with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Aid for Trade initiative (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/devel_e/a4t_e/aid4trade_e.htm) or the Trade Facilitation Agreement Facility (https://www.tfafacility.org/), (2) Participation in interagency and multisectoral committees, networks, and platforms, such as the Committee on Trade and Environment (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/envir_e/cte00_e.htm) or the Enhanced Integrated Framework (https://www.enhancedif.org/en), (3) Development and dissemination of guidelines, standards, and tools for trade sector engagement with other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Trade Policy Review Mechanism (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/tpr_e/tpr_e.htm) or the Trade Monitoring Database (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/tpr_e/trade_monitoring_e.htm), and (4) Advocacy and communication to raise awareness and mobilise support for trade issues and policies among other sectors and stakeholders, such as the Public Forum (https://www.wto.org/english/forums_e/public_forum_e/public_forum_e.htm) or the World Trade Report (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/publications_e/world_trade_report_e.htm).

matrix_cell_text_full: The WTO cooperates with various institutions to promote trade and development. It works with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, based on the coherence mandate in the Marrakesh Decision of 1994 (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/marrakesh_decl_e.htm), to ensure consistency and complementarity of global economic policies (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/coher_e.htm). Likewise, the WTO collaborates with the United Nations (UN) and its specialized agencies, such as the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), under the arrangements for effective cooperation signed in 1995, to address the linkages between trade and other policy areas, as specified in Article V of the WTO Agreement (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf). Furthermore, the WTO partners with the International Trade Centre (ITC), a joint agency of the WTO and the UN, to provide trade-related technical assistance and capacity building for developing countries, as stated in the Doha Ministerial Declaration of 2001 (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/ddec_e.pdf). It also engages with the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), an international organization of national parliaments, to enhance the parliamentary dimension of the WTO and foster dialogue and accountability on trade issues, as agreed in the Memorandum of Understanding of 2018 (https://www.wto.org/english/forums_e/parliamentarians_e/parliamentarians_conf_e.htm). Additionally, the WTO participates in various collaborative initiatives with like-minded groups of members and other stakeholders, such as the Joint Statement Initiative on E-commerce (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/ecom_e/joint_statement_e.htm), the Joint Statement on Investment Facilitation (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/minist_e/mc12_e/briefing_notes_e/bfinvfac_e.htm#:~:text=Originally%20launched%20by%20a%20group,of%20the%20economy%20(goods%20and), and the COVAX Facility on COVID-19 vaccines (https://www.wto.org/english/news_e/roadmap_igo_01jun21_e.htm), to advance discussions and actions on emerging and pressing trade challenges.

Instead, as an intergovernmental organization that regulates and facilitates international trade it has a global reach, with 164 member states representing over 98% of global trade and global GDP (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/org6_e.htm). The WTO's authority extends to the trade practices within these member states, irrespective of their location or the extent of their territorial waters and exclusive economic zones. It does not exercise jurisdiction in the same way a state does as its main purpose is to reduce tariffs and other barriers to trade.

matrix_cell_text_full: The WTO has a comprehensive strategy in place to achieve its objectives and mandates in ensuring that trade flows as smoothly, predictably, and freely as possible. It operates a non-discriminatory trading system that spells out the rights and obligations of its members (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/inbrief_e/inbr_e.htm). The WTO agreements, which are the result of negotiations, cover a wide range of activities including agriculture, textiles and clothing, banking, telecommunications, government purchases, industrial standards and product safety, food sanitation regulations, intellectual property, and more (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/fact2_e.htm). The WTO’s strategic plans are largely the outcome of negotiations between the members. The current round of trade negotiations, known as the Doha Development Agenda, was launched in 2001 (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dda_e/dda_e.htm) to succeed the Uruguay Round negotiations (1986–94) (https://www.wto.org/gatt_docs/english/sulpdf/92160001.pdf). The WTO has expanded its scope to include cooperation with the UN system, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), and other international partners on a wide range of issues (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/coher_e/mdg_e/global_partnership_e.htm). The WTO’s annual budget is contributed by its members based on their proportion of international trade (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/secre_e/budget_e.htm). The current budget proposal for the WTO Secretariat for the biennium 2024-2025 (https://docs.wto.org/dol2fe/Pages/SS/directdoc.aspx?filename=q:/WT/BFA/W643.pdf&Open=True) requests a modest increase of 7.4% in 2024 and 0.9% in 2025, amounting to CHF 211.76 million and CHF 213.7 million respectively. The WTO’s regulatory mechanisms are based on a number of simple, fundamental principles that run throughout all of its documents. These principles include trade without discrimination, national treatment (treating foreigners and locals equally), and the commitment to lowering trade barriers (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/utw_chap1_e.pdf).

matrix_cell_text_full: The WTO derives its mandate from the Marrakesh Agreement Establishing the World Trade Organization (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf), which entered into force on 1 January 1995 and established the WTO as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) (https://www.wto.org/english/res_e/booksp_e/agrmntseries2_gatt_e.pdf). Specifically, Articles II and III of the Marrakesh Agreement define the scope and functions of the WTO, and Article IV outlines the structure and decision-making of the WTO. Additionally, the WTO's Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU), which is annexed to the Marrakesh Agreement, sets out the rules and procedures for the settlement of disputes between WTO members (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dispu_e/dsu_e.htm). The DSU establishes the jurisdiction of the WTO panels and the Appellate Body, which are the adjudicating bodies of the WTO dispute settlement system. The DSU also provides for the implementation and enforcement of the rulings and recommendations of the panels and the Appellate Body. This is structured under the Organization section of the WTO Agreement (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf), specifically in Articles IV-IX. The WTO operates through the Ministerial Conference of all the members, the General Council of representatives from all members, and a secretariat headed by a Director-General. It also has councils, committees, and other subsidiary bodies (Article IV, paragraph 2) (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf). In addition, the WTO assists members in the implementation of its agreements, policies, and programmes and provides technical cooperation and training upon request (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/devel_e/teccop_e/tct_e.htm). WTO's work is organised around three main areas: trade negotiations, trade disputes, and trade policy reviews. Each area is overseen by a specific council or body that works closely with the Director-General to implement strategies and programmes across all levels of the Organization (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/org1_e.htm). There is also the Trade Negotiations Committee (consisting of the Director-General and representatives from all members) that supervises the conduct of the multilateral trade negotiations and reports to the Ministerial Conference (https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dda_e/negotiating_groups_e.htm). Additionally, WTO operates six regional offices and liaison offices in 12 Member States (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/whatis_e/tif_e/org3_e.htm). Besides the Director-General, at the WTO headquarters, there is a clear line of duty within the leadership team comprising of four Deputy Directors-General and 16 Directors with portfolios focusing on different aspects of the WTO's mandate (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/dg_e/senior_management_e.htm). In addition, WTO/Europe coordinates with the European Union and its institutions and is the host organisation and partner of the European Trade Policy Forum (https://www.wto.org/english/thewto_e/countries_e/european_communities_e.htm).
